chapters.title: The physicist's way of seeing
chapters.subtitle: Models, measurement, powers of ten and estimation

sections.heading: 0.1 What we see and what we think
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Alexandria, around 200 BCE

Eratosthenes was told a curious thing. At Syene, a town far up the Nile to the south, there was a deep vertical well, and at noon on the longest day of the year the sunlight reached all the way to the bottom of it. That could only happen if the Sun stood exactly overhead. In Alexandria, on that same day at that same noon, an upright column cast a short but definite shadow. The Sun was not quite overhead there.

Two observations, from two cities. On their own they are just facts. What made Eratosthenes a physicist was what he did next: he asked what *picture of the world* would make both facts true at once, and then he asked what else that picture would let him work out. Hold on to his two facts. The chapter ends with his answer.

Everything in science starts with an ==observation==: something a careful person can see, hear or measure, and that another careful person could check. "The well is lit to the bottom at noon on the longest day" is an observation. "The Sun is directly over Syene" is already a small step beyond it, and "the Earth is round" is a much bigger step. Those bigger steps are a ==model==: a picture of how things are, built to exp

sections.heading: 0.2 Measuring anything
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Sèvres, near Paris, 1879

In 1879 a metalworker named George Matthey made a small cylinder: 39 millimetres tall and 39 millimetres across, nine parts platinum to one part iridium. It went to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sèvres, just outside Paris, and sat under three glass bell jars, one inside the other, with six official copies kept alongside it. For the next 130 years, when anyone anywhere said "one kilogram", that is what they meant: exactly as much stuff as that cylinder, no more and no less. Every kitchen scale in Mumbai traced back, through a chain of copies, to a lump of metal in a French vault.

It had a flaw. Over the decades, tiny amounts of whatever floated in the air stuck to its surface, and its mass slowly changed. The changes were far too small to feel. They were not too small to measure, and a kilogram that drifts is a kilogram nobody can fully trust. So on 20 May 2019 the cylinder was retired. The kilogram is now defined by fixing a constant of nature called the Planck constant at exactly 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, together with the already-fixed metre and second. sections.heading: 0.3 Powers of ten
sections.excerpt:
In the store cupboard there is a 25 kg sack of rice. How many grains are in it? Nobody is going to count them. And yet, with a teaspoon and a kitchen scale, you can know the answer well enough to be sure of it.

:::predict
How many grains of rice are in a 25 kg sack?
- About ten thousand
- About a million
- About a hundred million
- About ten billion
???
About a million, and the next section of text shows how you can find that out for yourself in ten minutes. Most people guess far too high or far too low, because big numbers all feel the same. The point of this section is to make them feel different.
:::

Here is the chain. Count the grains in one level teaspoon. Suppose you get about 200 (your own count will replace that number). Weigh ten level teaspoons together, because a kitchen scale cannot weigh one grain or even one teaspoon honestly; suppose ten teaspoons come to 50 g, so one teaspoon is 5 g. Then 200 grains weigh 5 g, so there are 40 grains in a gram, 40,000 in a kilogram, and 40,000 × 25 = 1,000,000 in the sack. A million. If your teaspoon count is 20% different from mine, your answer will be 20% different too, and that is fine. The question was "how many, roughly?", and

sections.heading: 0.4 Guess like a physicist
sections.excerpt:
It is a monsoon afternoon in July, the lanes are rivers, and the news says 100 mm of rain has fallen on the city since morning. A hundred millimetres is ten centimetres: it would barely cover your ankle. How much water is that, over the whole of Mumbai?

:::predict
How much rain falls on the whole of Mumbai on a day with 100 mm of rainfall?
- A few swimming pools' worth
- A few thousand tonnes
- Tens of millions of tonnes
- More than the whole Arabian Sea
???
Tens of millions of tonnes. Hardly anyone guesses this right first time, because it needs two steps of reasoning rather than a feeling. By the end of this section you will be able to work it out on the back of a bus ticket.
:::

Physicists make rough estimates like this all the time, and they have a name for them: ==Fermi problems==, after Enrico Fermi, who was famous for working out surprising numbers on the back of an envelope. The method has two steps. First, find quantities you can estimate or look up. Second, find the relationship that joins them to the thing you want. Then check that the units come out right.

callouts.title: On a clear day you watch a ship sail straight away from Marine Drive, through binoculars. As it gets further away, what do you expect to see?
callouts.body:
- The whole ship shrinks evenly until it is a dot
- The bottom of the ship disappears first; the mast is the last thing you see
- The top of the mast disappears first; the hull is the last thing you see
???
The hull goes first and the mast last, as sailors have always reported. On a flat sea the whole ship would simply shrink. The bulge of water between you and the ship hides the lowest part first, which is exactly what a round Earth predicts.

callouts.title: Shadow of a ball, shadow of a plate
callouts.body: In a darkened room, shine a phone torch at a flat wall from a couple of metres back. Hold a cricket ball or an orange in the beam and watch its shadow on the wall as you turn the ball every which way: the shadow is always a circle. Now hold a flat steel plate or a large coin in the beam and turn it slowly from face-on to edge-on. Its shadow changes from a circle to an ellipse to a thin line. That is Aristotle's lunar-eclipse argument in your hand: the Earth's shadow on the Moon is circular at every eclipse, whatever the Moon's position in the sky, so the Earth must be a sphere and not a flat disc.

callouts.title: > "The Greeks thought the Earth was flat, and Columbus proved it was round."
callouts.body: Educated people around the Mediterranean knew the Earth was round at least two thousand years before Columbus sailed. Eratosthenes did not set out to prove it was round. He assumed it, because Aristotle's evidence was already convincing, and used that model to do something new: measure how big the round Earth is.

callouts.title: Model
callouts.body:
? What is it?
A simplified picture or description of how part of the world works, built from observations and used to explain them and to predict new ones.
? Why is it called this?
From the Italian *modello*, an architect's small scale figure of a building, from Latin *modulus*, a small measure. A scientific model is a small mental working copy of something too big, too small or too hidden to take in all at once.
? What problem did it solve?
Observations on their own are a heap of separate facts: a curved shadow on the Moon, a well lit at noon, a ship's hull vanishing before its mast. A model ties the heap together into one picture so you can ask what else must be true.
? Why does it work?
Because it leaves out the details that do not matter for the question in hand, such as mountains and waves when you are sizing up the whole Earth, and keeps the geometry or mechanism that does.
? How does it help?
Once you have a model, you can calculate things nobody has directly measured yet, just as Eratosthenes used the round-Earth model and two shadows to work out the distance all the way round the planet.
?? How do we know?
A model earns our trust when it predicts a new observation before anyone looks, and fails the moment a careful test disagrees with what it predicts.
?? What it isn't
It is not the real thing itself, and it is not a guess made up without evidence. Pythagoras calling the Earth a sphere because spheres seemed perfect was a wish, not a scientific model.
?? Where does it stop working?
Every model has edges where its simplifications start to matter: a perfect sphere is fine for Eratosthenes, while satellite navigation has to allow for the real Earth bulging by about 21 km at the equator.

callouts.title: IB MYP science names *models* and *evidence* among the ideas every science shares. Cambridge IGCSE physics does not have a topic on this at all; its first topic is measuring. The habit is taken for granted, which is why we practise it here.
Measure one sheet of paper with an ordinary ruler
callouts.body: An ordinary school ruler has marks every millimetre, and a single sheet of notebook paper is about a tenth of a millimetre thick—far too thin to read between two marks. Solve it by measuring a stack. Count 50 leaves of a notebook: that is 50 physical sheets, with 100 numbered pages. Pinch the stack gently together without squashing the spine, and measure its thickness in millimetres. Divide your reading, and your ±0.5 mm ruler uncertainty, by 50. That ruler uncertainty contributes about one hundredth of a millimetre to your answer for one sheet. Uneven paper and how firmly you pinch the stack can add more uncertainty.

callouts.title: You weigh the same katori of rice five times on a kitchen scale, lifting it off and putting it back between weighings. What do you expect the five readings to look like?
callouts.body:
- Exactly the same number every time
- Numbers that differ by a gram or two
- Numbers all over the place
???
Usually the second. The scale rounds to the nearest gram, the katori lands in slightly different spots, the air moves. The spread of your five readings is a direct measure of your uncertainty, and it is worth doing: it turns a vague "about 150 g" into "150 g, give or take 2".

callouts.title: > "My scale gave the same reading five times, so it must be right."
callouts.body: Agreeing with itself is precision. Being right is accuracy. A scale can be beautifully precise and still read 20 g too high every single time. Check it: weigh something whose mass you know, such as a sealed 1 kg packet, and see what it says.

callouts.title: Uncertainty
callouts.body:
? What does it measure?
The half-width of the interval around a measured number within which the true value can reasonably be expected to lie, written as ± in the same units or as a percentage.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *incertus*, not settled or not sure. In everyday speech *uncertain* sounds like a confession of failure; in physics it is a statement of how finely an instrument can resolve the world.
? What problem did it solve?
Without stated uncertainties, two experimenters who measure 9.8 m/s² and 9.78 m/s² cannot tell whether they have discovered a real difference in gravity between two cities or merely met the scatter of their clocks and rulers.
? Why does it work?
Because every reading is nudged by small random variations and limited by the finest division on the scale; repeating a measurement or reading half a division estimates the spread of those nudges directly.
? How does it help?
It tells you how many digits you have earned the right to write down, whether a new measurement agrees with a theory's prediction, and which part of an experiment needs a better instrument first.
?? How do we know?
When the same bar or katori is measured dozens of times, the readings cluster around a central value with a reproducible spread that shrinks when you switch to a finer scale or average many trials.
?? What it isn't
It is not a human blunder or an arithmetic mistake: reading 46 mm when the mark is at 36 mm is an error to fix, whereas ±0.5 mm on a millimetre ruler is the honest limit of the ruler itself.
?? Where does it stop working?
Quoting the scatter of repeated readings only captures random spread; if your kitchen scale has a 20 g zero offset, tight scatter will hide that systematic bias until you calibrate against a known standard.

callouts.title: Cambridge IGCSE defines mass as "a measure of the quantity of matter in an object". When the kitchen scale says 1 kg, that is the mass it means. Weight is something different, a force, and it arrives in Chapter 3.
How many grains of rice are in a 25 kg sack?
callouts.body:
- About ten thousand
- About a million
- About a hundred million
- About ten billion
???
About a million, and the next section of text shows how you can find that out for yourself in ten minutes. Most people guess far too high or far too low, because big numbers all feel the same. The point of this section is to make them feel different.

callouts.title: A teaspoon of rice
callouts.body: Tip a level teaspoon of rice onto a plate and push the grains into groups of ten with a finger; count the groups. Do it three times with three fresh teaspoons: the counts will not agree exactly, and the spread between them is your uncertainty from Section 0.2. Then weigh ten level teaspoons on the kitchen scale, divide by ten for one teaspoon, and work out grains per gram, grains per kilogram packet, and grains per 25 kg sack. Write the sack's number in the form "something × 10 to a power". Everything goes back in the rice tin afterwards.

callouts.title: School exams call writing a number as *a* × 10*ⁿ* (where *a* is at least 1 and less than 10, and *n* is a whole number) *standard form* or *scientific notation*. So 86,400 s is written 8.64 × 10⁴ s, and 0.0032 m is 3.2 × 10⁻³ m. To multiply two numbers in standard form, multiply the front numbers and add the powers of ten; to divide, divide the front numbers and subtract the powers.
callouts.body:
:::

The [Powers of Ten explorer](#explore-scale) at the front of this book lets you climb this ladder with your thumb, from a proton out to the Milky Way, with a readout of how many times bigger each thing is than the last. Spend a few minutes there now. The feel for scale you get from it will be used in every chapter after this one.

callouts.title: > "Ten times bigger, and then ten times bigger again, is twenty times bigger."
callouts.body: It is a hundred times bigger. Each step on the ladder multiplies by ten; it does not add ten. Three steps is a thousand times, six steps a million times. The steps on Figure 0.3 are drawn equal in width, but each one is ten times the jump of the one before.

callouts.title: Order of magnitude
callouts.body:
? What does it measure?
The rough scale of a number, given by the nearest power of ten: whether something is measured in tens, thousands, millions or millionths.
? Why is it called this?
*Magnitude* comes from the Latin *magnitudo*, size, and *order* means rank or step on a ladder. Astronomers first ranked stars by brightness into first, second and third magnitude; physicists borrowed the phrase for steps of ten in size.
? What problem did it solve?
Human intuition treats big numbers as one blurry crowd, so a million and a billion feel like neighbours when one is a thousand times the other. Counting powers of ten turns impossible-looking comparisons into small steps you can count on your fingers.
? Why does it work?
Because when two quantities are multiplied or divided, their powers of ten simply add or subtract, letting you check the scale of an answer before touching a calculator.
? How does it help?
It lets you estimate how many grains of rice sit in a 25 kg sack or how many tonnes of rain fall on Mumbai in a day, and catch a thousand-fold mistake in a calculation at a glance.
?? How do we know?
When Fermi estimated ~100 piano tuners in Chicago by multiplying rough factors of ten, directory counts confirmed the real number was within the same order of magnitude.
?? What it isn't
It is not a licence to be sloppy when precision is available; it is the first check that tells you which ballpark your careful measurement must land in.
?? Where does it stop working?
When two competing effects nearly cancel out, such as comparing two masses that differ by one part in a million, rough powers of ten cannot tell which one wins.

callouts.title: How many seconds are there in a day? Write the answer in the form "a number times a power of ten", and say how many steps up the ladder a year is from a day.
callouts.body:
???
24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 86,400 s, which is 8.64 × 10⁴ s. A year is about 365 days, so about 3.16 × 10⁷ s. That is between two and three steps up the ladder, since 365 lies between 100 and 1,000.

callouts.title: How much rain falls on the whole of Mumbai on a day with 100 mm of rainfall?
callouts.body:
- A few swimming pools' worth
- A few thousand tonnes
- Tens of millions of tonnes
- More than the whole Arabian Sea
???
Tens of millions of tonnes. Hardly anyone guesses this right first time, because it needs two steps of reasoning rather than a feeling. By the end of this section you will be able to work it out on the back of a bus ticket.

callouts.title: A rain gauge on the balcony
callouts.body: Ask an adult before you set anything up on a balcony or windowsill. Find a tall glass or jar with straight vertical sides: a bottle with a narrow neck will not do, because then the depth of water inside no longer equals the depth of rain. Stand it in the open, away from the overhang of the roof, inside a bucket or weighed down so the wind cannot take it. After a day of rain, measure the depth of water with a ruler, in millimetres. That is your rainfall, in the same units the weather office uses. Compare it with the figure in the news for your part of the city, and then redo the whole-city sum with your own number.

callouts.title: > "An estimate is just a wild guess with a number on the end."
callouts.body: A guess is a feeling. An estimate is a chain: a few inputs you can defend, a relationship you can state, and units that check out. Anyone can look at the chain, point at the weakest link and replace it with a better number. That is why "about a hundred piano tuners" is worth far more than "lots".

callouts.title: A new tower near your school has 40 storeys. Estimate its height, and say which input you trust least.
callouts.body:
???
A storey is about 3 m (a ceiling a little above your reach, plus the floor between), so 40 × 3 m = 120 m, roughly. The storey height is the weak link: real storeys run from about 2.5 m to 4 m, so the answer could be 100 m or 160 m. Counting the storeys exactly does not help much; measuring one storey would.

callouts.title: The shadow at Syene
callouts.body:
Back to Alexandria. Here is everything Eratosthenes had.

1. At noon on the longest day of the year, sunlight reached the bottom of a vertical well at Syene, far to the south. So at that moment the Sun stood exactly overhead at Syene.
2. In Alexandria, to the north, at that same noon, an upright column cast a shadow. From the lengths of the column and its shadow, the sunlight was arriving at an angle of 1/50 of a full circle away from straight down: about 7°, or exactly 7.2°.
3. The distance from Alexandria to Syene was known: 5,000 stadia, a stadion being the length of a Greek running track.
4. The Sun is enormously far away, about 150 million kilometres, so its rays reach the whole Earth travelling almost exactly parallel to one another. If everyone on Earth pointed at the Sun at the same instant, all their arms would be parallel.

Use Figure 0.5. What two things did Eratosthenes have to *assume*, beyond his observations? How far is it all the way round the Earth, in stadia? And why, more than two thousand years later, can nobody say exactly how close he came?
???
He assumed two things. The Earth is a sphere, which Aristotle's evidence had made reasonable. And sunlight arrives in parallel rays, which is true because the Sun is so far away.

Then the reasoning runs like this. "Straight up" at Syene points at the Sun. "Straight up" at Alexandria points 7.2° away from the Sun. Since the sunlight is parallel at both places, "straight up" at the two cities must differ by 7.2°, and on a sphere that can only mean the two cities are 7.2° apart around its curve, which is 1/50 of the way round. So the whole way round is 50 times the distance between them: 50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia.

How good was that? The modern figure is 40,000 km. For Eratosthenes' number to equal it, a stadion would have to be 160 m. The trouble is that nobody knows which stadion he used; several lengths were in use. With the common Olympic stadion his answer comes out about 20% too big, roughly 48,000 km. With another stadion of about a sixth of a kilometre it comes out at about 41,700 km, about 4% too big. (Some books say "within 1%" for that stadion; redo the multiplication and you will find they are wrong.) So the honest statement is: the method was brilliant, the answer was somewhere between a few percent and about a fifth too large, and we cannot say exactly, because a measurement is a number *and* a unit, and the unit was never written down precisely enough.

There is a lovely echo. In 1791 the metre itself was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the pole. That made the circumference of the Earth 40,000 km *by definition*: Eratosthenes' question, answered by turning it into a unit.

One more thing. Mumbai lies south of the Tropic of Cancer, so twice a year, once in May and once in July, the noon Sun stands straight overhead and an upright stick casts no shadow at all. On those days Mumbai is Syene. A friend with a stick in a city far to the north could be Alexandria, and the two of you could measure the Earth with a phone call and a ruler.

chapters.title: How fast, how far
chapters.subtitle: Position, speed, velocity, acceleration and motion graphs

sections.heading: 1.1 Where and when
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Churchgate station, Mumbai, a weekday morning

The local pulls out so gently that for a moment it is the platform that seems to slide backwards, with its pillars and its tea stall and the people on it. Then your body catches up with what your eyes are saying and the world rights itself: the train is moving, the platform is still. But stop and ask how you know. If the windows were painted over and the ride were perfectly smooth, could anything inside the carriage tell you whether it was moving or standing at the platform? You could drop a coin, pour water, toss a ball, bounce it. Every one of those would happen exactly as it does in your kitchen.

Galileo made this point with a ship. Shut yourself in a windowless cabin on a ship moving steadily over calm water, and nothing you can do in the cabin will tell you whether the ship is moving or tied up at the quay. Steady motion cannot be felt. The word *steady* is doing all the work in that sentence; a braking train is felt by everybody, and that is the subject of Section 1.3 and of Chapter 2. But as long as the motion is steady, "is it moving?" turns out to be a question about what you are comparing the train with, and about n

sections.heading: 1.2 How fast, and which way
sections.excerpt:
Take the corridor again, with a phone stopwatch and a chalk mark every metre. Walk six metres in three seconds. Your ==speed== was 6 m ÷ 3 s = 2 m/s, two metres every second. That is the first and simplest number about motion: speed is distance divided by the time it took. A car that covers 150 km in 3.2 hours averaged 47 km/h. A student who walks 205 m at a steady 1.4 m/s takes 205 ÷ 1.4 = 146 s, about two and a half minutes. A cricket ball, a train, a planet: speed is always distance over time, and its unit in physics is metres per second.

:::note Speed
How fast something covers distance: distance travelled divided by the time taken, in metres per second (m/s). A scalar.
:::

But "the car averaged 47 km/h" hides everything that happened on the way: traffic, a stop for chai, a fast stretch on the Sea Link. The speedometer shows something different, the speed *right now*. To get at that, physicists take the distance covered in a shorter and shorter time: the last minute, the last second, the last hundredth of a second. As the interval shrinks, the average over it settles down to one value, the ==instantaneous speed==, the speed at that instant. Every speedometer is an instrument f

sections.heading: 1.3 Speeding up, slowing down and turning
sections.excerpt:
Back in the local. At a steady 60 km/h you feel nothing; you could be sitting in your kitchen. What you do feel is the pull-away from the platform and the brake coming into the next station: the moments when the velocity is *changing*. The rate of that change is what physicists call ==acceleration==, and getting it right needs more care than the everyday word suggests.

Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time the change took. Say a train starts from rest and reaches 30 km/h, which is 8.3 m/s, in 20 s. Its velocity changed by 8.3 m/s in 20 s, so its acceleration was 8.3 ÷ 20 = 0.42 metres per second *per second*: every second, it gained another 0.42 m/s. The unit is written m/s², "metres per second squared", which just means (metres per second) per second. Now say the same train, running at 30 km/h, brakes to a stop in 8 s. Its velocity changed by 8.3 m/s again, this time downwards, in 8 s: an acceleration of about 1.0 m/s², pointing backwards, against the direction of motion. If forward is the positive direction we write it as −1.0 m/s².

:::note Acceleration
The change in velocity divided by the time taken for the change, in m/s². It is a vector: it points in th

sections.heading: 1.4 Galileo's ramps
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Padua, about 1604

Galileo Galilei, working in Padua, wanted to know exactly how a falling thing speeds up. Does its speed grow steadily with time? Does the distance it has fallen grow steadily? Something else? A dropped ball reaches the floor in well under a second, far too fast for anything he had to time it. So he did something that looks like cheating and is actually one of the great ideas in physics: he slowed the fall down. A ball rolling down a gentle slope gathers speed in the same *way* as a falling ball, only more lazily. Make the slope shallow enough and you can watch the whole thing happen, and time it with a steady beat.

:::story p-galileo

:::predict
A ball starts from rest at the top of a long ramp. In the first second it rolls 10 cm. How far from the start is it after two seconds?
- 20 cm: twice the time, twice the distance
- 30 cm
- 40 cm: twice the time, four times the distance
???
40 cm. After three seconds it is 90 cm from the start, and after four seconds 160 cm. Doubling the time multiplies the distance by four; trebling it, by nine. Almost everyone's first instinct is 20 cm, and the next few paragraphs explain why that instinct is wrong.
:::

sections.heading: 1.5 The top of a throw
sections.excerpt:
Now the puzzle this chapter opened with. A physics lecture at MIT begins exactly this way: the lecturer tosses a marker into the air and asks, at the highest point, is its velocity zero? And is its acceleration zero? The first answer is easy. For one instant at the top the marker is going neither up nor down, so its velocity is zero. The second answer is the puzzle, and everything you have learnt in this chapter gives you a way to test it.

:::predict
At the very top of a toss the ball's velocity is zero. What is its acceleration at that instant?
- Zero: it has stopped, so nothing is changing
- 9.8 m/s² downwards, exactly as it is on the way up and on the way down
- 9.8 m/s² upwards, because the ball was going up
- Something smaller than 9.8 m/s², because the ball is barely moving
???
9.8 m/s² downwards, the same as at every other instant of the flight. Acceleration is the rate at which velocity *changes*, and at the top the velocity is changing as fast as ever: from a little upward to a little downward. It passes through zero without pausing there. The ball's position stops changing for an instant. Its velocity never stops changing at all.
:::

callouts.title: Your friend walks steadily along a corridor, bouncing a ball as she goes. To her the ball goes straight up and down beside her hand. You stand still at the end of the corridor and watch. What path do you see the ball trace?
callouts.body:
- Straight up and down, the same as she sees
- A series of curved arcs: up and forward, down and forward
- It depends how fast she walks: a zigzag if she hurries, straight up and down if she strolls
???
A series of curved arcs, however slowly she walks, because between one bounce and the next the ball has moved along the corridor with her. For her the ball goes straight up and down. Neither of you is wrong. You are describing the same motion in two different frames, and each description is exactly right in its own frame.

callouts.title: Toss an eraser in a moving ride
callouts.body: Next time you are sitting in a train or bus cruising smoothly on a straight stretch—never when the driver is braking or turning—toss a small rubber eraser twenty centimetres straight up from your lap and catch it. Watch where it lands. It comes straight back into your palm, not behind you, because the eraser already shares the carriage's forward velocity when it leaves your hand. To someone standing by the track, your eraser traced a forward parabola at the train's speed; to you, it went straight up and down.

callouts.title: > "The platform is really still and the train is really moving. The ground is the true frame; the train's view is an illusion."
callouts.body: For steady motion there is no experiment, inside or outside the train, that can crown one frame the true one. The ground is the handy frame, because we live on it, and that is all. Keep the word *steady*, though. The moment the train brakes you can tell, with your eyes shut, that something has changed. Steady velocity cannot be felt; a change of velocity can. That difference is the hinge of Chapter 2.

callouts.title: Cambridge IGCSE sorts quantities into *scalars*, which have size only, like mass, and *vectors*, which have size and direction, like weight. Distance is a scalar and displacement a vector in exactly that sense.
Investigation 1.2
callouts.body: Switch the live graph above to *Walk it yourself*. Press *Start* and drag the corridor-position slider to draw a trace that climbs steeply for 2 seconds, stays flat for 4 seconds, and slopes gently back to 0 m over the last 6 seconds. Read the velocity reported in each stage and check that it matches rise ÷ run on your graph.

In Section 0.2 every measurement carried an uncertainty from the finest mark on the instrument. If you mark a corridor every metre with chalk (±1 cm) and time a 6 m walk with a phone stopwatch (±0.2 s around 3.0 s) because of your thumb's reaction time, which measurement—distance or time—contributes nearly all the percentage uncertainty to your calculated speed?
???
The time. A 1 cm uncertainty in 600 cm is less than 0.2%, whereas 0.2 s in 3.0 s is nearly 7%. Improving the chalk marks with a millimetre ruler would not make your speed measurement any better; timing a longer walk or filming the walk would.

callouts.title: In Figure 1.2 your line and your friend's dashed line cross at 4 seconds. At that moment, which of these is true?
callouts.body:
- You are at the same place
- You are moving at the same speed
- Both
???
Only the first. Crossing lines mean the same position at the same time, nothing more. Your speed is the slope of your line, which is flat: zero. Your friend's slope is 0.5 m/s. You are standing still as she walks past you. The same thing happens at 8 seconds, when you overtake her on your way back, walking twice as fast as she does. Being in the same place at the same time says nothing about how fast either of you is going.

callouts.title: > "The graph shows the path the walker took."
callouts.body: The horizontal axis is *time*, not a direction in space. The walk in Figure 1.2 happened along one straight corridor; the graph's rising and falling shows position changing as the seconds pass. A curved position–time graph does not mean a curved path. When you meet the graph of a thrown ball in Section 1.5 this will matter.

callouts.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary calls this a *distance–time graph*, with speed as its gradient; IGCSE topic 1.2, Motion, uses the same graphs. Ours is a *position*–time graph, which is why it can slope downwards when you walk back. A graph of distance travelled can only ever climb.
Does a car's odometer measure distance or displacement? Does its speedometer show speed or velocity?
callouts.body:
???
The odometer adds up distance: every kilometre driven counts, whichever way you went, so a round trip still adds to it. The speedometer shows speed, the size of the velocity at that instant, with no direction. If it showed velocity it would need a compass as well.

callouts.title: An auto-rickshaw goes all the way round a roundabout at a perfectly steady 20 km/h. Is it accelerating?
callouts.body:
- No: its speed is constant, so its acceleration is zero
- Yes: its direction keeps changing, so its velocity keeps changing
- Only on the parts where the driver speeds up
???
Yes, the whole way round. Its velocity is changing because its direction is changing, even though its size is not. You can feel it: your body leans towards the outside the entire time you are on the curve.

callouts.title: > "A negative acceleration means slowing down."
callouts.body: Look at car (c) in Figure 1.3: it moves left and its velocity arrow is getting longer, so it is speeding up, yet its acceleration is negative because it points left and we called right positive. The sign depends on a choice you made. The arrows do not. Compare the directions of v and a: the same way means speeding up, opposite ways means slowing down, every time.

callouts.title: The IGCSE syllabus says a resultant force "may change the velocity of an object by changing its direction of motion or its speed". Both of those are changes of velocity, so both are accelerations. That is why physicists count turning a corner as accelerating.
A train is moving to the left and comes smoothly to a stop. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the direction of its acceleration, and what is its sign?
callouts.body:
???
The train is slowing, so its acceleration points opposite to its velocity: to the right. With right as positive, that is a positive acceleration, even though the train is slowing down.

callouts.title: A ball starts from rest at the top of a long ramp. In the first second it rolls 10 cm. How far from the start is it after two seconds?
callouts.body:
- 20 cm: twice the time, twice the distance
- 30 cm
- 40 cm: twice the time, four times the distance
???
40 cm. After three seconds it is 90 cm from the start, and after four seconds 160 cm. Doubling the time multiplies the distance by four; trebling it, by nine. Almost everyone's first instinct is 20 cm, and the next few paragraphs explain why that instinct is wrong.

callouts.title: Galileo's ramp with coins for bells
callouts.body: You need a straight board about 2 m long, such as a plank or a long shelf, a marble or a smooth small ball, and masking tape. Prop one end of the board on a single book, so that the slope is as gentle as it can be while the marble still rolls all the way down; a gentle slope makes the beats long and easy to hear. Put tape marks at 10, 40, 90 and 160 cm from the top, measuring with a tape. At each mark, tape a small folded tab of stiff paper or kitchen foil so its tip hangs down and gives a crisp *tick* as the marble brushes past, or set a coin just to the side of the marble's line so the marble grazes its rim (if the marble has to climb *over* a coin at the 10 cm mark, it is still moving so slowly that the coin's edge will stop it). Release the marble from rest at the top, with no push, and listen: the four clicks should come at an even beat, like a slow clock. If the beats bunch up, the release was a push or the board is not straight. Filming it in slow motion and counting frames between clicks is a stricter test, and the markers are optional: with video you can mark where the marble is at equal time steps instead. Everything here is kitchen-safe; keep the marble away from small children.

callouts.title: > "The ball speeds up steadily, so the distance must grow steadily too."
callouts.body: The speed grows steadily: 20, 40, 60 cm/s. The distance does not, because a faster ball covers more ground in each beat than it did in the last. Distance grows with the *square* of the time: 1, 4, 9, 16. Mixing these two up is the commonest slip in all of kinematics, and Galileo's marks are the cure.

callouts.title: A ball starts from rest and its speed grows by 4 m/s every second. After 2 seconds, is its speed 8 m/s or 16 m/s? How far has it travelled?
callouts.body:
???
Its speed is 8 m/s: it gained 4 m/s in each of two seconds. The 16 belongs to the *distance* pattern, not the speed. Its distance is ½ × 4 × 2² = 8 m, which you can also get as average speed × time: it averaged 4 m/s over the two seconds, so 4 × 2 = 8 m.

callouts.title: At the very top of a toss the ball's velocity is zero. What is its acceleration at that instant?
callouts.body:
- Zero: it has stopped, so nothing is changing
- 9.8 m/s² downwards, exactly as it is on the way up and on the way down
- 9.8 m/s² upwards, because the ball was going up
- Something smaller than 9.8 m/s², because the ball is barely moving
???
9.8 m/s² downwards, the same as at every other instant of the flight. Acceleration is the rate at which velocity *changes*, and at the top the velocity is changing as fast as ever: from a little upward to a little downward. It passes through zero without pausing there. The ball's position stops changing for an instant. Its velocity never stops changing at all.

callouts.title: Investigation 1.5
callouts.body: On a scrap of paper, sketch the three graphs of Figure 1.6—height, velocity and acceleration against time—for a simpler event: a ball held at a height of 1 m and dropped from rest at *t* = 0 s (taking upward as positive). Which half of Figure 1.6 do your three curves match? Then check your prediction in the live video tracker above.

callouts.title: Film your own toss
callouts.body: Find a wall with tiles, or stick strips of tape on a plain wall at measured 10 cm intervals, and measure a tile with a ruler so you know its real height. Set the phone camera to its slow-motion mode, which on many phones films at 120 or 240 frames a second; check what yours does. Prop the phone against a book a few metres back, in bright light, so that it does not move. Toss a ball about a metre straight up, catch it, and stop filming. Now step through the clip. Do not compare one frame with the next: at 240 frames a second the gap changes by less than a fifth of a millimetre per frame, which no camera will show you against a tile. Instead, mark the ball's height every tenth of a second, which is every 24th frame at 240 frames a second, every 12th at 120, every 3rd at 30. Write down the heights in tiles and work out the gaps. Going up they should shrink by about one tile each time, pass through almost nothing at the top, and grow by about one tile each time coming down. The live version of Figure 1.5 does the marking for you, frame by frame, and plots the graph; the video stays on your phone.

callouts.title: > "At the top it has stopped, so nothing is happening to it. It just hangs there for a moment."
callouts.body: It does not hang. The heights at 0.4 s and 0.5 s differ by 0.2 cm, and that is the nearest it ever comes to a pause. Its velocity is changing at 9.8 m/s every second through that instant, exactly as it was a moment before and will be a moment after. Zero velocity and zero acceleration are different things: one says the ball is not moving right now, the other would say its motion is not changing, and the second is false. There is a related wrong idea, that the push of your hand "runs out" at the top. Once the ball has left your hand there is no upward push on it at all, from the first instant of its flight. What carries it upwards is a question for Chapter 2.

callouts.title: IGCSE writes "the acceleration of free fall *g* is approximately 9.8 m/s²", which is exactly the number used here. You will also meet *g* written as 9.8 N/kg; that is the same number read from a different side, and Chapter 4 explains how.
Two trains on the Western line
callouts.body:
You are on a local heading north at a steady 60 km/h, by the window, with a clear view out of both sides of the carriage.

1. On one side, a train on the next track appears beside you and slides slowly past, so slowly that you watch one passenger reading his newspaper for five or six seconds before his window leaves yours behind. Relative to your window it is moving at about 10 km/h, forwards.
2. On the other side, a train flashes past in the opposite direction. Relative to your window it passes at about 120 km/h.
3. The passenger with the newspaper looks up, sees your carriage drifting backwards past his window, and says to his neighbour: "Look, that train is going backwards."

What is each of the other two trains doing relative to the track: how fast, and which way? And is the man with the newspaper wrong?
???
To change frames, add the frame's own velocity, as in Section 1.1. The slow train moves at 10 km/h forwards relative to you, and you move at 60 km/h north relative to the track, so relative to the track it is doing 60 + 10 = 70 km/h north: the same direction as you, slightly faster, which is why it overtakes so gently. The flashing train moves at 120 km/h relative to you, the other way; relative to the track that is 120 − 60 = 60 km/h south. It is doing exactly your speed, in the opposite direction, and the two speeds add up to the 120 km/h you saw. In metres per second, 10 km/h is about 2.8 m/s, a brisk walk, and 120 km/h is about 33 m/s.

The man with the newspaper is not wrong. In his train's frame your carriage really does move backwards, at 10 km/h. In the track's frame his train does 70 km/h north and yours 60. In your frame his train creeps forward at 10. Every one of those statements is a complete and correct description of the same motion, each in its own frame. What would be wrong is to say that one of them is what is "really" happening and the others are illusions. For steady motion, no frame has that right.

chapters.title: Why things change their motion
chapters.subtitle: Forces, free-body diagrams, Newton's laws and momentum

sections.heading: 2.1 Aristotle's world
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a weekday evening

Start with something you can do before you read another line. Put a book flat on the table and give it a shove. It slides a hand's width, slows, and stops. Shove it harder and it slides further, and stops. Flick a steel katori across the kitchen counter: the same. Everything you have ever pushed has behaved this way, and from all that experience you have built a rule without ever writing it down. It goes something like this: *things move while something pushes them. Take the push away and they slow down and stop. Moving needs a mover.*

That rule has a famous author. Aristotle, in ancient Greece, reasoned his way to the same conclusion from the same kind of evidence: a cart moves while the ox pulls it, and stops when the ox stops. Everything that moves, he said, is moved by something. For nearly two thousand years this was physics, and it deserves respect. Aristotle described what really happens on Earth, where every moving thing is rubbing against a floor or pushing through air. He was right about the facts. He was wrong about the cause, and the mistake is so natural that most people make it today. In 1985 two physicists, Halloun and Hestenes, g

sections.heading: 2.2 The arrow problem
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Alexandria, 6th century

Aristotle's rule had one awkward case, and thinkers argued about it for a thousand years. An archer draws a bow and lets go. The string pushes the arrow for a fraction of a second, and then the arrow is on its own, flying across a field with nothing touching it. If moving needs a mover, what is moving the arrow? Aristotle's own answer was that the air behind it pushes it along. In Alexandria, in the sixth century, a scholar named John Philoponus found that hard to believe, and argued instead that the bow must give the arrow something that stays with it as it flies. Five hundred years later, in Bukhara, Ibn Sina discussed the idea in his *Book of Healing* and gave the something a name, *mayl*, an inclination. In the fourteenth century, in Paris, Jean Buridan called it *impetus*, and worked out that it grows with the arrow's speed and with the quantity of matter in it. (The Paris scholars almost certainly never read Philoponus directly. The idea reached them through Arabic.)

This is good thinking, and the ==impetus== idea is not simply wrong. Buridan was right that a moving thing carries something, and right that the something depends on both speed

sections.heading: 2.3 The ball that never stops
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Padua, about 1604

Galileo Galilei spent years rolling balls down ramps in Padua, because falling is too fast to time and a ramp slows it down to a speed he could measure. You met those ramps in Chapter 1. Later, in the books he wrote as an old man, he described an experiment that he could only do in his head, and it is one of the great arguments in science. Imagine two ramps facing each other, like a letter V, and let a ball roll down one of them. It rolls up the other and climbs to very nearly the height it started from, falling a little short because of friction. Now make the second ramp less steep. The ball must travel further along it to climb back to its starting height, and it does. Make the ramp shallower still and the ball rolls further still, always climbing to the same height. Now lay the second ramp perfectly flat. The ball can never climb back to its starting height, however far it rolls. So, Galileo reasoned, it never stops.

Notice what kind of argument that is. No ramp is perfectly smooth, so no real ball ever rolls for ever; Galileo did not claim to have watched one. He watched the *trend*. Every time he reduced the steepness, the ball went further, and th

sections.heading: 2.4 Newton's first law
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A local train, Mumbai

Now go back to the braking train, and watch it from two places at once. First stand on the platform. The train is coming in at a steady speed. Everyone inside is moving at that same speed, feet, body and bag together. Then the brakes grip the wheels and the train slows. What slows the passengers? Think about what is touching each one. The floor touches their feet, and the floor is part of the train, so it drags their feet to a slower speed by friction. Nothing is touching their heads, shoulders or hands. Those parts carry on at the speed the train had a moment ago, exactly as Galileo's ball would. So each passenger's feet slow with the train while the rest of them keeps going, and from the platform you watch a whole compartment of people tilt towards the front. The bag on the floor had less grip than a pair of shoes, so it slides further before friction stops it.

:::predict
The train brakes hard. Watching from the platform, what happens to a passenger standing in the aisle?
- A forward push throws her forward.
- Her feet are slowed by the floor, while the rest of her carries on at the speed the train had.
- Nothing happens to her until she hits some

sections.heading: 2.5 Friction is a force
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, the kitchen counter

Rest your palm flat on the table and press down. The table presses up into your hand; you can feel it. Now keep pressing and slide your hand forward. A new push appears, dragging backward along your skin. Push down and forward at once and you feel both together. What you are feeling is the table's contact force, and it has two parts: one straight out of the surface, holding your hand up, and one along the surface, resisting the slide. The first part is the subject of Chapter 3. The second is ==friction==, and this chapter has been leaning on it since the first page without ever checking that it deserves the name. It does. Friction is as real a force as a shove, and it obeys rules you can measure in a kitchen.

:::note Friction
The part of the contact force between two touching surfaces that acts along the surfaces and opposes their sliding over each other. It is a real force, with a size you can measure and a direction you can predict.
:::

The rules for sliding friction were first written down by Leonardo da Vinci in his notebooks, between about 1493 and 1515, then forgotten; Amontons found them again on his own and published them in 1699. Fir

sections.heading: The tablecloth trick
sections.excerpt:
:::case The tablecloth trick
A magician at a birthday party lays a cloth on a table, sets out plates, glasses and a vase of flowers, grips the edge of the cloth and yanks. The cloth is gone and the dishes stand where they were, barely rattled. Afterwards, Kym and two friends argue about how it works.

1. One says the plates have to be heavy: "the heavier the plate, the more it stays put".
2. One says the cloth has to be slippery and without a hem.
3. One says the pull has to be fast and straight down over the table's edge, and that a slow pull would drag everything off.

Kym notices that the plates did move, a centimetre or so, in the direction of the pull.

Which of the three is right, and why did the plates move a little but not a lot? Does a heavier plate help?
???
The second and third are right. The first is the popular explanation, and it is wrong.

While the cloth slides under a plate, the only sideways force on the plate is the cloth's friction, which drags the plate the way the cloth is going. The plate starts to move, exactly as the first law says it must when a force acts. How *far* it moves depends on two things: how big that friction is, and how long it acts. A slippery

callouts.title: You shove a book across the table and let go. It slows down and stops. Why does it stop?
callouts.body:
- The push you gave it has been used up.
- Nothing is pushing it any more, so it stops on its own.
- Something is pushing it backwards the whole time it slides.
???
Something is pushing it backwards: the table, through friction. You cannot see that push, and that is exactly why it took two thousand years to notice. Aristotle would have chosen the second answer, and most students today choose the first. The rest of this chapter earns the third one, and Section 2.5 puts friction on the scales to prove it is a real force.

In Chapter 0 you kept observations and models apart. Sort these three sentences about a katori flicked across the counter: "it slid about 40 cm and stopped"; "it stopped because the push you gave it ran out"; "it stopped because the counter pushed back on it".
???
The first is the observation: anyone watching would agree on it. The other two are models, stories about the cause. Both explain the same observation, so the observation alone cannot choose between them. You need a new observation that the two models predict differently, which is what Section 2.3 provides.

callouts.title: A marble on three floors
callouts.body: Roll a marble with the same gentle flick across a thick rug or doormat, then across a bare tiled floor, and then along a smooth steel tray. Watch how far it goes each time. Nothing about your flick changed—if "the push inside the marble" were what kept it moving, it should run out after the same distance on all three. Instead, the smoother the surface, the further the marble rolls.

callouts.title: > "Even in deep space, a spacecraft has to keep its engines firing to keep moving."
callouts.body: In deep space there is no floor and almost no air, so there is nothing to push backwards on the spacecraft. Once its engines have brought it up to cruising speed, they are switched off and the craft coasts across millions of kilometres for months on end without burning a drop of fuel. Engines are needed only to speed up, slow down or turn.

callouts.title: Think of three things you pushed today that stopped after you let go. For each one, name what was touching it while it slowed down.
callouts.body:
???
Whatever you chose (a door, a chair, a cup slid across the table, a ball rolled on the floor), something was touching it as it slowed: the floor, the table, its hinges, and always the air. Each of those is a candidate for the hidden backward push. Nothing you pushed today stopped while touching nothing at all.

callouts.title: While the arrow flies, which way does the air push on it?
callouts.body:
- Forward, from behind, carrying it along (Aristotle's answer).
- Backward, against its motion.
- Not at all; the air does nothing.
???
Backward. Newton put it plainly when he explained his first law: a flying projectile keeps moving except in so far as the air's resistance slows it and gravity pulls it down. Ride a bicycle fast and you feel on your face which way air pushes on something moving through it. The air is the arrow's brake, and the planets, which meet almost no air, keep moving for ages.

callouts.title: > "The ball carries the force of my throw inside it, and when that force is used up it stops."
callouts.body: Apply the two-object test. After the ball leaves your hand, who is exerting "the force of your throw"? Not your hand: it is no longer touching the ball. There is no second object, so there is no such force. What the ball carries is motion, and motion only ever gets *changed*, by the air, by the Earth's pull and, finally, by the floor. A ball thrown in empty space would carry the same motion for ever.

callouts.title: Force
callouts.body:
? What is it?
A push or a pull exerted on one object by another object, with both a size (in newtons, N) and a direction.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *fortis*, strong. In everyday speech *force* can mean effort, energy, or willpower; in physics it means strictly an interaction between two bodies that can change an object's velocity or deform its shape.
? What problem did it solve?
As long as people treated "force" as something stored inside a moving arrow or thrown ball, they mixed up motion itself with the pushes and pulls that change motion. Requiring every force to have an identifiable second object cleared away imaginary internal pushes.
? Why does it work?
Because every push or pull in nature—whether by direct contact (a hand, a rope, a floor) or across space (gravity, electricity, magnetism)—acts between a pair of objects and combines with other forces as a vector arrow.
? How does it help?
By listing only the real forces acting on an object and adding their arrows, you can tell immediately whether the object's velocity will stay steady (net force zero) or change in a predictable direction.
?? How do we know?
Spring balances and force sensors show that identical stretches produce identical accelerations on the same mass, regardless of whether the pull comes from a hand, a hanging weight, or a magnet.
?? What it isn't
It is not a property carried inside a moving body: a fast cricket ball in mid-air has velocity, momentum and kinetic energy, and zero "force of the throw".
?? Where does it stop working?
In subatomic physics and general relativity, physicists often find it cleaner to work with energy, momentum, or spacetime curvature directly rather than forces, though for everyday mechanics force remains exact.

callouts.title: A crumpled paper ball flies across the classroom. While it is in the air, list every force acting on it, and for each force name the object that exerts it.
callouts.body:
???
Two forces. The Earth pulls it downward (gravity), and the air pushes on it, mostly backward against its motion. There is no forward force, because nothing is touching it from behind: your hand stopped acting the moment the ball left it. The ball keeps moving forward because nothing is stopping it, except, slowly, the air.

callouts.title: A steel katori is sliding across the kitchen floor. Imagine that at this instant someone switches friction off completely, like a light, so that the floor and the air no longer rub on it at all. What does the katori do?
callouts.body:
- Slows down and stops, a little later than it would have.
- Slows down more gently, but still stops eventually.
- Keeps sliding at exactly the same speed, in a straight line, for ever.
???
It keeps the same speed in a straight line, for ever. Of the 478 students in Halloun and Hestenes' study, 47 per cent chose one of the first two kinds of answer. If you did too, you are in large company, and the reasoning below is aimed at you.

callouts.title: Ice on a thali, ice on a cloth
callouts.body: Wet a large steel thali and set it flat on the counter. Lay a folded cotton cloth beside it. Take an ice cube from the freezer, let it sit for half a minute so its surface starts to melt, and flick it gently across the cloth. Note where it stops. Now flick it the same way across the wet thali. Keep a hand ready at the far edge. **Predict first:** how many times further will it go on the steel? Then try a third surface (the tiled floor, a plastic tray) and arrange the three in order of friction. What you are watching is Galileo's trend. The less the surface rubs, the longer the cube keeps the motion you gave it. Wipe up the water afterwards: a wet tile is slippery for people too.

callouts.title: Investigation 2.3
callouts.body: Use the ramp model with its friction slider. Set the second ramp at 30° and release the ball: note the height it reaches. Lower the ramp to 15°, then 5°, then flat, and write down how far along the ramp it travels each time. Then set friction to zero and repeat. Which setting lets the ball reach exactly its starting height? What happens on the flat ramp when friction is zero, and what happens when it is not?

callouts.title: > "The ball never stops" means balls never stop.
callouts.body: Every real ball stops, because every real ball meets friction and air. Galileo's claim is about what *would* happen with those removed: nothing would slow the ball, so nothing would stop it. The claim is tested not by watching a ball roll for ever, which is impossible, but by watching the stopping fade exactly as the friction fades. The cloth, wet thali and air cushion let you compare the effect of rubbing without making a floor slippery.

callouts.title: You push a box across the floor and let go. It slides on for a moment, slowing down. While it slides, which way does the total force on it point: forward, backward, or nowhere?
callouts.body:
???
Backward. The only horizontal force left is friction from the floor, which pushes against the sliding. That backward force is what makes the velocity shrink. If the total force pointed nowhere, the velocity would not change, and the box would slide on at the same speed.

callouts.title: The train brakes hard. Watching from the platform, what happens to a passenger standing in the aisle?
callouts.body:
- A forward push throws her forward.
- Her feet are slowed by the floor, while the rest of her carries on at the speed the train had.
- Nothing happens to her until she hits something.
???
Her feet are slowed and the rest of her carries on. There is no forward push; there is a *backward* force, friction on her shoes, and it acts only on her feet. The top of her keeps the old velocity because nothing has yet acted to change it. That is why braking feels like a shove from behind, and why the dozing man looked round for the shover.

callouts.title: The coin, the card and the glass
callouts.body: Stand an empty glass on the table, lay a stiff card (a playing card or an old visiting card) flat across its rim, and put a coin on the card right above the middle of the glass. Flick the card sharply sideways with a finger, hitting its edge. Done well, the card shoots away and the coin drops straight into the glass. Now do it badly on purpose: pull the card away slowly. The coin rides along with it. The physics is the first law plus a very short time. While the card moves, its friction drags the coin sideways, but a sharp flick is over in a few hundredths of a second. If it lasts 0.05 seconds and the card's friction coefficient on the coin is about 0.3 (a guess), the coin picks up a sideways speed of only about 0.15 metres per second and has slipped about 4 millimetres, far less than the glass is wide, before there is no card under it and the Earth's pull takes over. Pull for half a second instead and the slip grows a hundredfold, to about 37 centimetres: the coin simply goes with the card. Short time, small change in motion. Keep that thought for the chapter's case file.

In Chapter 1 you threw a ball straight up and watched the very top of its flight, where for an instant it is still. Suppose you toss your keys up on the platform while you wait for the next train. At the top, is any force acting on them? And does Newton's first law say they should stay there?
???
The Earth is pulling the keys down the whole time, so a force is acting, and the first law says their velocity *must* be changing. It is: from upward to downward, through zero. Zero speed for an instant does not mean zero acceleration. If no force acted, the law says the keys would hang at the top for ever. They do not, which is proof enough that a force is there.

callouts.title: Investigation 2.4
callouts.body: Take two identical toy cars, and load one with ₹5 coins taped on top. Give each the same gentle push with a ruler laid flat and released from the same bend. Which is harder to get moving? Which rolls further once it is going, and why might that be a trickier question than it looks? (Think about friction on the wheels.)

callouts.title: Your IGCSE syllabus words the first law as: an object either remains at rest or continues in a straight line at constant speed unless acted on by a resultant force. "Resultant force", "net force" and "unbalanced force" all mean the same thing, which is what is left over after the pushes and pulls cancel. The syllabus also defines mass as a measure of the quantity of matter in an object.
Inertia
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The property of every piece of matter that keeps it at rest if it is at rest, or moving in a straight line at constant speed if it is already moving, unless a net force acts on it.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *inertia*, idleness or sluggishness, from *iners*, unskilled or inactive. Kepler introduced the word into physics for a body's reluctance to start moving, and Newton widened it to cover keeping moving as well, so the "lazy" name is half misleading: a fast-moving planet has inertia too.
? What problem did it solve?
For two thousand years people followed Aristotle in assuming that every moving thing needs a continuing push to keep going, which left nobody able to explain why an arrow keeps flying after it leaves the bowstring.
? Why does it work?
Because steady motion in a straight line and rest are the same physical state seen from two different steadily moving reference frames; neither needs a cause, and only a *change* of velocity requires a force.
? How does it help?
It explains why passengers lurch toward the front of a braking Mumbai local train (their feet are slowed by the floor while their upper bodies keep the train's old velocity), and how spacecraft cruise across the solar system with their engines off.
?? How do we know?
Galileo's facing ramps, ice cubes sliding across a wet steel thali versus a cloth, air-hockey pucks, and spacecraft in deep space all show that as rubbing and air resistance are removed, stopping fades away toward never.
?? What it isn't
It is not a force stored inside the moving object (that was the medieval *impetus* mistake), and saying "it kept moving because of inertia" is a label, not a cause: it kept moving because nothing stopped it yet.
?? Where does it stop working?
Newton's first law holds in any non-accelerating (inertial) reference frame; inside a braking train or a spinning merry-go-round, objects appear to veer on their own unless you account for the frame's own acceleration.

callouts.title: A friend says: "Newton's first law means that a moving object keeps a constant acceleration unless a force acts on it." Fix the sentence, and say why the fix matters.
callouts.body:
???
Replace "acceleration" with "velocity". A body with no net force on it keeps a constant *velocity*: the same speed in the same direction. Its acceleration is zero. If a body kept a constant non-zero acceleration with no force acting, its velocity would be changing by itself, which is exactly what the law rules out.

callouts.title: You walk forward across the kitchen floor. Which way does the floor's friction push on the sole of your shoe?
callouts.body:
- Backward, against the way you are walking.
- Forward, the way you are walking.
- Nowhere: there is no friction while you walk normally.
???
Forward. As you step, your foot tries to slide *backward* against the floor, and friction opposes that slide, which means it pushes your foot forward. Friction is what lets you walk at all; on wet ice it is nearly gone, and so is your ability to go anywhere. Friction opposes the *sliding of surfaces across each other*, which is not always the same as opposing the direction you happen to be moving.

callouts.title: Investigation 2.5
callouts.body: Put a ₹5 coin on a closed hardback atlas and tilt the book slowly until the coin, once nudged, slides down at a steady speed. Hold that angle and measure it with a phone app (phyphox has an inclinometer). The sliding coefficient of friction is the tangent of that angle: 15° gives about 0.27, 20° gives about 0.36. Try a plastic cover, a cloth cover and a steel thali, and rank them. To compare contact areas, use a small rectangular eraser or wooden block on its broad face and then on a narrow face, keeping the same pair of materials touching. A coin on its edge would roll, which tests something different from sliding friction.

callouts.title: The IGCSE syllabus describes solid friction as the force between two surfaces that may impede motion and produce heating. Notice the word "may". Friction impedes a sliding book, and it also lets you walk and a car accelerate; it opposes sliding between surfaces, whichever way that works out for the object.
Friction
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The force along two touching surfaces that opposes their sliding, or tending to slide, across each other.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *frictio*, a rubbing, from *fricare*, to rub.
? What problem did it solve?
On Earth, pushed books and rolling balls always slow down and stop, which fooled observers for centuries into thinking motion dies out on its own. Recognising friction as an invisible backward push from the floor rescued the law of inertia.
? Why does it work?
Even surfaces that look polished are microscopic mountain ranges that touch only at their tips; pressing the surfaces together squashes more tips into contact and lets surface molecules tug on one another, resisting any slide.
? How does it help?
It lets you calculate how far a braking car or a flicked coin will slide, explains why a magician must yank a tablecloth fast, and shows why your shoes can push you forward when you walk.
?? How do we know?
Leonardo da Vinci and Guillaume Amontons measured the pull needed to drag blocks across tables and found that friction grows in proportion to the pressing force and barely changes when a brick is turned from its broad face onto its narrow edge.
?? What it isn't
It does not always oppose an object's overall motion (forward friction from the ground is what accelerates a runner or a bicycle), and static friction before sliding is not fixed at its maximum value: it matches whatever sideways push is applied, up to the slip limit.
?? Where does it stop working?
The simple rule that friction equals a constant coefficient times the normal force (*f* = μ*N*) is a working approximation that breaks down when surfaces melt, peel, lubricate, or stick at the atomic scale.

callouts.title: A book rests on a level table and nobody touches it. How much friction acts on the book?
callouts.body:
???
None at all. Friction before sliding takes whatever value is needed to stop the surfaces slipping, up to a limit, and with no sideways push there is nothing to oppose. The old recipe "friction equals the coefficient times the pressing force" gives only the *maximum* friction can reach before the book slips, not the friction acting at any moment.

callouts.title: The tablecloth trick
callouts.body:
A magician at a birthday party lays a cloth on a table, sets out plates, glasses and a vase of flowers, grips the edge of the cloth and yanks. The cloth is gone and the dishes stand where they were, barely rattled. Afterwards, Kym and two friends argue about how it works.

1. One says the plates have to be heavy: "the heavier the plate, the more it stays put".
2. One says the cloth has to be slippery and without a hem.
3. One says the pull has to be fast and straight down over the table's edge, and that a slow pull would drag everything off.

Kym notices that the plates did move, a centimetre or so, in the direction of the pull.

Which of the three is right, and why did the plates move a little but not a lot? Does a heavier plate help?
???
The second and third are right. The first is the popular explanation, and it is wrong.

While the cloth slides under a plate, the only sideways force on the plate is the cloth's friction, which drags the plate the way the cloth is going. The plate starts to move, exactly as the first law says it must when a force acts. How *far* it moves depends on two things: how big that friction is, and how long it acts. A slippery cloth makes the friction small. A fast pull makes the time short.

Put in numbers, with inputs that are guesses. A sliding coefficient of 0.3 between cloth and plate and a pull that takes 0.1 seconds give the plate a speed of about 0.3 metres per second and a slip of about 1.5 centimetres while the cloth is under it. Once the cloth is gone the plate slides on the bare table and stops within about another 1.5 centimetres. Halve the pulling time to 0.05 seconds and the slip drops to about 4 millimetres, a quarter as much. Stretch the pull to half a second and the plate slides about 37 centimetres: off the table. That is Kym's centimetre, explained, and the magician's speed, explained.

**The numbers, if you want to follow the calculation.** While the cloth slides, the plate's acceleration is *a* = μ_k *g* ≈ 0.3 × 9.8 ≈ 3.0 m/s². Its displacement during the pull is ½*at*². A 0.05 s pull gives 0.0038 m, about 4 mm; a 0.10 s pull gives 0.015 m, or 1.5 cm; a 0.50 s pull gives 0.375 m, about 38 cm. The same model shows why a slower pull can carry the plate off the table.

Now the heavy plate. Friction grows in proportion to how hard the surfaces press together, so a plate twice as heavy feels twice the friction from the cloth. But it also has twice the mass, so twice the force produces exactly the same change in motion. The acceleration of a plate dragged by a cloth is the coefficient times 9.8 metres per second squared, whatever the plate weighs. Heavy plates do not help. Smooth plates, a smooth hemless cloth, and a short, sharp pull do.

If you try it, use plastic plates and a tea towel, and ask an adult first.

chapters.title: Turning, balancing and machines
chapters.subtitle: Moments, levers, centre of mass and equilibrium

sections.heading: 3.1 Adding forces
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A school sports ground, Mumbai

Sports day, and the tug of war is on. Two teams dig their heels into the dry ground, lean back and pull. For a long moment the rope does not move; then one team gives, and the other hauls them over the line. Think about the rope, or better, think about a loaded cart with a rope tied to each side and two teams pulling it in opposite directions, which is the same contest with a clearer middle. Two forces act on the cart at once. What does it do?

You already know the answer from experience. If the pulls are equal, the cart stays put. If one side pulls harder, the cart goes that way, and the harder the difference, the more briskly it goes. A force has a size and a direction, and when several forces act on one object at the same time, forces in the same direction add up and forces in opposite directions cancel. What is left over after the cancelling is called the ==net force==, and it is the net force, never any single push on its own, that decides how the motion changes.

:::note Net force
The total of all the forces acting on an object, after opposing forces have cancelled. Your school syllabus calls it the resultant force. If it is zero, the

sections.heading: 3.2 Why heavy things are hard to start
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A traffic signal, Mumbai

The light goes green. A scooter is away before you have finished looking at it; a loaded truck beside it rolls forward so slowly that you could keep pace on foot for the first few metres. Both engines are working hard. The difference is in what the force has to move. Here is your probable explanation: *heavy things are hard to get going because they are heavy.* It sounds like it cannot be wrong, and it mixes up two different things, which this section separates.

Start with a cleaner experiment than a traffic signal. Put a cart on a smooth track where friction barely matters, and push it with a steady force, the same every second. What does the cart do?

:::predict
You push a cart along a very smooth track with a steady force, never bigger, never smaller. What does the cart do?
- Moves at a steady speed set by how hard you push.
- Speeds up, and keeps speeding up for as long as you push.
- Speeds up at first, then settles at a steady speed.
???
It keeps speeding up. A steady force gives a steady *change* in velocity, every second the same extra speed. Two-thirds of Halloun and Hestenes' 478 students chose the first answer, and so did 44 per cent o

sections.heading: 3.3 Can a table push?
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Kym's desk, Mumbai

A book lies on the desk. The Earth pulls it down with its weight, about 10 newtons for a big textbook. It does not move. By everything in this chapter so far, the net force on it must be zero, so something must be pushing it *up* with 10 newtons, and the only thing touching it is the desk. Ask people whether a desk can push and about half say no. "The desk is just in the way. It stops the book falling, but it doesn't *push*; pushing is something living things do." A researcher named Minstrell, who studied high-school students' ideas about forces, found that only around half of them would say a table pushes up on a book. The other half are not foolish. A desk looks utterly passive. Where would a push come from?

:::predict
A book lies still on the desk. Which is true?
- The desk pushes up on the book, exactly as hard as the Earth pulls it down.
- The desk does not push; it just blocks the book from falling.
- The desk pushes up, but less than the book's weight, which is why the book presses into it.
???
The first. Zero net force needs an upward push equal to the weight, and the only candidate is the desk. The rest of this section shows where the push com

sections.heading: 3.4 Every push has a partner
sections.excerpt:
:::scene London, 1687

In the *Principia*, after the first two laws, Newton wrote a third, and it is the one that people find hardest to believe. Press a stone with your finger, he said, and the stone presses your finger. Whenever one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts a force of the same size, in the opposite direction, on the first. Forces never come singly. Every push has a partner, and the two partners act on different objects. That is ==Newton's third law==.

:::note Newton's third law
Whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force of equal size and opposite direction on object A. The two forces are of the same type and always act on different objects.
:::

Your finger on the stone is easy to accept, because you can feel the stone pressing back. The law bites when the two objects are very different. A marble hits a moving train. Which feels the bigger force at the instant they meet, the marble or the train? Almost everyone says the marble, because the marble is the one that gets smashed. Newton says the forces are exactly equal. The marble is smashed because it is small and fragile and the same force gives it an enormous

sections.heading: 3.5 Momentum and rockets
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Thumba, Kerala, 21 November 1963

Before any formula, feel it. A cricket ball comes at you at 20 km/h and you catch it: easy. The same ball at 100 km/h: your hands sting, and the keeper wears gloves for a reason. Now a tennis ball at 100 km/h: the same speed, far less sting. There is a quantity here that is bigger for a faster ball *and* bigger for a heavier one, and the simplest way to think of it is *how hard the thing is to stop*. Newton called it the quantity of motion. Buridan, back in Chapter 2, had almost found it: his impetus grew with speed and with the amount of stuff, and so does this. We call it ==momentum==, and it is simply mass times velocity. A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m/s carries 0.16 × 30 = 4.8 kilogram-metres per second of it. Momentum has a direction, the direction of the velocity, and that matters in a moment.

:::note Momentum
How much motion an object has: its mass multiplied by its velocity, in kg·m/s. It points the way the object is moving. Hard to stop means a lot of momentum.
:::

What changes momentum? A force, acting for a time. Catch the fast ball with stiff arms and your hands stop it almost instantly, with a large force; let your hands ride back w

sections.heading: The mosquito and the windscreen
sections.excerpt:
:::case The mosquito and the windscreen
A car on the Bandra–Worli Sea Link is doing 90 km/h, which is 25 metres every second. A mosquito drifting the other way meets the windscreen. In about a thousandth of a second, the mosquito goes from drifting to travelling with the car. The driver notices nothing.

1. A mosquito's mass is about 10⁻⁵ kg, a hundredth of a gram.
2. The car's mass is about 1,200 kg.
3. Newton's third law says the force of the windscreen on the mosquito and the force of the mosquito on the windscreen are equal and opposite.

Which feels the bigger force? And if the forces are equal, why is only the mosquito destroyed?
???
They feel exactly the same force. The third law allows no exception for size or speed.

Estimate it. The mosquito's momentum changes by about 10⁻⁵ kg × 25 m/s = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m/s, in about 0.001 s. Force × time = change in momentum, so the force is about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.001 = 0.25 N: a quarter of a newton, about the weight of a 25 g biscuit, on each of them.

Now the second law, separately for each. The mosquito gets an acceleration of 0.25 N ÷ 10⁻⁵ kg = 25,000 m/s², about two and a half thousand times the acceleration of a falling stone. The car

callouts.title: You push a loaded trolley along a smooth level corridor at a steady walking pace. While it moves at that steady speed, the forces on it are:
callouts.body:
- Unbalanced, with more force forward than backward; that is why it keeps moving.
- Balanced: the net force is zero.
- Unbalanced, with more force backward; the trolley is always fighting friction.
???
