Balanced. Steady speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing, and Chapter 2 says that happens only when the net force is zero. Your forward push is being cancelled by friction and air pushing back. Balanced forces do not mean "not moving". They mean "not changing its motion".

callouts.title: Investigation 3.1
callouts.body: Make your own force meter. Hang a small plastic bag from a rubber band and put one ₹5 coin in it; measure how far the band stretches. Then two coins, then four. Is the stretch for four coins twice the stretch for two? Now loop two identical rubber bands side by side and hang four coins from the pair: predict the stretch before you look. This is how a spring balance turns a stretch into a force reading.

callouts.title: IGCSE writes "resultant force" where this book says "net force"; some school sheets say "unbalanced force". All three mean the same thing: what is left after the pushes and pulls have cancelled. The syllabus also covers the *turning effect of forces* (topic 1.5.2, moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot, and the principle of moments for an object in equilibrium) and *centre of gravity* (topic 1.5.3, finding it with a plumb line and how its height and base width govern stability).
Two friends push a stalled scooter in the same direction with 200 N and 150 N. Friction and the rough road resist with 350 N. What is the net force on the scooter, and what does it do?
callouts.body:
???
200 + 150 − 350 = 0 N. The net force is zero, so the scooter's velocity does not change. If it was at rest, it stays at rest, which is why the friends feel they are pushing hard and getting nowhere. One more push of any size would tip the balance and start it moving.

callouts.title: You push a cart along a very smooth track with a steady force, never bigger, never smaller. What does the cart do?
callouts.body:
- Moves at a steady speed set by how hard you push.
- Speeds up, and keeps speeding up for as long as you push.
- Speeds up at first, then settles at a steady speed.
???
It keeps speeding up. A steady force gives a steady *change* in velocity, every second the same extra speed. Two-thirds of Halloun and Hestenes' 478 students chose the first answer, and so did 44 per cent of more than 2,000 American school students on a national test. If the cart settled at a steady speed, the net force on it would have to be zero, which means something else, friction or air, had grown to cancel your push. On a very smooth track, nothing does.

callouts.title: Investigation 3.2
callouts.body: Stand on a bathroom scale next to a sturdy table. Read the scale. Predict what the reading will do when you press down on the table with one hand, then do it. Now lift gently on the underside of the table instead (do not pull it over). What happens to the reading, and what does that tell you about which force the scale is measuring?

callouts.title: Your syllabus says weight is a gravitational force on an object that has mass, and gives *g* = 9.8 two ways: as 9.8 N/kg (the pull on each kilogram) and as the acceleration of free fall, 9.8 m/s². They are the same number seen from two sides. When someone says they "weigh 40 kg" they mean their mass; in a physics answer, write mass in kg and weight in N.
Newton's second law (F = ma)
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The rule that an object's acceleration equals the net force acting on it divided by its mass, pointing in the direction of the net force.
? Why is it called this?
Isaac Newton placed it second among the three laws of motion at the front of his *Principia* in 1687; Leonhard Euler first wrote it in its modern algebraic dress, *F* = *ma*, in the eighteenth century.
? What problem did it solve?
Knowing that forces change motion is only half the story: you need to know *how much* a given push changes the motion of a light scooter compared with a loaded truck, and how to combine several pushes acting at once.
? Why does it work?
Because every force acting on a body contributes independently to changing its velocity, while the body's mass measures how much matter must be accelerated together.
? How does it help?
With one equation you can work out the acceleration of anything from a mosquito hitting a windscreen to a rocket lifting off from Thumba, once you add up all the forces on it and divide by its mass.
?? How do we know?
Cart-and-pulley experiments on low-friction tracks show that doubling the net force doubles the acceleration, while doubling the cart's mass halves the acceleration to within experimental uncertainty.
?? What it isn't
*F* in *F* = *ma* is never a single push in isolation when other forces act; it is always the *net* (resultant) force left after opposing forces such as friction and air drag have cancelled.
?? Where does it stop working?
It holds for objects whose mass stays constant and whose speeds are small compared with the speed of light; for a rocket burning half its mass as fuel, or a particle near light speed, you must write the law in terms of rate of change of momentum.

callouts.title: A trolley and its load have a mass of 60 kg. You push with 80 N, and friction pushes back with 50 N. What is the trolley's acceleration?
callouts.body:
???
Net force = 80 − 50 = 30 N. Acceleration = 30 N ÷ 60 kg = 0.5 m/s². Only the net force counts; using the 80 N on its own would give the wrong answer.

callouts.title: A book lies still on the desk. Which is true?
callouts.body:
- The desk pushes up on the book, exactly as hard as the Earth pulls it down.
- The desk does not push; it just blocks the book from falling.
- The desk pushes up, but less than the book's weight, which is why the book presses into it.
???
The first. Zero net force needs an upward push equal to the weight, and the only candidate is the desk. The rest of this section shows where the push comes from, because "it must" is a poor reason to believe anything.

callouts.title: The spring, the foam, the ruler and the table
callouts.body: **Step 1.** Press your palm down on a spring, or a rubber ball, or a folded sponge. It squashes, and you can feel it pushing back; the harder you press, the harder it pushes. Nobody doubts that a spring pushes. **Step 2.** Lay a book on a thick sponge or a folded towel. The sponge dents under it and stays dented. The dent is the sponge's way of pushing up with exactly the book's weight: it squashed until its push matched the load, and there it stopped. **Step 3.** Lay a 30 cm steel ruler across the gap between two stacks of books, and put a ₹5 coin in the middle. Add more coins, one at a time, with your eye level with the ruler. It sags, visibly, a little more with every coin, and for every coin it holds. The ruler is doing exactly what the sponge did: bending until its push upward matches the weight on it. **Step 4.** Now lay the book on the table. The table is a ruler that is very, very stiff. It sags under the book by an amount far too small to see, and that tiny sag is its push. Press gently on the book with your palm and the table bends a tiny bit more and pushes a little harder, just as the ruler did. Keep the ruler on the desk for a day: it is the table's argument in a form you can watch.

callouts.title: At school you may see the table's push called the normal force, the normal contact force or the normal reaction. "Normal" means at right angles to the surface. IGCSE topic 1.5.1 also asks you to sketch and interpret load–extension graphs for springs, use *k* = *F*/*x* for the spring constant, and identify the *limit of proportionality* where the graph stops being a straight line through the origin.
When you jump off a low wall, for the moment you are in the air you feel weightless. Has gravity switched off? What has changed?
callouts.body:
???
Gravity has not switched off; it is what brings you down. What has gone is the normal force. On the ground, the floor pushed up on your feet and your body felt that push as "weight". In the air, nothing supports you, so there is no push to feel, and you are falling freely. Astronauts in orbit feel the same, for the same reason (Chapter 5).

callouts.title: Kym and her father hook two luggage scales together and pull against each other. Dad is stronger and pulls harder. Which scale shows the bigger reading?
callouts.body:
- Dad's scale.
- Kym's scale.
- Both read the same.
???
Both read the same, whoever "pulls harder". The pull of each scale on the other is one pair of forces, equal and opposite. Of about 900 university students asked the truck-and-car version of this question before their physics course, 73 per cent said the bigger object pushes harder. After the course, 39 per cent still did. Do the experiment.

callouts.title: Two luggage scales
callouts.body: If you can borrow two hanging luggage scales, ask an adult to help hook them securely together. Pull gently against a partner, keep well below both scales' load limits, and stop if a hook slips. Read both displays at the same moment while the scales are held steady: they should agree within their measurement uncertainty. Change the gentle pull together and compare again. If you have only one scale, follow the paired-scale drawing below instead; you can still work through the idea. The dial says kg, which is a weight reading divided by 9.8: a reading of 10 kg means the hook is being pulled with about 98 N.

callouts.title: This is Newton's third law. School books often say "every action has an equal and opposite reaction". Two words make that safe: the two forces act on *different objects*, and they act *at the same instant*. There is no first push followed by a reply. "Reaction" is a name, not a delay.
If every pull your tug-of-war team gives the rope is matched by an equal pull from the rope on your team, how can your team ever win?
callouts.body:
???
Because the pair acts on different objects: the rope's pull on you is matched by your pull on the rope, and neither of those is the whole story of what happens to *you*. To see which way your team moves, add up the forces *on your team*: the rope's pull one way and the ground's friction on your feet the other. The team with the better grip gets more friction from the ground than the rope can match, and goes backward, dragging the rope and the other team with it. A tug of war is won through the shoes.

callouts.title: A light 1 kg cart and a heavy 3 kg cart sit at rest on a smooth track with a compressed spring between them. You burn the thread holding them together so the spring pushes both carts apart. Once they are clear of the spring, how do the magnitudes of their momenta and their speeds compare?
callouts.body:
- The light cart has three times the momentum and three times the speed of the heavy cart.
- Both carts have the exact same size of momentum, and the light cart moves three times as fast.
- Both carts move off at the same speed, so the heavy cart has three times the momentum.
???
Both carts have the exact same size of momentum (pointing in opposite directions, so they still add to zero), and the 1 kg cart moves three times as fast as the 3 kg cart. By Newton's third law, the spring pushes both carts with equal and opposite forces for the exact same time, giving them equal and opposite impulses (*F* Δ*t*). Since *m*₁*v*₁ = *m*₂*v*₂, a third of the mass means three times the speed.

A spacecraft far from any planet switches off its engines. It keeps going at the same speed. A friend says: "The push from the engines is stored inside it, and it will slow down when that push runs out." What is wrong with that, and what does the spacecraft actually carry?
???
Apply Chapter 2's test: who exerts "the push from the engines" after they are off? Nobody. There is no stored force, and nothing to run out. What the spacecraft carries is momentum, mass times velocity, and momentum changes only when a force acts. With no force, it keeps the same velocity for ever, just as the arrow would in empty space.

callouts.title: The balloon rocket
callouts.body: Thread a drinking straw onto a long piece of string and tie the string tight between two chairs, or a door handle and a chair, a few metres apart. Blow up a balloon, hold the neck pinched, and tape the balloon to the straw with the neck pointing backward along the string. Let go. The balloon runs the length of the string with its air jetting the other way. Try a bigger balloon, and a balloon with the neck pinched half shut so the air leaves more slowly: which goes further, and which goes faster? The balloon is not pushed by its air hitting the room. It is pushed by the air it is throwing out, at the moment of throwing.

callouts.title: Investigation 3.5
callouts.body: On a glass table or a large wet steel thali, flick one ice cube into another that is at rest, head on. Watch what happens to each. Then try a big cube into a small one, and a small cube into a big one. In which case does the first cube stop dead, and in which does it bounce back? Avoid glancing hits and spinning cubes, which make the result hard to read.

callouts.title: IGCSE has a topic called Momentum (1.6). Expect to use momentum = mass × velocity and to work out the total before and after a collision. The habit to keep from this book is to decide first which objects you are counting, because only the total for the whole group stays the same.
Momentum
callouts.body:
? What does it measure?
How much directed motion an object carries, and how hard it is to stop: its mass multiplied by its velocity (*p* = *mv*), in kg·m/s.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *momentum*, movement or moving power, contracted from *movimentum* (from *movere*, to move). Newton called it *quantitas motus*, the quantity of motion.
? What problem did it solve?
Collisions between carts, billiard balls or a mosquito and a car involve forces that spike and vanish in a millisecond, too fast to track instant by instant. Momentum lets you relate the motion after a collision to the motion before without knowing the messy details in between.
? Why does it work?
Because by Newton's third law, when two objects push on each other, they exert equal and opposite forces for the exact same time, so whatever momentum one loses (*F* × *t*), the other gains.
? How does it help?
It explains why a wicket-keeper draws her hands back to catch a fast cricket ball over a longer time, how recoil speeds can be predicted after a collision, and how a rocket accelerates in empty space by throwing exhaust gas backward.
?? How do we know?
From Christopher Wren and Christiaan Huygens' colliding-pendulum tests in the 1660s to modern air-track carts and particle accelerators, the vector sum of *mv* before and after an isolated collision always matches.
?? What it isn't
It is not kinetic energy (½*mv*²), which has no direction and can be turned into heat during an inelastic crash even while total momentum stays strictly unchanged.
?? Where does it stop working?
Conservation of momentum never stops working anywhere in physics, provided you include all interacting parts of the system (even the small momentum carried away by light or electromagnetic fields).

callouts.title: An astronaut is floating in the middle of a space-station module, out of reach of every wall, holding a spanner. She wants to drift to the window. What should she do?
callouts.body:
???
Throw the spanner directly away from the window. Her push on the spanner is matched by the spanner's push on her, and the total momentum of astronaut plus spanner stays zero: the spanner goes one way with some momentum, and she goes the other way with the same amount. Because her mass is much bigger, she drifts slowly, but she drifts. There is nothing else to push on, so this is the only way.

callouts.title: The mosquito and the windscreen
callouts.body:
A car on the Bandra–Worli Sea Link is doing 90 km/h, which is 25 metres every second. A mosquito drifting the other way meets the windscreen. In about a thousandth of a second, the mosquito goes from drifting to travelling with the car. The driver notices nothing.

1. A mosquito's mass is about 10⁻⁵ kg, a hundredth of a gram.
2. The car's mass is about 1,200 kg.
3. Newton's third law says the force of the windscreen on the mosquito and the force of the mosquito on the windscreen are equal and opposite.

Which feels the bigger force? And if the forces are equal, why is only the mosquito destroyed?
???
They feel exactly the same force. The third law allows no exception for size or speed.

Estimate it. The mosquito's momentum changes by about 10⁻⁵ kg × 25 m/s = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m/s, in about 0.001 s. Force × time = change in momentum, so the force is about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.001 = 0.25 N: a quarter of a newton, about the weight of a 25 g biscuit, on each of them.

Now the second law, separately for each. The mosquito gets an acceleration of 0.25 N ÷ 10⁻⁵ kg = 25,000 m/s², about two and a half thousand times the acceleration of a falling stone. The car gets 0.25 N ÷ 1,200 kg, about 0.0002 m/s², a change of speed too small for any instrument in the car to register. The ratio of the two accelerations is the ratio of the two masses, about a hundred million to one. The mosquito is destroyed not because it felt a bigger force but because its body is tiny and fragile and the same force wrenched it to the car's speed in a millisecond.

Notice, too, that "the car was going faster" explains nothing. From the driver's seat the car is still and the mosquito is the one travelling at 90 km/h. Speed belongs to a point of view; the pair of forces does not.

(The mosquito's mass is an order-of-magnitude figure from a physics textbook; the car's mass and the thousandth of a second are our guesses. Change them and the conclusion does not move.)

chapters.title: Round in circles
chapters.subtitle: Centripetal force, orbits, rolling and angular motion

sections.heading: 4.1 Heavier falls faster?
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Delft, 1586

Picture a church tower in a Dutch town, and two men at the top with lead balls in their hands. Simon Stevin was an engineer and mathematician who thought the way to settle an argument was to try it. His friend Jan Cornets de Groot had climbed the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk with him. One ball weighed ten times as much as the other. About 30 feet below them, roughly 9 m, lay a wooden board. They let go of both balls at the same moment, and listened.

The argument they were settling was nearly two thousand years old. Aristotle had taught that heavier things fall faster, and faster in proportion to their weight. If that were right, the heavy ball should hit the board when the light one was still only a tenth of the way down, about 8 m above it, and the listeners would hear two thuds well apart. A few people had doubted this. In Alexandria in the sixth century, John Philoponus wrote that when you drop two very different weights, the difference in their fall times is tiny. But almost nobody had done the experiment carefully and written it down.

They heard one thud.

:::fig c4_two_predictions() | What Aristotle's rule predicts for two lead balls, one ten times heavier

sections.heading: 4.2 Air gets in the way
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a monsoon afternoon

Stand under a balcony in July and watch the rain. Those drops have fallen from clouds that can be a few kilometres up. If a drop kept speeding up all the way down at 9.8 m/s every second, from 4000 m it would arrive at about 280 m/s, over 1000 km/h. The monsoon would be a hail of bullets. A big drop does sting a little, but it arrives at the speed of a bicycle, not a rifle shot. Something stops the speeding up. That something is the air, and this section is about what it does and when it matters.

Start with a feeling. Fill a bucket with water, hold your hand flat and sweep it through, then turn your hand edge-on and sweep again. Flat, the water fights you; edge-on, it hardly does. Your hand has to shove the water out of its way, and the faster you move, the more water you must shove each second and the harder you must shove it. Air does the same thing to anything moving through it, more gently, because air is far thinner than water. The force is called ==drag==. Drag always points against the motion, and it grows with speed: for most everyday objects, roughly with the speed squared, so doubling the speed makes the drag about four times as big.

sections.heading: 4.3 On the Moon
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Hadley Rille, the Moon, 2 August 1971

The last moonwalk of Apollo 15 was nearly over. David Scott, the mission's commander, stood in front of the television camera with a geological hammer in one hand and a falcon's feather in the other. The hammer had a mass of 1.32 kg. He held them out at about the same height, roughly 1.6 m up, in front of the camera, and let go of both at the same moment.

:::predict
On the Moon there is no air. A hammer and a feather are let go together from the same height. Which lands first?
- The hammer: it is far heavier
- The feather: it is lighter and the Moon's pull is weak
- They land together
???
They land together. With no air to hold the feather back, nothing separates them: the Moon pulls the hammer much harder, and the hammer is exactly that much harder to get moving. NASA's transcription of the moment has Scott saying that "Mr Galileo was correct in his findings".
:::

Three things happened in that drop, and it is worth taking them apart. First, the hammer fell. Many people are sure that there is no gravity where there is no air. In one survey, 81% of 13-year-olds did not think there is gravity in space. But the hammer fell, and so did

sections.heading: 4.4 Thrown sideways
sections.excerpt:
:::scene At home, at the kitchen table

Put two coins at the edge of a table. Nudge one so that it just drops off the edge. At the same instant, flick the other hard so that it flies out sideways. The flicked coin travels much farther before it lands. Does it stay in the air longer? Most people feel that it must: it was moving faster, it had more "force" behind it, so surely it had more to carry it. That feeling has a name, and you met it in Chapter 2.

:::recall 2
"The flicked coin keeps going forward because it carries the push of your finger with it, and when that runs out it falls." What is wrong with this picture?
???
This is the impetus idea from Chapter 2. Once the coin has left your finger, nothing pushes it forward. Its sideways speed simply stays, because a force is needed to *change* motion, not to keep it going. And it starts falling at once, not when something runs out: the Earth's pull acts from the first instant.
:::

:::predict
Two coins leave the edge of a table at the same instant. One is nudged so that it just drops; the other is flicked so that it flies out sideways. Which hits the floor first?
- The dropped coin: the flicked one is going faster and stays up lon

sections.heading: 4.5 Going round
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, on a local train

The train takes a curve and everyone standing sways the same way, outward from the bend, grabbing the handles. It feels exactly like being pushed. Ask anyone what pushed them and they will say "centrifugal force", the force that flings you outward when you go round a corner. The feeling is real. The force, as we will see, is not what it seems, and the test is simple enough to do on the kitchen floor.

Cut a gap about 5 cm wide in the rim of a paper plate. Put a marble inside and roll it round and round against the rim, fast. It circles until it reaches the gap.

:::predict
A marble rolls round the inside of a paper plate with a gap cut in its rim. When the marble reaches the gap, which way does it go?
- Outward, away from the centre of the plate, flung by the spinning
- Straight on, along the direction it was moving at that instant
- It keeps curving round for a while, then straightens out
???
Straight on, along the line it was moving on at that instant: a tangent to the circle. It does not fly outward, and it does not keep curving. In the 1980 study, 30% of students drew a curved path for a ball let go from a string; the marble disagrees with the

sections.heading: The ball off the Sea Link
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Bandra–Worli Sea Link, Mumbai

:::case The ball off the Sea Link
This is a thought experiment, not an activity to try on a bridge or from a vehicle. Picture a computer model of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, with three identical tennis balls released from the same height above the water. A friend is predicting what the model will show.

1. You drop the first ball straight down.
2. At the same instant your friend throws the second ball out horizontally, gently.
3. Also at the same instant, a third ball is thrown out horizontally, as hard as possible.
4. Your friend says: "The hard-thrown ball has the most force, so it stays up longest. The dropped one hits first."
5. A car is driving along the bridge beside you at a steady speed. Its passenger holds a fourth ball out of the window and simply lets go of it.

Ignore the air. Which of the first three balls hits the water first? Where do they land, compared with one another? And where does the fourth ball land: behind the car, beside it, or ahead of it?
???
The first three balls hit the water at the same instant. Each starts with no downward speed, and each is pulled down at 9.8 m/s² from the moment it is released; a sideways throw

callouts.title: You drop a cricket ball and a ₹1 coin from the same height at the same moment. Which lands first?
callouts.body:
- The cricket ball, because it is heavier
- The coin, because it is smaller and slips through the air
- They land together, or so nearly that you cannot tell
???
They land together, or so nearly that you cannot tell. Both are small and heavy for their size, so from a table's height the air hardly touches either of them. Try it over a steel thali: you hear one clink. The feeling that the ball should win comes from watching light, wide things like paper and feathers, which are a different story.

callouts.title: Equivalence of mass
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The exact equality between an object's inertial mass (its stubbornness against any accelerating force in *F* = *ma*) and its gravitational mass (how strongly gravity pulls on it in *W* = *mg*).
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *aequivalere*, to have equal value or power. Physicists distinguish the two roles mass plays—resisting acceleration versus feeling gravity—and call their identity the *equivalence principle*.
? What problem did it solve?
There is no obvious reason why the mass that makes a loaded truck sluggish on a level road should be the exact same number that sets how hard the Earth pulls it downward; in electricity, by contrast, a particle's charge and its mass do not have a fixed ratio.
? Why does it work?
Because gravity couples to the very same property of matter that gives it inertia, so in *m*_inertial × *a* = *m*_gravitational × *g*, the two *m*'s cancel identically for lead, wood, water and feathers alike.
? How does it help?
It guarantees that every object in free fall accelerates at the exact same rate *g* at a given place, and it gave Albert Einstein the starting clue for general relativity: inside a freely falling lift, gravity disappears for everything at once.
?? How do we know?
Newton tested pendulums filled with gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, salt, wood, water and wheat; Loránd Eötvös tested materials with a torsion balance to one part in 10⁸; and the MICROSCOPE satellite tested titanium and platinum in orbit in 2022 to one part in 10¹⁵, finding zero difference.
?? What it isn't
It does not mean all objects feel the same gravitational *force*: a 10 kg lead ball feels ten times the downward pull of a 1 kg ball, and needs ten times the force to achieve the same acceleration.
?? Where does it stop working?
No experiment has ever found a breakdown of the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass, down to a quadrillionth of a part.

callouts.title: At school you will see *g* written two ways: 9.8 m/s², the acceleration of free fall, and 9.8 N/kg, the gravitational field strength, the pull on each kilogram. They are the same number seen from two sides. IGCSE calls the pull on an object its weight, "a gravitational force on an object that has mass", measured in newtons.
Free fall
callouts.body:
? What is it?
Motion under the pull of gravity alone, with no air resistance, hand, floor or string pushing on the object.
? Why is it called this?
*Free* here means free of every other force besides gravity. The word *fall* misleads people into thinking it applies only on the way down: a ball thrown straight up is in free fall on the way up, at the very top, and on the way down, from the instant it leaves your hand.
? What problem did it solve?
Everyday falls in air mix two things together, Earth's downward pull and the air's upward drag, so a feather lags behind a stone and people concluded for two millennia that heavier things naturally fall faster.
? Why does it work?
Earth pulls a body of ten times the mass with ten times the gravitational force, and by Newton's second law (*a* = *F*/*m*) ten times the mass also takes ten times the force to achieve the same acceleration; the two factors of ten cancel out completely.
? How does it help?
It tells you that every dense object near Earth's surface changes its vertical velocity by 9.8 m/s every second downward, letting you time the depth of a well or predict the arc of any thrown ball.
?? How do we know?
Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot dropped two lead balls of 10-to-1 weight 30 feet onto a board at Delft in 1586 and heard a single thud, and David Scott dropped a 1.32 kg geological hammer and a falcon feather in the Moon's vacuum on 2 August 1971 and watched them hit the lunar soil side by side.
?? What it isn't
It is not motion at terminal speed: once air drag grows to balance a raindrop's weight, the drop is no longer in free fall and falls at a steady speed instead of accelerating.
?? Where does it stop working?
Near Earth's surface *g* ≈ 9.8 m/s² stays nearly constant over everyday heights, and weakens noticeably only when you climb hundreds of kilometres toward orbit.

callouts.title: In a computer model, a glass marble and a cricket ball are released together from a height of 4 m. A friend says the ball will land first because it is heavier. What do you say, and how long does the fall take? Keep real drops at table height over a clear space; this higher drop is a calculation.
callouts.body:
???
They land together, or so close that you cannot tell. Both are dense, so air barely matters over 4 m, and with air out of the way everything accelerates at 9.8 m/s². The time comes from 4 = ½ × 9.8 × *t*², so *t* = √(8 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.9 s.

callouts.title: Take two identical sheets of paper. Crumple one into a tight ball and leave the other flat. Hold them at the same height and let go together. Which lands first?
callouts.body:
- The flat sheet, because it is spread out
- The crumpled ball, by a lot
- Together: they weigh the same, so the Earth pulls them the same
???
The crumpled ball, by a lot. The Earth does pull them the same: same paper, same weight. The difference is the air. The flat sheet pushes a wide area of air out of its way and the drag soon matches its tiny weight; the ball slips through. Same weight, different fall. So weight was never the whole story.

callouts.title: Four sheets of paper
callouts.body: Take four identical sheets of paper, A4 from the printer is ideal, and clear a space on the floor. **Predict first, every time.** First: one sheet flat against one sheet crumpled into a tight ball; drop them together from shoulder height. Second: one crumpled sheet against two sheets crumpled together into one ball, so the second ball has twice the weight but about the same size and shape. Drop them together several times and watch which lands first. The weights are the same in the first race and different in the second, yet the air decides both. Write down what you saw.

callouts.title: > "At terminal speed the drop has stopped speeding up, so gravity has stopped pulling on it."
callouts.body: Gravity is pulling exactly as hard as ever. The drag has simply grown until it pulls back equally hard, so the two forces cancel and the speed stays constant. Take the air away, as on the Moon, and the drop would go on speeding up all the way down.

callouts.title: Two skydivers jump in the same spread-eagled position, one much heavier than the other. The heavier one ends up falling faster. Why, if both are pulled towards Earth with the same acceleration at the start?
callouts.body:
???
Both start at 9.8 m/s², but the heavier skydiver has more weight to balance. Drag grows with speed, so she must reach a higher speed before the drag on her matches her larger weight. Her terminal speed is higher.

callouts.title: IGCSE calls drag through air "air resistance". The rule you will need is the one from Chapter 2: an object keeps a constant speed in a straight line unless a resultant force acts. At terminal speed the resultant force is zero, so the speed is constant.
On the Moon there is no air. A hammer and a feather are let go together from the same height. Which lands first?
callouts.body:
- The hammer: it is far heavier
- The feather: it is lighter and the Moon's pull is weak
- They land together
???
They land together. With no air to hold the feather back, nothing separates them: the Moon pulls the hammer much harder, and the hammer is exactly that much harder to get moving. NASA's transcription of the moment has Scott saying that "Mr Galileo was correct in his findings".

callouts.title: > "There's no gravity on the Moon, because there's no air."
callouts.body: The hammer fell. The Moon pulls everything near it, at about a sixth of Earth's rate. Air and gravity have nothing to do with each other: air is the stuff that gets in the way of falling, and taking it away lets things fall freely, which is why the feather kept up.

callouts.title: Suppose Stevin and de Groot had done their experiment on the Moon, dropping their two lead balls about 9 m onto a board. What would they have heard, and when?
callouts.body:
???
One thud, as at Delft: the balls fall together whatever they weigh, and with no air there is nothing to separate them. They would have waited longer for it, about 3.3 s instead of 1.4 s, because the Moon's pull is weaker (9 = ½ × 1.67 × *t*² gives *t* ≈ 3.3 s).

"The flicked coin keeps going forward because it carries the push of your finger with it, and when that runs out it falls." What is wrong with this picture?
???
This is the impetus idea from Chapter 2. Once the coin has left your finger, nothing pushes it forward. Its sideways speed simply stays, because a force is needed to *change* motion, not to keep it going. And it starts falling at once, not when something runs out: the Earth's pull acts from the first instant.

callouts.title: Two coins leave the edge of a table at the same instant. One is nudged so that it just drops; the other is flicked so that it flies out sideways. Which hits the floor first?
callouts.body:
- The dropped coin: the flicked one is going faster and stays up longer
- The flicked coin: it hits the floor harder and sooner
- Both at the same moment
???
Both at the same moment. Listen: one clink. From a table about 75 cm high, both are in the air for 0.39 s, however hard you flick. Flicking changes how far the coin goes, not how long it takes to fall.

callouts.title: Independence of perpendicular motions
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The rule that a projectile's horizontal motion and vertical motion happen simultaneously without affecting each other: horizontal velocity stays constant (when air drag is negligible) while vertical velocity changes downward at *g*.
? Why is it called this?
*Perpendicular* means at right angles (horizontal and vertical), and *independent* means neither motion speeds up, slows down, or alters the clock of the other.
? What problem did it solve?
Before Galileo, gunners and philosophers thought a cannonball flew in a straight line until its "impetus" was spent and only then dropped to the ground, making it impossible to calculate trajectories or explain why a flicked coin and a dropped coin land at the same instant.
? Why does it work?
Because Newton's second law (*F* = *ma*) is a vector equation: a vertical force (gravity) has zero component along the horizontal axis, so it produces zero horizontal acceleration while producing the full downward acceleration *g* vertically.
? How does it help?
It turns any two-dimensional throw or jump into two simple one-dimensional sums linked by the same flight time *t*: use the vertical motion to find how long the object is in the air, and multiply by the horizontal speed to find where it lands.
?? How do we know?
Stroboscopic photographs of two balls released together—one dropped from rest, one projected horizontally—show both balls on the exact same horizontal line in every flash from release to floor.
?? What it isn't
It does not mean the path is straight, and it does not mean the total speed stays constant: the horizontal speed *v*_x stays constant while the downward speed *v*_y grows, so the combined speed √(*v*_x² + *v*_y²) increases as the projectile falls.
?? Where does it stop working?
When air resistance is large (as for a fast cricket ball, a badminton shuttlecock, or a spinning ball), quadratic drag couples the horizontal and vertical speeds so that a fast sideways throw slightly increases the drag opposing the vertical fall.

callouts.title: > "The flicked coin stays up longer because it is going faster."
callouts.body: Going faster sideways has no effect on falling. Both coins start with no downward speed and both are pulled down at 9.8 m/s², so they reach the floor together. Speed sideways only decides where the coin lands, not when.

callouts.title: A ball is thrown horizontally from a balcony and takes 1.2 s to reach the ground. The same ball is then thrown horizontally from the same spot at twice the speed. How long does it take to reach the ground now, and what changes?
callouts.body:
???
Still 1.2 s. The time to fall depends only on the height and on *g*; the sideways speed does not touch it. What changes is where the ball lands: twice the sideways speed for the same time means it lands twice as far out.

callouts.title: Investigation 4.4
callouts.body: In the live figure, launch two balls from the same height at the same instant, one dropped and one thrown sideways. Predict which lands first and where, then run it. Then double the sideways speed and predict again. Finally set the launch angle upward and watch the sideways steps: do they change size while the ball rises and falls?

callouts.title: A marble rolls round the inside of a paper plate with a gap cut in its rim. When the marble reaches the gap, which way does it go?
callouts.body:
- Outward, away from the centre of the plate, flung by the spinning
- Straight on, along the direction it was moving at that instant
- It keeps curving round for a while, then straightens out
???
Straight on, along the line it was moving on at that instant: a tangent to the circle. It does not fly outward, and it does not keep curving. In the 1980 study, 30% of students drew a curved path for a ball let go from a string; the marble disagrees with them every time.

callouts.title: Your syllabus never uses the word "centrifugal". IGCSE describes circular motion as "motion in a circular path due to a force perpendicular to the motion". In an exam, name the real inward force: the tension in the string, the friction of the road, or the gravitational pull of the Sun.
callouts.body:
:::

Now the honest part about "centrifugal force", because you will keep hearing the words. Someone who insists on describing the world from inside the turning train, treating the carriage as if it were standing still, finds that Newton's rules do not quite work there: things seem to slide outward with nothing pushing them. To make the rules work in that spinning view, they have to add an outward force by hand. Physicists call that a fictitious force. It has no source; nothing is doing the pushing. Seen from the platform, there is no such force, just a passenger carrying straight on and a train turning. Both descriptions can be made to agree, but the one from the platform is the simpler and truer one, because in it every force has something causing it.

callouts.title: > "A force throws me outward when the train goes round a bend."
callouts.body: Nothing pushes you outward. Your body carries straight on while the train turns, and then the handle or the carriage wall pushes you inward to bring you round. The only real force in the turning is the inward one. The outward feeling is your own straight-line motion meeting a turning vehicle.

callouts.title: Centripetal force
callouts.body:
? What is it?
Any net force that points inward toward the centre of a curve and keeps an object moving along a circular path by continually turning its velocity vector.
? Why is it called this?
Isaac Newton coined *vis centripeta* in 1687 from Latin *centrum* (centre) and *petere* (to seek), to contrast with Christiaan Huygens' earlier *vis centrifuga* (centre-fleeing).
? What problem did it solve?
People felt tugged outward on a bend or when whirling a sling and assumed circular motion was driven by an outward push, which left them unable to explain why a stone released from a sling flies along the tangent rather than straight out from the centre.
? Why does it work?
By Newton's first law, a body with no force on it goes straight at constant speed; to bend that straight path into a circle at speed *v* and radius *r* requires an inward acceleration of *v*²/*r* toward the centre at every instant.
? How does it help?
It lets you calculate the road grip a car needs on a bend (four times as much grip at twice the speed), why water stays in an overhead swinging bucket, and how gravity holds the Moon and satellites in orbit.
?? How do we know?
Roll a marble round the inside of a paper plate with a gap cut in its rim: the instant the rim's inward push ends at the gap, the marble travels straight along the tangent, never outward.
?? What it isn't
It is not a new fifth force of nature to add alongside tension, friction or gravity on a free-body diagram; it is simply the job description for whichever real force (string tension, road friction, or gravity) is pointing toward the centre.
?? Where does it stop working?
If the required inward force *mv*²/*r* exceeds what the string or road friction can supply, the string snaps or the tyres skid and the object leaves the circle along a straighter path.

callouts.title: A racing car goes round a bend at a perfectly steady 120 km/h. Is it accelerating? If so, which way?
callouts.body:
???
Yes. Its speed is steady but its direction is changing, and velocity includes direction, so its velocity is changing: that is an acceleration. It points towards the centre of the bend, where the friction of the road on the tyres is pulling the car.

callouts.title: Investigation 4.5
callouts.body: In the live figure, whirl the ball on its string and press "release" at three different points of the circle. Before each release, point to where you think the ball will go. Then switch on the "from the ball's seat" view and see the same event from inside the turning: notice that the pretend outward force appears there and nowhere else.

callouts.title: The ball off the Sea Link
callouts.body:
This is a thought experiment, not an activity to try on a bridge or from a vehicle. Picture a computer model of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, with three identical tennis balls released from the same height above the water. A friend is predicting what the model will show.

1. You drop the first ball straight down.
2. At the same instant your friend throws the second ball out horizontally, gently.
3. Also at the same instant, a third ball is thrown out horizontally, as hard as possible.
4. Your friend says: "The hard-thrown ball has the most force, so it stays up longest. The dropped one hits first."
5. A car is driving along the bridge beside you at a steady speed. Its passenger holds a fourth ball out of the window and simply lets go of it.

Ignore the air. Which of the first three balls hits the water first? Where do they land, compared with one another? And where does the fourth ball land: behind the car, beside it, or ahead of it?
???
The first three balls hit the water at the same instant. Each starts with no downward speed, and each is pulled down at 9.8 m/s² from the moment it is released; a sideways throw changes nothing about the fall (Section 4.4). Your friend has the impetus idea from Chapter 2: there is no "force" stored in the hard-thrown ball, only a larger sideways speed that stays constant. The dropped ball lands straight below the railing; the gently thrown one lands some way out; the hard-thrown one lands farther out still, each in proportion to the sideways speed it was given, because all three are in the air for the same time.

The fourth ball lands beside the car, directly below where the passenger's hand is at that moment. When it was released it already had the car's forward speed, and nothing acts to slow that sideways motion, so it keeps pace with the car while it falls. Seen from the car it drops straight down; seen from the railing it traces the same kind of curve as the thrown balls. (With air, all four would fall a little short and a little late; the hard-thrown ball would lose the most.)

sections.heading: 5.1 The apple and the Moon
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Woolsthorpe, 1666

In 1666, in the plague years, Isaac Newton was 23 and at home at Woolsthorpe, his family's farmhouse in Lincolnshire. Sixty years later he told a friend, William Stukeley, that his thinking about gravity had been "occasion'd by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood". There really was an apple tree in the garden. The apple did not hit him on the head; that detail was added later, and the story itself rests on an old man's memory, so hold it lightly. But the question he asked is well recorded, and it is a wonderful one.

An apple falls. Everybody knows that. Newton's question was: how high does the pull that drops the apple reach? To the top of the tree, obviously. To the top of the air? And if it reaches that far, why should it stop? What if it reached the Moon?

Here is why the question had teeth. Chapter 2's law says a thing left alone moves in a straight line at a steady speed. The Moon does not: it goes round Earth, roughly in a circle, once in about 27.3 days. Chapter 4's last section says that anything going round must be pulled towards the centre by some force, or it would fly off along a tangent. So something is pulling the Moon to

sections.heading: 5.2 Newton's cannon
sections.excerpt:
:::scene In orbit, 400 km above Mumbai

The International Space Station circles about 400 km above the ground; on some evenings it can be seen from Mumbai as a bright, steady point crossing the sky in a few minutes. Use Section 5.1's rule to find Earth's pull up there: the station is at 6771 km from Earth's centre against 6371 km for us, and the square of 6371/6771 is 0.885. Gravity on the station is 89% of gravity in Mumbai. And yet the astronauts float. Before reading on, decide what you think is going on.

:::predict
Gravity at the space station's height is about 89% of its strength on the ground. Why doesn't the station fall down?
- Its engines keep pushing it up
- It is above the air, and gravity cannot act where there is no air
- It is falling, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground keeps curving away beneath it
- There is no gravity in space, whatever the sum says
???
It is falling, and it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away as fast as it falls. The station is in free fall all the time, exactly like the dropped hammer, and it never lands because Earth is round. Its engines are off almost all the time, and gravity has nothing to do with air.
:::

Newton

sections.heading: 5.3 Ellipses
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Hven, 1576

Newton's law was the explanation. The thing it explained had been found a lifetime earlier by two men who could hardly have been more different. Tycho Brahe built an observatory, Uraniborg, on the small island of Hven, and for about twenty years measured the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, without a telescope, more carefully than anyone before him. His positions disagreed with the printed tables, and his were the better ones.

:::scene Prague, 1600

Johannes Kepler arrived in Prague to work for Tycho in February 1600. Tycho died in October 1601, and Kepler got his data: twenty years of Mars. Kepler believed, as everyone did, that a planet moves in a circle, and he set out to find the circle that fitted Tycho's Mars. He could not. His best circle missed some of Tycho's positions by eight minutes of arc, a little more than an eighth of a degree. That is a tiny angle, small enough that many would have blamed the measurements. Kepler trusted Tycho. Eight minutes of arc, he decided, were enough to throw out two thousand years of circles.

sections.heading: 5.4 Weighing the Earth
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Clapham, 1798

Newton's law says that every mass pulls every other mass. Not just planets: a book pulls a cup, you pull the person next to you on the train. Nobody notices, because for everyday masses the pull is absurdly small, and for a hundred years after Newton nobody managed to measure it. Then Henry Cavendish, a man in his late sixties who lived at Clapham on the edge of London, and who was so shy that, the story goes, he spoke to his housekeeper only by written notes, set out to catch it.

:::predict
Two 1 kg bags of rice sit on a table 1 m apart. Do they pull on each other?
- No. Gravity is something planets and stars have, not bags of rice
- Yes, but far too weakly to notice, about a hundred-billionth of their weight
- Yes, about as strongly as a fridge magnet pulls a coin
???
Yes, far too weakly to notice. Each bag pulls the other with about 0.000 000 000 067 N, roughly 150 billion times less than the weight of either bag. It is real, and Cavendish measured a pull of this kind in 1798.
:::

sections.heading: 5.5 Predicting the sky
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Cambridge, August 1684

In August 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley visited Newton in Cambridge with a question: if the Sun pulled on a planet with a force weakening as the inverse square of the distance, what path would the planet follow? Newton answered at once: an ellipse. He had worked it out, he said, but he could not find the paper. Halley pressed him to write it up properly. The result, three years later, was the *Principia*, the book that contains everything in this chapter so far. The Royal Society was supposed to print it, but it had spent its money on a *History of Fishes* that did not sell, so Halley paid for the printing himself.

What Halley had seen was that a law like Newton's does more than describe. If you know where a body is and how fast it is moving, the law tells you where it will be next, and next after that, for as long as you care to calculate. Newton's law and his laws of motion allow only certain paths around the Sun: circles, ellipses, and two open curves for things moving too fast to be held. Find which one a body is on, and its future is written.

The law also lets you weigh things you cannot visit. Kepler's third law, *P*² = *a*³, holds for t

sections.heading: 5.6 The slow road to the Moon
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Sriharikota, 14 July 2023

At 14:35 on 14 July 2023, an LVM3 rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at Sriharikota, carrying Chandrayaan-3: a propulsion module, a lander called Vikram and, inside the lander, a small rover called Pragyan, about 3.9 tonnes in all. The Moon is about 384,000 km away, and the rocket had put the spacecraft into an orbit whose far point was planned at about 36,500 km. It would not reach the Moon for another three weeks, and it would get there by going round the Earth, again and again, in loops that grew.

Why loops? Why not point the rocket at the Moon and fire? Here is the picture to hold on to from this chapter. Once a rocket's engine stops, the spacecraft is simply falling, coasting on an orbit under gravity alone, exactly like the cannonball or the Moon. It needs no push to keep going (Chapter 2). An engine firing does not "push it outward"; it changes the spacecraft's speed along its path, and that moves it onto a *different* orbit. The whole art of flying to the Moon is choosing a sequence of orbits and the short burns that hop between them. ISRO's own updates record the sequence, and it is a lesson in Kepler.

sections.heading: The comet that came back
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Near Dresden, Christmas night 1758

:::case The comet that came back
Edmond Halley, the man who had paid to print Newton's *Principia*, predicted that a particular comet would return in 1758. He died in 1742. As 1758 approached, three people in Paris, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, spent months on a calculation Halley had not done, working out step by step how the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn would alter the comet's path. They announced that it would pass closest to the Sun around the middle of April 1759, some months later than a simple return would suggest.

1. The comet was first spotted on 25 December 1758 by Johann Georg Palitzsch, a farmer and amateur astronomer near Dresden.
2. A comet spends almost all of its time far from the Sun, moving slowly, and races through its closest approach in a matter of weeks.
3. The Paris calculators included the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn, the two giant planets, and no others.
4. For a bound two-body orbit, Newton's law gives an ellipse. When a third body pulls as well, there is no simple general formula for the paths, so astronomers follow the tugs step by step.

A sceptic says: "Halley said 1758. It wasn'

callouts.body:
"Nothing is pushing the Moon along its orbit, so it ought to slow down and eventually stop." What is wrong here?
???
The Moon needs no push to keep moving; that is the lesson of Chapter 2. A force is needed only to change motion. Earth's pull does change the Moon's motion, but sideways: it bends the path into a circle without speeding the Moon up or slowing it down. No force along the orbit is needed, and none acts.

callouts.title: A weather satellite is launched to a height of one Earth radius (6,371 km) above the ground, so it is twice as far from the Earth's centre as you are in Mumbai. How strong is the Earth's gravitational pull on the satellite up there, compared with its weight on the ground?
callouts.body:
- Zero: it is far out in space, beyond the atmosphere
- Half as strong, because it is twice as far from the Earth's centre
- One quarter as strong, because it is twice as far from the Earth's centre
???
One quarter as strong. Distance in Newton's law is measured from the Earth's centre, so climbing one Earth radius above the surface doubles your distance from the centre (*r* goes from 1 *R*_E to 2 *R*_E). Under an inverse-square rule, twice the distance means 1/2² = 1/4 of the pull, so *g* up there is about 9.8 ÷ 4 = 2.45 m/s².

callouts.title: > "The Moon falls 1.36 mm closer to Earth every second."
callouts.body: It falls 1.36 mm below the straight line it would otherwise have followed. But in that same second it also moves about 1 km sideways, and the straight line leads slightly *away* from Earth, so the two effects cancel and the Moon's distance stays about the same. It is always falling and never arriving.

callouts.title: Universal gravitation
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The law that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres (*F* = *Gm*₁*m*₂/*r*²).
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *gravitas*, heaviness or weight (from *gravis*, heavy), combined with *universal* because Newton showed in 1687 that one and the same attraction governs falling stones on Earth and planets in the sky.
? What problem did it solve?
Since antiquity, Earth and the heavens were thought to obey different laws: heavy things fell toward the Earth while planets moved in eternal circles for reasons of their own. Nobody knew what held the Moon in its path or why Kepler's three laws held.
? Why does it work?
Because gravitational influence spreads out across three-dimensional space so its strength thins out with the surface area of a sphere (4π*r*²), weakening as 1/*r*² while pulling in proportion to how much mass each body has.
? How does it help?
It lets us weigh the Earth in a shed (Cavendish, 1798), weigh the Sun and Jupiter from the periods of their satellites, predict the return of Halley's comet, and discover Neptune by pen and paper from the wobble of Uranus.
?? How do we know?
Newton's apple-and-Moon test showed that the Moon's inward acceleration at 60 Earth radii (0.00272 m/s²) is 1/60² = 1/3600 of *g* at Earth's surface (9.8 m/s²), and Cavendish directly measured the tiny attraction between lead spheres in 1798.
?? What it isn't
It is not a force that requires air or stops at the top of the atmosphere: at the International Space Station 400 km up, Earth's gravity is still 89% as strong as on the ground in Mumbai.
?? Where does it stop working?
Newton's inverse-square law is extraordinarily accurate across the solar system and gives way to Einstein's general relativity only in very strong gravitational fields, such as near the Sun (where Mercury's orbit precesses by an extra 43 arcseconds per century) or around black holes.

callouts.title: Suppose Earth kept the same mass but swelled to twice its radius, and you stood on the new surface. By what factor would your weight change?
callouts.body:
???
It would fall to a quarter. Your weight is Earth's pull on you, and you would be twice as far from Earth's centre. Twice the distance, under an inverse-square rule, means one quarter of the pull. Your mass would not change at all.

callouts.title: Gravity at the space station's height is about 89% of its strength on the ground. Why doesn't the station fall down?
callouts.body:
- Its engines keep pushing it up
- It is above the air, and gravity cannot act where there is no air
- It is falling, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground keeps curving away beneath it
- There is no gravity in space, whatever the sum says
???
It is falling, and it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away as fast as it falls. The station is in free fall all the time, exactly like the dropped hammer, and it never lands because Earth is round. Its engines are off almost all the time, and gravity has nothing to do with air.

In Chapter 4 you dropped a cricket ball and a coin. Now an astronaut of 70 kg and a space station of 420 tonnes are both falling round the Earth. Does the heavier one fall faster and pull away from the lighter one?
???
No. Everything falls alike when nothing but gravity acts, whatever its mass, because a heavier thing is pulled harder and is exactly that much harder to accelerate. The station and the astronaut fall round the Earth together, so neither drifts towards the other. That is why she floats in the middle of the cabin.

callouts.title: The phone that reads zero
callouts.body: You can inspect the live figure's trace without dropping a phone. For the physical version, ask an adult first and use only a phone they agree can be dropped onto a thick cushion. Install the free phyphox app, which uses the phone's own motion sensor, and open "Acceleration (with g)". Held still, it reads about 9.8 m/s²: that is the sensor feeling the phone's weight, the way you feel yours through your feet. Put a thick, soft pillow on the floor. Hold the phone flat above it, no higher than your knee, about 40 cm, start recording, and let it drop. Then look at the graph. For about 0.29 s, while the phone was falling, the reading dropped to about zero. Nothing was pushing on the sensor, so it felt no weight, although the Earth's pull on it never changed. For that third of a second your phone was an astronaut. The live figure for this section does the same thing with the book's own sensor reading.

callouts.title: > "There's no gravity in space. That's why astronauts float."
callouts.body: At the station's height gravity is about 89% of its strength on the ground, and it is what keeps the station from flying off in a straight line. The astronauts float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together, so nothing pushes up on them. They still have weight; they do not feel it.

callouts.title: Orbit
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The closed or open path of a body falling freely under gravity while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the body it circles.
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *orbita*, the wheel-rut or track left by a cartwheel (from *orbis*, a wheel or ring), adopted by medieval and Renaissance astronomers for the track of a planet across the sky.
? What problem did it solve?
Ancient astronomers imagined solid crystal spheres carrying the Moon and planets around, and modern intuition still imagines rockets must keep their engines firing to hold a satellite up.
? Why does it work?
Because at orbital speed (about 7.7 km/s at 400 km altitude), in each second the satellite falls toward Earth by the exact same 4.3 metres that the round Earth's surface curves away beneath it.
? How does it help?
It explains why astronauts float weightless inside the Space Station (craft and crew fall together with no floor pressing up), and how ISRO raised Chandrayaan-3 to the Moon using short engine burns at perigee and days of engine-off coasting.
?? How do we know?
Every satellite ever launched switches its main engine off once it reaches orbital speed and coasts for years, and a phone dropped 40 cm onto a pillow reads 0 m/s² on its accelerometer during the fall for the exact same reason.
?? What it isn't
An orbit is not a place where gravity has switched off; without gravity pulling inward at every instant, the spacecraft would fly off in a straight line into deep space.
?? Where does it stop working?
In low Earth orbit below a few hundred kilometres, wisps of thin upper air slowly drag on a satellite and bleed off its speed, causing the orbit to spiral down unless boosted from time to time.

callouts.title: Anna says a satellite in orbit is in free fall. Tom says it cannot be, because its acceleration is not 9.8 m/s². Who is right?
callouts.body:
???
Anna. Free fall means that gravity is the only force acting, and that is true of a satellite. The acceleration is smaller than 9.8 m/s² only because gravity is weaker up there (about 8.7 m/s² at 400 km), not because anything else is acting.

callouts.title: IGCSE defines weight as "a gravitational force on an object that has mass", so in an exam an astronaut in orbit *has* weight; say that she "feels weightless" because she is in free fall. When the syllabus says that gravity "keeps an object in orbit", think of a satellite that keeps falling towards the Earth and keeps missing it. The orbital speed formula is *v* = 2π*r*/*T*: the circumference divided by the time for one circuit.
Mars's orbit, drawn to scale on a page, looks like which of these?
callouts.body:
- A clearly squashed oval, like a rugby ball seen from the side
- A perfect circle with the Sun at its centre
- Almost a circle, but with the Sun noticeably off-centre
???
Almost a circle, with the Sun noticeably off-centre. Mars's orbit is only slightly stretched (its eccentricity is about 0.09), so the outline looks round. But the Sun is not at the middle: it sits about 9% of the way from the centre to the edge, so Mars is about 17% closer to the Sun at one end of its orbit than at the other.

callouts.title: Two pins and a loop of string
callouts.body: Ask an adult for two drawing pins and push them into a flap cut from a cardboard box, about 5 cm apart. Tie thread into a loop that fits loosely round both pins, put a pencil inside the loop, pull it taut and trace all the way round. You have drawn an ellipse, and the pins are its two foci. Now move the pins closer together and draw again, then farther apart. **Predict first:** what happens to the shape each time? To draw Mars's orbit to scale, make the loop so that the pencil reaches about 10 cm from the midpoint, and put the pins 0.9 cm either side of the midpoint. Mark one pin "Sun". It barely looks like an ellipse at all, and that is the point.

callouts.title: > "The Sun sits at the centre of the ellipse, and planets move in long, squashed ovals."
callouts.body: The Sun sits at one focus, not at the centre, and the other focus is empty. And the planets' ellipses are very nearly circles: Earth's distance from the Sun changes by only about 3% over a year. Textbook drawings stretch the ellipse so that you can see its shape; the real thing is round with an off-centre Sun.

callouts.title: A distant object goes round the Sun at an average distance of 50 astronomical units, fifty times Earth's distance. How long is its year?
callouts.body:
???
About 354 Earth years. Kepler's third law gives *P*² = 50³ = 125,000, so *P* = √125,000 ≈ 354 years. The farther out, the slower the journey and the longer the path.

callouts.title: Two 1 kg bags of rice sit on a table 1 m apart. Do they pull on each other?
callouts.body:
- No. Gravity is something planets and stars have, not bags of rice
- Yes, but far too weakly to notice, about a hundred-billionth of their weight
- Yes, about as strongly as a fridge magnet pulls a coin
???
Yes, far too weakly to notice. Each bag pulls the other with about 0.000 000 000 067 N, roughly 150 billion times less than the weight of either bag. It is real, and Cavendish measured a pull of this kind in 1798.

callouts.title: > "Gravity is a thing planets and stars have. Small objects don't have gravity."
callouts.body: Every mass pulls every other, including you and this book, and Cavendish measured the pull between lead balls in 1798. It is just extraordinarily weak unless one of the masses is enormous. Earth's pull on you is strong only because Earth has six million million million million kilograms of stuff doing the pulling.

callouts.title: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has a radius of 2.58 × 10⁶ m and a mass of 1.35 × 10²³ kg. What is the acceleration of free fall at its surface?
callouts.body:
???
About 1.35 m/s², a little less than on our Moon. The acceleration at a world's surface is *GM*/*R*²: 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.35 × 10²³ ÷ (2.58 × 10⁶)² ≈ 1.35 m/s². A hammer dropped on Titan would take about 1.5 s to fall 1.6 m.

callouts.title: IGCSE wording: mass is "a measure of the quantity of matter in an object", and weight is "a gravitational force on an object that has mass". Write mass in kg and weight in N, and remember that *G* (the constant in Newton's law) and *g* (9.8 N/kg at Earth's surface) are different things.
callouts.body:
:::

## 5.5 Predicting the sky

callouts.title: Uranus kept drifting away from the position that Newton's law predicted for it. Which of these was the right explanation?
callouts.body:
- Newton's law weakens even faster than the inverse square far from the Sun
- An unseen planet beyond Uranus was pulling on it
- The old measurements of Uranus were simply wrong
???
An unseen planet. Urbain Le Verrier treated the drift as a perturbation and calculated, from Newton's law alone, where a planet must be to cause it. He posted the position to the Berlin observatory. On the night the letter arrived, 23 September 1846, Galle and d'Arrest pointed their telescope at the predicted spot and found Neptune within about a degree of it.

callouts.title: > "Halley discovered Halley's comet."
callouts.body: Comets had been seen for thousands of years. What Halley did was new in a different way: he predicted that one of them would come back, in 1758, because a body on a closed orbit under Newton's law must return. He discovered the comet's *future*. The farmer who first spotted it on its return, on Christmas night 1758, was Johann Georg Palitzsch.

callouts.title: Why do astronomers say that Neptune was the first planet discovered through mathematics, when Galle found it with a telescope?
callouts.body:
???
Because the telescope was pointed where the mathematics said to look. Le Verrier calculated Neptune's position from the way Uranus was being pulled off course, using Newton's law of gravitation; Galle only had to confirm that something was there. Uranus itself had been seen through a telescope before anyone calculated where to look.

callouts.title: Chandrayaan-3 arrives near the Moon on 5 August, falling towards it faster and faster. To be captured into orbit around the Moon, what must it do with its engine?
callouts.body:
- Fire to speed up, so that it can catch the Moon
- Fire against its motion, to slow down
- Nothing: the Moon's gravity will capture it by itself
???
Fire against its motion, to slow down. Arriving at the Moon it is moving too fast for the Moon's weak pull to hold: left alone, it would swing past and fly back out, as the fast cannonball did. ISRO's engine fired backwards for 1835 seconds, about half an hour, starting at 19:12 on 5 August, and the craft dropped into an orbit round the Moon of 164 km by 18,074 km.

callouts.title: > "The engine burns pushed Chandrayaan-3 outward, away from the Earth."
callouts.body: Each burn pushed the craft *along* its path, making it faster at the low point of its orbit. The effect showed up half an orbit later, on the far side, as a higher high point. Nothing pushed it outward; gravity did the turning, as it always does, and a faster start simply let it climb farther before gravity brought it round.

callouts.title: Once the propulsion module was in its near-circular orbit of about 153 km by 163 km round the Moon, did it need to keep its engine running to stay there?
callouts.body:
???
No. In orbit it was falling freely round the Moon, held in its curve by the Moon's gravity alone, like Newton's cannonball or the Moon round the Earth. An engine is needed only to change from one orbit to another. With no air at the Moon to drag on it, it could circle for a very long time with the engine off.

callouts.title: Investigation 5.6
callouts.body: Open the Chandrayaan-3 tab in [The Sky](#explore-sky) explorer and step through the burns. Before each one, predict where on the orbit the engine will fire and which part of the orbit will change. Then watch the time for one lap grow from about 12 hours to about 24 hours, and work out from Kepler's third law roughly how much bigger the orbit's average size must have become.

callouts.title: The comet that came back
callouts.body:
Edmond Halley, the man who had paid to print Newton's *Principia*, predicted that a particular comet would return in 1758. He died in 1742. As 1758 approached, three people in Paris, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, spent months on a calculation Halley had not done, working out step by step how the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn would alter the comet's path. They announced that it would pass closest to the Sun around the middle of April 1759, some months later than a simple return would suggest.

1. The comet was first spotted on 25 December 1758 by Johann Georg Palitzsch, a farmer and amateur astronomer near Dresden.
2. A comet spends almost all of its time far from the Sun, moving slowly, and races through its closest approach in a matter of weeks.
3. The Paris calculators included the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn, the two giant planets, and no others.
4. For a bound two-body orbit, Newton's law gives an ellipse. When a third body pulls as well, there is no simple general formula for the paths, so astronomers follow the tugs step by step.

A sceptic says: "Halley said 1758. It wasn't closest to the Sun until 1759. So Newton's law got it wrong, and the Paris sums were just luck." Was the comet obeying Newton's law? Why did the three calculators need months, and what would have happened to the prediction if they had ignored Jupiter and Saturn?
???
The comet obeyed Newton's law precisely; that is why the Paris prediction worked. The law says every mass pulls every other, so the comet is pulled not only by the Sun but by Jupiter and Saturn as it passes near them, and over decades in the outer dark, where it moves slowly, those tugs have time to shift its path and its timetable by months. Halley's prediction used the Sun alone and could only be rough. To do better you must follow the comet step by step, adding up the three pulls at each stage, and in 1758 that meant months of hand arithmetic shared among the three of them. Ignoring the two giant planets would have given a date well off the true one, so the sceptic has it backwards: the months of sums were not luck, they were the law being taken seriously. Palitzsch spotted the comet as it came in, on Christmas night, on its way to the closest approach that the calculators had placed in the spring. The comet carries Halley's name because he was the first to know it would come back.
