sections.heading: 6.1 Pressure
sections.excerpt:
Press the flat end of a pencil gently into a lump of dough or plasticine. Now turn it round and press its point in with a similar push. Same sort of force; a much deeper dent. What changed was the area the push was spread over.

That is the whole idea of this section, and it is worth a number. Suppose an elephant of 4 tonnes stands on four feet, each about the size of a large dinner plate (we will call it 0.1 m², a made-up but reasonable figure). Its weight, about 39,000 N, is spread over 0.4 m². Now suppose a 60 kg person balances on the heel of one stiletto shoe, a heel about 1 cm² across (also a made-up figure). Her weight is about 590 N, spread over a hundredth of a hundredth of a square metre. Divide force by area in each case and the heel comes out pressing about sixty times harder on the floor than the elephant does. The elephant wins on force by a huge margin. The heel wins on force *per area*, and it is force per area that dents a wooden floor.

Force per area is called ==pressure==. Write it as pressure = force ÷ area, or *p* = *F*/*A*. The unit is the newton per square metre, which has its own name, the ==pascal== (Pa): 1 Pa is 1 N pushing on 1 m². A pascal is a very sma

sections.heading: 6.2 The ocean of air
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Florence, 1643

In the 1640s, pump-makers in Italy had a problem they could not solve. A pump that drew water up a pipe worked beautifully up to a height of about ten metres, and then stopped. Build the pipe taller and the water simply would not follow. Nobody knew why. Evangelista Torricelli, a mathematician in Florence, turned to mercury. Mercury is far denser than water; if the ten-metre limit had anything to do with weight, a column of mercury should stop much lower.

He filled a glass tube, closed at one end, with mercury, put his finger over the open end, turned it upside down into a dish of mercury, and took his finger away. The mercury in the tube dropped, and then stopped, standing about 76 cm above the level in the dish. Above it, at the top of the sealed tube, was a space with almost nothing in it. On 11 June 1644 he wrote to his friend Michelangelo Ricci and gave the reason in one line: *we live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air*.

Here is the idea in that sentence. Air has weight. Not much per litre, but the atmosphere is many kilometres deep, and all of it is sitting on you. Picture a column of air one square centimetre across, standing on the back o

sections.heading: 6.3 Nothing sucks
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Regensburg, 1654

Otto von Guericke, from Magdeburg, had an air pump. In 1654, or a few years later (the accounts disagree), he fitted two copper hemispheres together to make a hollow ball, pumped the air out of it, and hitched a team of horses to each side. The horses heaved. The two halves would not come apart. Let the air back in, and the same two halves come apart with no effort at all. How many horses were there? One letter says twelve, popular accounts say sixteen, one says thirty, so we will leave it at "teams of horses".

Ask almost anyone what held the hemispheres together and they will say the vacuum sucked them. It is one of the most natural wrong sentences in physics, and it is worth taking apart, because there is a true sentence underneath it that explains far more.

Think about what was on each side of the copper. Outside: ordinary air, pressing inward on every square centimetre of the ball with about 10 N, as it presses on everything. Inside: almost nothing. Before the pump ran, the air inside pushed outward exactly as hard as the air outside pushed in, and the two halves could be lifted apart with a finger. The pump removed the inside push and left the outs

sections.heading: 6.4 Deeper means more
sections.excerpt:
Dive to the bottom of the deep end of a swimming pool and your ears tell you, sharply, that something has changed. The further down you go, the more it hurts. Nothing about the water has changed; there is simply more of it above you, and all of it is pressing.

Let us count the pressing. Mark out a square metre of pool floor and look at the water standing on it. If the pool is 1 m deep, the column above that square is 1 m³ of water, which has a mass of 1,000 kg and a weight of about 9,800 N. Spread over 1 m², that is 9,800 Pa of pressure from the water, on top of the 101,000 Pa the air was already pressing with at the surface. Make the pool 2 m deep and the column holds twice the water, so the water's pressure doubles to 19,600 Pa. The pattern is simple: the pressure from the weight of the water is the depth, times the water's density, times *g*. Physicists write it *p* = *ρgh*, where *ρ* (the Greek letter rho) is the density and *h* the depth.

Now notice what is *not* in that formula. The area of your square was 1 m². Make it 2 m² and the column above it holds twice the water, but the weight is spread over twice the area, and force ÷ area is unchanged. The size of the patch cance

sections.heading: 6.5 Why ships float
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Syracuse, c. 250 BCE

You may know the story. A king suspects that his goldsmith has mixed silver into a golden crown. Archimedes puzzles over it in the public bath, notices the water rise as he climbs in, shouts "Eureka!" and runs home through the streets with no clothes on. It is a wonderful story, and historians treat it as a legend. It was first written down by Vitruvius about two centuries after Archimedes lived, and nothing earlier backs it up.

The best critic of the story was a 22-year-old. In 1586 the young Galileo Galilei wrote a short paper called *La Bilancetta*, "the little balance". He pointed out that measuring a crown by the water it displaces would need a precision no bowl and no eye could manage: the difference between gold and gold-with-silver would be a change in water level too small to see. Then he proposed a method that would work. Hang the crown from one arm of a balance and weigh it in air. Lower it into water and weigh it again. The water pushes up on it, so it weighs less, and the amount it loses tells you the volume, and therefore the density. That instrument is a hydrostatic balance, and it rests on a principle Archimedes really did state. The

sections.heading: The egg that changed its mind
sections.excerpt:
:::case The egg that changed its mind
Kym puts a raw egg into a tall glass of tap water. It sinks to the bottom and stays there.

1. She takes the egg out, stirs salt into the water a spoon at a time until no more will dissolve easily, and puts the egg back. Now it floats, with a little of its shell above the surface.
2. Very gently, she pours fresh tap water on top of the salt water, down the side of the glass so that the two barely mix. The egg sinks a little and then stops, hanging in the middle of the glass, well below the surface and well above the bottom.
3. Her cousin says: "The salt made the egg lighter, and the fresh water on top made it heavier again."

What really changed between the three stages, and why does the egg hang in the middle at stage 2 instead of floating at the top or sinking to the bottom?
???
The egg never changed. Its weight was the same in all three stages, and so was its volume. What changed was the water around it.

In plain tap water, the water the egg displaced weighed less than the egg, so the buoyant force was smaller than its weight and it sank. Dissolving salt made the water denser, so the same volume of displaced water weighed more. Once that we

callouts.title: A 1 kg packet of atta lies flat on the kitchen table. You stand it up on its narrow end. Compared with lying flat, the packet standing on its end pushes on the table with
callouts.body:
- more force and more pressure
- the same force but more pressure
- the same force and the same pressure
???
The same force but more pressure. The packet's weight has not changed: about 9.8 N either way. But standing on its end it rests on a much smaller patch of table. If the packet is about 20 cm by 12 cm by 5 cm, the flat face is 240 cm² and the end is 60 cm², four times smaller. Same force, four times the pressure: about 400 Pa lying flat, about 1,600 Pa standing up.

callouts.title: > "Pressure pushes downward."
callouts.body: In a pile of books it does. In a fluid it does not. Water at a given depth pushes sideways on the wall of the tank, upward on the underside of a boat and downward on the floor of the tank, all with the same pressure. If water only pushed down, the side holes in a leaking bucket would not spurt, and nothing would ever float. Most of this chapter depends on the sideways and upward pushes.

callouts.title: Pressure
callouts.body:
? What does it measure?
How concentrated a force is over a surface: the perpendicular force divided by the area it presses on (*p* = *F*/*A*), measured in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).
? Why is it called this?
From the Latin *pressura*, a pressing or squeezing, from *premere*, to press. In everyday speech people use *force* and *pressure* as synonyms, which obscures the crucial part: the area.
? What problem did it solve?
Force alone cannot explain why a blunt knife squashes a tomato while a sharp knife slices it under the same push, why an elephant dents a wooden floor less than a stiletto heel, or why pump-makers in Florence could never lift water higher than 10.3 metres.
? Why does it work?
Because materials yield or punctured skins give way when the local force on each tiny patch of surface exceeds what its bonds can hold, and in a fluid at rest, moving molecules bombard every surface from all sides with a push proportional to depth (*p* = *ρgh*).
? How does it help?
It explains how the ocean of air holds up 76 cm of mercury in Torricelli's barometer, why a postcard stays on an upturned glass of water, why dams are built thick at the base, and how hydraulic brakes multiply force.
?? How do we know?
Florin Périer carried Torricelli's mercury tube up the Puy de Dôme on 19 September 1648 and watched the column drop by about 8 cm as a tenth of the atmosphere was left below his feet, while an identical tube down in Clermont stayed steady all day.
?? What it isn't
It is not a directed vector that points only downward, and low pressure never "sucks" or pulls: fluids only push, and things move toward low pressure because higher pressure on the other side pushes them there.
?? Where does it stop working?
The smooth continuum picture of pressure works down to microscopic scales and breaks down only in an ultra-high vacuum where single gas molecules hit a wall miles apart rather than as a steady rain.

callouts.title: Investigation 6.1
callouts.body: Press the flat end of a pencil, then its point, into a lump of dough or plasticine with what feels like the same push. Measure the two dents. Which end made the deeper dent, and which end did you push harder with? (Your hand may give the answer away: most people cannot help easing off when the point goes in.) Then trace one of your shoes on squared paper, estimate its area in m², and work out the pressure you exert on the floor when standing on both feet versus balancing on one foot.

callouts.title: A sharp knife slices a tomato with a gentle push. A blunt knife, pushed just as hard, squashes it. Explain the difference using pressure.
callouts.body:
???
The force is the same, but the sharp edge meets the tomato's skin along a far narrower strip, so the same force is spread over a much smaller area. Force ÷ area is much larger, and the skin gives way. The blunt edge spreads the same force over a wider strip; the pressure is too low to cut, so the tomato squashes instead.

callouts.title: Pascal's brother-in-law carries a mercury barometer from the town of Clermont to the top of the Puy de Dôme, a mountain nearby. At the summit, compared with the town, the mercury column will stand
callouts.body:
- taller, because the air is thinner and lets the mercury rise
- shorter, because there is less air above pressing on the dish
- exactly the same, because a column of mercury weighs the same wherever it is
???
Shorter. At the top of the Puy de Dôme the mercury stood about 3 inches (about 8 cm) lower than it had in the town. The column is held up by the air pressing down on the dish; take some of that air away by climbing above it, and it holds up less.

callouts.title: > "The empty space at the top of Torricelli's tube sucks the mercury up and holds it there."
callouts.body: Empty space cannot pull on anything; there is nothing in it to do the pulling. The mercury is *pushed* up, by the weight of the air pressing down on the open dish. Périer's climb is the proof: emptiness at the top of the tube was the same on the mountain, yet the column fell. What changed was the amount of air pushing from outside.

In Chapter 4 you saw that a hammer and a feather fell together on the Moon, where there is no air. Suppose an astronaut set up Torricelli's barometer there. Would the mercury be pulled down by gravity, and how tall would the column be?
???
Gravity on the Moon is real (the hammer fell), so the mercury would be pulled down into the dish like anything else. But with no air there is nothing to press on the mercury in the dish, so nothing pushes any of it up the tube. The column would drain to the level of the dish: a reading of zero. Gravity does not need air, and the barometer measures the air, not gravity.

callouts.title: Torricelli's mercury column is about 76 cm tall. How tall would the column be if he had used water instead, and why?
callouts.body:
???
About 10.3 m. The air can only hold up a column whose weight per area matches the air's pressure. Water is 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so it takes 13.6 times the height to weigh the same: 0.76 m × 13.6 ≈ 10.3 m. That is also why pumps of Torricelli's day could not lift water more than about 10 m.

callouts.title: You fill a glass to the brim with water, lay a wet postcard flat over the top so that it seals the rim, hold the card in place, and turn the whole thing upside down over the sink. Then you take your hand away from the card.
callouts.body:
- The card falls and the water comes out
- The card stays and the water stays in the glass
- The card stays but the water trickles out round its edges
???
With a good seal, the card and water stay in place. Air outside pushes up on the card, while water inside pushes down. The pressure near the top of the sealed glass becomes slightly lower than the outside air pressure. Pressure then rises down through the water: a 10 cm depth adds about 980 Pa. At the card, the inside and outside pressures nearly match, with a small difference supporting the card's weight. So 980 Pa is the pressure *change* through the water, not the whole downward pressure on the card. Let air slip past the rim and the balance can no longer hold the water in.

callouts.title: > "Sucking pulls the drink up the straw."
callouts.body: Nothing pulls. You lower the pressure in your mouth; the air pressing on the drink's surface pushes it up. The test is Torricelli's: however hard anyone sucks, no drink rises more than about 10 m, because that is as much water as the atmosphere can push up. If sucking were a pull, a strong enough suck could lift water any height at all.

callouts.title: "Suction" is not in your IGCSE syllabus, and "upthrust" is not either. When an exam asks why the card stays on the glass or why a drink rises in a straw, write that the air pressure outside is greater and *pushes*. IGCSE topic 2.1.3 also requires Boyle's law (*p*₁*V*₁ = *p*₂*V*₂ for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature) and its explanation in terms of molecules colliding with the container walls.
A rubber suction hook sticks to a bathroom tile for weeks and then falls off. What held it up, and what changed when it fell?
callouts.body:
???
Pressing the cup flat pushed most of the air out from under it. The air in the room then pressed the cup against the tile (about 10 N on every square centimetre of the cup) with nothing inside pushing back. It fell when air had slowly leaked in round the rim: once the pressure under the cup matched the room's, the pushes balanced and only the weak rubber was holding it.

callouts.title: Two containers are filled with water to exactly the same depth, 2 m. One is a swimming pool 50 m long. The other is a vertical pipe 10 cm across. At the bottom, the water pressure is
callouts.body:
- higher in the pool, because there is far more water
- higher in the pipe, because the water is squeezed into a narrow space
- the same in both
???
The same in both. The pressure at the bottom depends only on the depth and the density of the water: about 19,600 Pa from 2 m of water, on top of the air's 101,000 Pa. The pool holds thousands of times more water, but that water is spread over thousands of times more floor. The pipe's narrowness changes nothing either. Depth decides.

callouts.title: > "A bigger lake pushes harder on the dam."
callouts.body: Only the depth at the dam matters, together with the water's density. In connected, still water, the pressure increase below the surface is *ρgh*. Water also presses sideways, so the depth sets the pressure on the dam; the ground supports the reservoir's weight. A small reservoir and a huge one at the same depth push on their dams with exactly the same pressure.

callouts.title: Your IGCSE syllabus writes the rule as Δ*p* = *ρg*Δ*h*. The Δ (delta) means "change in": go Δ*h* deeper, and the pressure rises by *ρg*Δ*h*. It is the same statement as *p* = *ρgh* measured from the surface.
Investigation 6.4
callouts.body: Before you open the live tank: a plastic bottle has three small holes in its side, one near the top, one in the middle, one near the bottom, and it is full of water. Which jet leaves its hole fastest, and why? One warning for the real experiment: do not judge by where the jets land on the ground, because the lowest hole is also closest to the ground and has the shortest time to fly. Compare how hard each jet comes out.

callouts.title: A river is in flood, and water is seeping under the levee that protects a town. Engineers stack sandbags in a ring round the leak on the town side and let the leak fill the ring. The small puddle inside the ring stops the leak. How can a little water hold back a whole river?
callouts.body:
???
Only depth matters. Water rises inside the ring until its surface is level with the river's. Then the pressure at the leak from the water in the ring equals the pressure from the river at the same depth, the pushes balance, and the leak stops flowing. The river's enormous width is irrelevant, exactly as the length of a reservoir is irrelevant to its dam.

callouts.title: A whole orange floats in a bowl of water. You peel it carefully and put the peeled orange back in. It
callouts.body:
- floats higher, because it is lighter now
- sinks
- floats exactly as before
???
Many oranges sink after peeling. The peel contains tiny pockets of air; removing it can raise the orange's average density above water's, even though the orange is now lighter. Your orange may behave differently, so record what actually happens. The rule is still the comparison of average densities: peeling changes both mass and volume, and "lighter" alone cannot tell you whether it floats.

callouts.title: > "Heavy things sink. Light things float."
callouts.body: A 50,000-tonne ship floats and a coin you can hide in your fist sinks, so weight cannot be the rule. The rule is density, and it is *average* density that counts: the steel of the hull plus all the air inside it, taken together, average out lighter than water. The coin is steel all the way through. Compare densities, never weights.

In Chapter 3 you met the idea that a table cannot push up on a book, because it is "just in the way". Now a 50,000-tonne ship sits on the sea. Is the water pushing up on it? With how much force, and how does water, which has no stiffness at all, manage to push?
???
The water pushes up on the hull with a force exactly equal to the ship's weight, otherwise the ship would be sinking or rising. A table pushes by being squashed a tiny bit and springing back. Water pushes by its pressure: the molecules of water keep hitting the hull's underside, and because pressure grows with depth, the hits on the bottom of the hull add up to more than the hits on anything above. The push is the sum of countless small collisions. It is as real a force as the table's, and it points up.

callouts.title: Some school books call the water's upward push "upthrust". The IGCSE syllabus itself does not use that word, and neither do most physicists; we say *buoyant force*. If you meet "upthrust" in a worksheet, it means the same thing: the weight of the fluid the object displaces.
An orange, an egg and a foil boat
callouts.body: Three sinkers and floaters, all over a bowl or a bucket. First the orange: float a whole orange or mosambi, then peel it and try again (predict first, see above). Second the egg: put a raw egg gently into a glass of tap water; it sinks. Take it out, stir in a heaped spoon of salt until it dissolves, put the egg back. Keep going, a spoon at a time, until the egg lifts and floats. Nothing about the egg changed; the water did. Third the boat: compress a sheet of aluminium foil into a tight ball and lower it into the water. If it still floats, trapped air may be keeping its average density low; press it more tightly and try again. Take a fresh sheet of the same size and fold it into a boat with high sides: it floats. Now load the boat with ₹1 coins, one at a time, and count how many it carries before it sinks. Then rebuild it wider or deeper and see whether it carries more. The steel ship in the harbour is this boat, scaled up.

callouts.title: Investigation 6.5
callouts.body: Before you open the live tank: an object has a density of 500 kg/m³ and floats in fresh water. What fraction of it is below the surface? Now the tank is filled with sea water instead. Does the object float higher or lower? Use the slider to check your two answers.

callouts.title: A loaded cargo ship sails from the Arabian Sea up a river into fresh water. Does it float higher or lower in the river?
callouts.body:
???
Lower. To float, the ship must displace its own weight of water. Fresh water is less dense than sea water (1,000 kg/m³ against about 1,025), so the same weight of fresh water takes up more volume. The hull has to sink a little deeper to push that much aside.

callouts.title: The egg that changed its mind
callouts.body:
Kym puts a raw egg into a tall glass of tap water. It sinks to the bottom and stays there.

1. She takes the egg out, stirs salt into the water a spoon at a time until no more will dissolve easily, and puts the egg back. Now it floats, with a little of its shell above the surface.
2. Very gently, she pours fresh tap water on top of the salt water, down the side of the glass so that the two barely mix. The egg sinks a little and then stops, hanging in the middle of the glass, well below the surface and well above the bottom.
3. Her cousin says: "The salt made the egg lighter, and the fresh water on top made it heavier again."

What really changed between the three stages, and why does the egg hang in the middle at stage 2 instead of floating at the top or sinking to the bottom?
???
The egg never changed. Its weight was the same in all three stages, and so was its volume. What changed was the water around it.

In plain tap water, the water the egg displaced weighed less than the egg, so the buoyant force was smaller than its weight and it sank. Dissolving salt made the water denser, so the same volume of displaced water weighed more. Once that weight passed the egg's weight, the net force pointed up and the egg rose until just enough of it was submerged to displace exactly its own weight.

Pouring fresh water gently on top made two layers: dense salt water below, lighter fresh water above. The egg is denser than the fresh water, so it sinks through that layer. It is less dense than the salt water, so it cannot sink into that. It settles at the boundary, with its lower part in salt water and its upper part in fresh, at the depth where the weight of the two kinds of water it displaces adds up to exactly its own weight. Nothing was made lighter or heavier; the egg found the one level where the water's push matched its weight. Buoyant force is the weight of the fluid displaced, and dissolving salt changes how much a litre of fluid weighs. That is the whole case.

sections.heading: 7.1 What is energy?
sections.excerpt:
Here is a sentence from a thousand school books: "The ball rolls because it has energy." Now swap one word: "The ball rolls because it has *movability*." Both sentences feel like explanations. Neither is one. A name is a label, and a label is not a reason. Richard Feynman, the physicist whose way of teaching this book borrows from, called this the difference between knowing the name of a thing and knowing the thing. So before we use the word energy, we have to earn it. What is it, if saying it explains nothing by itself?

Feynman had a story for that, told with a child's toy blocks. Here it is in our own words, with marbles. A boy has 28 marbles, and his mother counts them every evening. Twenty-eight. Twenty-eight. Twenty-eight. One evening she counts 26. She looks under the sofa and finds two. Rule one: before you say that any have vanished, look harder. Another evening: 25, and the window is open, and three marbles are lying on the lawn outside. Rule two: things can leave the room, so count what has gone out as well as what is in. Another evening the marble box is locked and she cannot open it. But she knows that the empty box weighs 400 g and each marble 10 g (made-up numbers),

sections.heading: 7.2 mv or mv²?
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Leiden, 1722

In the early 1700s the best minds in Europe were quarrelling about a quantity. A moving body carries something: the heavier and faster it is, the more it carries, and when it hits something it hands it over. The followers of Descartes said the right measure of this "force of motion" was mass times speed, *mv*. The followers of Leibniz said it was mass times speed *squared*, *mv*², which they called *vis viva*, "living force". The two sides argued for years, and the argument was partly about words. It was settled, as far as experiment can settle it, in Leiden, with a box of clay.

Willem 's Gravesande dropped brass balls into soft clay at different speeds and measured the dents. A ball arriving twice as fast made a dent four times as deep. Twice the speed, four times the effect: that is *mv*² behaviour, since doubling *v* doubles *mv* but quadruples *mv*².

:::scene Cirey, 1740

Eighteen years later, Émilie du Châtelet wrote 's Gravesande's result into her book *Institutions de physique*, and took Leibniz's side. She did not prove the case, and in a sense there was nothing to prove: both quantities are real, and both are conserved in their own way. The quarrel

sections.heading: 7.3 Stores and transfers
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a monsoon afternoon

The lift is out of order, and you are climbing. Each floor is about 3 m higher than the last. By the fourth floor your legs have an opinion about this. In physics there is a precise word for what your legs are doing, and it is a word you already use for something else.

==Work==, in physics, is done when a force moves something along its own direction: work = force × distance moved along the force. Gravity pulls down on you with your weight. Suppose you have a mass of 40 kg; then that pull is 40 × 9.8 ≈ 392 N. To climb one floor you must push yourself up 3 m against it, so the work is 392 N × 3 m ≈ 1,176 J. Climb four floors and it is about 4,700 J. Notice what does *not* count. Standing on the landing holding your school bag out at arm's length is exhausting, and does no work on the bag at all: the force on the bag points up, and the bag does not move. Homework is also not work in this sense, however it feels.

:::note Work
Energy transferred by a force pushing or pulling something along its own direction: work = force × distance. A force that moves nothing does no work, however hard it pushes.
:::

sections.heading: 7.4 Where does it go?
sections.excerpt:
Bounce a tennis ball on the hard floor of the compound and listen. Thock. Thock. Thock. Each bounce is lower than the last, and the gaps between the sounds get shorter, until the ball is just buzzing against the ground and then lying still. If energy is never destroyed, the ball's energy has to be somewhere. Where?

:::predict
A ball dropped from 1.0 m bounces back to 0.64 m. Where is the energy that would have taken it the other 0.36 m?
- It was used up in the bounce
- It is in the ball, the floor and the air, as a little extra warmth and as the sound you heard
- It went back into the ground's gravity
???
In the ball, the floor and the air, as warmth and sound. The ball squashed and sprang back, and squashing is never a perfect spring: some of the ordered motion of the ball became disordered jiggling of the molecules of the rubber and the floor. That is thermal energy. A little more left as the sound wave you heard. The books balance: 0.64 of the energy came back as height, 0.36 went into warmth and sound.
:::

You can measure this with your phone. The free phyphox app has an acoustic stopwatch that starts and stops on loud sounds. Set it going and drop the ball. The time between

sections.heading: 7.5 Power and the bill
sections.excerpt:
Look at the labels in the kitchen. The mixer-grinder might say 500 W. An LED bulb might say 10 W. The geyser in the bathroom might say 2000 W. None of these numbers is an amount of energy. They are *rates*: how many joules the device moves every second while it is on. That rate is ==power==, and its unit, the ==watt==, is one joule per second. A 500 W mixer moves 500 J of electrical energy into motion, noise and warmth every second it runs; in a minute, 30,000 J.

In the payment comparison, energy is like the amount paid; power is like the amount paid each second. A faster rate need not mean a larger total: how long it continues matters too.

:::note Power
How fast energy is transferred: power = energy ÷ time, in watts.
:::

:::eq
**power = energy ÷ time**, or *P* = *E* ÷ *t*
:::

:::note Watt (W)
One joule per second. A kilowatt (kW) is 1,000 W.
:::

Power is about time; energy is not. Haul a television up four floors with a rope and pulley in two minutes, or carry it up the stairs in five, and you have done the same work either way, the same *mgh*. The pulley just did it at two and a half times the power. Your own climb from Section 7.3 gives a feel for the numbers. Climbing one

sections.heading: 7.6 Energy for a city
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, 2022

Stand on a terrace in Mumbai after dark and look at the lights. Every one of them is the end of a chain, and the chain almost always starts with something falling or something burning.

The burning chain is the common one. In a thermal power station, coal, oil or gas is burned to boil water into high-pressure steam (chemical store to thermal store). The steam pushes against the blades of a turbine and spins it (thermal to kinetic). The turbine spins a generator, which pushes current out along the wires (kinetic to electrical). At every step the books balance, and at every step some energy goes where nobody wanted it. The result, for a coal-fired station, is that about 40% of the coal's chemical energy leaves as electrical energy and about 60% leaves as warmth, through the chimney and through the cooling towers that let the leftover heat into the air. This is unavoidable for any station that works by burning something, and it is why power stations have cooling towers at all: they have an enormous amount of thermal energy to get rid of.

The falling chain is the one from the start of this chapter. Rain fills a reservoir in the hills; the water's gravitational s

sections.heading: The perpetual-motion machine
sections.excerpt:
:::case The perpetual-motion machine
A video has been going round the class. A wheel studded with magnets spins on a stand, and a bulb wired to it glows. The man in the video says the wheel "runs on magnetism", that it has been turning for a year with no battery and no plug, and that for ₹4,999 he will sell you the plans to build one that powers your whole flat.

1. The video is 40 seconds long and loops.
2. The man says the bearings are "so smooth there is almost no friction".
3. He will sell the plans, but not a working machine.
4. He says the bulb is a 100 W bulb.

Using nothing but the bookkeeping rule from Section 7.1, say whether such a machine could light a 100 W bulb for a year with nothing going in. Then say whether it could even keep turning for a year with no bulb at all.
???
Lighting the bulb is impossible. A 100 W bulb moves 100 J every second out of the electrical store into light and warmth. For the books to balance, 100 J every second must be coming *out* of some other store: a battery emptying, fuel burning, water falling, something getting colder. Magnets sitting on a wheel are not a store that empties by being near a bulb; nothing about them changes from one hour

callouts.title: School calls the place where energy sits a *store*, and the way it moves from one place to another a *transfer*. The IGCSE list of stores is kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic (strain), nuclear, electrostatic and internal (thermal); transfers happen by forces (mechanical work done), by electrical currents (electrical work done), by heating, and by electromagnetic, sound and other waves. This chapter's "places" are exactly those stores.
callouts.body:
:::

Older school books often speak of "forms of energy" such as "light energy", "sound energy", "heat energy" or "electrical energy". Newer syllabuses distinguish **stores** (where energy sits before and after) from **pathways** (how it is travelling in between). Here is how the two ways of speaking translate into each other:

| What an older book calls it | What it really is | Store or pathway? |
|---|---|---|
| Kinetic / motion energy | **Kinetic store** (½*mv*²) | Store (in a moving object) |
| Potential / height energy | **Gravitational store** (*mgh*) | Store (in a raised mass + Earth field) |
| Strain / spring energy | **Elastic store** (½*kx*²) | Store (in a stretched or squashed object) |
| Internal / thermal energy | **Thermal (internal) store** | Store (particles' motion and interactions) |
| Food / fuel / battery energy | **Chemical store** | Store (in chemical bonds) |
| Atomic / mass energy | **Nuclear store** | Store (in atomic nuclei) |
| Static / capacitor energy | **Electrostatic / Magnetic stores** | Store (in electric or magnetic fields) |
| "Mechanical / push energy" | **Mechanical work pathway** (*W* = *Fd*) | Pathway (energy on the move via a force) |
| "Electrical energy" | **Electrical work pathway** (*E* = *VIt*) | Pathway (energy on the move via a current) |
| "Heat flowing" | **Heating pathway** | Pathway (energy moving due to a temperature gap, not a store inside an object) |
| "Light energy" / "Sound energy" | **Radiation / wave pathway** | Pathway (energy travelling as light or sound waves) |

callouts.title: A cup of hot chai is left on the table and goes cold. The chai had thermal energy and now has less. Which is true?
callouts.body:
- The missing energy was destroyed when the chai cooled
- The missing energy is now in the table, the cup and the air of the room, which are all a tiny bit warmer
- The missing energy turned into coldness
???
It is in the table, the cup and the air. The chai's thermal energy moved, by heating, into everything around it. The room is so much bigger than the cup that its temperature barely rises, which is why you cannot feel where the energy went. But the books balance: what the chai gave out, the room took in, to the joule. Coldness is a lack of thermal energy, never a thing that energy turns into.

callouts.title: > "Energy is a kind of fuel inside things. When it runs out, they stop."
callouts.body: Energy is a number, worked out from formulas, and the number for the whole system never runs out. A ball rolling across the floor does stop, but its energy is still there, spread as a little extra warmth through the floor, the ball and the air. The fuel picture gets one thing right: a store can empty. It gets the big thing wrong: whatever leaves one store turns up, in full, in another.

callouts.title: Conservation of energy
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The law that the total energy of all the stores involved in any event stays exactly the same before and after: energy shifts between stores and never appears from nowhere or vanishes into nothing.
? Why is it called this?
*Energy* comes from Greek *energeia*, activity or operation (coined by Aristotle from *ergon*, work), and *conservation* comes from Latin *conservare*, to keep safe or preserve unbroken.
? What problem did it solve?
Before the 1840s, motion, heat, light, electricity and food seemed like separate worlds, and when a rolling ball stopped or a cup of chai cooled, its vigour seemed to disappear. Conservation of energy revealed that nothing disappeared: one currency was paying for all of them.
? Why does it work?
Experiments reveal the rule: whenever one store decreases by a number of joules, other stores gain that same amount, provided we include everything receiving energy. Measuring all the stores in joules lets us check the balance. The account comparison helps us keep track; it does not explain why nature follows this rule.
? How does it help?
It lets you calculate the speed of a roller coaster at the bottom of a hill without tracking every curve on the way down, audit a power station's efficiency, and unmask any perpetual-motion machine as impossible before looking at its gears.
?? How do we know?
Julius Robert Mayer, James Prescott Joule (stirring water with paddle-wheels driven by falling weights in the 1840s) and generations of experiments since have checked the exchange rates across mechanical, electrical, chemical and nuclear stores and never found a missing joule.
?? What it isn't
It does not mean *useful* energy stays constant: friction and heating continually spread concentrated energy out into random molecular jiggling in the surroundings, which is why your electricity bill charges for "units consumed".
?? Where does it stop working?
In nuclear reactions where mass changes noticeably, you must include mass itself as an energy store via Einstein's *E* = *mc*²; with mass-energy included, the books balance everywhere from atoms to stars.

callouts.title: A friend says, "Energy is what makes things go." Try the swap test on that sentence: replace "energy" with a made-up word, and say whether the sentence still sounds like an explanation. What does that tell you?
callouts.body:
???
"Movability is what makes things go" sounds exactly as convincing, and it says nothing at all. So the original sentence was a label, not an explanation. Energy explains things only when you use its formulas: the ball reaches 4.4 m/s at the bottom because the 0.98 J it had as height has become 0.98 J of motion, and ½*mv*² = 0.98 J gives 4.4 m/s. The numbers do the explaining; the name never does.

callouts.title: You drop a marble into a tray of flour, first from 25 cm and then from 1 m. From 1 m it hits the flour at twice the speed. Compared with the first dent, the second dent will be about
callouts.body:
- twice as deep
- four times as deep
- eight times as deep
???
The marble arrives with four times the kinetic energy. If the flour resisted with the same steady force in both drops, the second dent would be about four times as deep. Real flour need not do that: its resisting force can change with packing and penetration. Predict a deeper dent, measure what happens, and treat the depth ratio as a test of this extra assumption, not as a score for your experiment.

callouts.title: > "Twice as fast means twice the energy."
callouts.body: Twice the *momentum*, yes. Energy goes with speed squared, so twice as fast means four times the energy. The clay knew this in 1722, and it is why the difference between 50 km/h and 100 km/h is a difference of four, not two, in what a crash has to absorb.

callouts.title: Kinetic energy (½mv²)
callouts.body:
? What does it measure?
The energy an object has because it is moving, equal to half its mass times the square of its speed (½*mv*²), measured in joules.
? Why is it called this?
From the Greek *kinetikos*, of motion (from *kinein*, to move). Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz called *mv*² *vis viva* ("living force") in 1686; William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and William Rankine introduced the modern term *kinetic energy* in the 1850s.
? What problem did it solve?
Seventeenth-century thinkers quarrelled over whether a moving body's "force of motion" was *mv* or *mv*². Willem 's Gravesande and Émilie du Châtelet showed that *mv* counts how long a force acts (momentum), while ½*mv*² counts how far a force pushes (work and dent depth).
? Why does it work?
A ball dropped from four times the height has four times the gravitational work (*mgh*) done on it, yet because distance in free fall grows as *t*², it lands at only twice the speed; for energy to balance work, motion energy must grow with the *square* of speed.
? How does it help?
It explains why a marble dropped from four times the height arrives with four times the kinetic energy. A fourfold dent depth follows only if the resisting force stays the same. The same reasoning gives four times the braking distance at twice the speed when the braking force is unchanged.
?? How do we know?
's Gravesande's brass-ball experiments in soft clay linked the effect of impact to speed squared. At home, the marble-into-atta activity lets you investigate how reliably dent depth follows that rule for your flour.
?? What it isn't
It is not a vector with a direction like momentum (*mv*): two cars crashing head-on can have zero total momentum between them and a huge combined kinetic energy that crumples both bonnets.
?? Where does it stop working?
The formula ½*mv*² is the low-speed approximation to Einstein's relativistic energy. It works extremely well at everyday speeds; near the speed of light it needs replacing with the relativistic formula.

callouts.title: Marble into flour
callouts.body: Spread atta or maida about 3 cm deep in a shallow tray and smooth the top flat. Keep the tray on the floor and the marble away from small children. Hold the marble 25 cm above the surface, measure the height with a ruler, and let it go. Lift the marble out gently with a spoon. Lay a ruler across the undisturbed flour beside the dent and use a blunt stick to compare the bottom of the dent with that original surface. Smooth and repack the flour in the same way before repeating from 1 m. Predict first, then compare your dents. Do each height three times and record the spread as well as the average. Stop if the marble reaches the tray bottom. A deeper dent shows more work done pushing flour aside; an exact fourfold depth is not guaranteed. Then try 50 cm and see whether your results support "depth goes with height" for this tray.

callouts.title: A scooter is going at 20 km/h. The rider speeds up to 60 km/h. By what factor has the scooter's kinetic energy increased?
callouts.body:
???
Nine times. The speed has tripled, and kinetic energy goes with the square of speed: 3² = 9. Its momentum has only tripled.

callouts.title: Two beads, a glass one and a steel one three times heavier, are released together from the same height on the ideal track. Neither spins and there is no friction. At the bottom, which is moving faster?
callouts.body:
- The steel bead, because it had more energy to begin with
- The glass bead, because it is lighter and easier to get moving
- Both have the same speed
???
Both have the same speed. The steel bead did start with three times the energy (three times the mass, same height). But it also needs three times as much energy to reach any given speed, because kinetic energy is ½*mv*². The mass appears on both sides of *mgh* = ½*mv*² and cancels out, leaving *v* = √(2*gh*), which has no *m* in it. More energy, more mass, same speed. The hammer and feather on the Moon were saying the same thing.

In Chapter 4 a hammer and a feather, dropped together on the Moon, landed together. Back on Earth, in a vacuum tube, a 1 kg ball and a 0.1 kg ball are dropped from 2 m and land together at the same speed. Does the heavier ball arrive with more kinetic energy, the same, or less, and how can that be if their speeds are equal?
???
Ten times more. Kinetic energy is ½*mv*²: same *v*, ten times the *m*, ten times the energy. There is no contradiction, because the heavier ball also started with ten times the gravitational energy (*mgh* with ten times the *m*). Same speed does not mean same energy; it means energy and mass grew in step. Equal falling speeds are a statement about *v*, and energy is about *mv*².

callouts.title: IGCSE asks you to show energy transfers with flow diagrams (Core) and Sankey diagrams (Supplement). A Sankey diagram is an arrow that splits, with each branch's width showing how much energy went that way; the widths of all the branches add up to the width of the arrow that came in. That adding-up is conservation of energy drawn as a picture. You will meet one in Section 7.6.
Investigation 7.3
callouts.body: Before you open the live track: the bead starts at 1.0 m and the far bump is 0.8 m high. Will it get over the bump? Now set the friction slider a little above zero and predict again. Then run both and watch the three bars; check that they always add to the same total.

callouts.title: Does the energy that goes into the gravitational store when you carry a 2 kg bag of rice up one floor depend on whether you take the stairs or the lift? On how fast you climb? On how high the floor is?
callouts.body:
???
Only on the height (and on the mass and *g*): PE = *mgh*. Stairs, ramp or lift give the same answer for the same floor. Climbing faster changes how quickly the energy is transferred (that is power, Section 7.5), never how much.

callouts.title: A ball dropped from 1.0 m bounces back to 0.64 m. Where is the energy that would have taken it the other 0.36 m?
callouts.body:
- It was used up in the bounce
- It is in the ball, the floor and the air, as a little extra warmth and as the sound you heard
- It went back into the ground's gravity
???
In the ball, the floor and the air, as warmth and sound. The ball squashed and sprang back, and squashing is never a perfect spring: some of the ordered motion of the ball became disordered jiggling of the molecules of the rubber and the floor. That is thermal energy. A little more left as the sound wave you heard. The books balance: 0.64 of the energy came back as height, 0.36 went into warmth and sound.

Back in Chapter 2, people said a rolling ball stops because it "runs out of push". You learned that nothing was pushing it in the first place: friction was slowing it. Now a classmate says the ball stops because it "runs out of energy". Is that better?
???
A little, and still wrong. The ball's own store of kinetic energy does empty. But the energy has not run out of existence; friction moved it, joule for joule, into warmth in the ball, the floor and the air. "Runs out of push" imagined a push that was never there. "Runs out of energy" imagines a destruction that never happens. The honest sentence is: friction spread the ball's energy into the surroundings as thermal energy, where it can no longer move the ball.

callouts.title: > "The ball stops bouncing because its energy ran out."
callouts.body: Its *useful* energy ran out. The energy itself went, bounce by bounce, into slightly warmer rubber, slightly warmer floor and a series of sounds, and it is all still there, spread far too thin to lift anything. "Lost" is a word to avoid in physics, and your IGCSE syllabus never uses it. Say "spread out into the surroundings as thermal energy", which is both true and exactly what happened.

callouts.title: If a teacher or a textbook says energy is "lost" or "wasted", they mean it has spread out into the surroundings as thermal energy and is no longer useful. The IGCSE subject content never uses "lost" or "wasted"; it uses *useful energy output* and *total energy input*, and defines efficiency as the first divided by the second.
An old-style bulb is fed 60 W and gives out 5 W of light. What is its efficiency, and where does the other 55 W go?
callouts.body:
???
Efficiency = 5/60 ≈ 0.083, about 8%. The other 55 W goes out as thermal energy: the bulb and the air around it get warm. All 60 W leaves the bulb every second; only 5 W of it leaves as the light you wanted.

callouts.title: The bill arrives and says 320 units consumed this month. Which of these is true about that energy?
callouts.body:
- It was destroyed by the appliances in the flat
- It is all still in the flat somewhere, stored up
- It was delivered into the flat and has since left it as light, sound and, most of all, warmth into the surroundings
???
It was delivered and has since left, mostly as warmth. "Units consumed" measures energy *delivered* to the flat: 320 kWh, about 1.15 × 10⁹ J. Every joule of it is still in existence. The fan turned it into moving air, which rubbed itself to a stop and became warmth; the bulbs turned it into light, which was absorbed by the walls and became warmth; the geyser turned it into hot water, which went down the drain or cooled in the tank. The flat is not warmer, because the warmth leaked out into the Mumbai evening, where it is spread across a city and an ocean and is useless to anyone. "Consumed" is the bill's word for "delivered and then spread out". Nothing was destroyed, and that is the answer to the chapter's question.

callouts.title: > "A kilowatt-hour is the amount of power we used."
callouts.body: A kilowatt-hour is an amount of *energy*: a kilowatt (power) kept up for an hour (time), which is 3.6 million joules. The power at any moment is what the appliance labels say. You will also see "watts per hour" written in advertisements; it is a muddle. Watts are already "joules per second", so nothing needs dividing by hours.

callouts.title: Investigation 7.5
callouts.body: Walk round the flat and read the wattage label on five things that plug in. Guess how many hours each one runs in a day, multiply, and add up the watt-hours. Divide by 1,000 to get units. Then look at last month's bill. Which single appliance do you think accounts for most of the bill, and why does running time matter as much as wattage?

callouts.title: Which transfers more energy in a day: a 2,000 W geyser switched on for 15 minutes, or a 10 W LED bulb left on for 24 hours?
callouts.body:
???
The geyser. 2,000 W × 0.25 h = 500 Wh, half a unit. The LED: 10 W × 24 h = 240 Wh, about a quarter of a unit. The high-power devices that run for long stretches, geysers and air conditioners, decide most bills; a bulb left on matters far less than it feels like it should.

callouts.title: Of Tata Power's 1,377 MW, 447 MW is hydro, about a third of the capacity. Over the year 2021–22, what fraction of the electricity it actually generated came from the hydro stations?
callouts.body:
- About a third, the same as the capacity share
- More than a third, because falling water is free and the hydro stations would be run as much as possible
- Less than a third
???
Less than a third: about 22%. The filing reports 5,512 million units from the thermal units that year and 1,596 million from hydro, and 1,596 out of 7,108 is 22.5%. Capacity is a maximum rate. How much energy a station actually delivers depends on how much of the year it runs near that rate, and the hydro stations ran well below their maximum for much of the year while the thermal units ran closer to theirs. Megawatts tell you what *could* be delivered; million units tell you what *was*.

callouts.title: > "We're told to conserve energy. But physics says energy is always conserved anyway, so why bother?"
callouts.body: Two different meanings of one word. The *law* of conservation says the total never changes. The *advice* to conserve says: do not turn useful, concentrated energy (coal, gas, the water behind a dam) into useless spread-out warmth faster than you need to. The law is about the total. The advice is about the useful part, which really does run down.

callouts.title: A coal-fired power station is about 40% efficient. Does that mean 60% of the coal's energy was destroyed?
callouts.body:
???
No. All of the coal's chemical energy is accounted for: about 40% left as electrical energy, and about 60% left as thermal energy, warming the air and the cooling water. Conservation holds exactly. Efficiency measures how much came out in the form we wanted, never how much survived.

callouts.title: The perpetual-motion machine
callouts.body:
A video has been going round the class. A wheel studded with magnets spins on a stand, and a bulb wired to it glows. The man in the video says the wheel "runs on magnetism", that it has been turning for a year with no battery and no plug, and that for ₹4,999 he will sell you the plans to build one that powers your whole flat.

1. The video is 40 seconds long and loops.
2. The man says the bearings are "so smooth there is almost no friction".
3. He will sell the plans, but not a working machine.
4. He says the bulb is a 100 W bulb.

Using nothing but the bookkeeping rule from Section 7.1, say whether such a machine could light a 100 W bulb for a year with nothing going in. Then say whether it could even keep turning for a year with no bulb at all.
???
Lighting the bulb is impossible. A 100 W bulb moves 100 J every second out of the electrical store into light and warmth. For the books to balance, 100 J every second must be coming *out* of some other store: a battery emptying, fuel burning, water falling, something getting colder. Magnets sitting on a wheel are not a store that empties by being near a bulb; nothing about them changes from one hour to the next. So there is no store to pay 100 J a second from, and the bulb cannot be lit by the wheel. Either the video is edited, or something off-camera is feeding it.

Without the bulb, the wheel could coast by spending its initial kinetic energy. "Almost no friction" is not none: the bearings and air gradually transfer that energy into warmth, so the wheel slows unless another store supplies energy. Whether it could coast for a year depends on the starting energy and the rate of loss; a 40-second video cannot establish that. Turning for a long time is different from supplying useful power forever. Selling plans alone gives you no working machine to test.

The rule to carry away: whenever anyone claims to get energy out, ask which store it is coming from. If there is no store emptying, there is no energy coming out. In nearly two centuries of careful counting, the books have never once failed to balance.
