sections.heading: 8.1 Hot and cold aren't substances
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Munich, 1798

Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, worked at the arsenal in Munich, among cannon. A cannon barrel starts as a solid metal casting, and the bore is drilled out with a slowly turning borer. Everyone knew the metal got hot. What struck Rumford was that it never stopped getting hot. Drill for an hour, and the metal was hot; drill for another hour, and it was just as hot again.

That was a problem for the best theory of the day. Most scientists then said heat was a fluid, called *caloric*, that sat inside things and flowed from hot to cold the way water runs downhill. Drilling, they said, squeezed caloric out of the metal, as wringing squeezes water from a cloth. But a cloth runs dry. Rumford fitted a blunt borer to a cannon barrel, sank the barrel in a box of water, and set the borer turning. No fire anywhere.

:::predict
If heat were a fluid stored inside the metal, what should happen as the boring goes on, hour after hour?
- The metal runs out of heat, and the water stops warming
- The water keeps warming for as long as the borer keeps turning
- The water cools, because the borer is scraping heat away
???
The water kept warming. After two and a half hours it boi

sections.heading: 8.2 Heat vs temperature
sections.excerpt:
A bucket of warm bath water sits on the bathroom floor at 40 °C. On the kitchen counter is a spoonful of water from the chai pan, at 90 °C. Which one has more "heat" in it? Most people answer "the spoon, obviously", and the question is a trap, because after Section 8.1 you know that neither has any heat in it. What each one has is internal energy, and that is a different question, with a surprising answer.

:::predict
The bucket (10 kg of water at 40 °C) and the spoonful (5 g at 90 °C) are both left in a room at 30 °C until they match it. Which gives out more energy to the room as it cools?
- The spoonful: it is far hotter
- The bucket: it holds far more water
- About the same: the spoon is hotter, the bucket is bigger, and the two balance
???
The bucket, by a very long way. The spoonful cools by 60 °C and gives out about 1,256 J. The bucket cools by only 10 °C and gives out about 418,600 J, roughly 333 times more. Hotter is not the same as having more energy to give.
:::

Here is the picture to keep. ==Temperature== is about the *average* particle: how fast, on average, each one is jiggling. A thermometer reads that average. Internal energy is the *total* over every particle in th

sections.heading: 8.3 Why metal feels colder
sections.excerpt:
Morning. The thali and the chopping board have sat on the counter all night, side by side, breathing the same air. You lay a hand on each. The steel is cold. The wood is, if anything, faintly warm. Everyone who has ever stepped from a bathroom's tiles onto a bedroom rug knows this feeling, and almost everyone draws the same conclusion from it.

:::predict
A kitchen thermometer is laid flat on the thali for a minute, then on the board for a minute. What does it read?
- Lower on the steel
- Lower on the wood
- The same on both
???
The same on both. Two objects left together in one room for a night end up at the room's temperature, both of them. Your hand reported something real, but it was not temperature.
:::

What your skin feels is the *rate* at which energy leaves it. Your hand is warmer than the room; the counter and everything on it are at the room's temperature, perhaps 30 °C. Energy flows from your hand into whatever you touch. The steel carries that energy away from the contact point quickly so the surface stays cool and keeps drawing more, and your skin loses energy fast: fast loss is what "cold" means to your nerves. The wood takes energy slowly; the surface under your pal

sections.heading: 8.4 Sweaters don't make heat
sections.excerpt:
Mumbai gives you about one week a year that calls for a sweater, so the sweater lives in a cupboard and comes out smelling of naphthalene. When you pull it on, it feels warm within a minute. Where did the warmth come from? Ask a class of children and many will tell you the sweater makes heat, or that it keeps the cold out. Both sound right. Both are tested by the same experiment.

:::predict
Two ice cubes come out of the freezer. One is wrapped snugly in a woollen sweater; the other sits bare on a saucer beside it. Which melts first?
- The wrapped one: sweaters are warm
- The bare one
- They melt together: the room is the same for both
???
The bare one melts first. The wrapped one lasts far longer. If the sweater made heat it would melt its cube faster. It does the opposite, because what a sweater does is slow down the flow of energy, whichever way that energy is going.
:::

A sweater makes nothing. Your body does: it runs at about 37 °C and gives out energy all day. In the open, that energy conducts into the air next to your skin, and the warmed air drifts away and is replaced by cooler air, so the loss goes on and on. A sweater slows the loss. The wool fibres themselves are poor

sections.heading: 8.5 Hidden heat
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Glasgow, 1761

Joseph Black, who lectured at Glasgow, noticed something that everyone before him had walked past. Take a lump of ice that is already melting and warm it steadily. The thermometer does not rise. The ice goes on melting, you get more water, and the water stays at the ice's temperature until the last of the ice is gone. Only then does the thermometer begin to climb. Energy was flowing in the whole time. Where was it going? Black called it *latent* heat, from the Latin for hidden. He never properly published the idea; it survives in notes of his lectures.

:::predict
A steel tumbler holds ice and water, well stirred, with a kitchen thermometer in it. Plenty of ice is still floating. Over the next ten minutes, in a warm Mumbai kitchen, the reading will:
- Rise steadily, as the warm room heats the water
- Stay at 0 °C until the ice is gone, then rise
- Fall, as the ice cools the water further
???
It stays at 0 °C for as long as there is ice to melt, and only then starts to rise. Energy is pouring in from the kitchen the whole time. All of it is going into melting, and none into raising the temperature.
:::

Where does it go? In ice, water molecules hold one anoth

sections.heading: 8.6 The matka and the monsoon
sections.excerpt:
Section 8.3 made a promise: nothing left in a room ends up colder than the room. Yet in May, the water in the matka on the counter is cooler than the kitchen air around it, and has been all afternoon. Ask why, and the usual answer is that clay is cold. You now know that cannot be right: clay left in a room is at the room's temperature, like steel and wood. Something is going on at the surface of that pot that was not going on with the thali.

:::predict
Fill two steel tumblers with tap water. Wrap one in a cloth soaked in water and the other in a dry cloth, and stand both in front of a fan for an hour. Can the wet-wrapped tumbler's water end up *colder than the room's air*?
- No. Moving air can only bring something down to the air's own temperature
- Yes, a little below the air temperature
- Yes, as cold as a fridge
???
Yes, below the air temperature, by an amount that depends on how damp the air already is. Moving air alone never cools anything below its own temperature; a fan on a dry tumbler does nothing. The wet cloth is the whole trick, and the reason is evaporation.
:::

Water does not have to boil to become vapour. At any temperature, the fastest particles at a liquid's surf

sections.heading: May or July?
sections.excerpt:
:::case May or July?
A cousin visiting from a dry inland town is baffled by Mumbai's matkas, which never make the water as cold as hers at home. "Mine drops the water by more than ten degrees," she says. "Yours barely does anything. When does it work best here?" You pull two typical afternoons out of the weather record for the airport at Santacruz:

- **May:** air 34.3 °C, relative humidity about 65%. The weather table gives the wet-bulb temperature as 28.7 °C.
- **July:** air 29.4 °C, relative humidity about 81%. Wet-bulb temperature 26.7 °C.
- Her town, for comparison: air 38 °C, humidity 20%, wet-bulb about 21 °C.

A perfect matka could bring its water down to the wet-bulb temperature and no lower; a real one stops a little above it.

Two questions. In which month does a Mumbai matka cool its water *further below the air*? And in which month is the water in it actually *colder*? Explain both with the numbers.
???
**Further below the air: May.** In May the floor is 34.3 − 28.7 = 5.6 °C below the air; in July it is 29.4 − 26.7 = 2.7 °C below. May has about twice the room to cool, because its air, though hotter, is drier. In her town the gap is 38 − 21 = 17 °C, which is why her mat

callouts.title: If heat were a fluid stored inside the metal, what should happen as the boring goes on, hour after hour?
callouts.body:
- The metal runs out of heat, and the water stops warming
- The water keeps warming for as long as the borer keeps turning
- The water cools, because the borer is scraping heat away
???
The water kept warming. After two and a half hours it boiled, and the metal showed no sign of running dry. Whatever the water was getting, the metal was not storing a fixed amount of it. Something else was supplying it, for as long as the borer turned.

callouts.title: > "When I open the fridge, the cold comes out into the kitchen."
callouts.body: Cool air really can spill out of the open fridge and brush your legs. But that air is not carrying a substance called cold. It has a lower temperature than your skin, so energy passes from your skin into it. Meanwhile warmer kitchen air enters the fridge and transfers energy to its colder interior. What moves is air and energy, not a cold fluid.

callouts.title: Internal energy
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the jiggling, rotating and interacting particles that make up an object.
? Why is it called this?
Nineteenth-century physicists introduced "internal energy" to distinguish the energy stored *inside* a body's microscopic motion and bonds from the bulk kinetic or potential energy of the whole body moving through space, and to stop calling stored energy "heat".
? What problem did it solve?
The caloric theory treated heat as an indestructible fluid inside materials, which could not explain why Rumford's blunt cannon borer or two rubbed hands can generate warmth endlessly without the metal or skin ever running dry.
? Why does it work?
Atoms and molecules are in ceaseless motion and pull or push on their neighbours. Doing mechanical work (like Joule's paddle or rubbing an eraser) or transferring energy across a temperature difference (heating) both feed into the same microscopic store.
? How does it help?
It unifies mechanics and thermal physics under a single currency, the joule, so that 4186 J of falling weights and 4186 J from a flame produce the exact same 1 °C rise in a kilogram of water.
?? How do we know?
Joule's paddle-wheel experiments showed a fixed conversion rate between mechanical work and warming, and Perrin's measurements of Brownian motion showed suspended grains kicked harder as the temperature rose.
?? What it isn't
It is not a substance called "heat" or "cold" stored in pores, and it does not carry a memory of whether it arrived by heating or by mechanical work.
?? Where does it stop working?
Knowing a body's total internal energy alone does not tell you which way energy will flow when it touches another body; for that you need the average per particle, which is temperature.

callouts.title: At school this topic is called *transfer of thermal energy*. IGCSE uses "heating" as the name of a process and "internal energy" for what an object holds. The old noun survives in one place: "specific heat capacity", which you meet in the next section.
The bucket (10 kg of water at 40 °C) and the spoonful (5 g at 90 °C) are both left in a room at 30 °C until they match it. Which gives out more energy to the room as it cools?
callouts.body:
- The spoonful: it is far hotter
- The bucket: it holds far more water
- About the same: the spoon is hotter, the bucket is bigger, and the two balance
???
The bucket, by a very long way. The spoonful cools by 60 °C and gives out about 1,256 J. The bucket cools by only 10 °C and gives out about 418,600 J, roughly 333 times more. Hotter is not the same as having more energy to give.

callouts.title: Temperature vs internal energy
callouts.body:
? What is it?
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of each jiggling particle in an object; internal energy is the total energy added up over all the particles in the object.
? Why is it called this?
"Temperature" comes from Latin *temperatura*, a due measure or proportion, first used by physicians for the balance of warmth in the body. "Internal energy" was coined in nineteenth-century thermodynamics for the energy held *inside* a body's particles, to stop people calling it "heat inside".
? What problem did it solve?
People confused "how hot something is" with "how much energy it has to give", so a spoonful of boiling water seemed to hold more "heat" than a bucket of warm bath water. Separating average per particle from total across the crowd cleared up the muddle.
? Why does it work?
When two objects touch, fast-jiggling particles collide with slower-jiggling ones and hand energy across. Direction of flow depends only on which side has the higher *average* jiggle (temperature), while the *total* amount of energy transferred depends on how many particles there are and what they are made of.
? How does it help?
It tells you both which way energy will flow (always higher temperature to lower) and how much energy is needed to warm a given mass by a given number of degrees (*E* = *mc*Δ*T*).
?? How do we know?
Leave a 10 kg bucket at 40 °C and a 5 g spoonful at 90 °C in a 30 °C room: a thermometer reads higher in the spoon, yet a calorimeter shows the bucket gives out over three hundred times more energy as it cools.
?? What it isn't
Temperature is not a count of joules in an object, and internal energy is not a substance called "heat" sitting in a tank.
?? Where does it stop working?
During melting or boiling, energy pours into a substance and increases its internal energy without raising its temperature at all, because the energy goes into pulling particles apart rather than speeding them up.

callouts.title: > "A thermometer measures how much heat something has."
callouts.body: A thermometer measures the average jiggle of the particles touching it, which is temperature. It knows nothing about how many particles there are. The spoonful of chai water reads 90 °C and has about 1,256 J to give; the bucket reads 40 °C and has 418,600 J. To know the energy you need the mass and the material as well as the temperature.

The bucket of bath water is left overnight and is at room temperature by morning. Its 418,600 J have gone. Were they used up?
???
No. They spread into the room: into the air, the floor, the walls, and out through the windows. The room is warmer by an amount too small to notice, because the energy is now shared among a far larger crowd of particles. The total is unchanged; it has only spread out, which is the pattern Chapter 7 found everywhere.

callouts.title: Investigation 8.2
callouts.body: Fill one steel tumbler with dry sand and another with the same mass of water. Stand both in the sun on a windowsill and read a kitchen thermometer in each every five minutes. Predict first: which climbs faster, and by about how many times? Then watch them cool in the shade.

callouts.title: IGCSE writes the specific heat capacity as c = ΔE/(mΔθ), with θ for temperature, and under *2.1.3* and *2.2.1–2.2.2* asks you to convert between Celsius and kelvin (*T* = *θ* + 273) and to compare the thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases along with everyday applications and consequences. It also describes a temperature rise as "an increase in the average kinetic energies of all of the particles". The word *average* is the whole of this section.
A kitchen thermometer is laid flat on the thali for a minute, then on the board for a minute. What does it read?
callouts.body:
- Lower on the steel
- Lower on the wood
- The same on both
???
The same on both. Two objects left together in one room for a night end up at the room's temperature, both of them. Your hand reported something real, but it was not temperature.

callouts.title: Which plate melts the ice?
callouts.body: Take an aluminium kadhai or pan that has been sitting at room temperature (never one from the stove) and turn it upside down. Beside it put the wooden chopping board. Touch both: the metal feels colder. Now predict: on which one will an ice cube melt first? Put one cube from the freezer on each and watch. On aluminium the cube slumps into a puddle within a few minutes; a commercial version of this demonstration melts its cube in under about four minutes. On the wood it is still a cube long after. The "colder" plate melted it faster, because it fed energy into the ice faster. Melting a 10 g cube takes about 3,340 J whichever plate it sits on; the plate only decides how quickly that energy arrives.

callouts.title: > "Metal is colder than wood. You can feel it."
callouts.body: You can feel energy *leaving your hand* faster. A thermometer finds the same temperature on both. "Cold" is a report from your nerves about the rate of loss, and metal conducts your hand's energy away about a hundred times faster than wood does. Nor does the metal pull cold into you: energy only ever flows out of the warmer thing, which is your hand.

callouts.title: Investigation 8.3
callouts.body: Stand a stainless-steel spoon, an aluminium or brass spoon if you have one, and a wooden or plastic spoon upright in a mug, with a tiny dab of butter or vaseline stuck near the top of each handle at the same height. Ask an adult to pour warm water into the mug so the bowls of all three spoons sit in the same water. Predict which handle melts its dab first. Watch the dabs rather than touching the warming metal.

callouts.title: IGCSE lists this under *2.3.1 Conduction*, and asks you to describe experiments that show which materials are good thermal conductors and which are good insulators. "Insulator" here means a poor conductor, which is the next section.
Two ice cubes come out of the freezer. One is wrapped snugly in a woollen sweater; the other sits bare on a saucer beside it. Which melts first?
callouts.body:
- The wrapped one: sweaters are warm
- The bare one
- They melt together: the room is the same for both
???
The bare one melts first. The wrapped one lasts far longer. If the sweater made heat it would melt its cube faster. It does the opposite, because what a sweater does is slow down the flow of energy, whichever way that energy is going.

callouts.title: The sweater and the ice
callouts.body: Put two ice cubes of the same size on two saucers. Wrap one saucer, cube and all, in a woollen sweater or a thick folded towel; leave the other bare. Predict how long each will take to melt. Check every fifteen minutes. The bare cube goes first. When the wrapped one is finally a puddle, ask: did the wool make heat, or slow it?

callouts.title: > "A sweater keeps the cold out."
callouts.body: Cold is not a substance that comes in (Section 8.1). Energy leaks *out* of you into cooler surroundings, and the sweater slows that leak. Your school book may say woollens "keep warmth close to the body"; read "keep" as "slow its escape", never "make".

callouts.title: A Styrofoam box keeps ice cold for a picnic. Does the box make cold, keep cold in, or slow energy flowing in from outside? One such box, with walls 2.5 cm thick, sitting in 35 °C air, still lets about 3.4 kg of ice melt a day. What would make it lose less?
callouts.body:
???
It slows energy flowing in: Styrofoam conducts at about 0.010, worse than wool, because it is mostly trapped air. The ice melts anyway, because the flow is slowed and never stopped. Thicker walls, a smaller box (less area), or a cooler place to stand it would all cut the flow. Nothing can "keep cold in", because cold is not a thing.

callouts.title: A steel tumbler holds ice and water, well stirred, with a kitchen thermometer in it. Plenty of ice is still floating. Over the next ten minutes, in a warm Mumbai kitchen, the reading will:
callouts.body:
- Rise steadily, as the warm room heats the water
- Stay at 0 °C until the ice is gone, then rise
- Fall, as the ice cools the water further
???
It stays at 0 °C for as long as there is ice to melt, and only then starts to rise. Energy is pouring in from the kitchen the whole time. All of it is going into melting, and none into raising the temperature.

callouts.title: Latent heat
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The energy required to change one kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid, or from liquid to gas, without any change in its temperature.
? Why is it called this?
Joseph Black coined *latent heat* in 1761 from the Latin *latere*, to lie hidden, because the energy poured into melting ice or boiling water did not show up on a thermometer.
? What problem did it solve?
Everyone before Black assumed that adding heat to a body must always raise its temperature, which could not explain why a pan of melting ice stays stubbornly at 0 °C in a warm room instead of turning into water all at once.
? Why does it work?
In a solid or a liquid, particles interact with one another. Rearranging ice's open lattice into mobile liquid water (334 kJ/kg), or separating liquid molecules into steam (2256 kJ/kg at 100 °C), requires energy. During each phase change, added energy changes the particles' interactions rather than raising the temperature; molecules themselves keep their size.
? How does it help?
It explains why ice cools a drink far better than cold water at 0 °C, why steam burns are far worse than boiling-water burns, and why sweating and a clay matka cool by evaporation.
?? How do we know?
Heat a weighed block of ice at a steady rate with a thermometer in it: the temperature pauses flat at 0 °C while the ice melts, then climbs, and pauses flat nearly seven times longer at 100 °C while the water boils away.
?? What it isn't
It is not energy that disappears: every joule spent melting ice or boiling water is stored in the looser state and comes back out as warmth when the water freezes or the steam condenses.
?? Where does it stop working?
Evaporation from a liquid surface happens at any temperature below boiling, and the exact latent heat of vaporisation shifts slightly with temperature and pressure (about 2400 kJ/kg for warm sweat, against 2256 kJ/kg at 100 °C).

callouts.title: > "While the ice melts, the heat just disappears."
callouts.body: It is spent, and stored. It went into pulling the particles out of their fixed pattern, and it is held in the looser arrangement of the liquid. Freeze the water again and every joule comes back out. Nothing disappeared; it changed form, as energy always does.

callouts.title: Investigation 8.5
callouts.body: Stir ice and water in a steel tumbler with a kitchen thermometer in it, and read it every minute for twenty minutes. Plot the readings. Mark the minute the last sliver of ice vanishes. Where on your graph is Black's hidden heat?

callouts.title: IGCSE puts this under *2.2.3 Melting, boiling and evaporation*. Evaporation is the part this section has not touched yet: water leaving as vapour well below 100 °C. It is where the next section begins.

Fill two steel tumblers with tap water. Wrap one in a cloth soaked in water and the other in a dry cloth, and stand both in front of a fan for an hour. Can the wet-wrapped tumbler's water end up *colder than the room's air*?
callouts.body:
- No. Moving air can only bring something down to the air's own temperature
- Yes, a little below the air temperature
- Yes, as cold as a fridge
???
Yes, below the air temperature, by an amount that depends on how damp the air already is. Moving air alone never cools anything below its own temperature; a fan on a dry tumbler does nothing. The wet cloth is the whole trick, and the reason is evaporation.

"Hot air rises because heat rises." Chapter 6 found a floating orange and a sinking peeled one. Use it to say what really pushes warm air up.
???
Heat does not rise; it is not a thing that can rise. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, and the denser air pushes it up, just as water pushes up anything less dense than itself. The orange floated for the same reason. Take away the surrounding cooler air and warm air would go nowhere.

callouts.title: Two tumblers in the sun: black paper and kitchen foil
callouts.body: Take two identical steel tumblers. Wrap one tightly in matte-black chart paper (or paint it with washable black poster paint) and wrap the other shiny-side-out in kitchen aluminium foil. Fill both with equal measures of water from the same tap, cover both with identical cardboard lids to stop evaporation, and stand them side by side in direct sunshine for thirty minutes. Predict which climbs further on a kitchen thermometer, and by how much. Then bring two identical hot tumblers indoors into the shade, wrapped the same way, and check which cools faster: the best absorber is also the best emitter.

callouts.title: A matka without a matka
callouts.body: Fill two identical steel tumblers with water from the same tap. Wrap one in a cloth soaked in water and wrung out; wrap the other in a dry cloth. Stand both in front of a fan. Read a kitchen thermometer in each every ten minutes for an hour, and keep the wet cloth damp. Write down the room's temperature too. The wet tumbler ends up below the room; the dry one does not. Do it once in May and once in July, and compare how far below the room each one got.

callouts.title: > "The matka's water is cold because clay is cold."
callouts.body: Clay left in a room is at the room's temperature, like the thali and the board. The water is cooler because of what happens at the pot's surface: water seeps out and evaporates, and the escaping particles take energy with them. A glazed pot of the same clay, which cannot sweat, does nothing.

callouts.title: IGCSE places evaporation under *2.2.3*, convection under *2.3.2 Convection*, and infrared transfer under *2.3.3 Thermal radiation* (asking which surfaces are the best and worst emitters, absorbers and reflectors, and how a vacuum flask or building insulation combines all three mechanisms under *2.3.4 Consequences of thermal energy transfer*). Cambridge Lower Secondary calls what the matka does "evaporative cooling". When an exam asks why evaporation cools, name the escaping particles: the fastest ones leave, so the average energy of the rest falls.
May or July?
callouts.body:
A cousin visiting from a dry inland town is baffled by Mumbai's matkas, which never make the water as cold as hers at home. "Mine drops the water by more than ten degrees," she says. "Yours barely does anything. When does it work best here?" You pull two typical afternoons out of the weather record for the airport at Santacruz:

- **May:** air 34.3 °C, relative humidity about 65%. The weather table gives the wet-bulb temperature as 28.7 °C.
- **July:** air 29.4 °C, relative humidity about 81%. Wet-bulb temperature 26.7 °C.
- Her town, for comparison: air 38 °C, humidity 20%, wet-bulb about 21 °C.

A perfect matka could bring its water down to the wet-bulb temperature and no lower; a real one stops a little above it.

Two questions. In which month does a Mumbai matka cool its water *further below the air*? And in which month is the water in it actually *colder*? Explain both with the numbers.
???
**Further below the air: May.** In May the floor is 34.3 − 28.7 = 5.6 °C below the air; in July it is 29.4 − 26.7 = 2.7 °C below. May has about twice the room to cool, because its air, though hotter, is drier. In her town the gap is 38 − 21 = 17 °C, which is why her matka seems to work and ours seems not to.

**Colder water: possibly July.** The lowest a perfect matka could reach is 28.7 °C in May and 26.7 °C in July. July's water can be the colder drink, because July's air is cooler to begin with; the matka simply adds less to it. Both pots will sit a degree or two above these floors in practice, because energy leaks in through the clay from the room.

So the cousin is right that the matka does very little in July: the air is already close to its balance point, and evaporation is slow. She is wrong that it does nothing in Mumbai. It works in May, and it works best of all in the dry months before the monsoon, when the air has the most room for vapour.

sections.heading: 9.1 Things that swing
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Pisa, about 1583

The story goes that a young Galileo, in the cathedral at Pisa, watched a lamp swinging on its chain and noticed that each swing took the same time whether the lamp swung wide or barely moved. It is a lovely story, and it comes from one source only: Viviani, Galileo's assistant in his old age, writing long afterwards. The lamp that hangs in the cathedral today was installed after Galileo had left Pisa. So treat the lamp as a legend. What is true is that Galileo did study swinging pendulums, carefully and for years, and that what the legend has him notice is real.

You can notice it yourself on the swing in the building compound. Push off and let it go. Each swing takes the same time as the one before, and as the swing dies down the time between swings hardly changes. The time for one complete swing, out and back, is the ==period==; the number of swings in a second is the ==frequency==, which is one divided by the period. A swing on chains about 2.5 m long has a period of about 3.2 s.

:::note Period
The time for one complete repeat of a motion that repeats, such as one full swing out and back. Symbol T, in seconds.
:::

:::note Frequency
How many repeats h

sections.heading: 9.2 Resonance
sections.excerpt:
:::scene London, June 2000

The Millennium Bridge, a new footbridge over the Thames, opened on 10 June 2000 with crowds pouring across it. Almost at once it began to sway from side to side, and the engineers closed it two days later. The sway came from the walkers themselves. As the deck moved a little, people adjusted their steps to keep their balance, fell into step with the sway, and pushed it further; the more it swayed, the more of them fell into step. Dampers costing about £5 million were fitted, and the bridge reopened in 2002. One textbook says it was closed "for the same reason" as a famous American bridge you will meet below. It was a different reason, and the difference is the point of this section.

Every swinging thing has a rhythm of its own, the rate at which it swings when you let it go and leave it alone: its ==natural frequency==. The swing in the compound, with its 3.2 s period, has a natural frequency of about 0.3 Hz. Push it once every 3.2 s, each time it comes back to you, and each push adds a little to the last; after ten pushes the child is flying. Push at random, and half your pushes fight the swing. sections.heading: 9.3 What a wave carries
sections.excerpt:
Fill a bucket to the brim and wait for the water to go still. Float a scrap of paper in the middle. Now dip a finger in at the edge, once. Rings spread out across the surface, reach the paper, and pass under it. Watch the paper.

:::predict
As the ripples reach the paper scrap and pass it, the scrap will:
- Be carried along with the ripples to the far side of the bucket
- Bob up and down, and stay roughly where it was
- Be pushed backwards, away from the ripples
???
It bobs and stays. Each ripple lifts it, moves it a little forward and then a little back, and sets it down almost exactly where it was. The ripples cross the bucket; the water, and the paper riding on it, does not.
:::

A ==wave== is a disturbance that travels away from the place where it was made. Your finger pushed the water down in one spot. That water pushed its neighbours, which pushed theirs, and the *push* travelled outward in a ring while each bit of water went up and down and came back to where it started. Out at sea it is the same on a bigger scale: a bit of water near the surface moves round in a small loop as a swell passes, forward at the crest, back in the trough, and ends up where it began. sections.heading: 9.4 Sound is a push passed on
sections.excerpt:
Tie a steel spoon to the middle of a metre of string. Wind the two ends of the string round your index fingers and press those fingertips gently into your ears. Now let the spoon swing and knock against the edge of a table. Through the string you hear a deep, clear bell, as if from inside your head. Let the string go slack and tap the spoon again: a faint tink. The spoon vibrated the same way both times. What changed was the road the vibration took to your ear.

:::predict
A friend taps one end of a long steel railing with a coin. You are at the other end, 100 m away, with one ear pressed against the rail and the other in the air. Which ear hears the tap first?
- The ear in the air
- The ear on the rail
- Both at once
???
The ear on the rail, by a clear margin. Sound travels through steel at about 5960 m/s and through warm air at about 349 m/s, so the rail delivers the tap in about 0.017 s and the air takes 0.29 s. The vibration travels about eighteen times faster in the steel.
:::

Here is what sound is. The spoon, struck, vibrates: its surface moves out and back many times a second. Each time it moves out it squeezes the layer of air next to it; each time it moves back it leaves

sections.heading: 9.5 Loud and high
sections.excerpt:
A baby wails in the next seat of the local train; a whistle shrieks on the platform; a friend hums in your ear. Each sound has two things you can tell at once: how loud it is, and how high. Children, and plenty of adults, run the two together, and say that a high sound is a loud one. The microphone in your phone can take them apart.

:::predict
You sing one steady note into a phone app that draws the sound wave, and then sing the same note more loudly. On the screen, the wave becomes:
- Taller, with the same spacing
- The same height, with the crests closer together
- Both taller and closer together
???
Taller, with the same spacing. Loudness is the size of the vibration, the wave's amplitude. The spacing of the crests is set by how often your vocal cords vibrate, which is the note, and you did not change the note.
:::

What you hear as ==pitch== is the frequency of the vibration reaching your ear: how many compressions arrive each second. Human ears work from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Below 20 Hz is infrasound, above 20,000 Hz ==ultrasound==, and you hear neither, though dogs, bats and dolphins hear well into the ultrasonic range. The ear is remarkably fine about pi

sections.heading: 9.6 Why a tabla sings
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Calcutta, 1920

Strike an ordinary drum and you get a thud with a vague sense of height, and no note you could hum. Strike a tabla and a clear, singing note rings out. In 1920 C. V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar published a short paper in *Nature* explaining why. Most drums, they showed, give out overtones that are out of tune with one another, so the sound is a clash with no clear pitch. The tabla and the mridangam are different: their overtones fall in tune, at whole-number multiples of the lowest one, as a string's do, and the reason is the *syahi*, the black loaded patch on the drumhead, which tunes the drumhead's modes into line. To see why that is remarkable, start with a string.

:::scene Florence, about 1589

The old story says Pythagoras discovered the laws of harmony by hearing blacksmiths' hammers and weighing them. It was first written down about six centuries after his time, and the physics in it is wrong: the weight of a hammer does not set its note. The true version has Galileo's father in it. Vincenzo Galilei, in Florence, hung weights from strings to tighten them and measured what he heard. To raise a string's note by an octave, doubling its frequency, you must

sections.heading: 9.7 The moving whistle
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Utrecht, 1845

In 1842 Christian Doppler, in Prague, read a short paper to a handful of members of the Royal Bohemian Society. If a source of waves moves towards you, he argued, the waves should reach you more often and the pitch should rise; if it moves away, the pitch should fall. His main example was the colours of double stars, and it was wrong. Three years later a Dutch scientist, Christophorus Buys Ballot, tested it. On the railway line between Utrecht and Maarssen he had horn players stand on an open wagon pulled by a locomotive, sounding one steady note, while musicians with perfect pitch stood by the track and wrote down what they heard. The note rose as the wagon came towards them and fell as it went away. A well-known textbook credits Doppler himself with the train. It was Buys Ballot.

You have done his experiment on every station platform. Stand behind the yellow line as a fast local comes through with its horn sounding. The note holds steady while the train is far off, then, as it passes, drops, and holds a new, lower note as it recedes. The driver, meanwhile, hears none of this.

sections.heading: The echo off the building
sections.excerpt:
:::case The echo off the building
A hot afternoon, 30 °C. You stand in the compound facing the building across the open ground and clap once, hard. The clap comes back to you from the wall. Your cousin says the wall "makes a new sound" when the clap hits it. You set the phyphox app's acoustic stopwatch going and clap again. It reads 0.29 s between the clap and its return.

Two questions. How far away is the wall? And is the echo a new sound?
???
**Distance.** The sound went to the wall and came back, so it travelled twice the distance in 0.29 s. At 30 °C sound travels at about 349 m/s, so the round trip is 349 × 0.29 ≈ 101 m, and the wall is about 50 m away.

**Not a new sound.** The compressions you made with your hands ran to the wall, pushed on it, and were pushed back: the same pattern of pushes, turned around. The wall adds nothing of its own, which is why an echo repeats what you said and never says anything else.
:::

callouts.title: Two pendulums hang from strings of the same length. One has a 10 kg bob, the other 100 kg. Both are pulled back 12° and released. Which swings faster?
callouts.body:
- The heavy one
- The light one
- Neither: they keep time with each other
???
They keep time with each other. Mass makes no difference to a pendulum's period. The heavier bob is pulled ten times harder by gravity and is ten times harder to get moving, and the two cancel exactly.

callouts.title: Weigh the Earth's pull with a key
callouts.body: Tie a key to a thread exactly one metre long, measured from the knot you hold to the middle of the key. Hold it against a door frame so the top cannot move, pull it aside less than 10° (about 15 cm at the bottom) and let go. Time ten complete swings with a phone stopwatch and divide by ten; you should get close to 2.0 s. Then work out g = 39.5 × length ÷ (period × period); the 39.5 is 2π squared. With 1.00 m and 2.01 s you get 9.8 m/s². Try a thread twice as long and see what happens to the period.

callouts.title: > "A heavier child makes the swing go faster, because gravity pulls harder."
callouts.body: Gravity does pull harder on the heavier child, and the heavier child is harder to get moving by exactly the same factor. The period comes out the same. Only the length of the chains (and the strength of gravity) decides how fast a swing swings.

callouts.title: Simple harmonic motion
callouts.body:
? What is it?
Any back-and-forth oscillation in which the pull back towards the resting position grows in direct proportion to the displacement from it.
? Why is it called this?
Nineteenth-century physicists called it "harmonic" because a pure musical tone has the exact same smooth sine-wave shape in time, and "simple" because it is the single fundamental rhythm out of which more complicated vibrations are built.
? What problem did it solve?
It explained why a pendulum, a mass on a spring, a plucked guitar string and a tuning fork all keep steady time as their swings die down, with a period independent of amplitude.
? Why does it work?
Pull the object twice as far from the middle and it has twice as far to travel back, but the restoring force is also twice as strong, accelerating it twice as hard; the extra distance and the extra acceleration cancel in the time of each swing.
? How does it help?
It lets clocks keep accurate time with pendulums or quartz crystals, and lets you measure local gravity (*g*) simply by timing a pendulum of known length.
?? How do we know?
Time ten swings of a 1.00 m pendulum pulled back 5° and then 12°: both give 2.01 s per swing, and swapping a light key for a heavy stone changes nothing.
?? What it isn't
Not every repeating motion is simple harmonic: a ball bouncing up and down on a hard floor repeats, but the force on it is not proportional to distance from a midpoint and its period shrinks as the bounces get smaller.
?? Where does it stop working?
Pull a pendulum out to large angles (such as 60°) and the restoring pull along the arc grows more slowly than the angle itself, making the period about 7% longer than Galileo's small-swing rule predicts.

callouts.title: At school, a motion that repeats like this is called an *oscillation*, and the period and frequency are defined exactly as here. The pendulum formula belongs to IB Diploma physics (topic C.1, simple harmonic motion); IGCSE asks for period and frequency only.
Resonance
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The large build-up of oscillation that happens when a system is pushed repeatedly at a frequency matching its own natural frequency.
? Why is it called this?
From Latin *resonare*, to sound back or echo, first used in acoustics for a musical string or air column that begins to hum in sympathy when its own note is sung nearby.
? What problem did it solve?
It explained how very gentle periodic forces, too weak to move an object far in a single push, can selectively make one particular string vibrate, shatter a wine glass, or set a footbridge swaying.
? Why does it work?
When each push arrives in step with the object's natural swing, it always pushes in the direction the object is already moving, so every cycle adds energy instead of cancelling the previous cycle.
? How does it help?
Engineers use it to tune radios and musical instruments so they respond strongly to one frequency, and to design dampers on bridges and tall buildings so they do not sway dangerously.
?? How do we know?
Drive an oscillator across a range of frequencies and measure its amplitude: the swing peaks sharply at the natural frequency, and adding friction (damping) lowers and broadens that peak.
?? What it isn't
It is not just shaking something violently at any frequency, and not every bridge failure is resonance: the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a steady wind by aerodynamic flutter, making its own rhythm.
?? Where does it stop working?
If the swing grows so large that the restoring force is no longer proportional to displacement, the natural frequency itself shifts with amplitude and the simple resonance curve bends over.

callouts.title: A singer, the story always goes, can shatter a wine glass with her voice. For the glass to break, which matters more?
callouts.body:
- Being loud enough: any note will do if it is loud
- Singing the right note: the glass's own natural frequency, however softly
- Both the right note and enough sound energy
???
Both are needed. Near the glass's natural frequency, each wave of sound arrives in time with its flexing and adds energy. But the sound must also supply enough energy to overcome the losses and bend the glass far enough to break. MIT physics lecturers demonstrate it with amplified sound at the right note. A quiet right note is not enough. This is a demonstration to watch, not to try at home.

A parent gives a swing one small push every 3.2 s, and after a minute the child is swinging two metres high. Is energy being made from nothing?
???
No. Each push does a little work and adds a little energy; resonance makes the twenty small contributions add up instead of cancelling. Meanwhile friction and the air drain some away every swing. The swing grows until the drain per swing matches the push per swing.

callouts.title: > "Resonance is just a fancy name for shaking something hard."
callouts.body: Shaking *in time* is the point. The right rhythm makes sound much more effective, but breaking a glass still needs enough sound energy. Nor is every violent oscillation resonance: the Tacoma bridge drove itself with a steady wind, which is flutter, and the Millennium Bridge was driven by walkers who adjusted their steps to it.

callouts.title: Soldiers crossing a bridge are ordered to break step and walk out of rhythm. Why?
callouts.body:
???
Marching in step delivers a push to the bridge at one steady frequency. If that frequency is near the bridge's natural frequency, the pushes add up and the bridge could swing dangerously. Breaking step scatters the pushes across many rhythms, so they mostly cancel.

callouts.title: As the ripples reach the paper scrap and pass it, the scrap will:
callouts.body:
- Be carried along with the ripples to the far side of the bucket
- Bob up and down, and stay roughly where it was
- Be pushed backwards, away from the ripples
???
It bobs and stays. Each ripple lifts it, moves it a little forward and then a little back, and sets it down almost exactly where it was. The ripples cross the bucket; the water, and the paper riding on it, does not.

callouts.title: Wave
callouts.body:
? What is it?
A travelling disturbance that carries energy and information from one place to another without carrying matter along with it.
? Why is it called this?
From the Old English *wagian*, to move to and fro, first applied to the ridges on the sea and then extended by physicists to sound, ripples on strings, and light.
? What problem did it solve?
It showed how energy can cross a bucket, a concert hall, or an ocean while the water or air stays in its own neighbourhood, and gave one mathematical rule (*v* = *f*λ) for ripples, sound and light alike.
? Why does it work?
Each piece of the medium is coupled to its neighbours: displace one bit and it pulls or squeezes the next bit, handing the motion and energy onward while restoring forces pull the original bit back to its resting place.
? How does it help?
Knowing a wave's frequency and wavelength gives its speed immediately, and knowing that waves add where they meet explains echoes, beats, musical notes, and interference.
?? How do we know?
Float a scrap of paper on rippled water or track air in a sound tube: the crests race across from one side to the other while the paper scrap only bobs in a small loop about the same spot.
?? What it isn't
It is not a stream of water or air travelling from source to receiver: wind and ocean currents move matter, whereas sound and sea swells move only a pattern of motion and energy.
?? Where does it stop working?
When a water wave runs into shallow water near a beach, the bottom slows the trough while the crest overtakes it and topples forward as surf; there the wave breaks and really does throw water up the sand.

"The swell carries the water along, the way a thrown ball carries its push inside it." Chapter 2 had something to say about pushes carried inside things. What really travels in the swell?
???
Nothing carries a push inside it, and the swell carries no water. Each bit of water is pushed by its neighbour, moves round a small loop, and pushes the next; it is the pattern of pushes that moves on, together with the energy. Unlike the ball in Chapter 2, each bit of water is pulled back by its neighbours after every loop.

callouts.title: Measure a ripple
callouts.body: In a bucket or a wide parat of still water, float a paper scrap and dip one finger at the edge at a steady rhythm, once a second. Watch the scrap stay put. Estimate the distance between crests with a ruler held above the water, and the time between crests from your dipping; divide one by the other for the speed. Does dipping harder change the spacing of the crests, or only their height?

callouts.title: > "Waves at the beach push the water up the sand, so waves do carry water."
callouts.body: At the shore, yes: when a wave runs into shallow water it breaks, and the water in it tumbles forward. That is a wave falling apart. Out at sea, where the wave is a wave, the water goes round in loops and stays.

callouts.title: IGCSE puts all of this under *3.1 General properties of waves*, with the same words: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, and the two kinds, transverse and longitudinal. Learn to draw a wave and label the first two.
A friend taps one end of a long steel railing with a coin. You are at the other end, 100 m away, with one ear pressed against the rail and the other in the air. Which ear hears the tap first?
callouts.body:
- The ear in the air
- The ear on the rail
- Both at once
???
The ear on the rail, by a clear margin. Sound travels through steel at about 5960 m/s and through warm air at about 349 m/s, so the rail delivers the tap in about 0.017 s and the air takes 0.29 s. The vibration travels about eighteen times faster in the steel.

callouts.title: The spoon bell
callouts.body: Tie a steel spoon to the middle of a metre of thread. Wrap the ends round your index fingers, press those fingertips lightly into your ears, lean forward and let the spoon knock the edge of a table. Then take your fingers out and knock it again. Try a fork, a steel ladle and a wooden spoon: which gives the deepest bell?

callouts.title: > "The air from the loudspeaker travels across the room to my ear."
callouts.body: Each layer of air moves back and forth a tiny distance about its own place and shoves the next layer. The push travels; the air stays. It is the paper scrap in the bucket again, a thousand times a second.

callouts.title: IGCSE topic *3.4 Sound* asks for this: sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions, it needs a medium, and an echo is a reflection. Cambridge Lower Secondary puts it as "no sound in a vacuum".
You sing one steady note into a phone app that draws the sound wave, and then sing the same note more loudly. On the screen, the wave becomes:
callouts.body:
- Taller, with the same spacing
- The same height, with the crests closer together
- Both taller and closer together
???
Taller, with the same spacing. Loudness is the size of the vibration, the wave's amplitude. The spacing of the crests is set by how often your vocal cords vibrate, which is the note, and you did not change the note.

callouts.title: Investigation 9.5
callouts.body: Put a phone playing music face down on a light table or a cardboard box and rest your fingertips on the surface. Turn the volume up: you feel the surface vibrate harder, and the vibration you feel is the amplitude. Turn it down until you can only just feel it, then listen: is that also the point where you can only just hear it?

callouts.title: > "That whistle is so high it's deafening. High sounds are loud sounds."
callouts.body: Height and loudness are different properties of the same wave. A whistle can be high and faint; a drum can be low and deafening. The ear is more sensitive to some frequencies than others, so a modest amplitude at a frequency it likes can sound loud; the loudness still comes from the amplitude.

callouts.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary states it as "loudness ↔ amplitude, pitch ↔ frequency", which is this section in six words. IGCSE (*3.4 Sound*) adds the audible range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, defines ultrasound as sound above 20 kHz, and asks for pulse-echo applications of ultrasound in sonar, medical scanning and non-destructive testing of materials (*d* = ½*vt*).
Blow across the mouth of an empty glass bottle and you get a low toot. Pour water into the bottle, so the air column above the water is shorter, and blow again. The note:
callouts.body:
- Goes up
- Goes down
- Stays the same, because the bottle is the same bottle
???
It goes up. In a narrow-necked bottle, air in the neck moves in and out against the springiness of the air inside. Adding water leaves less air to squeeze, making that spring stiffer and the note higher. This is not quite the straight-pipe vibration above.

callouts.title: A bottle organ
callouts.body: Line up three identical glass bottles. Leave one empty, half-fill the second with water and nearly fill the third. Blow gently across the mouth of each (practise: a thin, steady stream of air just over the rim). Predict which gives the highest note before you blow. Then tap the bottles with a spoon instead: is the order the same? Blowing sounds the air inside; tapping sounds the glass and the water in it, which is a different vibration altogether.

callouts.title: > "All overtones are whole-number multiples of the fundamental."
callouts.body: That is true for an ideal string and for a pipe open at both ends. A pipe closed at one end gives only the odd multiples, and a plain drumhead's overtones are not whole-number multiples at all; that is why most drums have no clear note. The tabla is the exception, and the syahi is the reason.

callouts.title: Two wind instruments are the same length. One is a pipe open at both ends; the other is closed at one end. Which can play the lower note?
callouts.body:
???
The closed one. Its fundamental fits a quarter of a wavelength into the pipe, so its wavelength is four times the length; the open pipe's fundamental fits half a wavelength, so its wavelength is only twice the length. The closed pipe's fundamental is an octave lower, at half the frequency.

callouts.title: The driver of the train hears the horn, which is mounted on the train with her. Compared with the horn's true note, she hears:
callouts.body:
- A higher note, because the train is moving fast
- A lower note
- The true note
???
The true note. She and the horn move together, so each compression reaches her exactly as often as the horn makes it. The shift happens only between things moving towards or away from each other.

callouts.title: Investigation 9.7
callouts.body: Use the moving-whistle model above to compare an approaching horn with a receding one. Keep the horn’s own note fixed, change only its speed, and predict which setting makes the bigger change. If you happen to hear a steady passing horn from a safe place indoors, listen for the same drop; there is no need to go near traffic or a platform edge.

callouts.title: > "The horn gets louder as the train comes, and that is why it sounds higher."
callouts.body: Louder and higher are separate (Section 9.5). The pitch rises because the compressions arrive more often, and that depends on the train's speed, never on how loud the horn is.

callouts.title: IGCSE leaves out the Doppler effect for sound. Under *6.2.3* it asks for *redshift*: the increase in the wavelength of light from galaxies that are moving away from us, which is the horn's falling note, for light. IB Diploma physics covers both as topic C.5. You will meet redshift again in Chapter 15.
The echo off the building
callouts.body:
A hot afternoon, 30 °C. You stand in the compound facing the building across the open ground and clap once, hard. The clap comes back to you from the wall. Your cousin says the wall "makes a new sound" when the clap hits it. You set the phyphox app's acoustic stopwatch going and clap again. It reads 0.29 s between the clap and its return.

Two questions. How far away is the wall? And is the echo a new sound?
???
**Distance.** The sound went to the wall and came back, so it travelled twice the distance in 0.29 s. At 30 °C sound travels at about 349 m/s, so the round trip is 349 × 0.29 ≈ 101 m, and the wall is about 50 m away.

**Not a new sound.** The compressions you made with your hands ran to the wall, pushed on it, and were pushed back: the same pattern of pushes, turned around. The wall adds nothing of its own, which is why an echo repeats what you said and never says anything else.

chapters.volumeTitle: Volume III · Waves, Sound and Light
chapters.title: Rays, mirrors and eyes
chapters.subtitle: Law of reflection, Snell's law refraction, lenses and RGB colour
chapters.hookSummary: Take a pencil and draw this: you, a mango on the table, and arrows showing how you see it. Do it before you read on.

sections.heading: 10.1 Does anything leave your eyes?
sections.excerpt:
Take a pencil and draw this: you, a mango on the table, and arrows showing how you see it. Do it before you read on.

Most people draw at least one arrow that starts at the eye and points at the mango. In one study, students were asked to draw how a person sees a balloon, and 86 in every 100 drew arrows going out from the eye. Among adults asked straight out whether anything leaves the eye when you look, 69 in 100 said yes. If that is what you drew, you are in old and distinguished company. Euclid, the geometer, and Ptolemy, the astronomer, both believed that the eye sends out rays which reach out and touch what you see. The idea fits how looking feels. Looking is something you *do*. You point your eyes, you choose, you stare. A gaze has a direction, and a direction feels like something going out.

:::scene Cairo, c. 1011

Around the year 1011, in Cairo, a scholar called Ibn al-Haytham set out to test the idea instead of arguing about it. (The story goes that he was in confinement at the time, having pretended to be mad to escape the Caliph's anger over a failed scheme to tame the Nile. Historians doubt it.) He put two observations together. First: look at the Sun, or at a very bri

sections.heading: 10.2 Straight lines and shadows
sections.excerpt:
Ibn al-Haytham's dark room is the oldest camera in the world, and you can build one from a shoebox. Shut yourself in a dark room with one small hole in the shutter, and the sunlit street outside appears on the opposite wall: dim, in colour, moving, and upside down. People walk along the wall with their feet in the air. The Latin name for such a room, ==camera obscura==, means "dark chamber", and it is where the word *camera* comes from.

Why upside down? Because light goes straight. Light from the top of a tree outside travels in a straight line through the hole. A straight line that comes in high at the hole carries on downwards, so it lands low on the wall. Light from the tree's roots comes in low and lands high. Every point of the scene outside sends light through the hole to exactly one point on the wall, and so the whole picture arrives turned over, top to bottom and left to right. Nothing "flips" the light. Straight lines through one small opening simply cross there.

:::note Camera obscura
A dark room or box with a small hole in one side. Light from outside passes straight through the hole and forms an upside-down picture on the opposite wall. A pinhole camera is a small one

sections.heading: 10.3 Mirrors
sections.excerpt:
Stand in front of the bathroom mirror and ask a question you have probably never asked: where is your face? Not the real one; the one you are looking at. Most people say it is on the glass, like a picture stuck to the surface. Here is a test. Walk up to the mirror and touch it with a fingertip. Your fingertip's image meets your finger at the glass, which is what you would expect if the image were on the surface. Now look at your face. Your real face is an arm's length in front of the glass. Your face in the mirror is an arm's length *behind* it. The image of anything is as far behind the mirror as the thing is in front, so if you stand 1.0 m from a mirror, your image is 1.0 m behind the glass and 2.0 m from you.

The mirror can do this because it is smooth on the scale of light. A rough page sends light every way; a mirror sends each ray off in one definite direction, following one rule. Draw a line at right angles to the mirror's surface, which physicists call the ==normal==. The angle between the arriving ray and the normal is the angle of incidence; the angle between the departing ray and the normal is the angle of reflection; and they are equal. Light leaves at the angle it arr

sections.heading: 10.4 Bending light
sections.excerpt:
Stand at the side of a tank of water in an aquarium and look at a fish near the glass. Look up through the surface and you may see the fish a second time, in a different place. Wade into a swimming pool and look down: your legs are short and your feet are nearer the surface than they should be. Stand a pencil in a glass of water and look at it from the side: it looks broken at the waterline. In all three cases, light has changed direction on its way from the thing to your eye, and your eye, as always, has traced the light straight back to a place where the thing is not.

Before the explanation, commit to an answer.

:::predict
You are standing at the edge of a clear pool and see a shell on the bottom. You reach straight for where you see it. Where is the shell really?
- Exactly where you see it.
- Nearer the surface than it looks.
- Deeper than it looks.
???
Deeper than it looks. Looking straight down, the water makes everything look shallower by a factor of about three-quarters: a shell under 10 cm of water appears to be under about 7.5 cm, and a pool floor 2 m down looks about 1.5 m down. People hurt their necks diving into unfamiliar ponds for exactly this reason. The shell has

sections.heading: 10.5 Lenses and the eye
sections.excerpt:
Put a single drop of water on a sheet of clear plastic, lay it on a newspaper, and look down through the drop. The letters under it are bigger. A drop of water is a lens: a curved surface that bends light, and bends it more at the edges than in the middle, so that rays spread apart by the small letters are gathered together again before they reach your eye. A magnifying glass and the lens in your eye are *converging* lenses: they gather spreading light and bend it back together. Other lenses spread light farther apart; you will meet those in spectacles below.

Hold a magnifying glass in sunlight and it gathers the Sun's parallel rays to one bright, hot point, the ==focal point==. Never do this towards your eyes, or anyone's, and never look at the Sun through any glass. Do this instead: in a dim room, hold the magnifier a hand's width from a wall opposite a bright window and move it slowly back and forth. At one distance a small, sharp picture of the window appears on the wall, upside down, exactly like the pinhole camera's but far brighter, because the whole width of the lens is collecting light and delivering it to the picture. Now test an idea.

:::note Focal point
The point wher

sections.heading: 10.6 How fast is light?
sections.excerpt:
In a monsoon storm, the lightning comes first and the thunder after. Count the seconds between them: sound in warm air travels at about 340 m/s, so every three seconds is about a kilometre. The flash arrives so soon that it seems to arrive instantly. Does that prove light is extremely fast? Only that it is much faster than sound. In 1638 Galileo could say only that light was extremely fast, perhaps instantaneous. "Too fast to measure" is where things stood for nearly forty years, until an astronomer noticed that a moon was running late.

:::predict
Suppose the Sun switched off at this instant. How long before Mumbai goes dark?
- At the same instant.
- About eight minutes later.
- About a day later.
???
About eight minutes later. The Sun is 149,600,000 km away, and light covers 299,792 km every second, so the light reaching you now left the Sun 499 seconds ago, about 8.3 minutes. For eight more minutes after the switch-off, the sky over Mumbai would look exactly as it does now. You never see the Sun as it is; you see it as it was.
:::
