sections.heading: The disappearing coin
sections.excerpt:
:::case The disappearing coin
A steel tumbler stands on the kitchen table, 8 cm deep and empty. You put a ₹1 coin on the bottom, against the far wall. You sit down and lower your head until the near rim of the tumbler just hides the coin: your line of sight skims the rim at 45° and reaches the bottom 8 cm beyond the near wall, which is exactly where the coin lies. You do not move your head at all. A friend slowly pours water into the tumbler, right up to the brim.

The coin comes back into view.

- The coin did not move: it is heavy and sits where you put it.
- Your head did not move.
- The tumbler did not move.

So what changed, and where did the coin appear?
???
The light did. Before, light from the coin had to travel in a straight line to your eye, and the rim was in the way. Now the light leaves the coin, travels up through the water, and bends at the surface as it comes out into the air, away from the normal. A ray that leaves the coin at 32° to the vertical comes out of the water at 45°, which is exactly the angle that skims the rim and reaches your eye.

The sum, line by line:

- Empty tumbler: the 45° sightline reaches the bottom 8 cm × tan 45° = 8.0 cm from the near wall.

callouts.title: You are in a room with no window. The door is shut and every crack is sealed, so that no light at all gets in. You wait five minutes for your eyes to get used to the dark, then hold your hand up in front of your face. What do you see?
callouts.body:
- Your hand, dimly. Eyes adjust.
- Only a faint outline where your hand is.
- Nothing at all, however long you wait.
???
Nothing at all. Eyes do adjust in the dark, and remarkably well. Your eye works across a range of brightness from the faintest thing it can detect to something ten billion (10¹⁰) times brighter, and the cells it uses in dim light get by on about a thousandth of the light the colour-seeing cells need. But adjusting means collecting the little light there is more carefully. If there is none, there is nothing to collect. A bedroom that seems pitch dark usually has a sliver of light under the door or round a curtain, and after a few minutes that sliver is enough to show shapes. A truly sealed room shows you nothing, and that is the answer to this chapter's big question.

callouts.title: The darkest room in the flat
callouts.body: Tell an adult what you are doing and where you will be. Find the darkest room, usually a bathroom with no window. Leave your phone outside: a phone is a lamp. Switch the light off, shut the door, and if light leaks under it, lay a towel along the gap. Count slowly to sixty to let your eyes adjust, then hold your hand in front of your face and wave it. Now open the door the width of a finger and watch. The moment a sliver of light comes in, your hand appears, because light from the crack is bouncing off your hand and into your eye. Shut the door and it goes again. Your hand did not change. The light did.

callouts.title: > "Looking is something I do. I point my eyes at things. Something must go out of them."
callouts.body: Nothing goes out. Your eye only collects. Pointing your eyes chooses *which* light to collect, the way turning a bucket in the rain chooses which drops to catch; the bucket sends nothing out. You already accept this for hearing. You turn your head towards a sound, and you never imagine that your ears send anything out to fetch it. Seeing is the same kind of thing, with light in place of sound. The test is the sealed room. If your eyes sent anything out, you would see your hand there. You don't.

callouts.title: Someone with an oily, shiny nose dabs face powder on it, and the shine is gone. What did the powder do to the light?
callouts.body:
???
The thin film of oil was a smooth surface, a tiny mirror. It sent the lamp's light off in one direction, and from that direction you saw a bright highlight. Powder is rough. Light hitting it goes off in every direction, evenly, so no direction gets a highlight. Nothing changed about the light arriving; only what the nose did with it.

callouts.title: At school you will "draw and use ray diagrams". A ray isn't a thing that exists. It's a pencil line showing the direction light goes, and the rules for drawing it (straight, bouncing, bending) are the subject of this chapter.
callouts.body:
:::

Before you build the camera, decide something about the hole.

callouts.title: A camera in a shoebox
callouts.body: Ask an adult to help with the cutting. You need a shoebox, kitchen foil, a pin, tracing paper or baking paper, and tape. Cut a hole about 3 cm across in the middle of one end of the box, tape foil over it, and prick the foil once with the pin. Cut away most of the opposite end and tape tracing paper over it as a screen. Put the lid on. In a dim room, point the pinhole at a bright window and look at the screen with a dark cloth over your head and the box, so no stray light reaches the paper. The window appears on it, upside down. Move the box nearer the window and the picture grows. Then, with the adult, make the pinhole a little bigger with a pencil tip, and see whether your prediction held. Never point the box, or your eyes, at the Sun.

A torch beam looks bright on a wall 1 m away and much fainter on a wall 10 m away. A friend says the light "runs out of push" on the way, the way a rolling ball slows to a stop. What is really happening?
???
Nothing slows the light. It arrives at full speed either way, and in empty space it would carry on for ever with nothing pushing it, just as the ball on Galileo's frictionless ramp would. What changes is that the beam spreads out as it travels, because its rays fan out in straight lines from the torch. The same light is shared across a bigger patch of wall, so each bit of wall gets less. The light is spread thinner; none of it has been used up.

callouts.title: > "A shadow is a black thing that an object throws onto the wall."
callouts.body: Nothing is thrown. A shadow is not a thing; it is a patch of wall that light fails to reach because an opaque object is standing in the way of the straight rays from the lamp. Shine a second lamp on that patch from the side and the shadow fills with light at once, because nothing was sitting on the wall waiting to be pushed off.

callouts.title: In a camera obscura the picture is upside down. A friend says "the hole flips the light over". Give the real reason.
callouts.body:
???
The hole does nothing to the light. Light from each point outside travels in a straight line through the hole. Lines from high points pass through heading downwards and land low; lines from low points land high. Because all the lines cross at one small opening, the picture is turned over, top to bottom and also left to right.

callouts.title: Virtual image
callouts.body:
? What is it?
An image formed at the place where diverging light rays appear to come from when traced straight back, even though no light actually passes through that place.
? Why is it called this?
From medieval Latin *virtualis*, having the effect or appearance without the physical substance, used in optics since the seventeenth century to contrast with a *real* image where rays genuinely meet on a screen.
? What problem did it solve?
It explained why your face in a flat mirror looks as though it sits behind the glass at a definite distance, and why a magnifying glass makes letters look larger and farther back without projecting them onto a wall.
? Why does it work?
Your eyes and brain judge the position of any point by the angle at which two or more rays from it enter the pupil, always assuming the rays travelled in straight lines; a mirror redirects the rays so their straight-back extensions cross behind the glass.
? How does it help?
It lets you locate exactly where an image sits in any mirror or lens by drawing two rays and extending the reflected or refracted lines backwards with a ruler.
?? How do we know?
Focus a camera on a smudge on the mirror's glass and your reflected face is blurry; refocus to twice your distance from the mirror and your face becomes sharp, proving the rays enter the lens as if coming from behind the glass.
?? What it isn't
It is not an optical illusion in your head and it does not sit on the surface of the mirror; the diverging light rays entering your eye are completely physical.
?? Where does it stop working?
Because no light actually reaches the image's location behind the mirror, you can never catch a virtual image on a piece of paper put there; to put it on a screen or a retina, a second lens (such as your eye's) must bend the diverging rays back together into a real image.

callouts.title: You can see yourself from head to waist in a small mirror on the wall. You step back, away from the mirror. Now you see
callouts.body:
- more of yourself: the mirror shows you down to your knees.
- less of yourself.
- exactly the same amount.
???
Exactly the same. To see your feet, light from your feet has to reach your eyes after one bounce, and by the equal-angles rule it bounces off the mirror exactly halfway between the height of your feet and the height of your eyes. That halfway point does not move when you step back; only the angle changes. A mirror shows all of you if it is half your height, wherever you stand. A person 1.50 m tall needs a mirror 0.75 m tall, with its bottom halfway between your eyes and your feet, and its top halfway between your eyes and the top of your head. Stepping back shows you more of the *room*, never more of yourself.

callouts.title: Investigation 10.3
callouts.body: Put the object 20 cm in front of the mirror and find the image. Move the object to 40 cm and 10 cm. Record both distances each time. Then write one sentence about what the mirror does to distance, and one about what it does to left and right.

callouts.title: Your syllabus asks you to "define and use the terms normal, angle of incidence" and angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the mirror. Measure from the glass instead and every answer comes out wrong.
Your friend stands 1.5 m in front of a flat mirror. How far from her is her image? She steps back another 0.5 m. How far is it now?
callouts.body:
???
The image is as far behind the mirror as she is in front: 1.5 m behind, so 3.0 m from her. After stepping back she is 2.0 m from the mirror, her image is 2.0 m behind it, and the distance between them is 4.0 m. The image moved back by the same amount she did.

callouts.title: You are standing at the edge of a clear pool and see a shell on the bottom. You reach straight for where you see it. Where is the shell really?
callouts.body:
- Exactly where you see it.
- Nearer the surface than it looks.
- Deeper than it looks.
???
Deeper than it looks. Looking straight down, the water makes everything look shallower by a factor of about three-quarters: a shell under 10 cm of water appears to be under about 7.5 cm, and a pool floor 2 m down looks about 1.5 m down. People hurt their necks diving into unfamiliar ponds for exactly this reason. The shell has not moved. Where it *appears* has.

callouts.title: Refraction
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The bending of a wave when it crosses at an angle from one medium into another in which its speed is different.
? Why is it called this?
From Latin *refractus*, broken back, because a straight stick or pencil standing at a slant in water looks broken at the waterline.
? What problem did it solve?
It explained why pools look shallower than they are, why lenses can bring light to a focus, why swimming underwater blurs your vision, and why hot road tarmac shimmers with mirages.
? Why does it work?
When a wavefront meets a slower medium at a slant, the edge of the wave that enters first slows down first while the other edge keeps travelling faster outside, swinging the whole wave round towards the normal.
? How does it help?
From a material's refractive index (*n* = *c*/*v*) you can calculate how much any surface bends light, design spectacle and camera lenses, and trap light inside optical fibres by total internal reflection.
?? How do we know?
Shine a narrow beam of light from air into a flat-sided tank of water or glass block with a protractor underneath: the beam bends towards the normal on entering and bends back by the exact same angle on leaving.
?? What it isn't
The water does not pull on the light, and the underwater coin or fish has not floated upward; only the light's path has bent at the boundary.
?? Where does it stop working?
A ray meeting the boundary straight on along the normal slows down without bending at all, and inside a single medium whose refractive index varies slightly with wavelength, different colours bend by slightly different amounts (dispersion, which Chapter 11 uses to split white light).

callouts.title: Investigation 10.4
callouts.body: Set the ray to arrive at 45° from the air and read the angle in the water. Then send the ray up from the water and increase its angle slowly. Find the angle at which it stops getting out. Write down both numbers.

callouts.title: Your syllabus explains refraction "in terms of change of speed", and that is the right way. Some books say light bends when it enters a "denser medium". They mean a material that is slower for light, which is not the same as heavier: diamond slows light far more than water does, but the word to use is speed.
Does a ray bend towards the normal or away from it when it goes (a) from air into water, (b) from water into glass, (c) from glass into air?
callouts.body:
???
Towards the normal whenever the light slows down, away whenever it speeds up. Air (1.00) to water (1.333): slower, so towards. Water (1.333) to glass (1.52): slower again, so towards. Glass (1.52) to air (1.00): faster, so away from the normal.

callouts.title: With the window's picture sharp on the wall, you cover the top half of the lens with a card. What happens to the picture?
callouts.body:
- The top half of the picture disappears.
- The bottom half of the picture disappears.
- The whole picture stays, but fainter.
???
The whole picture stays, fainter. Light from every point of the window passes through every part of the lens, and every part bends it to the same spot on the wall. Covering half the lens removes half the light from each point of the picture, and none of the picture itself. The lens is a collector, and you have made it a smaller collector.

callouts.title: Investigation 10.5
callouts.body: Focus the eye on the far tree, then on the near book, and watch what the lens does. Then cover half the pupil. Predict first whether the picture on the retina loses its top, its bottom, or only some brightness.

callouts.title: > "The lens in my eye does the focusing."
callouts.body: Mostly it is the cornea, the clear front window, which does about two-thirds of the bending because the jump in speed from air into it is the biggest on the way. The lens fine-tunes: it fattens for near things and flattens for far ones. Proof of the cornea's share: underwater, where the jump at the cornea almost vanishes, everything blurs, though your lens is working exactly as before.

callouts.title: Why is everything blurry when you open your eyes underwater, and why does a swimming mask fix it?
callouts.body:
???
Most of your eye's focusing happens where light passes from air (index 1.00) into the cornea (1.38). In water (1.33) the change in index at the cornea falls from 0.38 to 0.05, so the cornea hardly bends the light, and the lens alone cannot bring the picture to a point on the retina. A mask holds a layer of air against your face, so light again enters the cornea from air and the cornea gets its two-thirds back.

callouts.title: Suppose the Sun switched off at this instant. How long before Mumbai goes dark?
callouts.body:
- At the same instant.
- About eight minutes later.
- About a day later.
???
About eight minutes later. The Sun is 149,600,000 km away, and light covers 299,792 km every second, so the light reaching you now left the Sun 499 seconds ago, about 8.3 minutes. For eight more minutes after the switch-off, the sky over Mumbai would look exactly as it does now. You never see the Sun as it is; you see it as it was.

Sunlight takes 8.3 minutes to reach your skin, and you feel its warmth. Does anything from the Sun's surface travel to you along with the light?
???
No material does. The Sun's hot gas stays at the Sun, just as the water of a wave stays in the sea while the wave crosses it. What arrives is energy, carried by the light wave, and you feel that energy as warmth. Light is the clearest case yet of Chapter 9's rule: a wave carries energy without carrying stuff, and this one does it across 150 million kilometres of empty space.

callouts.title: > "Light is instant. Flick the switch and the room is lit at the same moment."
callouts.body: Too fast to notice is not the same as instant. Light crosses a room in a few billionths of a second, crosses the Earth's orbit in 16.6 minutes and reaches us from the Sun 8.3 minutes after leaving it. The switch and the far wall are lit at very slightly different moments, and with a fast enough clock you could measure the gap. Fizeau did, in effect, with a wheel.

callouts.title: Lightning flashes, and you count six seconds before the thunder. How far away did it strike? Does the time the light took matter in your sum?
callouts.body:
???
Sound at about 340 m/s covers about 2,000 m in six seconds, so the strike was about 2 km away. The light from the flash covered that 2 km in about seven millionths of a second, far less than the time it took you to blink, so for this sum you can treat the flash as arriving the instant it happened. Compared with sound, light is as good as instant. Compared with Fizeau's wheel, it is not.

callouts.title: The disappearing coin
callouts.body:
A steel tumbler stands on the kitchen table, 8 cm deep and empty. You put a ₹1 coin on the bottom, against the far wall. You sit down and lower your head until the near rim of the tumbler just hides the coin: your line of sight skims the rim at 45° and reaches the bottom 8 cm beyond the near wall, which is exactly where the coin lies. You do not move your head at all. A friend slowly pours water into the tumbler, right up to the brim.

The coin comes back into view.

- The coin did not move: it is heavy and sits where you put it.
- Your head did not move.
- The tumbler did not move.

So what changed, and where did the coin appear?
???
The light did. Before, light from the coin had to travel in a straight line to your eye, and the rim was in the way. Now the light leaves the coin, travels up through the water, and bends at the surface as it comes out into the air, away from the normal. A ray that leaves the coin at 32° to the vertical comes out of the water at 45°, which is exactly the angle that skims the rim and reaches your eye.

The sum, line by line:

- Empty tumbler: the 45° sightline reaches the bottom 8 cm × tan 45° = 8.0 cm from the near wall.
- Full tumbler: the same sightline, bent to 32° in the water, reaches 8 cm × tan 32° = 5.0 cm from the near wall.
- So the strip of bottom you can now see has grown by 8.0 − 5.0 = 3.0 cm.

Any coin lying in that extra 3 cm strip of bottom appears. Your eye traces the arriving ray straight back along its 45° line, so the coin seems to lie higher up and nearer to you than it is, as though it had floated. It has not. Dip your finger in and you will find it exactly where you put it. The water did not lift the coin. It bent the light.

chapters.title: Light as a wave
chapters.subtitle: Diffraction, interference, polarisation and the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.heading: 11.1 White is a mixture
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Cambridge, 1666

Isaac Newton, twenty-three years old, darkened his room, made a small hole in the window shutter, and let a thin beam of sunlight cross the room to the far wall. Then he put a glass prism in the beam. The white spot on the wall stretched into a band of colours: red at one end, through yellow and green and blue, to violet at the other. People had seen a prism's colours for centuries. The obvious explanation, the one most people reach for, is that the glass *stains* the light: white light goes in pure, and the glass adds colours to it.

Newton did not trust the obvious explanation, so he designed a test for it. Six years later, in a letter to the Royal Society dated 6 February 1672, he called it his *experimentum crucis*, the decisive experiment. Before you read what he found, decide what you expect.

:::predict
Newton lets the band of colours fall on a board with a small hole in it, so that only the red light passes through. He puts a second prism in that red beam. What comes out of the second prism?
- A new band of colours. The second prism adds colours just as the first did.
- Light of a different colour: the red has been changed again.

sections.heading: 11.2 Colour is in the light
sections.excerpt:
:::recall 10.1
A friend says your eyes "see colour" the way a torch shines: the eye sends out something that colours what it looks at. Where is the colour of a ripe mango actually decided?
???
Nothing leaves the eye, as the sealed dark room showed. The mango's colour is decided by two things: which wavelengths of the arriving light the mango's skin sends back and which it absorbs, and how the three kinds of colour-sensing cell in your eye respond to the mix that reaches them. Change the light that arrives and the mango's colour changes, as this section shows.
:::

A ripe mango is yellow. A leaf is green. A red kurta is red, and most people would say it is red whatever light you shine on it: red is simply what it is. This section is about why that is only half true, and the test is one you can do tonight.

:::predict
In a dark room, you light a green leaf with nothing but a phone screen showing pure red. What colour does the leaf look?
- Green. A leaf is green.
- Red, like everything else in the room.
- Black, or very nearly.
???

sections.heading: 11.3 Blue sky, orange sunset
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Marine Drive, this evening

The Sun is low over the Arabian Sea, orange and swollen. Overhead the sky is still blue. If you ask ten people why, you will hear that the sky is blue because it reflects the sea, that the sunset is orange because the Sun is cooling for the night, and that Mumbai's sunsets are orange because of the traffic. The first two are wrong and the third is unproven, and the real reason is the same for the blue overhead and the orange at the horizon.

Start with what light does to air. Light is a wave, and the wave shakes the tiny electric charges, the electrons, inside each molecule of air as it passes. A shaken charge sends out light of its own, in every direction, like a tiny radio antenna. So every molecule the sunlight passes becomes a faint new source of light, re-sending a little of what reached it in all directions. Physicists call this ==scattering==. Most of the sunlight passes straight through; only a tiny share is re-sent. But the air is deep, and that tiny share is the whole sky.

:::note Scattering

sections.heading: 11.4 Why the sea is blue
sections.excerpt:
:::scene The Mediterranean, September 1921

The liner *Narkunda* is steaming east towards Bombay, and a young physicist from Calcutta is standing at the rail, looking at the sea through a small crystal. C. V. Raman is on his way home to India, and the Mediterranean is a deep, dark blue. He knows the standard explanation. Lord Rayleigh, the English physicist, had said that the sea is blue because it reflects the sky. Raman has with him a Nicol prism: a crystal cut so that it lets through only light whose sideways shaking lies in one direction. He is about to use it to take the sky out of the sea.

:::predict
Light reflected off the surface of water is polarised, as you are about to learn, so a Nicol prism held at the right angle can block the reflected sky almost completely. Raman holds the prism to his eye and turns it until the reflected sky is gone. What does the sea look like now?
- Grey or dark. Its blue was the sky's, and it has gone with the sky.
- Still blue. The water itself is sending blue light up to the eye.
???
Still blue. With the reflected sky removed, the sea's blue remained, so the colour must be coming from inside the water. Raman argued that the water was doing wh

sections.heading: 11.5 Light is a wave
sections.excerpt:
:::scene London, 24 November 1803

Thomas Young let a narrow sunbeam into a dark room. Into the beam he held a thin card, about a thirtieth of an inch wide (under a millimetre), edge-on, so that the light passed on both sides of it. On the wall behind, inside the card's shadow, where it should have been darkest, he saw fine stripes: bright, dark, bright, dark. The light that had passed on the two sides of the card had spread into the shadow from both edges, met there, and *interfered*.

You know what that word means from Chapter 9. Drop two stones into still water and watch where the two sets of ripples cross. Where a crest from one meets a crest from the other, the water is lifted twice as high. Where a crest meets a trough, they cancel, and the water is flat. The pattern of doubled and flattened places is interference, and nothing but a wave can do it. Two balls do not add up to nothing; two cricketers' throws do not cancel. Young's stripes were bright where light met light in step, crest with crest, and dark where it met out of step, crest with trough. Dark stripes made by *adding* light together are the surest sign of a wave there is.

:::fig c11_young() | Two sources of light

sections.heading: 11.6 The colour that changed
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Calcutta, February 1928

Everything scattered so far came back the colour it went in. The blue of the sky is sunlight's own blue, re-sent; the blue of the sea is the same. In the seven years since the *Narkunda*, Raman and his students at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta had gone on studying how liquids scatter light, and he now had a young colleague, K. S. Krishnan. In February 1928 they shone light of a single colour into clear liquids and looked carefully at what came out sideways.

:::predict
Light of one pure colour is shone into a clear liquid, and you look at the light scattered out sideways. Its colour is
- all exactly the colour that went in.
- all a different colour.
- almost all the colour that went in, with a tiny fraction of a different colour.
???
Almost all the same, with a tiny fraction shifted to a different colour. Krishnan's diary records the work day by day from 5 February. On 9 February Raman said it should be called the "Raman–Krishnan effect". sections.heading: The sunglasses test
sections.excerpt:
:::case The sunglasses test
Take a pair of polarised sunglasses to Marine Drive an hour before sunset, with an adult, and first check the glasses on a phone screen: through genuinely polarised lenses the screen goes dark at some angle as you turn them. Then, from the sea wall, do three things and write down what you see.

1. Look at the glare on the water about 37° below the horizon, roughly a third of the way from straight ahead to straight down, and slowly tilt your head towards one shoulder. The glare brightens as you tilt, and fades again as you straighten up.
2. Look at the sea's own colour, the blue in the water between the patches of glare, while tilting. It stays blue.
3. Look at the blue sky about a quarter of the way round from the Sun and tilt again. It darkens and brightens a little as you turn. Never look at the Sun itself, with or without sunglasses.

Three patches of light. One is strongly polarised, one is partly polarised, and one hardly at all. Which is which, and what does the one that stays blue tell you about where the sea's colour comes from?
???
The glare off the water (1) is strongly polarised: it is sunlight reflected off the surface, shaking parallel to th

callouts.title: Newton lets the band of colours fall on a board with a small hole in it, so that only the red light passes through. He puts a second prism in that red beam. What comes out of the second prism?
callouts.body:
- A new band of colours. The second prism adds colours just as the first did.
- Light of a different colour: the red has been changed again.
- Red light, bent, and nothing else.
???
Red light, bent, and nothing else. The second prism bends the red beam but adds no colour to it and takes none away. Newton tried each colour in turn and got the same result. So the prism cannot be adding anything. The colours were in the sunlight all along, mixed together so that they looked white, and the prism only sorts them. White light is a mixture. That was the point of the letter.

callouts.title: Your syllabus calls this topic "dispersion", and it asks for the order: red is bent least and violet most. Whether you say "deviated" or "bent", the colours leave the prism in the order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
Why can you only ever see a rainbow with the Sun behind you?
callouts.body:
???
The light that makes a rainbow enters a raindrop, is bent, reflects off the inside of the back of the drop, and is bent again on the way out. After that bounce it is travelling back towards the Sun's side of the sky. So the only drops that can send colour to your eye are the ones on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun, which puts the Sun behind you.

A friend says your eyes "see colour" the way a torch shines: the eye sends out something that colours what it looks at. Where is the colour of a ripe mango actually decided?
???
Nothing leaves the eye, as the sealed dark room showed. The mango's colour is decided by two things: which wavelengths of the arriving light the mango's skin sends back and which it absorbs, and how the three kinds of colour-sensing cell in your eye respond to the mix that reaches them. Change the light that arrives and the mango's colour changes, as this section shows.

callouts.title: In a dark room, you light a green leaf with nothing but a phone screen showing pure red. What colour does the leaf look?
callouts.body:
- Green. A leaf is green.
- Red, like everything else in the room.
- Black, or very nearly.
???
Black, or very nearly. A leaf looks green in daylight because its surface sends back the green part of the light that reaches it and absorbs most of the rest. Red light has no green in it, so there is nothing for the leaf to send back, and it absorbs most of the red. Nothing much reaches your eye from the leaf, and nothing much is what black means. A phone screen's red is not perfectly pure, so expect "dark and strange" rather than perfectly black.

callouts.title: A banana by phone-light
callouts.body: In a room as dark as you can make it, open a plain, full-screen red image on a phone, or any app that fills the screen with red, and turn the brightness up. Put a banana, a green leaf and something blue on the table, and light them with the phone from a hand's width away. Say what colour each looks before you check with the room light. Then try a blue screen, and a white one. If you have a magnifying glass, or the water-drop lens from Section 10.5, look closely at the white screen: it is made of tiny red, green and blue dots, with no white dot anywhere.

callouts.title: Investigation 11.2
callouts.body: Before you touch the controls, write down what colour red light and blue light will make together, and what cyan and magenta paint will make. Then mix them and compare. Which of your two guesses was based on paintbox experience?

callouts.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary calls this "adding and subtracting colours". Adding is for light (red, green and blue make white); subtracting is for paints and filters (each one removes colours). Keep the two lists apart, because the answers come out different.
A spot of red light and a spot of green light overlap on a white wall. What colour is the overlap, and why is it not the muddy brown you get from mixing red and green paint?
callouts.body:
???
Yellow. Both lights reach your eye, so your "red" and "green" cones fire together, which is exactly what yellow light makes them do. Paints subtract: red paint removes green and blue, green paint removes red and blue, and together they remove nearly everything, so the mixture is dark and dull. Light adds; paint takes away.

callouts.title: Rayleigh scattering
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The redirection of light in all directions by particles much smaller than the wavelength of the light, which scatters short wavelengths (blue and violet) far more strongly than long ones (orange and red).
? Why is it called this?
Named after Lord Rayleigh, who worked out in 1871 that when small particles scatter light, the scattered intensity scales as one over the fourth power of the wavelength (1/λ⁴).
? What problem did it solve?
It explained two everyday mysteries with a single rule: why the daytime sky away from the Sun is blue, and why the Sun itself turns yellow, orange and red when seen through a long slant of air at sunset.
? Why does it work?
A passing light wave shakes the electrons in each air molecule, and an oscillating charge radiates light like a tiny antenna; higher-frequency (shorter-wavelength) oscillations radiate much more strongly, so blue at 450 nm is scattered nearly six times as strongly as red at 700 nm.
? How does it help?
It explains the colour of the sky, the redness of a totally eclipsed Moon lit by light bent through the Earth's rim of air, and why Raman could argue that water molecules themselves give the deep sea its blue.
?? How do we know?
Shine a white torch beam through a glass of water faintly clouded with a drop of milk: looked at from the side, the scattered light is bluish; looked at end-on through the glass, the remaining beam is yellow-orange.
?? What it isn't
Air is not blue like tinted glass (if it were, the noon Sun seen through it would look blue), and the sky is not blue because it reflects the sea.
?? Where does it stop working?
Once the scattering particles are as big as or bigger than the wavelength of light, such as water droplets in a cloud or fog, the 1/λ⁴ rule no longer holds; all visible wavelengths scatter about equally and the cloud looks white or grey.

callouts.title: Astronauts on the Moon stood in full sunlight, with no air above them at all. What colour was the daytime sky over their heads?
callouts.body:
- Blue, like ours.
- A paler, whiter blue.
- Black, with the Sun blazing in it.
???
Black, with the Sun blazing in it. There is no air to scatter the sunlight sideways into your eyes, so the only direction light arrives from is the Sun itself. Everywhere else in the sky there is nothing to see, which is black. Blue sky needs air. It is the air you are looking at.

callouts.title: A sky in a glass
callouts.body: Fill a clear glass with water and stir in a few drops of milk, enough to make the water very faintly cloudy; if it goes white, start again with more water. Take it into a dark room with a torch. Shine the torch at the glass from one side and look at the glass from another side: the water has a faint bluish tinge. Now look at the torch *through* the glass: the beam coming through is yellowish-orange. The milk droplets are playing the part of the air, scattering the shorter wavelengths sideways and letting the longer ones through. It is a model of the sky, not the sky itself: milk droplets are much bigger than air molecules, so the six-to-one rule does not hold exactly, but the two colours come out the right way round.

callouts.title: Investigation 11.3
callouts.body: Set the Sun straight overhead and read off the colour of the sky and of the Sun. Lower the Sun to 10° and then to 3°, and write down how the two colours change. Then switch the air off and say what you see.

callouts.title: > "The sky is blue because it reflects the sea."
callouts.body: Go to Nagpur, in the middle of the country and hundreds of kilometres from any sea, and the sky is just as blue. The sky's blue comes from the air itself scattering sunlight, and it arrives from every direction at once, including straight overhead, where no sea could be reflected. The sea, as it happens, has borrowed some of *its* blue from the sky, which is the mystery of the next section.

callouts.title: A friend says the air is blue the way tinted glass is blue, so you see blue when you look through it. What is wrong with that picture?
callouts.body:
???
Look *through* tinted blue glass at the Sun and the Sun looks blue. Look through the air at the Sun and it looks yellow-white at noon and orange at sunset: the air removes blue from the light that passes straight through it. The blue you see is in the *rest* of the sky, away from the Sun, where the removed blue has been re-sent towards you. That is scattering, and it is the opposite of tinting.

callouts.title: Light reflected off the surface of water is polarised, as you are about to learn, so a Nicol prism held at the right angle can block the reflected sky almost completely. Raman holds the prism to his eye and turns it until the reflected sky is gone. What does the sea look like now?
callouts.body:
- Grey or dark. Its blue was the sky's, and it has gone with the sky.
- Still blue. The water itself is sending blue light up to the eye.
???
Still blue. With the reflected sky removed, the sea's blue remained, so the colour must be coming from inside the water. Raman argued that the water was doing what the air does: its molecules scatter the sunlight that enters it, blue most of all, and send some of it back up. He wrote a letter to the journal *Nature* on board, and when the *Narkunda* docked at Bombay he posted it. The sea's blue is a cousin of the sky's, made in the water rather than above it.

Chapter 9's sound waves were pushes passed along the direction of travel. Could a sound wave in air be polarised the way light can?
???
No. Polarisation is the direction of a wave's *sideways* shaking, and sound in air has none: the air moves back and forth along the direction the sound travels, with no sideways motion to point one way or another. Light does shake sideways, which is why it can be polarised, and why a polarising filter can tell glare from the light of the water beneath it.

callouts.title: > "Polarised sunglasses are just dark glasses with a fancy name."
callouts.body: Dark glasses dim everything equally. Polarised glasses block one direction of shaking, so they dim glare off water far more than they dim the water itself, and turning them changes what you see. Test a pair on a phone or laptop screen before you trust them: the screen's light is polarised, so through genuinely polarised lenses the screen goes dark at some angle as you rotate them. Ordinary tinted lenses do nothing of the kind.

callouts.title: Looking at the glare on a pond through polarised sunglasses, you turn your head sideways through 90°, and the glare gets much brighter. Why?
callouts.body:
???
The glare is light reflected off the water, and it shakes mostly side to side, parallel to the surface. Upright, the glasses pass only up-and-down shaking, so they block most of the glare. Turned through 90°, they pass side-to-side shaking instead, which is exactly the glare's direction, so now it comes through.

callouts.title: Interference
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The combining of two or more overlapping waves, adding together to make a larger wave where they meet in step (crest on crest) and cancelling out where they meet out of step (crest on trough).
? Why is it called this?
Thomas Young introduced the word *interference* into optics in 1801, from the everyday sense of two things crossing and acting on each other, to name the way two overlapping light waves reinforce or cancel.
? What problem did it solve?
It settled the long argument over whether light has wave properties: streams of simple particles do not cancel each other to make darkness, whereas two overlapping beams of light produce alternating bright and dark stripes.
? Why does it work?
A wave's displacement can be positive (a crest) or negative (a trough); where two waves cross, the medium responds to the sum of both displacements at each instant.
? How does it help?
It explains the bright and dark fringes behind narrow slits, the swirling colours of soap bubbles and oil films on wet roads, the rainbow thrown by a CD's tracks, and the bronze-green sheen of a peacock's feather.
?? How do we know?
Hold a sub-millimetre card edge-on in a narrow sunbeam in a dark room, as Young did in 1803, or shine a laser through two narrow slits: the centre of the shadow is crossed by fine bright and dark stripes that vanish the moment you block either side.
?? What it isn't
Destructive interference does not destroy energy: the energy missing from the dark stripes is shifted into the bright stripes beside them, keeping the total energy unchanged.
?? Where does it stop working?
Two ordinary torches shining on a wall show no interference stripes because their waves shift out of step with each other billions of times a second, blurring the bright and dark fringes into smooth illumination before your eye can register them.

callouts.title: A small round disc is lit by a tiny, bright source of light. At the exact centre of its shadow, the light is
callouts.body:
- as dark as the shadow gets, since the disc is directly in the way.
- about the same as the rest of the shadow.
- a bright spot.
???
A bright spot. François Arago set up the experiment and looked, and there it was: a point of light at the centre of the shadow, exactly where the wave theory said the light spilling round the whole edge of the disc arrives in step. Fresnel won the prize in 1819. Poisson was never convinced, and the spot now carries his name as well as Arago's, which is a fair reward for an honest wrong prediction. Others had seen the spot long before, without understanding what they were looking at.

callouts.title: Investigation 11.5
callouts.body: Set the two sources close together and note how far apart the stripes are. Move the sources apart and watch the stripes. Then shorten the wavelength. Write one rule for what makes the stripes wider.

callouts.title: Interference and diffraction appear in Cambridge Lower Secondary Stage 9 and again in IB, and IGCSE light stays mostly with rays. Keep both pictures and know which to use: rays for mirrors and lenses, waves for stripes and for the colours of films and bubbles.
Your shadow in sunlight has fuzzy edges. Is that light diffracting round you?
callouts.body:
???
Mostly not. The Sun is a disc, not a point, so each point on it casts a slightly shifted shadow of you, and the fuzzy band at the edge is where some of the Sun is hidden and some is not (Section 10.2). Diffraction round something as big as a person does happen, but the spreading is a tiny fraction of a millimetre, far too small to see at that scale. Diffraction shows itself at edges less than a millimetre across.

callouts.title: Light of one pure colour is shone into a clear liquid, and you look at the light scattered out sideways. Its colour is
callouts.body:
- all exactly the colour that went in.
- all a different colour.
- almost all the colour that went in, with a tiny fraction of a different colour.
???
Almost all the same, with a tiny fraction shifted to a different colour. Krishnan's diary records the work day by day from 5 February. On 9 February Raman said it should be called the "Raman–Krishnan effect". On 28 February 1928 they announced it: when light of one colour enters a liquid, a small fraction of the scattered light comes out a different colour, and the amount of the change depends on the liquid. India now keeps 28 February as National Science Day.

callouts.title: Your syllabus topic is "Electromagnetic spectrum". You need the order of the family by wavelength (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma), and the fact that all of them travel at the same speed in a vacuum. The Ladder of Light is that order, with real sources on it.
Put these in order of wavelength, longest first: X-rays, radio waves, visible light, infrared.
callouts.body:
???
Radio waves (metres and more), infrared (longer than red light), visible light (about 400 to 700 nm), X-rays (far shorter than violet). All four travel at the same speed in empty space; only the wavelength, and with it the number of waves per second, is different.

callouts.title: The sunglasses test
callouts.body:
Take a pair of polarised sunglasses to Marine Drive an hour before sunset, with an adult, and first check the glasses on a phone screen: through genuinely polarised lenses the screen goes dark at some angle as you turn them. Then, from the sea wall, do three things and write down what you see.

1. Look at the glare on the water about 37° below the horizon, roughly a third of the way from straight ahead to straight down, and slowly tilt your head towards one shoulder. The glare brightens as you tilt, and fades again as you straighten up.
2. Look at the sea's own colour, the blue in the water between the patches of glare, while tilting. It stays blue.
3. Look at the blue sky about a quarter of the way round from the Sun and tilt again. It darkens and brightens a little as you turn. Never look at the Sun itself, with or without sunglasses.

Three patches of light. One is strongly polarised, one is partly polarised, and one hardly at all. Which is which, and what does the one that stays blue tell you about where the sea's colour comes from?
???
The glare off the water (1) is strongly polarised: it is sunlight reflected off the surface, shaking parallel to the surface, and at Brewster's angle, 53° from the normal and so about 37° below the horizon, it is completely polarised. Upright lenses, which pass only up-and-down shaking, block it; tilt your head and the lenses start to pass side-to-side shaking, and the glare returns.

The sky (3) is partly polarised, because it is sunlight scattered sideways by the air, and scattering sorts the shaking only partly, so the sky dims and brightens without going black.

The sea's own blue (2) is hardly polarised at all, so tilting changes nothing. That is Raman's result from the rail of the *Narkunda*: with the polarised reflected sky removed, the blue is still there, so it is coming from inside the water, where sunlight is scattered, blue most of all, and sent back up. The sky is blue because the air scatters sunlight, the sunset is orange for the same reason seen along a longer path, and the sea is blue partly because it reflects that sky and mostly because the water scatters light itself. The same rule, three times, and a different share of it in each.

sections.heading: 12.1 Rubbing moves charge
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a dry evening in winter

Comb your hair quickly with a plastic comb, then turn on a tap until a thin, smooth stream falls into the basin. Bring the comb close without touching the water. The stream leans towards the comb. A balloon rubbed on your hair does the same, and will also lift scraps of paper and cling to a wall for a minute; you met it in *The Invisible World*, sorting pepper from salt. Now it is time to ask what the rubbing did.

Say your first thought out loud. Most people's is: *the rubbing made electricity*. It has one thing right, which is that rubbing is involved. But two strips of sticky tape show that whatever rubbing does, it does to *two* things at once.

:::predict
Stick two strips of tape, each about four centimetres long, side by side on a table, then peel both off quickly and hold them dangling near each other. They swing *apart*. Now stick one strip on top of another, press them together, peel the pair off the table, and pull them apart. Hold the two strips near each other. What happens?
- They swing apart, as before.
- They swing towards each other.
- Nothing: pulling them apart cancels the effect.
???

sections.heading: 12.2 A loop, not a pipe
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, your table

For the rest of this chapter you need a small kit from an electronics shop: a 9 V battery (the rectangular kind with two snap terminals), two resistors marked 330 Ω, two red LEDs, one white LED, and four leads with crocodile clips. Everything runs on that battery. An adult should help check the connections; a short circuit can still make a battery or wire hot. Nothing goes anywhere near a wall socket; Section 12.6 explains why.

Here is the first experiment; predict before you do it. Clip one lead from the battery's + terminal to one leg of a red LED. That is a wire from battery to "bulb", which is exactly what the tidy story says you need.

:::predict
One lead joins the battery's + terminal to one leg of the LED. Nothing else is connected. What does the LED do?
- It lights.
- It glows faintly, since only half the circuit is there.
- Nothing at all.
???
Nothing at all, however long you wait. The one-wire circuit is so natural that physics-education researchers have been studying it since 1980, and it never works. Now add the resistor and a second lead so that the path runs battery + → resistor → LED → battery −. The LED lights the instant the last clip

sections.heading: 12.3 What gets used up?
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, the first of the month

The electricity bill arrives on the phone. "Units consumed: 312." Somebody paid for something, and the natural thought is that it came down the wire and the flat used it up. The torch tells the same story: the bulb glows, the battery dies, so the bulb must be eating what the battery sends. The idea feels so obviously true that one group of physics teachers wrote that "it is clear to most pupils that something must get used up". Something does. The question is what, and the two red LEDs settle it.

:::predict
Put both red LEDs in the loop, one after the other: battery + → resistor → first LED → second LED → battery −. The current leaves the battery, passes the first LED and then the second. Which LED is brighter?
- The first, because it gets the current fresh from the battery.
- The second, because the first has slowed the current down and the second has a clearer run.
- They are equally bright.
???
Equally bright. Now swap the two LEDs over and look again. Nothing changes. If the first LED were using up some of the current, the second would always be the dimmer, whichever LED you put there. It never is.
:::

sections.heading: 12.4 Push and resistance
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a car starting on a winter morning

Watch a car start in the early morning with its headlights on. As the driver turns the key the lights dim for a second, then recover once the engine catches. A torch with tired cells is similar: the light is yellow and dull, and fresh cells make it white again, though both sets say 1.5 V on the side. A popular wrong idea hides in both scenes: *a battery always gives out the same current*. If it did, the headlights would not care about the starter motor and old cells would be as bright as new. Here is the test, with your kit.

:::predict
You have two red LEDs in the loop with the resistor and both are lit. You add a third red LED, in line with the others. What happens?
- All three stay as bright as before: the battery gives the same current, so each LED gets it.
- All three are dimmer.
- The first two stay bright and the third is dim, because it is last in line.
???
All three are dimmer, and equally so, because the same smaller current runs through each. The battery did not keep the current fixed. It kept its *push* roughly fixed, and with more in the loop to push through, less gets through.
:::

:::work
The battery's push is 9 V.

sections.heading: 12.5 Series and parallel
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a flat at night

The kitchen tube light flickers and dies. The fan keeps turning, the fridge hums, the hall light stays on. Nobody finds that remarkable, but after what you have just learned it should be. If everything in the flat were on one loop, like your three LEDs, a dead light would be a gap in the loop and the whole flat would go dark. It does not, so the wiring is arranged some other way. There are exactly two ways to put two things in a circuit, and your kit can do both. Predict first, with a question MIT asks its first-year students.

:::predict
One red LED with its own 330 Ω resistor is lit on the 9 V battery. You add a second red LED with its own 330 Ω, each resistor-and-LED pair running from the battery's + terminal to its −: two branches side by side. Compared with before, the first LED is now:
- Dimmer, because the two LEDs share the battery.
- Just as bright.
- Brighter.
???
Just as bright, or so close you cannot tell. Each branch has the full 9 V across it and carries its own 21 mA regardless of the other, so the battery now supplies 42 mA and does twice the work. (A real battery sags a little at the higher current.) Unclip one LED and the other do

sections.heading: 12.6 Safe at home
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, the cupboard by the front door

Use the drawing below to understand your flat's distribution board. If the labels on its switches are visible from outside, an adult can point them out. Do not open or remove any cover or touch the switches for this activity. Inside are devices guarding the flat's circuits; this section explains them without an experiment on the real board. The battery on your table pushes with 9 V. The wall sockets push with about 230 V, swinging back and forth fifty times a second, and that is a different world.

Electricity has two ways to hurt. The first is heat. Remember the one rule of your kit: never join the battery's terminals with a bare lead, because a lead has almost no resistance, a huge current flows, and lead and battery get hot. Such an accidental low-resistance path across a supply is a ==short circuit==, and at 230 V the current in one can set a cable on fire. The guard is simple and old: something in series with each circuit that opens if the current grows too large. A fuse is a strip of metal with a low melting point that melts and breaks the path. A circuit breaker is a switch that trips itself and can be reset; each small switch

sections.heading: The LED that wouldn't light
sections.excerpt:
:::case The LED that wouldn't light
A friend follows an online video and builds a circuit on the kitchen table: two AA cells in a holder, one white LED, and a lead from each end of the holder to each leg of the LED. Nothing. He swaps the two leads over: still nothing. He presses the clips harder: nothing. Then he takes a red LED from your kit, adds the 68 Ω resistor from the video's parts list, and connects it the same way. It lights at once. "The white LED is broken," he says, and reaches for the bin.

Clues from the datasheets:

- An AA cell has a nominal voltage of 1.5 V. Two in a row give 3.0 V.
- A red LED starts to pass current at about 1.8 to 2.4 V, typically 2.0 V.
- A white LED starts to pass current at about 2.8 to 3.8 V, typically 3.3 V.
- An LED passes current in one direction only.

Is the white LED broken? Why did it stay dark while the red one lit, and how would you light it safely?
???
It is almost certainly not broken. A white LED needs about 3.3 V across it before it passes much current, and two AA cells supply 3.0 V. There is not enough push. The red LED needs only about 2 V, so 3.0 V is plenty for it, with the 68 Ω resistor taking up the extra volt and holding t

callouts.title: Stick two strips of tape, each about four centimetres long, side by side on a table, then peel both off quickly and hold them dangling near each other. They swing *apart*. Now stick one strip on top of another, press them together, peel the pair off the table, and pull them apart. Hold the two strips near each other. What happens?
callouts.body:
- They swing apart, as before.
- They swing towards each other.
- Nothing: pulling them apart cancels the effect.
???
They swing towards each other. The side-by-side strips were treated the same way, so they ended up alike, and alike pushes apart. The stacked pair was pulled off each other, and whichever strip took something from the other, the two ended up *opposite*, and opposite pulls together. Rubbing does not make one kind of stuff. It leaves two things different from each other.

callouts.title: Investigation 12.1
callouts.body: Do the tape experiment on a dry evening, then again on a humid one, timing how long a strip keeps swinging away from its twin. Then try the comb on the tap. Write what you observe before you write why; the "why" column may say "don't know yet".

The comb pulls the stream of water sideways. In Chapter 3 every push had a partner. Does the water pull on the comb?
???
Yes, with exactly the same size of force, the other way. You do not notice because you are holding the comb, and the pull is tiny next to your grip. Hang the comb from a thread and bring something charged near it, and it swings. Attraction is never one-sided.

callouts.title: > "Rubbing makes electricity in the comb."
callouts.body: Rubbing makes nothing. It moves electrons from one material to the other, leaving exactly as much positive charge behind as negative charge it carried off, so comb and hair together have the total they had before, which is none. "Static electricity" is not a special kind of electricity either. It is the same charge you will meet flowing round a circuit in the next section, sitting still.

callouts.title: A rubbed balloon ends up with a charge of −3 units, where one unit is a very large number of electrons. It was rubbed on a woollen scarf. What charge does the scarf have, and how do you know without measuring it?
callouts.body:
???
+3 units. Both started neutral and electrons only moved between the two, so every electron the balloon gained is one the scarf lost. The scarf is short of exactly three units of negative charge, which leaves it positive by three, and the pair's total is still zero.

callouts.title: One lead joins the battery's + terminal to one leg of the LED. Nothing else is connected. What does the LED do?
callouts.body:
- It lights.
- It glows faintly, since only half the circuit is there.
- Nothing at all.
???
Nothing at all, however long you wait. The one-wire circuit is so natural that physics-education researchers have been studying it since 1980, and it never works. Now add the resistor and a second lead so that the path runs battery + → resistor → LED → battery −. The LED lights the instant the last clip touches. If it stays dark, turn the LED round: it lets current through one way only.

callouts.title: Electric current
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The rate at which electric charge flows past a point in a circuit, measured in coulombs per second, which are called amperes (A).
? Why is it called this?
Early experimenters pictured electricity flowing like a river and borrowed *current* from the Latin *currere*, to run; the unit *ampere* honours André-Marie Ampère, who worked out the magnetic forces between currents in 1820.
? What problem did it solve?
It replaced vague talk of "electric fire" with a countable quantity: how much charge passes any cross-section of a wire each second, which turns out to be the exact same number at every point round a simple closed loop.
? Why does it work?
A metal wire is already full of mobile electrons before a battery is connected; when the loop is closed, the battery's electric field pushes on electrons everywhere round the loop at once, and if charge ever piled up at one spot its repulsion would immediately even the flow out.
? How does it help?
Knowing that current is never used up around a loop lets you predict that two identical LEDs in series shine equally brightly, and lets a residual current device (RCD) spot a 30 mA leak through a person by comparing outgoing and returning currents.
?? How do we know?
Put an ammeter before a resistor and LED, between them, and after them on the return lead to the battery: all three readings match to the last digit.
?? What it isn't
Current is not stuff stored in a tank inside the battery and it is not used up by a bulb; what the battery supplies from its chemicals and the bulb converts into light and warmth is energy.
?? Where does it stop working?
While individual electrons in a thin copper wire carrying 21 mA drift along at less than a hundredth of a millimetre per second, the lamp still lights the instant the switch closes because the electric push travels round the loop at nearly the speed of light.

callouts.title: Build the loop
callouts.body: Clip a lead from the battery's + terminal to one end of a 330 Ω resistor, a second lead from the resistor's other end to one leg of a red LED, and a third from the LED's other leg back to the − terminal. It lights; if not, turn the LED round. Unclip any one clip and it goes dark; clip it back and it lights at once, wherever you broke the loop. Move the resistor to the other side of the LED: same brightness. Swap the two battery leads so the current runs the other way: dark. An LED is a one-way device, which is a clue for the chapter's case. Two rules, always: keep a resistor in the loop (Section 12.4 says why), and never join the battery's two terminals with a lead and nothing else. That is a path with almost no resistance, and lead and battery heat up fast.

callouts.title: Your Stage 7 book may describe electricity as a flow of electrons, and that is fine. In IGCSE you write *current*, charge flowing per second, and you will be asked for both arrows: conventional current from positive to negative, and free electrons from negative to positive. Both are right.
Two coulombs of charge pass a point in a wire every ten seconds. What is the current there, and what is the current at a point on the other side of the same loop?
callouts.body:
???
0.2 A at the first point: two coulombs divided by ten seconds. And 0.2 A at the other point too. Round a single loop, whatever passes one point must pass every other, or charge would be piling up somewhere, and piled-up charge pushes back until the flow evens out.

callouts.title: Put both red LEDs in the loop, one after the other: battery + → resistor → first LED → second LED → battery −. The current leaves the battery, passes the first LED and then the second. Which LED is brighter?
callouts.body:
- The first, because it gets the current fresh from the battery.
- The second, because the first has slowed the current down and the second has a clearer run.
- They are equally bright.
???
Equally bright. Now swap the two LEDs over and look again. Nothing changes. If the first LED were using up some of the current, the second would always be the dimmer, whichever LED you put there. It never is.

callouts.title: Investigation 12.3
callouts.body: Build the two-LED loop and do the swap. Then leave it running a minute and touch the resistor lightly. It is warm; the leads are not. Something is being delivered there, and this section names it.

The bill says "units consumed". In Chapter 7 energy was never used up. Reconcile the two.
???
A "unit" is a kilowatt-hour of energy, and what you buy is its *delivery* into the flat, where it ends up as light, motion, sound and, finally, warmth spread into the air. None is destroyed; it is spread out and no longer useful. The charge is not consumed either. It stays in the wires, going back and forth fifty times a second.

callouts.title: Voltage
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The energy transferred per coulomb of charge as it moves between two points in a circuit, measured in joules per coulomb, which are called volts (V).
? Why is it called this?
Named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first chemical battery (the voltaic pile) in 1800; its other name, *potential difference*, compares the electrical "height" at two points the way Chapter 7 compared heights on a hill.
? What problem did it solve?
People saw that current is the same before and after a lamp and asked what *does* get spent across the lamp; voltage separates the conserved carrier (coulombs of charge) from the energy each coulomb hands over (joules per coulomb).
? Why does it work?
A 9 V battery's chemical reactions do 9 J of work on every coulomb they pump from one terminal to the other; as that coulomb goes round the loop, it drops about 2 J at a red LED and 7 J at the resistor, arriving back at the battery ready to be lifted again.
? How does it help?
Multiplying voltage by current (*P* = *VI*) gives the exact power in watts delivered to any component, and adding the voltage drops round any loop always equals the battery's voltage.
?? How do we know?
Clip a voltmeter across a 9 V battery, then across the resistor (about 7 V) and across the red LED (about 2 V) in series: the drops across the components add up to the battery's rise.
?? What it isn't
Voltage is not a flow: charge flows *through* a wire (current), whereas voltage is a difference in energy per coulomb *across* two points, and you can have 230 V waiting across an open wall socket with zero current flowing.
?? Where does it stop working?
A real battery's terminal voltage is not completely fixed: when a starter motor or a low-resistance load draws a large current, the battery's own internal resistance uses up part of the joules per coulomb inside the cell and the terminal voltage sags.

callouts.title: > "The first LED uses up some of the current, so the second gets less."
callouts.body: The current is the same at every point round the loop. What each LED takes is a share of the *energy* each coulomb delivers, which shows up as a share of the battery's volts: 2 V across each red LED out of the 9. Swap the LEDs and nothing changes. Current goes round; energy is delivered.

callouts.title: In the loop with the resistor and one red LED, where is the current largest: as it leaves the battery's + terminal, as it passes through the LED, or as it returns to the − terminal?
callouts.body:
???
Nowhere: it is the same at all three points. If it were larger leaving than returning, charge would pile up somewhere in the loop every second, and the pile would push back until the flow evened out. What differs between the three places is the energy each coulomb has left to deliver: most as it leaves, less after the resistor, least after the LED.

callouts.title: You have two red LEDs in the loop with the resistor and both are lit. You add a third red LED, in line with the others. What happens?
callouts.body:
- All three stay as bright as before: the battery gives the same current, so each LED gets it.
- All three are dimmer.
- The first two stay bright and the third is dim, because it is last in line.
???
All three are dimmer, and equally so, because the same smaller current runs through each. The battery did not keep the current fixed. It kept its *push* roughly fixed, and with more in the loop to push through, less gets through.

callouts.title: Where this book says "the battery's push", IGCSE says the battery's *e.m.f.*, and where it says the volts across a component, IGCSE says the *p.d.*, the potential difference. Both are in volts. "E.m.f." once stood for electromotive force, but it is not a force at all; it is energy per coulomb, and the name is a historical leftover. IGCSE (*4.2–4.3*) also asks you to sketch *I*–*V* curves for an ohmic resistor, a filament lamp and a diode, and to use thermistors, LDRs and diodes (for rectification of AC to DC) in practical sensing and power circuits.

A friend's torch is dim with old cells. A meter across each old cell, with the torch off, reads 1.5 V, the same as a new cell. "So the cells are fine," says the friend, "the bulb must be going." What is wrong with that reasoning?
callouts.body:
???
A meter draws almost no current, so it reads the push with nothing asked of the cell. The bulb draws a real current, and an old cell's internal resistance takes a large share of the push inside the cell, leaving the bulb less. Swap in new cells: if the torch is bright again, the bulb was fine all along.

callouts.title: One red LED with its own 330 Ω resistor is lit on the 9 V battery. You add a second red LED with its own 330 Ω, each resistor-and-LED pair running from the battery's + terminal to its −: two branches side by side. Compared with before, the first LED is now:
callouts.body:
- Dimmer, because the two LEDs share the battery.
- Just as bright.
- Brighter.
???
Just as bright, or so close you cannot tell. Each branch has the full 9 V across it and carries its own 21 mA regardless of the other, so the battery now supplies 42 mA and does twice the work. (A real battery sags a little at the higher current.) Unclip one LED and the other does not even flicker.

callouts.title: Two LEDs, two ways
callouts.body: Build the series circuit: + → resistor → LED → LED → −. Both glow at the same, slightly dull level. Unclip one LED and the other goes dark, because the only path is broken. Now build the parallel circuit with both resistors: two branches, each resistor-then-LED, both starting at + and ending at −. Both LEDs glow at full brightness. Unclip one and the other carries on exactly as before. Last, in the series circuit, swap the order of an LED and the resistor: nothing changes, because order along a single path makes no difference to a current that is the same everywhere.

callouts.title: > "Bulbs in parallel share the battery, so each one is dimmer."
callouts.body: In parallel each branch has the whole voltage across it and draws its own current, so each bulb is as bright as alone. What is shared is the battery's *effort*: it supplies the sum of the branch currents and runs down faster. Brightness is shared out in series, where the push is divided.

callouts.title: Three identical resistors, each of resistance R, are connected in parallel. Without any arithmetic, what is their combined resistance? And how would you connect the three to get the largest possible total?
callouts.body:
???
R/3. Each branch passes the same current it would alone, so three branches pass three times the current for the same push, which is what a resistor of one third the value would do. For the largest total, connect them in series: 3R, since the charge has to pass through all three in turn.

callouts.title: In your flat, a 100 W reading lamp and a 2,000 W bathroom geyser are both plugged into the same 230 V mains supply (in parallel, as Section 12.5 showed). Which appliance has the *larger* electrical resistance?
callouts.body:
- The 2,000 W geyser, because it is much bigger and works much harder
- The 100 W reading lamp
- Both have the same resistance, because both run on 230 V
???
The 100 W reading lamp has twenty times the resistance of the geyser. Both receive the same 230 V push, and power is *P* = *VI*. To deliver 2,000 W at 230 V, the geyser must let a large current through (*I* = 2,000 ÷ 230 ≈ 8.7 A), which requires a *low* resistance (*R* = *V* ÷ *I* = *V*² ÷ *P* ≈ 26.5 Ω). The 100 W lamp lets only about 0.43 A through, so its resistance while hot is about 529 Ω. High-power mains appliances are low-resistance paths, which is why the geyser needs thick copper wiring and its own heavy-duty switch.

callouts.title: IGCSE has a topic called *Electrical safety* (4.4), and its hazards and devices are this section's. Where IGCSE says "circuit breaker", the electrician who comes to the flat says "MCB". Same thing.
callouts.body:
:::

Three facts about the supply. Its voltage in Maharashtra is declared as 230 volts, with 240 beside it in some documents, and the rules let it wander between about 195 and 253. It alternates: the push reverses a hundred times a second, fifty full swings, peaking at about 325 V each swing; "230" is the steady voltage that would give the same heating. And it is never, under any circumstances, for experiments. No wire near a socket, no probe, no finger, no coin. The whole of this chapter can be done with a 9 V battery, and that is where it stays.

callouts.title: Why must a fuse be connected in series with the circuit it protects, and not in parallel with it?
callouts.body:
???
In series, all of the circuit's current passes through the fuse, so when it grows dangerously large the fuse melts and breaks the only path. In parallel, the fuse would carry only part of the current, and melting it would leave the circuit's own path intact. A guard has to stand in the doorway, not beside it.

callouts.title: The LED that wouldn't light
callouts.body:
A friend follows an online video and builds a circuit on the kitchen table: two AA cells in a holder, one white LED, and a lead from each end of the holder to each leg of the LED. Nothing. He swaps the two leads over: still nothing. He presses the clips harder: nothing. Then he takes a red LED from your kit, adds the 68 Ω resistor from the video's parts list, and connects it the same way. It lights at once. "The white LED is broken," he says, and reaches for the bin.

Clues from the datasheets:

- An AA cell has a nominal voltage of 1.5 V. Two in a row give 3.0 V.
- A red LED starts to pass current at about 1.8 to 2.4 V, typically 2.0 V.
- A white LED starts to pass current at about 2.8 to 3.8 V, typically 3.3 V.
- An LED passes current in one direction only.

Is the white LED broken? Why did it stay dark while the red one lit, and how would you light it safely?
???
It is almost certainly not broken. A white LED needs about 3.3 V across it before it passes much current, and two AA cells supply 3.0 V. There is not enough push. The red LED needs only about 2 V, so 3.0 V is plenty for it, with the 68 Ω resistor taking up the extra volt and holding the current to a safe 15 mA or so. Some white LEDs sit at the low end of their range and will glow faintly on 3.0 V; this one did not.

The other two classic reasons for a dark LED were ruled out by the friend himself. He swapped the leads, so it was not the wrong way round, and the red LED lit on the same clips, so the loop was complete.

To light the white LED, give it more push and keep the resistor: on your 9 V battery with the 330 Ω, 9 − 3.3 = 5.7 V is left for the resistor and 5.7 ÷ 330 is about 17 mA, comfortably under the 30 mA the LED can take. Never connect any LED straight across a battery without a resistor: once an LED starts to conduct, nothing else stops the current climbing far past what it survives.

sections.heading: 13.1 Which metals stick?
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, the kitchen table

Gather what you can: every coin in the house, a steel spoon or two, a scrap of aluminium foil, a brass key, a steel safety pin, and the strongest fridge magnet you own. Before anything touches the magnet, write down what you expect. Most people expect that *magnets attract metals*. Children of three believe it, and most adults never find out otherwise, because the metals we meet most often, nails, pins and tins, happen to be the ones that stick.

:::predict
You hold the fridge magnet over, in turn: a ₹1 coin, a ₹2 coin, a ₹5 coin dated 2007, a ₹5 coin dated 2011, a steel spoon, the aluminium foil and the brass key. Which stick?
- All of them: they are all metal.
- All the coins and the spoon, which are steel; not the foil or the key.
- The ₹1, the ₹2 and the 2007 ₹5. Not the 2011 ₹5, the foil or the key. The spoon depends on the spoon.
???

sections.heading: 13.2 The Earth is a magnet
sections.excerpt:
:::scene London, 1600

Sailors had steered by compass for centuries without anyone knowing why the needle pointed north, and they had a stock of beliefs about it, one being that garlic would spoil it. William Gilbert, in London, tested such claims and dismissed the garlic as "fable and falsehood". Then he did something better: he ground a lump of lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, into a sphere, called it a *terrella*, a little Earth, and laid small needles on it. Over the sphere's equator a needle lay flat; towards its poles it tilted down, more steeply the nearer it got, just as compasses at sea were known to tilt as ships sailed north. Gilbert's conclusion, published in 1600, was that the Earth itself is a great magnet.

:::try Investigation 13.2
Make a compass. Stroke a steel sewing needle about twenty times with one end of your magnet, always the same way, lifting the magnet clear between strokes. Float the needle on a small leaf in a bowl of water away from steel, and wait: it turns and settles. Check it against a phone's compass app, then bring the fridge magnet near and watch which way it swings.
:::
