sections.heading: 13.3 Electricity makes magnetism
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Copenhagen, 21 April 1820

Hans Christian Ørsted was lecturing, with a battery and wires on the bench and a compass lying nearby. When he connected the wire and a current flowed, the compass needle twitched, so slightly that the audience did not notice. Ørsted did, and in the following weeks he tested it: reverse the current, and the needle twitched the other way. In July he published four pages in Latin, and the news crossed Europe. For the first time something electric had moved something magnetic: the first evidence, a textbook says, that the movement of charges had "any connection with magnets" at all.

Before this section explains the twitch, notice what does not twitch. A charged comb held near a compass does nothing to the needle as a magnet: charge sitting still has no magnetic effect. Charge *moving* does, and that one word is the hinge of the chapter.

:::predict
A wire runs north–south directly over a compass, and when a current flows the needle swings east. You reverse the current along the same wire. Now the needle:
- Swings east again, since the current is the same size.
- Swings west.
- Does not move: a current either side of the compass cancels out.
???
Swi

sections.heading: 13.4 The first motor
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Royal Institution, London, 3 September 1821

Seventeen months after the twitch in Copenhagen, Michael Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice turned laboratory assistant, stood a magnet upright in a dish of mercury and let a wire hang down into the mercury beside it, free to swing. When a current flowed, the wire began to circle the magnet, round and round, for as long as the current lasted. It was the first electric motor, and it ran on nothing but a current, a magnet and a force nobody had named yet. Do not copy the apparatus: mercury is poisonous.

The natural way to describe what Faraday saw is that the magnet pushed the electricity round the dish, as if stirring a fluid. Keep hold of Chapter 12: there is no electric fluid, only charge moving in a solid wire. So what did the magnet push? First, a question that catches most people out.

:::predict
Two long straight wires hang side by side a few centimetres apart, carrying the same current in the same direction, so each sits in the other's magnetic field. Do the wires:
- Push apart, like two like charges.
- Pull together.
- Do nothing to each other, since neither is a magnet.
???
Pull together. Currents in the same direction

sections.heading: 13.5 Magnetism makes electricity
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Royal Institution, London, 29 August 1831

Ten years on from the spinning wire, Faraday was still chasing the obvious question: if a current makes a magnet, should a magnet not make a current? He wound two separate coils on opposite sides of an iron ring, connected one to a battery through a switch and the other to a compass needle, and closed the switch. The needle jumped, then settled to zero while the current flowed steadily. He opened the switch and the needle jumped the other way, then settled. A steady current in the first coil did nothing to the second; only the *change*, at switching on or off, made anything happen. Eleven years after Ørsted, the connection ran both ways.

The result deserves a prediction. Faraday soon simplified it to a bar magnet and a coil of wire wired to a meter.

:::predict
You push the magnet into the coil and the meter needle kicks to the right. Now you hold the magnet perfectly still inside the coil. The meter:
- Shows a steady reading to the right while the magnet stays in.
- Falls back to zero.
- Kicks to the left.
???
Falls back to zero. A magnet sitting still inside a coil, however strong, produces nothing. Pull it out and the needle k

sections.heading: 13.6 Light is electromagnetic
sections.excerpt:
:::scene London, 1865

By the 1860s the rules were all in hand. Charges make electric fields. Magnetic field lines have no ends, because poles come in pairs. A changing magnetic field makes an electric field: Faraday's induction. A current makes a magnetic field: Ørsted's twitch, to which James Clerk Maxwell, a Scottish physicist working in London, added one piece of his own: a *changing electric field* makes a magnetic field too, with no current anywhere. He wrote the four rules as equations and asked what they allowed in empty space. The answer was a ripple. A changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field, which makes a changing electric field, and the pair travels on together, each making the other, at a speed fixed by two numbers already measured with coils and capacitors. Put them in and the speed comes out at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s: the speed of light, as Fizeau had measured it across Paris. Maxwell wrote: "We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena." Light was a wave of electric and magnetic fields. The "medium" he assumed was later found unnecessary; the wav

sections.heading: The trams and the magnetometer
sections.excerpt:
:::case The trams and the magnetometer
The Colaba observatory had recorded the Earth's magnetic field at the southern tip of Bombay every hour since 1846. Around 1904 its directors began a second observatory at Alibag, down the coast across the harbour, ran both at once for two years to match one record against the other, and then moved the magnetometers out of Bombay for good. The reason was that the city was about to electrify its trams: on 7 May 1907 the first electric tram ran from the Municipal Office to Crawford Market.

Some clues, with the guessed inputs marked:

- A tram line is fed with direct current, out along an overhead wire and back along the rails. For a line with several trams running, a few hundred amperes is a reasonable guess; take 500 A.
- Section 13.3's rule: a straight current makes 20 μT at 1 cm for each ampere, falling off in proportion to distance.
- Mumbai's horizontal field is about 38,400 nT. The observatory's purpose was to track the slow, small changes in it, hour to hour and year to year.

Why would trams a few hundred metres away spoil the readings, and why move the whole observatory out of the city instead of shielding the instruments?
???
A tram l

callouts.title: You hold the fridge magnet over, in turn: a ₹1 coin, a ₹2 coin, a ₹5 coin dated 2007, a ₹5 coin dated 2011, a steel spoon, the aluminium foil and the brass key. Which stick?
callouts.body:
- All of them: they are all metal.
- All the coins and the spoon, which are steel; not the foil or the key.
- The ₹1, the ₹2 and the 2007 ₹5. Not the 2011 ₹5, the foil or the key. The spoon depends on the spoon.
???
The third, as far as the Reserve Bank's own notices let us say. The ₹1, ₹2 and 2007 ₹5 are made of a steel that magnets grab. The ₹5 coins issued from 2010 are nickel brass, a copper alloy with no iron in it, expected not to stick, though no source this chapter rests on has tested one, so your magnet is the judge. Foil and brass never stick. And a spoon can go either way, which is the strangest result on the table and the one this section must explain.

callouts.title: Sort your family's coins with a magnet
callouts.body: Every Indian coin has its year stamped on it. Lay out all the coins you can borrow, sorted by value and then by year, and beside each write your prediction: sticks or not. Then test each with the fridge magnet and record what happened. Expect the recent ₹1 and ₹2 coins to stick, and the ₹5 coins to split by year. Coins from 2019 onwards are a newer series whose metals this book has not checked, so treat them as a real experiment. Then do the same for the spoons, bowl and handle separately, the foil, the key and the pin. Two cautions: keep magnets away from phones and bank cards, and keep small strong magnets away from small children, who can swallow them.

In Chapter 12 a rubbed comb lifted scraps of paper. Will the fridge magnet lift the same scraps? And will the comb lift the ₹1 coin?
???
Neither. These are two different forces. The comb's charge pulls feebly on anything at all by separating the charges inside it, enough for paper scraps but never for a coin. The magnet pulls strongly, but only on the few ferromagnetic materials. A charge sitting still has no magnetic effect whatever, as Section 13.3 shows with a compass.

callouts.title: > "Steel is magnetic, so anything made of steel will stick to a magnet."
callouts.body: Steel is a family of metals, and whether a magnet grabs one depends on how its atoms are stacked, not on the label. The ferritic stainless steel of Indian coins is strongly magnetic; the austenitic steel of many spoons and sinks is not, except faintly where it has been pressed or bent. The same goes for "it has nickel in it": behaviour belongs to the material, not to its ingredients.

callouts.title: A plain iron nail, which has never been a magnet, is picked up just as readily by the north end of a bar magnet as by its south end. Why is it never pushed away?
callouts.body:
???
Whichever pole approaches, it magnetises the nail with the *opposite* pole nearest: a north end makes the near end of the nail a south pole, a south end makes it a north pole. Either way the nearest poles are unlike, and unlike attract. Repulsion needs two things that are already magnets, which is why two fridge magnets can push each other apart and a magnet and a nail never do.

callouts.title: Investigation 13.2
callouts.body: Make a compass. Stroke a steel sewing needle about twenty times with one end of your magnet, always the same way, lifting the magnet clear between strokes. Float the needle on a small leaf in a bowl of water away from steel, and wait: it turns and settles. Check it against a phone's compass app, then bring the fridge magnet near and watch which way it swings.

callouts.title: The north end of a compass needle points north. Unlike poles attract. So what kind of magnetic pole is near the Earth's geographic North Pole?
callouts.body:
- A north magnetic pole, because the needle points towards it.
- A south magnetic pole.
- Neither: the Earth only steers the needle, it is not a magnet.
???
A south magnetic pole. The needle's north end points north because something *unlike* it is pulling, and unlike means south. Textbooks admit the muddle: the geographic term "North Pole" has come to be used, incorrectly, for the magnetic pole near it.

callouts.title: Magnetic field
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The condition a magnet or an electric current sets up in the space around it, giving every point a magnetic direction (the way a compass needle's north end points there) and a strength, measured in tesla (T).
? Why is it called this?
*Magnet* comes from Magnesia, the district where lodestones were found in antiquity; Michael Faraday introduced *magnetic field* in the 1840s to describe the region of space around a magnet or wire where magnetic forces act.
? What problem did it solve?
A magnet swings a compass needle and pulls on steel right through empty air or a wooden tabletop without touching them; the field replaces mysterious action at a distance with a measurable property at the exact spot where the compass sits.
? Why does it work?
Moving charges in a wire or aligned electron magnets in iron modify the space around them so that any other magnet or moving charge placed at a point experiences a torque or sideways force determined by the field right at that point.
? How does it help?
Mapping the field's direction and strength lets you navigate with a compass in the Earth's 44 μT field, calculate the sideways force inside an electric motor, and see why electric trams ruined the Colaba Observatory's readings a kilometre away.
?? How do we know?
Move a small compass or a phone's magnetometer step by step around a bar magnet or a current-carrying wire: at every point it settles along a definite direction and reports a strength that weakens predictably with distance.
?? What it isn't
Field lines are a drawing, not physical threads in space: the magnetic field exists smoothly in the gaps between the drawn lines, and iron filings only form separate threads because the magnetised filings stick end to end.
?? Where does it stop working?
A magnetic field exerts zero force on an electric charge that is sitting still relative to it; it pushes only on ferromagnetic materials, other magnets, and charges that are moving.

callouts.title: > "The Earth's North Pole is a north magnetic pole; that's why the compass points to it."
callouts.body: A compass's north end is attracted there, and attraction is between *unlike* poles, so the magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole is a south pole. The names clash because the needle's ends were named after the directions they point, long before anyone understood magnets. Keep the two meanings of "north" apart and the muddle disappears.

callouts.title: A compass in Mumbai points north. Does the Earth's magnetic field at Mumbai point north?
callouts.body:
???
It points north *and downward*, about 28° below the horizontal. Its northward part is larger than its downward part, so a freely tilting needle would lean down rather than point mostly into the ground. An ordinary compass is held level and shows only the horizontal part, which does point north. Gilbert saw the dip on his little Earth four centuries ago.

callouts.title: A wire runs north–south directly over a compass, and when a current flows the needle swings east. You reverse the current along the same wire. Now the needle:
callouts.body:
- Swings east again, since the current is the same size.
- Swings west.
- Does not move: a current either side of the compass cancels out.
???
Swings west. Ørsted saw exactly this, and it told him the direction of the current matters, which no earlier idea about electricity had suggested. Whatever the current makes around itself has a direction that follows the current's own.

callouts.title: Ørsted's twitch
callouts.body: Open “Add wire and Earth fields” beneath the wire-and-compass drawing. Predict the needle’s direction before reversing the current, then compare your prediction with the result. Move the model’s probe farther from the wire and notice how the deflection changes. This keeps the useful question without shorting a cell. For a physical version, use an adult-led school activity with a purpose-made, current-limited teaching kit; never connect bare wire directly across a battery.

callouts.title: > "A charged balloon should swing a compass needle; charge and magnetism are the same thing."
callouts.body: A charge sitting still has no magnetic effect at all, however much of it there is. Only *moving* charge makes a magnetic field: a current in a wire, or the electrons inside a magnet. Charge and magnetism are connected, which is this chapter's discovery, but they are not the same thing, and the field lines round a wire record what a compass would do; nothing streams out along them.

callouts.title: Your wire over the compass carries 1 A and swings the needle 27°. What two separate changes would each make the swing bigger, and roughly how?
callouts.body:
???
Double the current: the wire's field doubles to 40 μT at the same distance, and the needle swings to about 46°, since 40 against 38 is nearly an even match. Or halve the distance: at half a centimetre the field is also doubled. The field grows in proportion to the current and in inverse proportion to the distance.

callouts.title: Two long straight wires hang side by side a few centimetres apart, carrying the same current in the same direction, so each sits in the other's magnetic field. Do the wires:
callouts.body:
- Push apart, like two like charges.
- Pull together.
- Do nothing to each other, since neither is a magnet.
???
Pull together. Currents in the same direction attract and currents in opposite directions repel, the reverse of the rule for charges. Each wire feels a force because it carries a current *through the other's field*, and when you follow the rule below carefully the direction comes out as a pull. It is the force Faraday's wire felt from his magnet.

callouts.title: Follow the turn of a motor
callouts.body: Open “Step inside a motor” beneath the drawing. Follow the current on the two opposite sides of the coil and predict each sideways force. Then let it turn and look for the moment when the current must reverse to keep the turning effect in the same direction. A physical motor is a good adult-led school activity with a purpose-made, current-limited teaching kit. The bare-wire-and-magnet shortcut makes a near short circuit, so it is not a home build in this book.

callouts.title: IGCSE 4.5 calls this the "force on a conductor" and the "d.c. motor", and asks you to find the direction of the force using **Fleming's left-hand rule**: hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of your *left* hand mutually at right angles; point the **F**irst finger along the **F**ield (N to S) and the se**C**ond finger along the conventional **C**urrent (+ to −), and your **Th**umb points in the direction of the **Th**rust (force or motion). Keep your right hand for the next section, where **Fleming's right-hand rule** gives the direction of the induced current in a generator when a wire is moved by an outside force across a field.
A small motor's coil has 50 turns. The maker rewinds it with 100 turns of the same wire carrying the same current. What happens to its turning effect, and why?
callouts.body:
???
It doubles. Each turn is a loop pushed by the same sideways force, so a hundred loops are pushed round twice as hard as fifty. The turning effect grows in proportion to the number of turns, and to the current and the field.

callouts.title: You push the magnet into the coil and the meter needle kicks to the right. Now you hold the magnet perfectly still inside the coil. The meter:
callouts.body:
- Shows a steady reading to the right while the magnet stays in.
- Falls back to zero.
- Kicks to the left.
???
Falls back to zero. A magnet sitting still inside a coil, however strong, produces nothing. Pull it out and the needle kicks to the left; push it in faster and the kick is bigger. Current appears only while the magnetic field through the coil is *changing*.

callouts.title: Electromagnetic induction
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The production of a voltage round a loop of wire whenever the magnetic field threading through the loop changes.
? Why is it called this?
Faraday discovered it in August 1831 and called it *induction*, from Latin *inducere*, to lead in, because a changing magnetic field calls forth a voltage in a nearby coil without any wire touching between them.
? What problem did it solve?
Ørsted had shown in 1820 that an electric current makes magnetism, and for eleven years physicists failed to make a stationary magnet produce a current; Faraday saw that the secret was *change*, not steady strength.
? Why does it work?
A changing magnetic field creates an electric field that curls in a loop around the changing region; any charges in a wire placed along that loop are pushed round by that electric field, and the induced current always runs in the direction that opposes the change.
? How does it help?
Every power-station generator in the world spins magnets and coils past each other to generate alternating current by induction, and every grid transformer steps voltages up or down using a changing field in an iron core.
?? How do we know?
Connect a coil of wire to a sensitive meter and push a magnet in: the needle kicks one way while the magnet moves, drops dead to zero while the magnet sits still inside, and kicks the opposite way when you pull the magnet out.
?? What it isn't
A magnet sitting still beside a coil never generates electricity, and a generator does not create energy out of magnetism; it converts the mechanical work of steam, water or muscle that turns the shaft against magnetic drag.
?? Where does it stop working?
A transformer relies entirely on a *changing* magnetic field in its core, so if you connect its primary coil to a steady DC battery, it gives a single brief kick at switch-on and zero voltage thereafter.

callouts.title: Lenz's law
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The rule, stated by Heinrich Lenz in 1834, that any induced current always flows in the direction whose own magnetic field opposes the change that caused it.
? Why is it called this?
Named after the Baltic German physicist Emil (Heinrich) Lenz, who formulated it three years after Faraday's discovery of induction to give a single universal rule for the sign of every induced current.
? What problem did it solve?
Faraday's law tells you how *big* the induced voltage is from the rate of change of the magnetic field, whereas Lenz's law tells you *which way* the induced current flows without having to guess.
? Why does it work?
It is conservation of energy (Chapter 7) applied to electromagnetism: if pushing a north pole into a coil induced a south pole on the near face, the coil would suck the magnet in faster and faster, creating both kinetic and electrical energy out of nothing. Instead, the near face becomes a north pole that pushes back, so your hand must do mechanical work equal to the electrical energy generated.
? How does it help?
It explains why a generator becomes harder to crank the moment you switch on a heavy load, and how eddy-current brakes slow high-speed trains and rollercoaster cars smoothly without brake pads touching a wheel.
?? How do we know?
Drop a strong neodymium magnet down a vertical copper tube: although copper is not ferromagnetic and does not attract a stationary magnet, the falling magnet induces swirling currents in the copper that repel it from below and attract it from above, making it drift down like a feather in treacle.
?? What it isn't
It does not mean the coil permanently repels magnets; pull the same north pole *out* of the coil and the induced current reverses immediately to make a south pole on the near face that tries to hold the magnet back.
?? Where does it stop working?
If the loop of wire is open (switched off), an induced voltage still appears across its ends, but because no current can flow, there is no opposing magnetic force and the coil turns or the magnet falls freely.

callouts.title: IGCSE 4.5 lists "induction, a.c. generator" and "transformer": the ideas of this section, under those names.

A coil connected to a meter gives a small kick when a magnet is pushed in. Without changing the magnet, name two ways to make the kick larger, and say what would happen if you pushed the magnet in and left it there.
callouts.body:
???
Wind more turns onto the coil (double the turns, double the push), or move the magnet faster so that the field through the coil changes more quickly. Pushing the magnet in and leaving it gives one kick as it enters, then nothing: with the field no longer changing, the induced voltage is zero until something moves.

In Chapter 10 most people drew arrows leaving the eye to touch what it sees. Now that you know what light is, describe what actually happens when you see a lamp across the room.
???
Charges in the lamp's hot filament or glowing LED shake back and forth, and the shaking sends ripples of electric and magnetic field in every direction at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Some cross the room and enter your eye, where they are absorbed. Nothing leaves your eye. With the lamp off, no ripples are made and you see nothing, however hard you look.

callouts.title: A radio in the kitchen plays music that left a transmitter across the city. Sunlight comes through the window. Which is true?
callouts.body:
- They are different things: radio is a kind of electricity in the air, light is a kind of wave.
- They are the same kind of wave, differing only in how fast they wiggle.
- Radio is a wave; light is a stream of tiny particles, so they cannot be compared.
???
The same kind of wave, differing only in frequency. Radio waves wiggle a few hundred million times a second and are metres long; visible light wiggles about a million times faster and is less than a thousandth of a millimetre long. Both are ripples of electric and magnetic field travelling at one speed. (Chapter 15 has a surprise about the third option, which does not undo this one.)

callouts.title: > "Radio waves come from the current flowing in the antenna."
callouts.body: A steady current makes a steady magnetic field, and nothing travels away from it. Waves come only from charges that are *accelerating*: speeding up, slowing down or reversing. An antenna radiates because its current reverses millions of times a second. Shake a charge and you make a wave; let it drift steadily and you do not.

callouts.title: In an electromagnetic wave travelling east, the electric field wiggles up and down. In which direction does the magnetic field wiggle, and in which direction does neither of them point?
callouts.body:
???
North and south: the magnetic field is at right angles to the electric field and to the direction of travel. Neither field ever points east, along the wave's motion. Both wiggle sideways to it, which is what "transverse" meant in Maxwell's sentence.

callouts.title: The trams and the magnetometer
callouts.body:
The Colaba observatory had recorded the Earth's magnetic field at the southern tip of Bombay every hour since 1846. Around 1904 its directors began a second observatory at Alibag, down the coast across the harbour, ran both at once for two years to match one record against the other, and then moved the magnetometers out of Bombay for good. The reason was that the city was about to electrify its trams: on 7 May 1907 the first electric tram ran from the Municipal Office to Crawford Market.

Some clues, with the guessed inputs marked:

- A tram line is fed with direct current, out along an overhead wire and back along the rails. For a line with several trams running, a few hundred amperes is a reasonable guess; take 500 A.
- Section 13.3's rule: a straight current makes 20 μT at 1 cm for each ampere, falling off in proportion to distance.
- Mumbai's horizontal field is about 38,400 nT. The observatory's purpose was to track the slow, small changes in it, hour to hour and year to year.

Why would trams a few hundred metres away spoil the readings, and why move the whole observatory out of the city instead of shielding the instruments?
???
A tram line is a long straight current, and every long straight current is a magnet, exactly as Ørsted's wire was. Scale Section 13.3's number: 500 A at 200 m gives 20 μT × 500 ÷ 20,000, which is 0.5 μT, or 500 nT; at a kilometre it is still 100 nT. Against Mumbai's 38,400 nT that is about one part in eighty, which sounds small until you remember what the observatory was for: tracking changes far smaller than that, hour by hour. Worse, a tram's current is not steady. It rises as trams start, falls as they stop and vanishes at night, so the stray field would come and go with the timetable, forging "storms" in the record that were really the 5:30 service to Crawford Market.

Shielding is no answer, because a magnetometer's whole job is to feel the Earth's field, and anything that kept the trams' field out would keep the Earth's out too. The only cure was distance. Alibag is far enough from any tram for the stray field to fade to nothing, and the Earth's field there is almost the same as at Colaba: about 43.4 μT, dipping 27°. Running both observatories from 1904 to 1906 let the directors, Moos among them, tie the new record to the old. The 500 A and the 200 m are guesses; the physics that drove a scientific institution out of a city is the rule you tested with the wire-and-compass model.

sections.heading: 14.1 Day and night
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Kusumapura, near today's Patna, 499 CE

Every clear night the stars wheel slowly across the sky from east to west. The Sun does the same by day, and so does the Moon. For almost everyone who has ever lived, the explanation was obvious: the sky turns. You can see it turning. Around 499 CE, in Kusumapura on the Ganges, a mathematician named Aryabhata, then about twenty-three, wrote down a different idea in his *Aryabhatiya*. The sky, he said, stands still. It is the Earth that turns, once a day. He gave a picture to go with the claim: a person in a boat drifting down a river sees the trees on the bank slide backwards, although the trees are not moving. In the same way, people on the turning Earth see the fixed stars slide west.

Your first objection is probably the one everyone has had for fifteen hundred years. If Mumbai is being carried round the Earth's axis, it is moving fast: a point at Mumbai's latitude covers about 1,576 kilometres every hour, faster than any aeroplane you have flown in. Surely you would feel that. But think back to Chapter 2. You feel *changes* in motion: the lurch when the local brakes, the push in your back when it pulls away. Steady motion, with n

sections.heading: 14.2 Why seasons happen
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, early January

A January morning in Mumbai is the best the city's weather gets: the air is dry, the nights are almost cool, and January is, on average, the coolest month of the year. It is also the time when the Earth is nearest the Sun. Our orbit is not a perfect circle. In early January we pass about 147.1 million kilometres from the Sun; in early July, about 152.1 million. Light spreads out with distance by the same inverse-square rule that Chapter 5 found for gravity, so the Sun shines on the whole Earth about 7% more strongly in January than in July. That is real, and it is measurable. And it arrives in Mumbai's coolest month.

- It makes no difference at all; sunlight does not weaken with distance
???

sections.heading: 14.3 Phases of the Moon
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Marine Drive, just after sunset

The Sun has gone down into the Arabian Sea, and low in the west, not far from where it set, hangs a thin bright crescent with its horns pointing away from the sunset. Over the next two weeks the crescent fattens night by night into a half, then a swollen oval, then a full round Moon that rises in the east just as the Sun sets in the west. Then it thins again. The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days, which is where the word *month* comes from.

Ask around what makes the dark part of the crescent dark and a good many people, about four in ten in survey after survey, will tell you it is the Earth's shadow. It is a reasonable guess. Shadows are round, the Moon is round, and the Earth is right there with it. Hold the guess up against what you just saw.

:::predict
The crescent is hanging low in the west, near where the Sun went down. The Earth's shadow points directly away from the Sun. Where is the Earth's shadow right now, compared with the Moon?
- Falling on the Moon, making the dark part
- Pointing the opposite way, out towards the east, nowhere near the Moon
- Too short to reach the Moon at all
???
It points the opposite way. The Sun is below

sections.heading: 14.4 Eclipses
sections.excerpt:
Here is a coincidence so neat that it looks designed. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon: about 1,391,000 km across against 3,475 km. It is also about 400 times farther away: 149.6 million km against 384,400 km. Divide one by the other and both discs come out about half a degree wide in our sky, so nearly the same size that the Moon can just cover the Sun.

:::scene Kusumapura, 499 CE, again

Aryabhata, who gave us the boat, also wrote down what an eclipse is. The stories said a demon swallowed the Sun or the Moon. He said it was a shadow: the Moon's shadow falling on the Earth, or the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. Every eclipse since has agreed with him.

A shadow in sunlight has two parts. Behind the Moon there is a cone of complete darkness, the ==umbra==, where the whole Sun is hidden, and around it a wider, lighter region, the ==penumbra==, where only part of the Sun is covered. Hold your hand up to a window and look at its shadow on the floor: the sharp dark centre and the fuzzy grey edge are the same two parts. The Earth's umbra stretches about 1.4 million km out into space behind it, far beyond the Moon's distance.

sections.heading: 14.5 Tides at Haji Ali
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Haji Ali, Mumbai

A narrow causeway runs out from the shore at Worli to the white dargah of Haji Ali on its rock in the sea. Twice a day the sea rises over the causeway and cuts the dargah off; twice a day it falls and the path reappears, wet and crowded. The timing shifts, later each day by close to an hour, and the people who sell flowers at the shore end know the schedule better than any clock. The sea is answering the Moon. Chapter 5 told you that the Earth's pull reaches out across 384,000 km and holds the Moon in its orbit. The Moon's pull reaches back the same distance, and it moves the whole ocean.

Most people, asked how, say that the Moon pulls the water up towards it, and that is a good first half of the story. It raises an immediate problem.

The Moon pulls the sea towards it, and the sea heaps up a little on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. Yet there are two high tides a day at Haji Ali, about twelve and a half hours apart. Where does the second one come from?
- There is a second heap of water on the opposite side of the Earth, facing away from the Moon
- The Sun makes the second one
- The first heap sloshes back across the ocean and arrives a

sections.heading: The causeway timetable
sections.excerpt:
:::case The causeway timetable
Your cousin visited Haji Ali with you last Saturday. You reached the shore at 10:30 in the morning and the causeway was dry, with the sea at its lowest; that night the Moon was full. She wants to go back next Saturday at the same time, "because that's when it was open."

You have three clues from this chapter:

- High and low tide come about 50 minutes later each day, following the Moon.
- The two lows in a day are about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
- The biggest rise and fall come at new and full Moon; the smallest at the quarters.

(These Saturday times are made up for the puzzle. The real ones are in the tide tables.)

Will the causeway be dry next Saturday at 10:30? If not, when should she go, and what else will be different about the tide that day?
???
No. Seven days of 50-minute delays add up to about 5 hours 50 minutes, so last Saturday's 10:30 low falls at about 4:20 in the afternoon next Saturday. The other low of the day, 12 hours 25 minutes earlier, is at about 4 in the morning. At 10:30 she would arrive roughly halfway between a low and a high, with the sea rising over the causeway, the most dangerous time to be anywhere near it.

The toy ti

callouts.title: You are sitting in a local at Dadar, waiting to leave. Through the window, the train on the next track begins to slide slowly backwards. Looking only at that train, can you tell which of the two has started to move?
callouts.body:
- Yes: you can see which train is moving
- No: the view through the window is the same either way
- Only if you feel a jolt or look at the platform
???
The view through the window is the same either way, so the second answer is right, and the third tells you how to settle it: find something else to check against. Astronomers were in exactly this position for more than a thousand years. Watching the stars rise and set cannot tell you whether the sky turns or the Earth does; the two pictures predict the same view from the deck. Deciding between them needed a new kind of evidence, and it came from a pendulum.

callouts.title: > "You can see the Sun go round the Earth. It rises in the east and sets in the west, every day."
callouts.body: You can see the Sun *seem* to go round, and that is a different thing. The view would be exactly the same if the sky stood still and the ground under you turned east, and the Foucault pendulum shows that it is the ground that turns. Aryabhata saw the trap in 499 CE: what you watch from a moving platform is the world sliding the other way. Keep what you observe (the Sun crosses the sky) apart from the model that explains it (the Earth turns), as Chapter 0 asked you to.

callouts.title: IGCSE says the Earth "rotates on its axis, which is tilted, once in approximately 24 hours". Hold on to that *approximately*; 15° an hour is close enough for every question in this book.
Astronomers accepted that the Earth turns long before Foucault. What is wrong with saying "we know the Earth turns because we see the Sun and stars go round us every day"?
callouts.body:
???
Seeing the Sun and stars go round is exactly what you would see whether the sky turned or the Earth did; Aryabhata's boat shows why. The observation cannot choose between the two models. Foucault's pendulum can, because a swinging pendulum keeps its plane, so when the line of its swing turns relative to the floor, the floor must be turning.

callouts.title: The Earth is about 5 million kilometres closer to the Sun in early January than in early July. What does this do to Mumbai's January?
callouts.body:
- It makes January the warmest month
- It makes January a little warmer than it would otherwise be, but something much bigger is making it cool
- It makes no difference at all; sunlight does not weaken with distance
???
The second. The extra 7% of sunlight is real, and January is still the coolest month, so whatever sets the seasons must be far stronger than a 7% change and must be working the other way. A film called *A Private Universe* once put this question to newly graduated Harvard students and some of their professors. Most of those asked got it wrong, and the commonest wrong answer, there and in every survey since, is the one most people reach for first: that summer is when we are nearer the Sun.

callouts.title: The torch and the graph paper
callouts.body: Lay a sheet of graph paper on the table in a dim room and hold a phone torch about 20 cm straight above it. Count, roughly, how many squares the bright patch covers. Now keep the torch at the same height and tilt it so the beam comes in at a slant, as the winter Sun does. The patch stretches into a long oval and covers many more squares, and each square gets less light: tilt the beam 60° from straight down and the patch covers about twice the area, so every square gets about half the light. Nothing about the torch changed. The same light was spread over more ground.

callouts.title: Axial tilt and the seasons
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The 23.44° lean of the Earth's rotation axis away from upright on its orbital plane, which keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year and causes the cycle of seasons.
? Why is it called this?
*Axial* means belonging to the axis, the imaginary line from pole to pole around which the Earth spins; astronomers also call the angle the *obliquity of the ecliptic*, from Latin *obliquus*, slanting.
? What problem did it solve?
It explained why northern and southern hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same moment, and why Mumbai is coolest in January even though the whole Earth is five million kilometres closer to the Sun in early January than in July.
? Why does it work?
Because the axis keeps its direction in space as the Earth orbits the Sun, the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun around June (giving a high noon Sun whose light is concentrated on less ground, and longer days) and leans away around December (giving a lower, more spread-out noon Sun and shorter days).
? How does it help?
From your latitude and the 23.44° tilt alone you can calculate how high the noon Sun stands on the solstices and equinoxes anywhere on Earth, and why places inside the tropics see the noon Sun pass directly overhead twice a year.
?? How do we know?
Measure the noon shadow of a vertical stick in Mumbai across the year: it shrinks until the Sun is 85.6° high in June and stretches until the Sun is only 47.5° high in December, while a stick in Sydney does the exact reverse on the same dates.
?? What it isn't
Summer is not caused by the Earth moving closer to the Sun in its orbit, nor by the tilted hemisphere being a few thousand kilometres nearer the Sun.
?? Where does it stop working?
Angle of sunlight alone does not fix the warmest month at every place: oceans and land take weeks to warm, and in tropical Mumbai the June monsoon clouds and rain cool July below May even though the June Sun stands higher.

callouts.title: > "Summer is when the Earth is closer to the Sun."
callouts.body: The Earth is closest in early January, when Mumbai is coolest and Australia is hottest. A 7% change in sunlight, pointing the wrong way, cannot make a season. What makes a season is the tilt: how high the Sun climbs, and for how many hours it is up. A subtler version of the mistake says the tilted half is a little nearer the Sun and so warmer. The lean brings it a few thousand kilometres closer at most, against 150 million, and the whole Earth is five million kilometres nearer in January anyway.

callouts.title: IGCSE says the Earth "orbits the Sun once in approximately 365 days" and uses that to "explain the periodic nature of the seasons". The orbit explains why the seasons *repeat* every year. The reason there are seasons at all is the tilt of the axis, which the syllabus mentions without connecting it.

Work out how high the noon Sun stands in Mumbai (19.08° N) on 21 December, when the Sun is overhead at 23.44° S. Then say in one sentence why that number, and the length of the day, matter more to the seasons than the 5 million km the Earth moves closer to the Sun that month.
callouts.body:
???
The Sun is overhead 23.44° south of the equator, and Mumbai is 19.08° north of it, so they are 23.44 + 19.08 = 42.52° apart; the Sun's height is 90 − 42.52 = 47.48°, about 47.5°. A Sun at 47.5° spreads the same light over about 35% more ground than a Sun at 85.6°, and shines for about two hours less each day; the extra 7% of sunlight from being closer is smaller than either effect, and it arrives in the coolest month.

callouts.title: The crescent is hanging low in the west, near where the Sun went down. The Earth's shadow points directly away from the Sun. Where is the Earth's shadow right now, compared with the Moon?
callouts.body:
- Falling on the Moon, making the dark part
- Pointing the opposite way, out towards the east, nowhere near the Moon
- Too short to reach the Moon at all
???
It points the opposite way. The Sun is below the western horizon, so the Earth's shadow stretches out to the east, into the night sky on the other side. The Moon is in the west, almost in the Sun's direction. No shadow of ours can be on it. (The third answer is wrong too: the Earth's shadow is about 1.4 million km long and the Moon is only 384,000 km away. It does reach, on the rare nights when the line-up is exact; the next section is about those.) The dark part of the crescent is the Moon's own night side, seen from an angle.

callouts.title: The orange and the lamp
callouts.body: Darken a room so that one lamp or torch is the only light; a bare bulb across the room is ideal. Stand about two metres from it, hold an orange at arm's length a little above your head, and turn slowly on the spot, watching the orange. With your back to the lamp the orange is full: its whole lit side faces you. Turn a quarter and it is half lit, like a quarter Moon. Turn until the orange is almost between you and the lamp and only a thin crescent of light shows along its edge. The lit half of the orange always faces the lamp; your view of it is what changes. Nothing cast a shadow on the orange at any point, and nothing needs to.

"We see the Moon because it shines." Chapter 10 found that we see a thing when light from it enters our eyes. Where does the Moon's light come from, and why does that explain the phases?
???
The Moon makes no light; sunlight falls on it and some bounces off towards us, so we see the Moon the way we see a white wall in daylight. Because the light comes from the Sun, exactly half the Moon is lit at any time, the half facing the Sun. The phases are the changing fraction of that lit half we happen to be looking at as the Moon goes round us. A Moon that glowed by itself would look full every night.

callouts.title: > "The dark part of the Moon is the Earth's shadow falling on it."
callouts.body: The Earth's shadow always points directly away from the Sun. The crescent Moon hangs near the Sun in the sky, at sunset or sunrise, where our shadow cannot reach. The dark part is the Moon's own night side, which the Sun is not shining on, seen from an angle. The Earth's shadow does reach the Moon on rare occasions: only at full Moon, only when the line-up is exact, and then it is called an eclipse, which is the next section.

callouts.title: IGCSE asks for "approximately one month for the Moon to orbit the Earth" and the "cycle of phases". Two months hide in that *approximately*: the Moon goes once round relative to the stars in 27.3 days, but the phases take 29.5 days to repeat, because the Earth has moved on round the Sun meanwhile and the Moon must catch up. If a book says "the dark side of the Moon", read "far side".
Tonight the Moon is full. At roughly what time will it be highest in the sky, and where is the Sun at that moment?
callouts.body:
???
Around midnight. A full Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets, is highest when the Sun is lowest, at midnight, and sets at sunrise.

callouts.title: There is a new Moon every month, when the Moon lies in the Sun's direction. Why isn't there a solar eclipse every month?
callouts.body:
- There is, but each one is seen only from a small part of the Earth
- The Moon's orbit is tilted, so its shadow usually passes above or below the Earth
- The Moon is too small to cover the Sun most of the time
???
The second. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the plane of the Earth's orbit round the Sun. At the far point of that tilt the Moon sits about 34,000 km above or below the plane, and the Earth is only 6,371 km in radius, so in most months the Moon's shadow sails past, above or below us. Only twice a year, when the Sun lines up with the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the plane, can a shadow strike. Those are the eclipse seasons, and every eclipse falls in one of them.

callouts.title: > "The Sun and the Moon are the same size. You can see they are: they match in the sky."
callouts.body: They match in *apparent* size, which is a different thing from actual size. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, and the two 400s cancel, so both look about half a degree across. A coin held at arm's length can cover a building in just the same way. Apparent size is a size divided by a distance, and it tells you nothing about either on its own.

callouts.title: Eclipses are not in the IGCSE syllabus at all; Cambridge Lower Secondary covers them in Stage 7, alongside tides. One phrase to carry into any exam: the Sun and Moon have similar *apparent* sizes. Their actual sizes differ by a factor of about 400.
During a total lunar eclipse the Moon does not go black. It glows a dim copper red. Where is that light coming from?
callouts.body:
???
From the Sun, by way of the Earth's air. Sunlight grazing past the edge of the Earth is bent slightly inward by the atmosphere, into the shadow, and on the way through the air the blue light is scattered away while the red gets through, as at sunset (Chapter 11). What reaches the eclipsed Moon is the red light of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at that moment, and we see it bounced back.

callouts.title: The Moon pulls the sea towards it, and the sea heaps up a little on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. Yet there are two high tides a day at Haji Ali, about twelve and a half hours apart. Where does the second one come from?
callouts.body:
- There is a second heap of water on the opposite side of the Earth, facing away from the Moon
- The Sun makes the second one
- The first heap sloshes back across the ocean and arrives again half a day later
???
The first. There are two heaps, one under the Moon and one on the far side, and the Earth turns under both of them each day. The Sun raises smaller tides of its own, which add to or subtract from the Moon's. Why there should be a heap on the side *away* from the Moon is the real puzzle of this section, and the answer is in how gravity weakens with distance.

callouts.title: Tides
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The twice-daily rise and fall of the oceans caused by the difference in the Moon's (and the Sun's) gravitational pull across the width of the Earth.
? Why is it called this?
From Old English *tid*, meaning time or season, because the sea along the coast rises and falls on a regular schedule that shifts by about 50 minutes each day in step with the Moon.
? What problem did it solve?
If the Moon simply lifted the water facing it, there would be only one high tide a day; explaining why Haji Ali sees *two* high tides every 24 hours 50 minutes required Newton's insight that tides come from the *difference* in gravity from one side of the Earth to the other.
? Why does it work?
The Moon pulls the near ocean about 3.5% harder than the Earth's centre, and pulls the far ocean about 3.5% less hard than the Earth's centre; relative to the Earth, those small differences tug water sideways into two broad bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side, and the spinning Earth carries every coast through both bulges each day.
? How does it help?
It explains why high tides come about 12 hours 25 minutes apart, why the biggest *spring tides* happen at both new Moon and full Moon when Sun and Moon line up, and why *neap tides* happen at the quarter Moons.
?? How do we know?
Compare a harbour's tide table with the Moon's transit times and phases over a month: the two high waters track the Moon's 50-minute daily delay rather than the Sun's 24-hour clock, and the tidal range peaks every 14.8 days at new and full Moon.
?? What it isn't
The Moon does not lift water straight up against the Earth's gravity (which is ten million times stronger); the tiny horizontal component of the tidal force makes water *flow* along the ocean surface over hours.
?? Where does it stop working?
In a small body of water like a lake, a swimming pool or a bucket, both ends are at virtually the same distance from the Moon, so the difference in pull across it is too tiny to pile water up; and on the real Earth, continents and shallow shelves distort the two simple bulges into complex local schedules.

"The Moon is in space, and there's no gravity in space." Chapter 5 had an answer about the Moon falling round the Earth. What do the tides add to it?
???
Gravity does not stop at the top of the air. The Earth's pull reaches 384,000 km to the Moon and keeps it falling round us (Chapter 5), and the Moon's pull reaches 384,000 km back and moves the whole ocean twice a day. If there were no gravity in space there would be no orbit and no tides, and the causeway at Haji Ali would stay dry.

callouts.title: > "The Moon lifts the water up towards it."
callouts.body: Lifting is not what happens, and it could not make a second heap on the far side. The Moon's pull is a little stronger on the near side of the Earth than on the far side. Relative to the Earth as a whole, that tugs the near sea slightly towards the Moon and leaves the far sea slightly behind. Over hours, these tiny differences make water flow sideways along the surface into two heaps. The tide is water that has flowed along. Nothing picked it up.

callouts.title: Investigation 14.5
callouts.body: For one month, write down each day's high-tide times for Mumbai from a published tide table, and the Moon's phase from [The Sky](#explore-sky) or the night sky. Predict first: by how much will the high tide shift from one day to the next, and on which dates will the rise and fall be largest? If you go to see the causeway go under, go with an adult and stay on the shore; never set foot on the causeway when the tide is rising.

callouts.title: Are spring tides something that happens in spring?
callouts.body:
???
No. They happen twice every month, at new Moon and at full Moon, in every season, when the Sun's and the Moon's tidal bulges line up and add. The name means the water "springs up". Neap tides, the smallest, come at the two quarter Moons in between.

callouts.title: The causeway timetable
callouts.body:
Your cousin visited Haji Ali with you last Saturday. You reached the shore at 10:30 in the morning and the causeway was dry, with the sea at its lowest; that night the Moon was full. She wants to go back next Saturday at the same time, "because that's when it was open."

You have three clues from this chapter:

- High and low tide come about 50 minutes later each day, following the Moon.
- The two lows in a day are about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
- The biggest rise and fall come at new and full Moon; the smallest at the quarters.

(These Saturday times are made up for the puzzle. The real ones are in the tide tables.)

Will the causeway be dry next Saturday at 10:30? If not, when should she go, and what else will be different about the tide that day?
???
No. Seven days of 50-minute delays add up to about 5 hours 50 minutes, so last Saturday's 10:30 low falls at about 4:20 in the afternoon next Saturday. The other low of the day, 12 hours 25 minutes earlier, is at about 4 in the morning. At 10:30 she would arrive roughly halfway between a low and a high, with the sea rising over the causeway, the most dangerous time to be anywhere near it.

The toy timetable puts the next low near 4:20 in the afternoon. It cannot tell her when the causeway is safe to cross. She and an adult must use current local guidance and the published tide table, because real tides at Mumbai drift unevenly. One more change: a week after full Moon is the third quarter, so next Saturday's tides are neaps. The sea will rise and fall less than at the full-Moon spring tide she saw. About a fortnight after the first visit, around new Moon, the times come back near where they started and the big tides return.

sections.heading: 15.1 Light comes in packets
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Bern, 1905

In 1905 a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein, published four papers in the journal *Annalen der Physik*. One of them changed how we measure space and time; another gave the world E = mc², which you will meet in Section 15.3. But the Nobel Prize he was eventually given was for the first of the four, which was about something that looks small: what happens when light falls on a metal.

Here is the effect. Shine light on a clean metal surface and, for some metals and some colours of light, electrons come flying out of it. That is the ==photoelectric effect==, and after Chapter 11 you have a ready picture of it. Light is a wave; a wave carries energy; the energy shakes electrons loose. A brighter light is a bigger wave, so it should shake them out harder, and a very dim light should need a little time to build up enough energy before any electron can leave.

:::note Photoelectric effect
Electrons being knocked out of a material by light falling on it. Each electron is freed by one packet of light; the packet must carry at least the energy that binds the electron.
:::

:::predict

sections.heading: 15.2 The nucleus and radiation myths
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Kenilworth, Peddar Road, Bombay, 19 December 1945

A few minutes' walk from Haji Ali, in a house called Kenilworth on Peddar Road, a new institute opened its doors on 19 December 1945. Its founder, Homi Bhabha, had written to his father from Cambridge in 1928 that business and engineering were not for him and that he was burning to do physics; the bargain they struck was an engineering degree first. In March 1944 he wrote to the Sir Dorab Tata Trust proposing an institute for fundamental research, and the Tata Institute, TIFR, began in Bangalore that June before moving to Bombay. Among those who joined it was Bibha Chowdhuri, who had spent the war years leaving photographic plates on mountains at Darjeeling and Sandakphu so that cosmic rays, particles raining in from space, would streak across them, and had found in them the curved tracks of a new kind of particle.

Particles from space pass through you every day. The word for anything that streams out of a source, from radio waves and the remote's infrared to X-rays and the fragments of atoms, is ==radiation==, and it is a word that frightens people. Two fears are common. One is that all radiation is dangerous. The other,

sections.heading: 15.3 E = mc² and the Sun's fire
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Kungälv, Sweden, Christmas 1938

Lise Meitner had fled Germany that summer. She spent Christmas in the small Swedish town of Kungälv with her nephew Otto Frisch, and brought with her a letter from her old colleague Otto Hahn in Berlin. He had been firing neutrons at uranium and had found, among the products, barium: an atom only about half as heavy as uranium. It made no sense. Nuclei chipped; they did not halve. The story goes that the two of them walked out into the snow to think about it, and on that walk they saw what Hahn had done. The uranium nucleus had split in two. They called it ==fission==, and they worked out that the two pieces together have slightly less mass than the nucleus they came from, and that the missing mass had become about 200 million electronvolts of energy, more than a hundred thousand times what any chemical reaction releases per atom. Their paper appeared in *Nature* in February 1939.

:::note Fission
A heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter ones. The pieces have a little less mass than the original, and the difference comes out as energy.
:::

The mass had become energy by the rule from the third of Einstein's 1905 papers, *E* = *mc*². Mass

sections.heading: 15.4 What stars are made of
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Calcutta, 1920

Nobody can visit a star, and yet by 1920 astronomers had been reading the recipe of the Sun for sixty years. The trick is the spectrum from Chapter 11. Spread a star's light into a rainbow and it is crossed by dark lines, hundreds of them in sunlight; Joseph von Fraunhofer counted about 600 in 1815. Each kind of atom swallows its own set of colours, so each element leaves its own pattern of lines, like a barcode. In 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff matched one of the Sun's patterns to sodium, the first element ever identified in a star. Helium was found in the Sun's light before anyone had found it on Earth.

But the stars' barcodes differ. Some show strong hydrogen lines; some, the hottest and bluest, show almost none. The first guess was the obvious one: different lines, different ingredients. In Calcutta a young physicist, Meghnad Saha, saw another possibility. The lines an atom can make depend on where its electrons are sitting, and that depends on how hot the gas is. Heat a gas enough and its atoms lose electrons altogether; an atom with no electron cannot make its usual lines at all. sections.heading: 15.5 How far are the stars?
sections.excerpt:
Hold up your thumb at arm's length against the far wall of the room. Close one eye, then the other. The thumb jumps against the wall. Bring it closer to your face and the jump is bigger; hold it farther away and the jump shrinks. The jump is called ==parallax==, and it is the only direct way we have of measuring the distance to a star.

:::note Parallax
The apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when you look from two places. The farther the object, the smaller the shift. For a star, the two places are the Earth six months apart.
:::

:::predict
You hold a pen at arm's length and note how far it jumps against the wall when you switch eyes. A friend holds it twice as far from your eyes. How big is the jump now?
- Twice as big
- The same
- About half as big
???
About half as big. The shift depends on how far apart your eyes are compared with the distance to the pen, and doubling the distance halves the angle. Now imagine the pen is a star. Your eyes, 6 or 7 centimetres apart, are hopeless. The farthest apart two viewpoints can ever be, for anyone on the Earth, is the two sides of its orbit round the Sun, 300 million kilometres apart: look in January and again

sections.heading: 15.6 How stars die
sections.excerpt:
:::scene At sea, Bombay to England, 1930

In 1930 a nineteen-year-old from Madras, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, nephew of the C. V. Raman of Chapter 11, boarded the SS *Pilsna* at Bombay for England, where he was to study. He had finished college at nineteen. On the long voyage he began working on a problem that sounds harmless: what happens to a star like the Sun when its fuel runs out?

The answer begins with the squeeze. When the core of a Sun-like star has turned its hydrogen into helium, nothing holds it up against its own gravity, and it shrinks. The electrons in it are pressed closer and closer. Then a rule from the quantum world takes over, the Pauli principle: no two electrons can be in the same place at the same time doing the same thing. Press them closer than that rule allows and they push back, with a pressure that has nothing to do with their electric charge and is far stronger than ordinary repulsion. Think of a local at rush hour, where every seat is taken; however hard the crowd pushes at the doors, the seats do not get smaller. The electrons' rule is like that, only stricter. The shrinking stops, and what is left is a ==white dwarf==: the dead core of a star, held

sections.heading: 15.7 The stretching universe
sections.excerpt:
In Chapter 9 the horn of a local dropped in pitch as the train passed you: the sound waves from a source moving away are stretched, so their frequency falls. Light does the same. The lines in the spectrum of a star moving away from us sit at slightly longer wavelengths than they would in a laboratory, shifted towards the red; a star coming towards us shows them shifted towards the blue. The first is called a ==redshift==, and it is the hinge on which the biggest discovery in this book turns.

:::note Redshift
A stretching of light waves, so that every line in a spectrum appears at a longer wavelength than in the laboratory. It shows a source moving away, or, for distant galaxies, space stretching while the light travels.
:::

From 1912 Vesto Slipher measured the light of the spiral "nebulae", the faint smudges that Leavitt's tape would soon show to be other galaxies, and found nearly all of them redshifted: racing away, some at 1,800 km/s. Then Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason, in 1929 and 1931, put Slipher's speeds next to Cepheid distances and found a plain rule, now ==Hubble's law==: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, in proportion. The current value is about 22

sections.heading: The star that's mostly hydrogen
sections.excerpt:
:::case The star that's mostly hydrogen
An astronomer in 1920 lays three spectra on the desk. Star A is hot and blue, and shows almost no hydrogen lines. Star B is a little hotter than the Sun, and its hydrogen lines are the strongest thing in its spectrum. Star C is cool and red, and its hydrogen lines are faint again. Many of the dark lines in all three match metals known on Earth.

The astronomer concludes that Star B is made largely of hydrogen, Stars A and C of something else, and that the Sun, like the Earth's crust, is mostly the familiar heavy stuff.

Use Saha's idea and Payne's result to say what all three stars are really made of, and where the reasoning went wrong.
???
All three are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun: about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with about 2% left for everything else. Star A's hydrogen is so hot that it has lost its electrons, so it cannot make the lines. Star C is so cool that its electrons sit in the lowest level, and the visible hydrogen lines need an electron one step up. Star B is at the temperature where hydrogen shows best.
