callouts.title: Two lamps shine in turn on the same clean metal: a very bright red lamp and a dim violet one. Which knocks electrons out?
callouts.body:
- The bright red lamp, because it delivers far more energy
- Both, the red one more strongly
- Only the violet one, however dim it is
???
Only the violet one, for the calcium example below, and it works the instant it is switched on, however dim it is. Make the red lamp as bright as you like and nothing comes out. Make the violet lamp brighter and *more* electrons come out, each with the same top speed as before. Measured carefully, the effect breaks the wave picture in five places at once: a threshold colour below which nothing happens, whatever the brightness; no delay; a number of electrons that follows the brightness; a top energy that does not; and a top energy that rises in a straight line with the light's frequency.

callouts.title: Photon
callouts.body:
? What is it?
A single quantum packet of light (or any electromagnetic radiation), carrying an energy proportional to the wave's frequency: *E* = *hf*.
? Why is it called this?
Einstein called the packets *light quanta* in 1905; the physical chemist Gilbert Lewis coined *photon* in 1926 from the Greek *phos* (*phot-*), light, to match *electron* and *proton*.
? What problem did it solve?
In the photoelectric effect, dim violet light knocks electrons out of calcium instantly while blazing red light never knocks out a single one; waves that spread their energy smoothly could not explain why colour alone sets a sharp threshold.
? Why does it work?
Whenever light is emitted or absorbed by matter, it hands over its energy one whole packet at a time to one electron; if a single packet (*hf*) is smaller than the energy binding the electron, the electron cannot leave, no matter how many packets arrive per second.
? How does it help?
It explains the photoelectric effect, why ultraviolet light causes sunburn while infrared from a remote control cannot, how solar cells and camera sensors count light, and why atoms emit and absorb sharp spectral lines.
?? How do we know?
Shine monochromatic light on a clean metal in a vacuum and measure the stopping voltage of the freed electrons: below a threshold frequency no electrons appear at any brightness, and above it their maximum kinetic energy rises in a straight line with frequency, with slope *h*.
?? What it isn't
A photon is not a tiny hard marble with mass: it has zero rest mass, always travels at *c* in empty space, and still produces wave interference patterns when sent through two slits.
?? Where does it stop working?
In everyday lamps and radio antennas where trillions of photons arrive together, the individual packets blur into the smooth classical electromagnetic wave of Chapter 13.

callouts.title: See the invisible
callouts.body: Point a television remote at your phone's camera in a dim room, look at the screen, and press a button. The remote's tip flashes a pale light on the screen that your eyes cannot see in the room: infrared, at about 940 nm, a colour just beyond red. Only some cameras show it; if the back camera shows nothing, try the front one. This is light from a small lamp, a torch at a colour you cannot see. It is not the heat of a warm object, and the phone is not "seeing heat". Each of these photons carries about 1.32 eV, less than any visible photon, which is one reason the remote cannot hurt you.

"Light is a wave, full stop." Chapter 11 showed you Young's fringes and Arago's spot. Does the photoelectric effect mean Chapter 11 was wrong?
???
No. The fringes are real and only a wave makes them. The threshold in the photoelectric effect is real too, and only packets make it: a dim violet lamp frees electrons at once while a bright red one never does. Light travels like a wave and delivers its energy in packets of *hf*. Chapter 11 told you half of what light does; this section tells you the other half.

callouts.title: > "A brighter light must give each electron more energy."
callouts.body: Brighter light means more photons each second, and each photon's energy is fixed by the colour alone. So a brighter lamp frees more electrons, each with the same energy as before. If the colour is below the metal's threshold, a brighter lamp frees more of nothing. Remember the remote: it cannot free an electron from calcium however hard you press the button.

callouts.title: The photoelectric effect is not in IGCSE; it arrives in IB Diploma physics under E.2, Quantum physics. IGCSE topic 3.3 does ask for the electromagnetic spectrum: the remote's infrared is one rung of Chapter 11's ladder of light.

A made-up metal needs 2.3 eV to free an electron. Red light, 1.63 eV per photon, is shone on it ten times more brightly than before. Does anything come out? What about dim violet light at 3.26 eV per photon?
callouts.body:
???
Nothing comes out under the red light, however bright: each photon carries 1.63 eV, less than the 2.3 eV needed, and photons do not pool their energy. Dim violet light frees electrons at once, each leaving with up to 3.26 − 2.3 = 0.96 eV.

callouts.title: After a chest X-ray, is the patient radioactive?
callouts.body:
- Yes, for a few hours
- Yes, very slightly, for ever
- No
???
No. An X-ray is a beam of high-energy photons; they pass through the body, some are absorbed, and when the machine switches off there is nothing left behind. Being *exposed* to radiation and being *contaminated* with radioactive material are different things, and the difference is the whole answer to the second fear.

callouts.title: > "Anything that has been near radiation becomes radioactive."
callouts.body: The patient after a diagnostic X-ray and the spices after approved food irradiation do not become radioactive. That is different from radioactive *material* getting on or into something and continuing to emit. Some other radiation, including neutron beams, can change nuclei. Keep the kind and energy of the radiation in view, and keep "exposed" and "contaminated" apart.

callouts.title: IGCSE topic 5.1 is the nuclear model of the atom (Rutherford's gold-foil alpha-scattering evidence, proton number *Z*, nucleon number *A*, and isotopes) and 5.2 is radioactivity: background radiation sources, comparing α, β and γ in ionising effect, penetrating power and deflection in electric and magnetic fields, nuclear decay equations, half-life (subtracting background count rate first!) and safety. When the syllabus says "ionising", it means knocking electrons off atoms, and "contamination" there means what it means here: radioactive material where it should not be.
A packet of chilli powder has been irradiated with gamma rays to kill insects. Is the chilli radioactive?
callouts.body:
???
No. The kinds and energies used in approved food irradiation can kill insects without making the food radioactive. No radioactive material is put into the chilli. This controlled process is different from contamination with radioactive dust, or from other kinds of irradiation that can change nuclei.

callouts.title: If the Sun were a giant ball of coal, burning, how long could it keep shining as brightly as it does now?
callouts.body:
- About as long as it already has: billions of years
- A few million years
- A few thousand years
???
A few thousand years. Burning is chemistry, a few electronvolts per atom, and no chemical fuel the size of the Sun could last longer than that; besides, nothing like coal could survive at the Sun's temperature. The other old idea, that the Sun shines because it is slowly shrinking under its own gravity, reaches only about a hundred million years, and the rocks say that there was liquid water on the Earth nearly four billion years ago. Something far richer than burning is going on, and it is the opposite of fission.

callouts.title: Nuclear fusion
callouts.body:
? What is it?
The joining of two light atomic nuclei into a heavier nucleus whose mass is slightly less than the sum of the pieces, releasing the mass difference as energy according to *E* = *mc*².
? Why is it called this?
*Nuclear* refers to the atom's nucleus; *fusion* comes from Latin *fusio*, melting together, borrowed in the 1930s as the opposite of nuclear *fission* (splitting).
? What problem did it solve?
Neither chemical burning (which would last a few thousand years) nor gravitational shrinking (about a hundred million years) could explain how the Sun has shone for 4.5 billion years; fusing hydrogen into helium releases millions of times more energy per kilogram than any chemical reaction.
? Why does it work?
Quantum tunnelling lets some protons get past their electrical repulsion, and the strong nuclear force binds the final helium nucleus. Across the full reaction chain, four protons and two electrons become a helium-4 nucleus and two neutrinos. Comparing the masses of four hydrogen atoms with one helium atom accounts for the electrons: about 0.71% of the starting mass becomes released energy, yielding about 6.4 × 10¹⁴ J per kilogram of hydrogen.
? How does it help?
It explains what powers the Sun and every main-sequence star, how stars forge heavier elements out of hydrogen and helium, and why the Sun has used only about 0.03% of its mass in 4.5 billion years.
?? How do we know?
We measure the Sun's luminosity (3.8 × 10²⁶ W), compare hydrogen and helium atomic masses to verify the 0.71% mass difference, and detect the neutrinos streaming straight out of the Sun's core from the fusion reactions.
?? What it isn't
It is not chemical burning (which only rearranges outer electrons and leaves nuclei untouched), and it is not nuclear fission (which splits heavy nuclei like uranium).
?? Where does it stop working?
A star’s fusion rate depends strongly on temperature and density, as well as on the nuclei involved. It is not simply a switch that turns on when protons move fast enough to touch: tunnelling matters. Building nuclei heavier than iron generally absorbs energy instead of releasing it.

"Energy is never created. So where does the Sun's energy come from?" Chapter 7 kept a ledger with stores and transfers. What has to go in the ledger to make the Sun's accounts balance?
???
Mass. Four million tonnes of the Sun's mass disappear each second and the same amount of energy appears, at the rate *E* = *mc*². Once mass is counted as a store of energy, the Sun's books balance exactly: nothing is created, and the total of mass-energy stays the same. Chapter 7's rule survives; it just has a larger ledger than you knew.

callouts.title: > "The Sun is burning, like a huge fire."
callouts.body: Burning is a chemical change: atoms swap partners and their electrons rearrange, and the nuclei are never touched. A coal Sun would be ash in a few thousand years. The Sun shines by fusion, which changes the nuclei themselves, hydrogen into helium, and releases about a million times more energy per atom than any flame. Say "shining", or "fusing", and keep "burning" for the kitchen.

callouts.title: IGCSE 1.7.1 lists "nuclear" among the energy stores, and 6.2.1 treats the Sun as a star. The nuclear store is the mass of the Sun's hydrogen, released a little at a time as it becomes helium.
The Sun loses 4 million tonnes of mass every second. Is it in danger of running out soon? Use its mass, 2 × 10³⁰ kg, and its age.
callouts.body:
???
No. Four million tonnes is 4 × 10⁹ kg a second. In 4.5 billion years, about 1.4 × 10¹⁷ seconds, that comes to about 6 × 10²⁶ kg, which is 0.03% of 2 × 10³⁰ kg. Most of the Sun's hydrogen has not fused yet.

callouts.title: A hot blue star shows almost no hydrogen lines in its spectrum. Does that mean it contains almost no hydrogen?
callouts.body:
- Yes: no lines, no hydrogen
- No: it is so hot that its hydrogen atoms have lost their electrons, and cannot make the lines
- The lines are there but drowned out by the blue light
???
No. In the hottest stars nearly every hydrogen atom has been stripped of its electron, so there is nothing left to swallow the hydrogen colours, and the lines vanish. In the coolest stars the lines are weak for the opposite reason: the electrons all sit in their lowest level, and the visible lines need an electron one step up. The hydrogen lines are strongest in stars of middling temperature, and that is the trap: "different-looking spectrum" was read as "different stuff" when it mostly meant "different temperature".

callouts.title: > "Different lines in two stars' spectra mean they are made of different things."
callouts.body: Mostly they mean the stars are at different temperatures. Nearly all stars are made of the same stuff, hydrogen and helium with a sprinkling of everything else; what changes with temperature is which atoms still have the electrons they need to make their lines. Saha's equation lets you allow for that, and when Payne did, the differences in recipe almost vanished.

callouts.title: Investigation 15.4
callouts.body: Hold a CD at a slant under a white LED lamp, as in Chapter 11, and look at the rainbow it throws. Then try an old orange street lamp, if you can find one, and see where the light is and where it is missing. Never point a CD, or anything else, at the Sun.

callouts.title: Why did astronomers expect the Sun to be made of the same stuff as the Earth's crust, and what did they get wrong?
callouts.body:
???
Many of the Sun's dark lines matched elements known on Earth, and it seemed natural that a star should be made of the familiar stuff. The mistake was to read the strength of a line as the amount of the element. Line strength depends on temperature too, because only atoms with their electrons in the right places can make a given line. Once Saha's equation allowed for that, the Sun came out as mostly hydrogen and helium.

callouts.title: You hold a pen at arm's length and note how far it jumps against the wall when you switch eyes. A friend holds it twice as far from your eyes. How big is the jump now?
callouts.body:
- Twice as big
- The same
- About half as big
???
About half as big. The shift depends on how far apart your eyes are compared with the distance to the pen, and doubling the distance halves the angle. Now imagine the pen is a star. Your eyes, 6 or 7 centimetres apart, are hopeless. The farthest apart two viewpoints can ever be, for anyone on the Earth, is the two sides of its orbit round the Sun, 300 million kilometres apart: look in January and again in July.

callouts.title: > "A light-year is a length of time."
callouts.body: It is a distance: how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million kilometres. Proxima Centauri is 4.25 light-years away, which also tells you that its light took 4.25 years to arrive, so you see it as it was four years ago. But the unit measures the road, not the journey.

callouts.title: IGCSE 6.2.2 uses the light-year as the unit for the distances of stars and galaxies. Write it, and think of it, as a distance.
Leavitt's brighter-looking Cepheids pulsed more slowly. Why could she trust that "brighter-looking" meant "truly brighter"?
callouts.body:
???
Because all her Cepheids were in the Small Magellanic Cloud, at very nearly the same distance from us. When distance is the same for every star, the ones that look brighter are the ones that really are brighter. That is what let the pulse, which anyone can time, stand in for the true brightness, which nobody can see directly.

callouts.title: A white dwarf is held up by its crowded electrons. Add more mass to it. Does it get bigger or smaller?
callouts.body:
- Bigger: more stuff takes up more room
- Smaller
- The same size: the electrons are already as close as they can be
???
Smaller. More mass means more gravity, and the extra gravity crushes the electrons closer still. The more massive the white dwarf, the smaller it is, the opposite of everything you handle in daily life. Chandrasekhar's question on the *Pilsna* was where that ends.

callouts.title: IGCSE *6.1.2* and *6.2.1* ask for the accretion model of Solar System formation (gravity pulling a spinning cloud of gas and dust into a flat accretion disk, explaining why the four inner planets are small and rocky while the four outer planets are large and gaseous) alongside the life cycle of stars: nebula → protostar → main-sequence star → red giant (or red supergiant) → planetary nebula + white dwarf (or supernova → neutron star / black hole for the most massive stars).
Will the Sun become a white dwarf?
callouts.body:
???
Yes. The Sun's mass is 1 solar mass, below the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4, so when its fuel is spent its core can be held up by its electrons. Only a core above the limit must collapse further.

callouts.title: Every galaxy we measure, in every direction, is moving away from us, and the farther ones faster. Does that put us at the centre of the universe?
callouts.body:
- Yes: everything is moving away from here
- No: an observer in any galaxy would see exactly the same thing
- Only the nearby galaxies are really moving
???
No. Draw ants on a ruler at the 2, 4, 7 and 12 cm marks, and stretch the ruler so that it doubles in length in one minute. The ant at 2 cm sees the others move away at 2, 5 and 10 cm per minute: speed in proportion to distance, exactly Hubble's law. Now sit on the ant at 7 cm instead: it sees the others recede at 5, 3 and 5 cm per minute, the same law again. Every ant sees itself at the centre, and none of them is. None of the ants moved of its own accord. The ruler stretched.

callouts.title: A balloon universe
callouts.body: With an adult, draw a dozen dots on an uninflated balloon and one short wavy line between two of them. Inflate it slowly and compare the gaps: the farther-apart dots separate more. No dot on the surface is a special centre. The wavy line stretches too, modelling the stretching of light. Watch for a limit of the model: ink dots stretch with the rubber, whereas galaxies held together by gravity do not simply grow with expanding space. The balloon also has a centre inside it; our universe does not need that extra place in the picture.

callouts.title: > "The Big Bang was an explosion at a point in space, and the galaxies are flying away from it."
callouts.body: Nothing is flying out from a point into empty space. Space itself is stretching, everywhere, and the galaxies are carried apart with it, like the ants on the ruler. Every galaxy sees all the others receding, so none is at the centre, and there is no spot you could visit where it began. The rulers, balloons and loaves all have an edge and a middle; the universe has neither.

callouts.title: IGCSE 6.2.3 asks for two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang model: the redshift of light from distant galaxies (showing the universe is expanding, *v* = *H*₀*d*, with 1/*H*₀ giving an estimate for the age of the universe) and the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR, microwave radiation of a specific frequency observed at all points in space, produced shortly after the universe was formed and expanded into the microwave region of the electromagnetic spectrum). The syllabus also says all the matter in the universe was once "present at a single point"; read that as "far closer together, everywhere", because there is no point in today's space where it happened. "Theory" there means a well-tested explanation, never a guess.
As the raisin bread rises, do the raisins grow? Do galaxies grow as the universe stretches?
callouts.body:
???
No, and no. The dough between the raisins expands, and the raisins ride apart on it. Gravity holds each galaxy together against the stretching of space, so galaxies keep their size while the gaps between them grow. Only on the largest scales, between galaxies, does the stretching show.

callouts.title: The star that's mostly hydrogen
callouts.body:
An astronomer in 1920 lays three spectra on the desk. Star A is hot and blue, and shows almost no hydrogen lines. Star B is a little hotter than the Sun, and its hydrogen lines are the strongest thing in its spectrum. Star C is cool and red, and its hydrogen lines are faint again. Many of the dark lines in all three match metals known on Earth.

The astronomer concludes that Star B is made largely of hydrogen, Stars A and C of something else, and that the Sun, like the Earth's crust, is mostly the familiar heavy stuff.

Use Saha's idea and Payne's result to say what all three stars are really made of, and where the reasoning went wrong.
???
All three are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun: about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with about 2% left for everything else. Star A's hydrogen is so hot that it has lost its electrons, so it cannot make the lines. Star C is so cool that its electrons sit in the lowest level, and the visible hydrogen lines need an electron one step up. Star B is at the temperature where hydrogen shows best. The astronomer read line strength as amount, when it depends on temperature as much as on quantity. That is the mistake Saha's equation corrects and Payne's thesis exposed: the stars are mostly hydrogen, and the Earth is the odd one out.

explorers.summary: Trace how conservation laws, vectors, fields, and waves connect every chapter of The Moving World to Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8.

investigations.title: Charge moves; neutral objects respond
investigations.question: If both objects start neutral, can rubbing create net charge?
investigations.explanation: Rubbing moves electrons from one object to the other; it does not create charge. A positive electron deficit on one object exactly matches the negative excess elsewhere. A nearby neutral sample can rearrange its charges while its total charge stays zero.
investigations.limits: Counted charges and displacements are enlarged. Polarisation force is a qualitative proxy, not a molecular simulation.

investigations.title: Inside a conducting shell
investigations.question: Does a metal shell merely weaken the external electric field?
investigations.explanation: Mobile electrons in the metal rearrange until their field cancels the applied field inside the empty cavity. Compare the external field with the induced field, then add them. The transparent inspection view does not make a hole in the shell.
investigations.limits: Analytic conducting sphere in a uniform static field. The cutaway is a view, not a physical opening; this does not model radio-frequency shielding.

investigations.title: Slow electrons, fast signal
investigations.question: Must an electron travel from the battery to the LED before the LED responds?
investigations.explanation: The wire already contains mobile electrons all along its length. A change in the electric field reaches distant parts of the circuit quickly, while each electron drifts only a tiny distance. The two clocks separate those very different speeds.
investigations.limits: Illustrative 1 m wire, signal speed 10^8 m/s and chosen drift speed 0.1 mm/s; the two clocks have separate labelled scales.

investigations.title: Find the dark LED
investigations.question: Can a battery show its normal voltage and still fail under load?
investigations.explanation: Current must pass through the battery’s internal resistance as well as the LED and its resistor. More current causes a larger voltage drop inside the battery, so a battery can show its normal voltage without a load yet supply much less current when connected. The graph’s dot is where the source and load agree on one current and terminal voltage.
investigations.limits: Illustrative exponential I–V with nVt=0.08 V, calibrated to 20 mA at red 2.0 V / white 3.3 V; temperature, leakage, reverse breakdown and component specifications omitted.

investigations.title: Measure two branches
investigations.question: Do unequal parallel branches have equal current or equal voltage?
investigations.explanation: Parallel branches touch the same two junctions, so they share the same voltage difference. The branch with greater resistance carries less current. In series there is only one path, so both loads carry the same current even when their voltage drops differ.
investigations.limits: Ideal resistors and fixed 2 V LED drops in this topology lesson; these are separate from the nonlinear diagnostic model.

investigations.title: A fault in the case
investigations.question: Does a small current leaking to earth look like an overload?
investigations.explanation: Current leaving by live should return by neutral. A separate route to earth makes those currents unequal, so the residual-current device opens the switch. A balanced overload can have no such imbalance yet still require an overcurrent breaker.
investigations.limits: Prescribed prospective fault current, ideal latched 30 mA imbalance / 16 A overload comparisons, no real trip timing or body-resistance prediction; all routes are virtual.

investigations.title: Domains inside a magnet
investigations.question: When a magnet is cut, can one half contain only a north pole?
investigations.explanation: Neighbouring magnetic moments form domains whose different directions can largely cancel. An applied field favours some orientations, moving domain walls and turning moments. Cutting the material does not split those moments into isolated north and south poles: each piece remains a complete magnet.
investigations.limits: Schematic domains: field-dependent orientation and favourable-region growth, not a quantitative hysteresis or atomic-spin model.

investigations.title: A compass that can dip
investigations.question: Does a compass reveal the complete direction of Earth’s field?
investigations.explanation: A freely suspended needle can follow the full sloping magnetic field. Holding it level prevents vertical motion, so it can reveal only the horizontal projection. Rotating the device changes its measured components without rotating the world field.
investigations.limits: Centred ideal dipole, not a local geomagnetic forecast. Latitude controls the ideal dip, which differs from measured Mumbai values.

investigations.title: Add wire and Earth fields
investigations.question: Will reversing the wire current turn a compass exactly 180 degrees?
investigations.explanation: A compass follows the sum of all magnetic fields at its location. The wire’s field circles the wire and reverses with the current, while the northward background remains. Reversing only the wire therefore need not reverse the whole resultant field.
investigations.limits: Long straight wire, 38.4 microtesla horizontal background. The tram preset treats one distant current and omits the return conductor. Coil contributions use the on-axis Biot–Savart field of circular loops of 1 cm radius, spaced 1 mm apart. The centre probe is fixed in that mode; field-arrow scales are printed separately.

investigations.title: Step inside a motor
investigations.question: Why must the current reverse every half-turn?
investigations.explanation: Opposite sides of the coil carry opposite currents and feel opposite sideways forces, producing a turning effect. After half a turn, unchanged current would reverse that turning effect. The split ring swaps the current direction so the turning effect keeps the same sense.
investigations.limits: Uniform 0.5 T field, 10 turns of 0.04 m² area. Rotor inertia 0.08 kg·m² and damping 0.35 s^-1 are chosen model values; ideal instantaneous commutation. Holding freezes the rotor for inspection; open circuit removes electrical torque while a moving rotor coasts. Back emf is omitted.

investigations.title: Turn a generator
investigations.question: Does the largest flux always mean the largest induced voltage?
investigations.explanation: As the coil turns, the amount of magnetic field passing through it changes; this amount is called flux. Induced voltage follows how quickly the flux changes. At a maximum or minimum flux, the change is momentarily zero, so the voltage is zero even though the flux is large.
investigations.limits: Uniform field, ideal coil; mechanical rotation is supplied externally. Loading and self-inductance are omitted.

investigations.title: Two coils, one changing field
investigations.question: Can a steady direct current keep inducing voltage in a second coil?
investigations.explanation: A changing magnetic field in the shared core produces a voltage around each coil. More turns add more induced voltage, giving the turns ratio. Steady direct current leaves a steady field after switching, so it gives no sustained secondary voltage.
investigations.limits: AC control is RMS voltage, with an ideal resistive secondary load and no core losses/saturation. Separate steady DC comparison assumes 10 Ω primary winding resistance and schematic stored flux; switching transient omitted.

investigations.title: Two fields across a gap
investigations.question: Does either field point along the wave’s travel direction?
investigations.explanation: At a fixed point the electric and magnetic fields change together. Both point across the direction of travel, at right angles to one another. The moving curves show a travelling pattern of field values, not material moving along the curves.
investigations.limits: Plane wave; amplitudes use independent diagram scales. Wavelength spans are normalised and the animation is enormously slowed.

investigations.title: Earth turns beneath the sky
investigations.question: Which way must Earth turn for stars to seem to move west?
investigations.explanation: Earth turns eastward beneath the distant Sun and stars. The same surface observer moves between the lit and dark hemispheres, while the sky appears to move the other way. The local-horizon view describes those same directions from the observer’s turning frame.
investigations.limits: Ideal sphere and distant Sun; solar time, not Mumbai civil time. Star coordinates are illustrative.

investigations.title: Tilt, sunlight and daylight
investigations.question: If tilt is zero but the orbit remains, do the seasons remain?
investigations.explanation: A hemisphere tilted toward the Sun receives higher-angle sunlight over a smaller footprint and has longer daylight. The opposite hemisphere receives lower-angle sunlight and shorter days at the same time. Removing the tilt removes these seasonal differences in the circular-orbit model.
investigations.limits: Circular orbit isolates tilt. Bodies are enlarged independently of orbital distance so the axis and daylight arcs can be inspected. Daily geometry is approximate and ignores refraction and weather.

investigations.title: The Moon has to turn
investigations.question: Would a Moon that never rotated always show us the same face?
investigations.explanation: To keep one marked face directed toward Earth, the Moon must turn once while travelling once around Earth. A Moon with no axial rotation would keep its marked direction fixed in space, so Earth would see different sides. Sunlight sets the illuminated half independently of that face marker.
investigations.limits: Circular orbit with schematic sizes. Lunar libration is omitted; this is not a dated Moon-rise calculator.

investigations.title: Find an eclipse by geometry
investigations.question: Why can a new Moon miss the Sun–Earth line?
investigations.explanation: Most new or full Moons pass above or below the Sun–Earth line because the lunar orbit is tilted. Near the two places where the orbital planes cross, the bodies can align and a shadow can intersect the target. The close-up shows the same calculated alignment and shadow boundaries as the overview.
investigations.limits: Circular orbits and fixed nodes; no dated ephemeris. Earth, Moon, orbital distance and shadow widths share one scale in 3D. The linked cut states its longitudinal and transverse scales; the optional central detail enlarges all transverse distances together.

investigations.title: Subtract Earth’s central pull
investigations.question: Why is there an outward relative pull on the far side?
investigations.explanation: The Moon pulls the near side more strongly than Earth’s centre and the far side less strongly. Relative to the falling centre, the near side accelerates toward the Moon while the far side falls behind. That far-side relative arrow points outward even though the Moon’s absolute pull is still inward.
investigations.limits: Ideal equilibrium tide pattern, with arrows hugely enlarged. Continents, ocean dynamics and Haji Ali timing are not predicted.

investigations.title: Count photons and electrons
investigations.question: Can bright red light beat the threshold by pooling its photons?
investigations.explanation: In this model one electron receives energy from one photon. Below the threshold, adding more photons does not give any one electron enough energy to escape. Above it, photon energy sets the maximum electron kinetic energy, while photon flux controls how many electrons can be emitted.
investigations.limits: Single-photon calcium model with work function 2.71 eV. A uniform 0-to-maximum electron-energy distribution is illustrative; multiphoton effects are outside this model.

investigations.title: An atom is mostly space
investigations.question: If a nucleus were a 1 cm marble, how large would the atom be?
investigations.explanation: The chosen atom reference diameter is one hundred thousand times the nucleus diameter. A nucleus one centimetre across would therefore belong to an atom reference about one kilometre across. At a true common scale the nucleus is unresolved; the cloud outline is a probability-region symbol, not an orbit or a solid wall.
investigations.limits: Approximate 10^5 diameter ratio; a cloud outline is a probability-region symbol rather than a solid boundary.

investigations.title: Exposure, contamination and decay
investigations.question: Does switching off a beam remove radioactive dust?
investigations.explanation: An external beam stops exposing the object when its source is switched off. Radioactive dust is different: the emitting atoms remain on the surface until removed or decayed. Each nucleus has a random decay time, while many nuclei together approach the smooth exponential expectation.
investigations.limits: Simulated decay events; half-life is chosen in arbitrary model seconds. No dose or biological-effect calculation.

investigations.title: From the solar core to light
investigations.question: Does the Sun’s light come from chemical burning at its surface?
investigations.explanation: Fusion in the hot core combines hydrogen into helium and releases energy corresponding to the reduction in total rest mass. Neutrinos carry some energy straight out; most heats the Sun and is transported through the radiative and convective layers before escaping as light. The visible transport sequence is schematic, not a measured travel-time simulation.
investigations.limits: Net reaction and atomic masses are bookkeeping. Transport is a schematic stage sequence, not a simulated photon diffusion time.

investigations.title: A halo around L1
investigations.question: Is L1 a place where gravity is zero?
investigations.explanation: The Sun’s pull and Earth’s opposing pull do not cancel at L1. Their remaining inward acceleration is what a craft needs to follow Earth’s yearly orbital motion. The linked projections show one schematic three-dimensional path near that balance region; they are not a mission forecast.
investigations.limits: Point masses for the force account; its distance control does not relocate the independently schematic 177.86-day halo. No mission ephemeris or integrated restricted-three-body orbit.

investigations.title: Same hydrogen, different lines
investigations.question: Does a weak hydrogen line mean little hydrogen?
investigations.explanation: In cool hydrogen few electrons occupy the excited level needed for strong Balmer absorption. At very high temperature much hydrogen is ionised, again leaving few electrons in that level. Stronger lines at an intermediate temperature therefore need not mean more hydrogen; compare temperature first, then abundance.
investigations.limits: LTE Saha–Boltzmann population proxy at fixed electron density 10^20 m^-3, ground-state partition approximation. Line depths are illustrative, not an atmosphere fit.

investigations.title: From a blink to a distance
investigations.question: Can a star look faint because it is distant rather than weak?
investigations.explanation: Parallax compares a known baseline with a tiny apparent shift. For a Cepheid, a calibrated relation between pulse period and luminosity estimates how bright the star really is. Comparing that luminosity with the received mean flux gives distance through the inverse-square relation; the pulse and graph share one clock.
investigations.limits: Triangle uses logarithmic distance and exaggerated angles; numerical parallax is physical. Cepheid relation and icon radius/colour are illustrative; extinction, metallicity and calibration uncertainty omitted.

investigations.title: More mass, smaller dwarf
investigations.question: Does adding material always make a star bigger?
investigations.explanation: No two electrons can occupy the same complete quantum state. Compression fills higher-momentum states, creating pressure even when the gas is cold. More mass means stronger gravity and a smaller supported radius; at the limiting mass this ideal stable model fails rather than producing a real zero-size star.
investigations.limits: Zero-temperature ideal relation with 1.44-solar-mass limiting mass. Zero radius marks model breakdown, not a physical white dwarf of zero size.

investigations.title: Choose another galaxy
investigations.question: If every distant galaxy recedes, are we at the centre?
investigations.explanation: Multiplying every separation by the same factor increases a larger separation by a larger amount. Any chosen galaxy therefore finds the same distance–recession relation when measuring relative positions. Individual bound galaxies keep their sizes while the gaps expand in this model.
investigations.limits: Homogeneous low-redshift Hubble-flow model; local peculiar velocities and general-relativistic light propagation are omitted.

investigations.title: A pendulum and a turning Earth
investigations.question: Would a Foucault pendulum precess equally in Mumbai and at the equator?
investigations.explanation: At a pole, Earth turns the floor beneath the swing through one full rotation per sidereal day. At lower latitude only the component of Earth’s rotation along the local vertical contributes to the slow turning of the swing direction relative to the floor. That component vanishes at the equator.
investigations.limits: Small-amplitude ideal pendulum; precession is the local approximation, not a claim of one globally fixed swing plane at every latitude.

investigations.title: An axle parallel to Earth’s
investigations.question: Why does Ooty’s latitude match the telescope’s slope?
investigations.explanation: An axle parallel to Earth’s rotation axis lets a telescope compensate for Earth’s turn by rotating about that one axis. Its elevation above a level horizon equals the observatory’s latitude. Mesh openings much smaller than the wavelength can act approximately like a continuous conductor; that size comparison is qualitative here.
investigations.limits: Equatorial-mount geometry is exact; mesh reflection is a qualitative wavelength comparison, not an electromagnetic solver.

investigations.title: Read a track through emulsion
investigations.question: Can a flat microscope image hide motion through the plate?
investigations.explanation: At a known momentum, a heavier charged particle moves more slowly and has a larger scattering and ionisation proxy in this model. Emulsion grains record a track, but a flat projection hides its depth. Finite microscope resolution broadens the conditional mass and speed interval rather than uniquely identifying the particle.
investigations.limits: Highland x/X₀=.01 proxy, 1/β² grain-density proxy; transverse magnification and resolution are labelled. Interval conditions on known momentum/material and omits energy loss and sampling uncertainty. This does not reconstruct historical plates.

investigations.title: Nature and its mirror
investigations.question: Does a mirror image of the weak-decay pattern remain an allowed pattern?
investigations.explanation: The electrons are emitted more often on one side of the aligned nuclear spins. A mirror transforms a spin arrow, defined by a right-hand rule, differently from an ordinary motion arrow. The mirrored picture reverses their correlation; weak decay favours one correlation rather than treating its mirror as equivalent.
investigations.limits: Illustrative angular asymmetry parameter 0.8, not historical count data. Nuclear spin is an arrow, not a classical spinning ball.

investigations.title: Count states, not labels
investigations.question: Does exchanging two identical photons produce a new state?
investigations.explanation: Swapping the named particles A and B changes a labelled arrangement. Swapping identical bosons leaves the observable occupation unchanged, so it must not be counted again. Identical same-spin fermions cannot share one one-particle state; the available-state and energy assumptions remain fixed here.
investigations.limits: Fixed two particles, two available one-particle states; no fixed-total-energy constraint. Counts alone do not assign general probabilities or derive Planck’s law.

investigations.title: Measure a tiny displaced star
investigations.question: Does one noisy measurement prove a theory?
investigations.explanation: An uncertainty interval shows the range allowed by the measurement’s finite precision. If two predictions both lie inside it, this measurement cannot distinguish them. Reducing the uncertainty may exclude a prediction, but agreement with one result alone does not prove a theory.
investigations.limits: Solar-limb general-relativistic deflection 1.75 arcseconds, scaled by inverse impact parameter. The plot is simulated evidence, not the 1919 plates. The 3D ray bend is enlarged for inspection; use the labelled arcsecond plot for measurement.

investigations.title: Race a hoop and a cylinder
investigations.question: Does equal mass mean an equal finish time?
investigations.explanation: Mass farther from the axis needs more energy for the same spin rate. Less of the height loss becomes forward kinetic energy.
investigations.limits: Rigid objects, no slipping, constant slope and negligible rolling resistance. The bodies are equal in mass and radius. Household containers may have moving contents; that needs a different model.
investigations.materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: gentle book ramp, two sturdy round objects, clear desk; adult helps secure the ramp.
procedure: Choose two round objects and a gentle ramp over a clear desk, or use the model. Release together without a push.
Keep the ramp and starting height fixed. Compare finish times; repeat three times.
In the model, vary the inertia factor while leaving mass and radius fixed. Record model readings separately from physical observations.
investigations.worked: On a 30° ramp, a solid cylinder (k = 0.5) accelerates at 3.27 m/s²; a hoop (k = 1) at 2.45 m/s².
investigations.challenge: If you move the same mass towards the axis, which object now wins? Explain without calculating.

investigations.title: Balance is more than equal forces
investigations.question: Can forces balance while the object starts turning?
investigations.explanation: A balanced beam needs zero net force and zero net torque. The separate free-bar force pair shows how zero net force can coexist with a turning effect.
investigations.limits: Beam: massless rigid beam with two point loads on a fixed frictionless pivot, shown horizontal at release. An unbalanced beam has angular acceleration and a downward centre-of-mass acceleration; the support reaction is calculated from both. Pair mode: view from above of a free bar; equal opposite in-plane forces, no pivot.
investigations.materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: ruler, stable desk support, tiny known loads; no heavy balancing objects.
procedure: Balance a ruler across a stable narrow support on a desk; keep loads small and off feet. Or use the beam model.
Put loads on opposite sides. Keep one position fixed and find a position that balances.
Repeat with a different pivot. Record distance from pivot, not distance from the ruler end.
investigations.worked: A 0.2 kg load 0.2 m left balances 0.4 kg placed 0.1 m right of the pivot: both turning effects are 0.392 N·m.
investigations.challenge: Could two equal weights fail to balance? Give a placement and explain it.

investigations.title: Measure what a bounce returns
investigations.question: If 80% of the speed returns, does 80% of the energy return?
investigations.explanation: Height measures gravitational energy. Speed depends on the square root of height; speed ratio and energy ratio therefore differ.
investigations.limits: Vertical bounce from rest on a fixed floor, negligible air drag and rotation. Restitution is a ball/surface/impact-condition property, not a universal constant. Microphone echoes are not used as measurements.
investigations.materials: Soft ball, ruler, clear floor and optional local slow-motion clip. Supplied observations need no equipment.
procedure: Use the linked local video tracker to mark the highest point after each bounce; put a ruler in the same plane. Or use the supplied observations.
Keep ball, surface and camera position fixed. Enter successive drop and rebound heights in metres; repeat a height three times.
Compare your height ratios with the model. Explain where mechanical energy went and what measurement could test your account.
investigations.worked: From 1.00 m to 0.64 m: e = 0.80 and mechanical-energy fraction = 0.64; 36% became other stores and sound.
investigations.challenge: A ball returns to half its height. Is its speed ratio one half? Explain.

investigations.title: Make a sealed diver sink
investigations.question: What changes when a sealed packet sinks after a squeeze?
investigations.explanation: The air compresses, making the sealed packet smaller. The packet displaces less water, so buoyancy can drop below its unchanged weight.
investigations.limits: Illustrative sealed packet: 9 mL incompressible material plus 1 mL air at 101.325 kPa, mass 9.8 g. Slow, approximately isothermal compression; water compression is neglected. A real packet may be too dense to float.
investigations.materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: sealed flexible packet, water and plastic bottle; adult helps choose a barely floating packet.
procedure: Use the supplied packet model, or with an adult select a sealed condiment packet that barely floats inside a plastic water bottle.
Squeeze gently, release, and describe the change before explaining it. Keep the packet sealed.
Compare air-pocket volume and displaced water at several pressures. This model uses fixed packet mass, not water entering an open diver.
investigations.worked: Doubling pressure halves the 1 mL air pocket. Packet volume becomes 9.5 mL, below the 9.8 mL needed to support 9.8 g.
investigations.challenge: Would squeezing a completely solid incompressible packet work the same way? Why?

investigations.title: Warm it or squeeze it?
investigations.question: Can two different changes produce the same pressure?
investigations.explanation: Gas pressure depends on amount, volume and absolute temperature. Compression and warming are different changes that can produce the same pressure ratio.
investigations.limits: Fixed gas amount, ideal gas, equilibrium states. Baseline: 1 L at 300 K and 101325 Pa. No real container heating or molecular collision trajectories are simulated.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Choose the constant-temperature route and vary volume.
Choose the fixed-volume route and vary temperature in kelvin. Record the pressure each time.
Compare both with the baseline. Keep the amount of gas fixed; no heated sealed container is needed.
investigations.worked: 1 L at 600 K and 0.5 L at 300 K both give 202650 Pa for this fixed amount.
investigations.challenge: Does warming from 20°C to 40°C double pressure in a rigid container? Explain.

investigations.title: One yo-yo, two questions
investigations.question: Does a smaller axle make an unwinding yo-yo fall faster?
investigations.explanation: Unwinding couples the fall to spin through string tension. A small axle requires more spin for the same downward speed.
investigations.limits: Pendulum: point-bob approximation, small angle, no unwinding. Unwinding: fixed end, massless string, no slip on axle, no return tug, outer radius 4 cm and mass 1 kg. Illustrated angle is slowed.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Use Pendulum to vary string length and predict the period.
Use Unwinding to compare axle radii while outer radius and mass distribution stay fixed.
Trace the same height loss into translation and rotation; record a model reading and explain why the pendulum formula no longer applies.
investigations.worked: For k=0.5, R=4 cm and r=1 cm, a=g/9≈1.09 m/s². This is not free fall.
investigations.challenge: Why does the same yo-yo need different equations when it hangs and when it unwinds?

investigations.title: Calibrate a spring; question a rubber band
investigations.question: Must every stretch graph be a straight line?
investigations.explanation: A straight load–extension graph describes an approximately linear spring. Elastic recovery alone does not require a straight graph.
investigations.limits: Quasistatic loading; linear F=kx or illustrative nonlinear F=kx+800x³ (SI). The rubber-like curve is not a fit to a particular band and has no hysteresis. Do not stretch bands near eyes.
investigations.materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: small spring, ruler and tiny known loads over a desk; adult helps secure it.
procedure: Use a small spring and tiny known loads over a desk, or use the supplied observations. Mark the unloaded position.
Add loads gently and record extension, not total length. Repeat each load; hold the spring and ruler fixed.
Plot force against extension. Compare a straight-line model with the curved model. Real rubber may also show different loading and unloading paths.
investigations.worked: A 20 N/m linear spring stretches 0.10 m under 2 N, storing 0.10 J.
investigations.challenge: If a rubber band springs back, must its graph be a straight line? What would you measure?

investigations.title: Why a spinning top precesses
investigations.question: Does spin remove the downward force of gravity?
investigations.explanation: Gravity still acts. Its torque changes the direction of angular momentum, so the axis sweeps around.
investigations.limits: Fast symmetric top, slow steady precession, fixed tilt; ignores nutation and spin loss. m=0.1 kg, centre 0.04 m from support, I=0.0001 kg·m². Spin 80–160 rad/s; precession is much slower. No physical balancing required. Torque projection is drawn about the support; the centre is not the pivot.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Choose a tilt and spin rate in the virtual top.
Follow the angular momentum arrow and the horizontal torque that turns it.
Record precession at several spin rates and compare the inverse trend. This is a steady-precession approximation, not a full top falling to rest.
investigations.worked: At ω=80 rad/s, Ω≈4.9 rad/s. At 160 rad/s it is≈2.45 rad/s.
investigations.challenge: Which force disappeared when the top began to spin? If none, what changed?

investigations.title: A flying disc needs more than a parabola
investigations.question: What does a gravity-only prediction leave out?
investigations.explanation: Moving air produces lift normal to the flight velocity and drag opposite it in this simplified model. Spin helps orientation stability but does not supply forward energy.
investigations.limits: Two-dimensional illustrative flight from 1 m, mass 0.175 kg, area 0.057 m², density 1.2 kg/m³, fixed C_L=.30 and C_D=.12. No attitude, spin or stall dynamics; launch elevation is not angle of attack. This is not a prediction for a particular disc.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Choose the same launch speed and elevation for both models.
Compare range and flight time; record the model used beside every reading.
Explain which observations would need a better model: wind, changing angle of attack, wobble or spin loss. Use the virtual route indoors.
investigations.worked: At 10 m/s and 30° from 1 m above the floor, the gravity-only range is about 10.32 m.
investigations.challenge: Can a decorative spinning disc on a parabolic path demonstrate lift? Explain what is missing.

investigations.title: Shake, store, shine
investigations.question: Can a stationary magnet keep a flashlight lit?
investigations.explanation: Changing flux induces voltage. Hand work can become stored electrical energy, light and heat; taking energy out opposes the driving motion.
investigations.limits: Ideal rectified source E=2v, a 0.1 F capacitor charged through 10Ω, then discharged through a 10Ω lamp-equivalent. No LED threshold, real magnetic waveform or conversion efficiency is modeled. No mains or physical wiring needed.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Choose a representative magnet speed and a charging duration.
Stop shaking and increase the time since stopping. Watch the capacitor discharge into the lamp-equivalent load.
Record energy values and check the complete account, including winding heat. Compare with the linked generator.
investigations.worked: At 2 m/s the representative EMF is 4 V. A capacitor approaches but does not exceed that voltage in this circuit.
investigations.challenge: Where does the lamp energy come from after your hand stops? Why is the magnet not a fuel?

investigations.title: Measure waves with virtual chocolate
investigations.question: Are neighbouring hot regions a whole wavelength apart?
investigations.explanation: A simple standing wave has neighbouring antinodes half a wavelength apart. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
investigations.limits: One-dimensional ideal standing-wave pattern. A real oven has several cavity modes and nonuniform heating. Virtual food only; never modify an appliance or require a child to handle hot food.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Use the supplied virtual pattern. Enter adjacent hot-region spacing in centimetres and frequency in GHz.
Repeat several spacings and record the resolution. Compare the resulting estimates.
Explain why arbitrary melt spots in a real oven may not be adjacent antinodes. No appliance experiment is required.
investigations.worked: 6.1 cm and 2.45 GHz give λ=.122 m and speed≈2.989×10⁸ m/s.
investigations.challenge: A learner uses c=df. What factor is missing, and what observation justifies it?

investigations.title: One light clock, two observers
investigations.question: How can the same light have a longer path and the same speed?
investigations.explanation: The moving clock has a diagonal light path in the ground frame. Both accounts use the same light speed; the ground-frame tick interval is longer.
investigations.limits: Inertial frames, ideal mirrors 1 light-second apart transversely; units c=1. Ground-frame time drives both panels, and ship proper time is t/γ. No acceleration, journey turnaround or gravity. Light travel delay is not time dilation.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Begin at zero relative speed; both frame accounts coincide.
Set speed to0.6c and move the ground-time control through a complete tick.
Compare the same reflection events in both panels. The proper-time clock is aboard the carriage. This is a coordinate account, not delayed camera footage.
investigations.worked: At 0.6c, γ=1.25. A 2 s ship tick takes 2.5 s in the ground frame.
investigations.challenge: Is this just waiting longer for light to reach a camera? Explain how the two panels define their times.

investigations.title: Many samples, one probability law
investigations.question: Must exactly half of a small sample remain after one half-life?
investigations.explanation: Half-life is a probability statement. Individual lifetimes vary; an expectation curve describes the ensemble, and small samples fluctuate visibly.
investigations.limits: Independent exponential lifetimes with a fixed half-life of 2 model s; five pseudorandom seeded samples. Coins are a probability analogy, not the mechanism of nuclear decay. No radioactive material is used.
investigations.materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: coins or two-sided counters on a tray; no radioactive materials.
procedure: Use the virtual samples or toss a set of coins. Remove heads after each round and toss only the survivors.
Enter round number and survivor count. Repeat the whole experiment with the same initial number.
Compare separate runs with the expectation curve. Do not pool supplied model values with physical observations.
investigations.worked: For 64 initial nuclei, the expected number after 4 s is 16. A particular sample need not contain exactly 16.
investigations.challenge: If a nucleus survived ten half-lives, is it now more likely to decay in the next half-life?

investigations.title: Build a nucleon; explore the particle families
investigations.question: Is a proton elementary, or does it have constituents?
investigations.explanation: Protons and neutrons are composite. Quarks and leptons are elementary matter particles in the Standard Model; interaction bosons and the Higgs have different roles.
investigations.limits: Valence-quark bookkeeping, not a picture of quark orbits or a complete proton wavefunction. Additional sea quarks and gluons matter. Gravity is outside the Standard Model; most nucleon mass comes from strong-interaction energy, not simply quark Higgs masses.
investigations.materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
procedure: Compare uud and udd. Add charges before revealing the sum.
Select each particle family and read what the model can and cannot explain.
Connect the atom-scale, tracks and parity lessons. Write an evidence-based question that this simple constituent diagram cannot answer.
investigations.challenge: Why is a neutron neutral without each constituent being neutral? What important physics is missing from three colored circles?

investigations.title: Find the right model for a colourful surface
investigations.question: Must every rainbow-coloured object act like a prism?
investigations.explanation: Different mechanisms can sort or select wavelengths. A grating, a thin film, a prism and a polariser require different accounts.
investigations.limits: Schematics and links to the existing calculated optics lessons. Thin-film and grating colours depend on geometry and material; this directory is not a quantitative fit to a particular photographed surface. No laser is required. The filter panel uses Malus’s law for an ideal analyser and initially linearly polarised incident light; it is not a complete model of unpolarised glare.
investigations.materials: Model and linked experiments: nothing. Optional CD, soap-film image and polarising sunglasses; ordinary reflected light only.
procedure: Choose a surface and make a prediction before opening its linked experiment.
Observe changes with angle, filter rotation or illumination. Record what changed and what stayed fixed.
Return here and explain which model fits. A colour name alone is not an explanation. Use supplied descriptions if the objects are unavailable.
investigations.worked: Rotating a polariser can reduce a reflected glare patch while a neighbouring matte surface changes less.
investigations.challenge: What observation could distinguish a prism rainbow from colours produced by fine tracks?

investigations.title: A magnet falls through a conducting tube
investigations.question: Can a nonmagnetic metal slow a falling magnet?
investigations.explanation: Moving magnetic flux induces currents in the conducting tube. Their magnetic effect resists the motion, transferring energy into warming.
investigations.limits: Illustrative low-speed electromagnetic drag F=−bv, mass0.020 kg, one-metre tube. Constant b is a lumped approximation, not a conductivity measurement. No entry/exit field detail. The scene ends at first contact; contact energy is not modeled.
investigations.materials: Virtual experiment: no equipment. A physical magnet-and-tube demonstration requires adult handling of strong magnets.
procedure: Compare the virtual nonconducting tube with the conducting-tube model. No strong magnets are needed.
Change the drag coefficient and follow the shared time control. Record fall times and compare the two energy accounts.
Explain where gravitational energy goes before the magnet hits the bottom.
investigations.worked: With no electromagnetic drag, a one-metre fall takes about0.452 s. A conducting tube takes longer in this model.
investigations.challenge: Would cutting a lengthwise slot in the conducting tube change the braking? Explain using the current paths.

investigations.title: Listen to the time between bounces
investigations.question: What can three impact times tell you about the next bounce?
investigations.explanation: Between two floor impacts, a vertical ball rises and falls. The flight interval is proportional to its launch speed, so the ratio of consecutive intervals estimates restitution.
investigations.limits: Manual or supplied impact intervals; no automatic microphone detection. Negligible drag, short contacts, same-height floor, consecutive impacts. Echoes, missed impacts and varying restitution can invalidate the inference.
investigations.materials: Supplied intervals need nothing. Optional local audio editor or slow-motion recording for manually identified impact times.
procedure: Use the supplied intervals, or identify three consecutive floor impacts in a local recording using an audio editor or a slow-motion clip. A recording is not uploaded here.
Measure the time between the first two impacts, then the time between the next two. Enter both in seconds. Do not include the initial release-to-first-impact interval.
Repeat the identification and check for echoes or missed impacts. Compare with the video-height route.
investigations.worked: Intervals1.00 s and0.80 s give e=.80 and energy fraction.64; their peak heights are1.225 m and.784 m.
investigations.challenge: If you mistake an echo for the next impact, will the inferred restitution still be trustworthy?

investigations.title: Over the sea horizon
investigations.question: Will raising your eyes recover a ship hidden below the horizon?
investigations.explanation: The eye height changes the tangent to a spherical sea. The lowest visible part of a distant ship therefore changes. A flat model does not hide the hull.
investigations.limits: Geometric horizon on a smooth spherical Earth; no atmospheric refraction. Curvature is magnified in the 3D overview.

investigations.title: A sphere and a disc cast shadows
investigations.question: If a disc turns edge-on to the light, does its shadow stay circular?
investigations.explanation: Parallel projection preserves a sphere’s circular outline in every orientation. A disc’s projection narrows to a line as it turns edge-on.
investigations.limits: Parallel geometric projection of an opaque sphere and thin circular disc. No diffraction or extended light source.

investigations.title: Precise can still be wrong
investigations.question: If five readings agree, must their average be correct?
investigations.explanation: Scatter measures repeatability; an offset shifts every reading together. Compare both with the marked reference length.
investigations.limits: Five deterministic illustrative readings, not a statistical confidence interval. The reference is assumed known.

investigations.title: Length, area and volume
investigations.question: A cube becomes twice as wide. How do its face area and volume change?
investigations.explanation: Count the unit lengths, squares and cubes: scaling multiplies length by s, area by s² and volume by s³.
investigations.limits: Dimensionless unit cubes; the logarithmic Powers of Ten explorer remains the authority for physical sizes.

investigations.title: A shallow layer over a city
investigations.question: Can ankle-deep rain add up to millions of tonnes of water?
investigations.explanation: Volume is footprint area times rainfall depth. One cubic metre of fresh water has about one tonne of mass.
investigations.limits: A rectangular, illustrative city footprint; no drainage, infiltration or forecast. The rain depth in the overview is enormously enlarged.

investigations.title: Two shadows measure a world
investigations.question: Why can two parallel sunbeams make different stick shadows?
investigations.explanation: Local verticals point in different directions on a sphere. The shadow angle equals the central angle in this two-city meridian model.
investigations.limits: Parallel rays, cities on one meridian, spherical Earth. Stadion length remains an explicit assumption.

investigations.title: One bounce, two observers
investigations.question: Does the ball travel vertically or along an arc?
investigations.explanation: Subtract the chosen observer’s position from every event. Changing frame changes the drawn path, not which events occur together.
investigations.limits: Steady nonrelativistic motion; identical ideal bounces. Train and ball sizes are schematic; distances are metres.

investigations.title: Three trains, one clock
investigations.question: Which train is really going backwards?
investigations.explanation: A velocity is always measured relative to an observer. The 70 km/h train passes the 60 km/h train at 10 km/h; the opposite train passes at 120 km/h.
investigations.limits: Illustrative constant speeds, no timetable data; carriage sizes enlarged.

investigations.title: A graph is not a road
investigations.question: After an out-and-back walk, can average velocity be zero while average speed is positive?
investigations.explanation: Distance adds every segment travelled. Displacement compares only start and finish. The slope of position against time gives velocity. On the smooth-motion preset, reduce the secant interval to approach instantaneous velocity.
investigations.limits: Piecewise ideal walking velocities change instantaneously at the marked times; a real walker takes time to turn.

investigations.title: Negative need not mean slowing
investigations.question: Can a negative acceleration make something go faster?
investigations.explanation: Compare velocity and acceleration directions. The same direction increases speed; opposite directions decrease it, regardless of coordinate signs.
investigations.limits: One-dimensional constant acceleration; arrows for different quantities use separate labelled scales.

investigations.title: Equal beats, unequal gaps
investigations.question: Does twice the elapsed time mean twice the distance?
investigations.explanation: Constant acceleration gives distances proportional to t². A rolling solid sphere has smaller acceleration than a frictionless sliding particle because some energy becomes rotation.
investigations.limits: Uniform solid sphere rolls without slipping; slider is an ideal particle. No rolling resistance. Markers are equal-time samples.

investigations.title: Stop exactly at the top
investigations.question: At the highest point, which graph reaches zero?
investigations.explanation: The height has a maximum while velocity passes through zero. Acceleration remains −9.8 m/s² throughout the ideal flight.
investigations.limits: No air. The horizontal graph axis is time; it is not a horizontal flight direction.

investigations.title: After the hand lets go
investigations.question: What happens when friction approaches zero?
investigations.explanation: After release there is no forward hand force. A backward contact force changes velocity; when it is removed, the same velocity continues.
investigations.limits: A 1 kg book is pushed for 0.40 s to a selected release speed, then slides with constant kinetic friction and no air. Hand departure is visible; replay restarts after five seconds.

investigations.title: What pushes an arrow after release?
investigations.question: Once the string leaves the arrow, what supplies a forward force?
investigations.explanation: The bow supplied a contact force before release. After release gravity and air drag change the arrow’s velocity; no stored forward force is needed to keep it moving.
investigations.limits: Point-particle flight with linear drag, no lift or wind; the arrow is aligned with velocity. Body size is enlarged; no quantitative archery prediction.

investigations.title: Who pushed the passenger?
investigations.question: From the platform, what slows first when the train brakes?
investigations.explanation: The floor slows the passenger’s feet. An initially unrestrained upper-body marker keeps its old motion, so it advances relative to the braking carriage.
investigations.limits: Short-time rigid hinged-torso model with floor-driven feet and no muscle response or stepping. A separate loose bag slides on an ideal frictionless floor; no injury prediction. Coordinates transform using the same train clock.

investigations.title: At the contact
investigations.question: Does friction always equal its maximum value?
investigations.explanation: Static friction matches the applied force up to a limit. Once sliding begins, deforming and breaking contact junctions resist relative sliding.
investigations.limits: Schematic contact junctions; constant coefficients μs=0.50 and μk=0.35. Real contacts also involve adhesion and deformation.

investigations.title: A short push on a plate
investigations.question: Will doubling the plate’s mass stop it moving?
investigations.explanation: Friction grows with mass, but so does inertia. Pull duration controls the impulse and the resulting displacement; mass cancels in this ideal model.
investigations.limits: Constant sliding friction μ=0.30 on both cloth and bare table, no hem or tipping. This is a virtual experiment.

investigations.title: Pulls at an angle
investigations.question: Do two 5 N pulls always add up to 10 N?
investigations.explanation: Add vectors head to tail. The resultant depends on their directions; acceleration is the resultant divided by mass.
investigations.limits: Point-mass cart on a frictionless horizontal surface; force and acceleration scales differ.

investigations.title: Change the force; change the mass
investigations.question: If the same resultant acts on twice the mass, how does its acceleration change?
investigations.explanation: Apply the same net force to different masses or vary the force on a fixed mass; acceleration scales with force and inversely with mass (a = F/m).
investigations.limits: Point-mass cart on a frictionless horizontal surface; force and acceleration scales differ.

investigations.title: A table is a very stiff spring
investigations.question: If a tabletop hardly moves, how can it push?
investigations.explanation: A small deformation produces a restoring force. Stiffer supports need less deformation for the same force. On a slope, the normal balances the perpendicular part of weight. The table preset exposes schematic material sites whose small relative displacements are enlarged.
investigations.limits: Hooke-law support analogies; all deformation magnified. On the inclined support, separate static friction balances the downhill component.

investigations.title: One interaction, two objects
investigations.question: Can equal opposite forces give very different accelerations?
investigations.explanation: An interaction gives equal and opposite forces on two different objects. Their accelerations differ inversely with their masses. Selecting one object leaves its own force visible. The standing-person preset separates the two balanced forces on the person from their partners on Earth and floor.
investigations.limits: Two isolated bodies with a prescribed mutual force for a short instant; not a collision damage model.

investigations.title: Throw something, move yourself
investigations.question: What can an astronaut push on in empty space?
investigations.explanation: The astronaut and thrown object receive equal and opposite momentum. Repeated ejections use the same two-body accounting; there is no external air.
investigations.limits: Discrete ideal ejections, no gravity or drag; exhaust icons are parcels of finite mass, not literal molecules.

investigations.title: Air and gravity are separate controls
investigations.question: Would a feather fall slowly on the Moon because there is no air?
investigations.explanation: Gravity sets the initial acceleration. Drag grows with speed, shape and air density. Removing air restores equal acceleration regardless of mass.
investigations.limits: Vertical quadratic drag with assumed effective drag areas; fixed g, no tumbling, wind or changing atmosphere.

investigations.title: Drop from a moving car
investigations.question: Where does the ball land relative to the car?
investigations.explanation: The released ball retains the car’s horizontal velocity. It falls vertically in the car frame and along a parabola in the ground frame.
investigations.limits: Level constant-speed car; no air or rotation. Start height 0.75 m.

investigations.title: Turning a velocity arrow
investigations.question: How can speed stay constant while velocity changes?
investigations.explanation: Equal-length velocity arrows turn. Their vector difference points towards the centre. Releasing the constraint continues along the tangent.
investigations.limits: Planar circle of radius 2 m; release removes only the inward constraint. Floor view neglects vertical motion.

investigations.title: The apple, the Moon and a shared centre
investigations.question: Does the Moon move around an Earth that is perfectly fixed?
investigations.explanation: The two bodies orbit a common centre of mass. A separate comparison shows the inverse-square change in gravitational acceleration. The apple/Moon preset compares 4.90 m in one second with the gap below a lunar tangent in one minute.
investigations.limits: Circular two-body teaching orbit; Earth/Moon sizes and orbital separation enlarged independently for visibility. No tidal or solar perturbations.

investigations.title: A falling room and a relaxed spring
investigations.question: Does a zero accelerometer reading mean zero gravity?
investigations.explanation: A freely falling room and astronaut have the same gravitational acceleration. With no support force, the spring-mass sensor relaxes even though gravity remains strong.
investigations.limits: Ideal local free fall, ignoring gravity gradients and station rotation. Sensor is a spring analogy; no device is connected.

investigations.title: Kepler’s equal-time sweeps
investigations.question: Does a planet cover equal distances in equal times?
investigations.explanation: For equal amounts of time, the line joining the planet to the central body sweeps equal areas. The planet moves faster near the central body. Bigger orbits take longer: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.
investigations.limits: Two-body Newtonian ellipses; normalized units with GM=1. Eccentricity is user-selected, not necessarily a real planet.

investigations.title: A tiny pull twists a wire
investigations.question: What changes when the large lead balls switch sides?
investigations.explanation: Both gravitational torques change sign. The wire twists until its restoring torque matches the tiny gravitational torque.
investigations.limits: Assumed small-angle apparatus; includes attraction of both large balls on both small ones. The displayed twist is enormously enlarged. Not a reconstruction of Cavendish’s measured trace.

investigations.title: A small nudge leaves a message
investigations.question: Does adding one small planet leave the same predicted orbit?
investigations.explanation: Compare the two-body path with a restricted three-body calculation. The separate residual view reveals the small difference that is hard to see on the main orbit.
investigations.limits: Illustrative planet mass and prescribed circular orbit; not historical Neptune or Halley data. Heliocentric indirect acceleration is included.

investigations.title: Burn here, change the far side
investigations.question: Does a forward burn at perigee push the spacecraft radially outwards?
investigations.explanation: An impulse along the path immediately changes velocity; the larger apogee appears later. A retrograde lunar flyby burn can change positive orbital energy to a bound orbit.
investigations.limits: Educational impulsive two-body burns, separate Earth and Moon panels. The original mission explorer retains the published ISRO orbit sequence; this is not a flight trajectory reconstruction.

investigations.title: Pressure has no preferred direction
investigations.question: What changes when the same load is turned onto a smaller face?
investigations.explanation: Force stays fixed while force per area changes. In the immersed mode, forces are perpendicular to every face and pressure increases with depth.
investigations.limits: Uniform fresh-water density; rectangular body. Contact and immersed views use different arrow scales. Within the immersed view, equal-area face arrows share one gauge-pressure scale; values are printed. The immersed cube is held while pressure forces are measured; the arrows are not a complete free-body diagram. The solid has fixed 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.05 m dimensions and is turned onto one of three faces.

investigations.title: The outside air does the pushing
investigations.question: Can an empty space pull water up a tube?
investigations.explanation: A pressure difference supports a liquid column. Change the gas pressure at the top, the liquid density or the apparatus to see the same balance.
investigations.limits: Static columns, negligible liquid vapour pressure and capillary forces. Hemispheres use projected circular area; no hazardous apparatus is proposed. The glass inset is enlarged and shows initial forces only, not subsequent water flow.

investigations.title: Same depth, same pressure
investigations.question: Does a wide lake make more pressure than a narrow tube at the same depth?
investigations.explanation: Pressure at a point depends on depth, density and surface pressure. A dam’s total force adds a triangular distribution; a piston adds the same pressure everywhere.
investigations.limits: Static incompressible fresh water; vertical dam. Vessel shapes are illustrative and pressure probes are compared at equal depths.

investigations.title: The same steel, a larger hull
investigations.question: Can adding enclosed air change the steel’s weight?
investigations.explanation: The steel’s mass is fixed. A larger watertight envelope displaces more liquid before submerging. Cargo changes weight; salinity changes the displaced volume needed.
investigations.limits: Ideal rectangular watertight hull in calm liquid, with no stability or flooding model. The layered case uses an egg-shaped solid at a sharp density interface; no mixing, surface tension or real-egg variability.

investigations.title: Choose what you count
investigations.question: If the ball loses mechanical energy, must the total account fall?
