investigations.explanation: Choose the ball alone, ball plus Earth, or the surroundings too. Thermal accounts reveal where the mechanical energy went; gravitational energy belongs to the ball–Earth interaction.
investigations.limits: Ideal flights and instantaneous lossy impacts; 64% mechanical-energy retention per bounce. Thermal allocations 30/40/30% are illustrative, sound counted after absorption.

investigations.title: Two ways to stop a moving ball
investigations.question: When speed doubles, what happens to stopping time and stopping distance?
investigations.explanation: At fixed resisting force, impulse determines stopping time and work determines stopping distance. Momentum doubles, kinetic energy quadruples.
investigations.limits: Constant resisting force; no universal claim about real flour or clay crater depths.

investigations.title: Different routes, the same rise
investigations.question: Does a longer ramp store more gravitational energy than a lift to the same floor?
investigations.explanation: Only the rise changes the gravitational store. A ramp needs less force along a longer route. A perpendicular support force does no mechanical work during a horizontal move.
investigations.limits: Quasistatic motion, no friction or physiological energy costs. Ramp/stairs geometry is schematic.

investigations.title: Power is the rate, energy is the amount
investigations.question: Which uses more energy: a 2 kW geyser for 15 minutes or a 10 W lamp all day?
investigations.explanation: Power is the slope of cumulative energy. Duration matters as well as the wattage. One kWh is 3.6 MJ.
investigations.limits: Constant label power; ignores appliance duty cycles and billing tariffs.

investigations.title: Follow the shaft and the energy
investigations.question: Where does the rest of a power station’s input go?
investigations.explanation: A turbine turns a generator while the account splits electrical output from rejected energy. A finite spinning wheel slows when a lamp draws energy from it.
investigations.limits: Illustrative adjustable efficiencies, no present-day Mumbai supply claim. Rotor kinematics are schematic; the energy account is exact for the stated model.

investigations.title: Stevin’s wreath of spheres
investigations.question: Why do four beads on a gentle slope balance two on a steep one?
investigations.explanation: For a uniform chain, mass on each slope grows with its length while the downhill fraction shrinks inversely with length. Both downhill forces equal linear density × g × height.
investigations.limits: Uniform flexible chain on frictionless slopes, symmetric hanging portion. Geometry follows the selected height; beads represent equal chain lengths.

investigations.title: A heat engine needs two temperatures
investigations.question: Could an engine turn all incoming heat into work?
investigations.explanation: The reversible limit depends on hot and cold absolute temperatures. Work plus rejected energy always equals input; real performance can lie below that limit.
investigations.limits: Ideal reservoir model and schematic piston; temperatures are kelvin, not Celsius. The reversible limit is not a claim of an actual engine’s efficiency.

investigations.title: Turn a falling weight into warming
investigations.question: Will the water warm if no hot object touches it?
investigations.explanation: The falling weight does work on the paddles. In this insulated model, every joule lost from its gravitational store becomes water internal energy.
investigations.limits: Ideal insulated calorimeter; the paddle timing is illustrative. Particle motion is magnified, not a molecular dynamics simulation.

investigations.title: A hot spoonful and a warm bucket
investigations.question: Which sample can transfer more energy while reaching room temperature?
investigations.explanation: Temperature changes the spread of particle speeds; it does not tell you how much water there is. Follow the amount bars when you change mass, then compare the energy bars for cooling to 30 °C. A tiny hot sample can release less energy than a warm bucket; enough hot water reverses that comparison. The equally enlarged marker windows show motion, not literal amounts.
investigations.limits: Both samples are liquid water with constant specific heat 4186 J/(kg K). Equal-size sampling windows and 64 markers per window are not physical volumes or molecule counts. The 3D amount bars and each diagram bar pair have a common linear scale; very small quantities make hairline bars. Maxwell curves describe classical translation, while water heat capacity includes interactions and other motion.

investigations.title: Insulation works in both directions
investigations.question: Will wrapping ice in a sweater melt it faster?
investigations.explanation: An insulating layer increases thermal resistance. It slows energy transfer from warm skin to a cool room, and from a warm room to cold ice.
investigations.limits: Steady one-dimensional conduction; convection and radiation are omitted. Layer thickness in the scene is enlarged.

investigations.title: Energy enters while the thermometer waits
investigations.question: During melting, where does the incoming energy go?
investigations.explanation: During a phase-change plateau, energy changes particle interactions and the phase fraction rather than increasing the temperature. Ice has an open structure; liquid water is denser near melting.
investigations.limits: One kilogram of pure water at atmospheric pressure. Ice and liquid arrangements are schematic; particle size stays fixed. Steam is represented as separate markers.

investigations.title: The fastest escape from a matka
investigations.question: Why does the same pot cool less below the air temperature in humid July?
investigations.explanation: Escaping water molecules remove energy. Humid air reduces net evaporation. The wet-bulb temperature is a lower limit for an ideal evaporative cooler under these conditions.
investigations.limits: Uses the book’s three illustrative weather cases, not live weather. Warm-water vaporisation cost is approximated as 2400 J per gram. The particle view illustrates selection, not measured rates.

investigations.title: A coastal circulation loop
investigations.question: What pushes warm air up above the land?
investigations.explanation: Warm air has fewer kilograms in the same volume at equal pressure. Cooler, denser surrounding air provides a buoyant upward push. The arrows show rising air over the warmer side, a return flow aloft and cooler air flowing in near the surface. Cool the land below the sea temperature to reverse the loop; equal temperatures remove this thermal drive.
investigations.limits: An illustrative sea-breeze loop, not a weather or monsoon forecast. Density uses the ideal-gas relation at a common pressure.

investigations.title: An engine needs a cold destination
investigations.question: Can all the energy from a hot reservoir become work in one cycle?
investigations.explanation: A cyclic heat engine transfers some incoming energy into work and rejects the rest to a colder reservoir. Even a reversible engine has the limit 1 − cold temperature / hot temperature, in kelvin.
investigations.limits: The animated piston illustrates a cyclic engine, not a pressure-volume calculation for a particular gas. Efficiency is a chosen fraction of the Carnot limit. The piston marks a repeated cycle schematically; its stroke is not a work measurement. The green output arrow vanishes at zero work; the paired energy bars supply the quantitative account.

investigations.title: What sets a pendulum’s clock?
investigations.question: Does increasing the mass shorten the period?
investigations.explanation: A heavier bob feels a larger gravitational pull, but it is harder to accelerate by the same factor. Dividing tangential force by mass gives the same acceleration at the same angle. Red arrows show gravitational g; green arrows show the acceleration along the arc. The string also keeps the bob on its circular path. The readout keeps actual forces in newtons. Length changes the clock; mass does not.
investigations.limits: Point bob and massless string; no damping. The amplitude correction is valid for the offered angles up to 40 degrees. The displayed swing is a harmonic motion at the corrected period, rather than an exact nonlinear integration. Red gravitational g and green tangential-acceleration arrows use one fixed scale for both bobs; they do not depict total acceleration or force. Their tails are offset outside the bob for visibility.

investigations.title: Push in time, then add damping
investigations.question: Can the same small drive produce different amplitudes?
investigations.explanation: A periodic force adds energy efficiently near the natural rhythm. In steady motion, input per cycle balances damping losses. Stronger damping limits the response.
investigations.limits: Linear oscillator with RK4 transient motion, drive work and damping loss. The separate amplitude curve is the steady response; a manual impulse acts on the current transient.

investigations.title: A steady flow can feed a twist
investigations.question: Does the wind need to arrive in rhythmic gusts?
investigations.explanation: A twisting deck changes how the steady wind pushes on it. If the wind’s turning push tends to act in the same direction as the deck’s motion, it adds energy on average. Damping removes energy. When input wins, the twist grows without the wind needing rhythmic gusts.
investigations.limits: A prescribed small-amplitude torsional energy model, not a CFD model or reconstruction of Tacoma’s collapse. It shows feedback separately from externally timed resonance. The plotted energy is a cycle-averaged envelope. The side inset enlarges the central twist angle fourfold and states the actual angle; the 3D deck uses the unscaled angle.

investigations.title: Follow a parcel beneath a wave
investigations.question: Does a marked parcel travel with the crest?
investigations.explanation: Watch the red parcel circle the black mean-position mark in the enlarged inset. A crest travels onward, but that parcel returns near its starting place. The inset is the same surface motion enlarged40× in both directions. The whole-wave view keeps the smaller physical displacement; deeper parcels move less.
investigations.limits: Linear deep-water gravity wave; controls keep kA≤0.189. The framed 3D local copy and the right-hand calculated inset magnify displacement40× in both directions, with the same clock and the same parcel state as the main view. No Stokes drift, breaking or finite-depth dispersion.

investigations.title: A compression crosses the air
investigations.question: Will one air particle travel from the speaker to your ear?
investigations.explanation: Watch the red air parcel: it moves back and forth near the black mean position while the pattern travels on. Blue shows pressure; red shows local displacement, each divided by its own maximum. Pressure is highest where neighbouring parcels crowd together, not where one parcel is furthest from its mean. Those two peaks are a quarter of a wavelength apart.
investigations.limits: A one-dimensional plane sound wave shown inside a volume. Regular marker rows represent mean positions, not a frozen molecular lattice; random thermal motion is omitted. Motion and time are magnified/slowed.

investigations.title: One clap, two legs of the journey
investigations.question: If the echo returns after 0.29 seconds, did sound travel one wall-distance or two?
investigations.explanation: The same pulse travels to the reflecting wall and returns. Distance to the wall is sound speed times return delay divided by two.
investigations.limits: Ideal flat reflector, sound speed 349 m/s for the warm-air example. The pulse drawing is not a pressure amplitude measurement.

investigations.title: Two separate sound controls
investigations.question: Can a higher-pitched sound also be quieter?
investigations.explanation: Frequency controls pitch; amplitude controls the oscillation size. At fixed medium, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
investigations.limits: Synthetic sine tone, never a calibrated sound-level meter. Playback is optional and stops when this experiment closes or leaves view.

investigations.title: A drumhead has nodal lines
investigations.question: How does a circular skin differ from a string?
investigations.explanation: A node is a line or point that stays still while nearby parts of the skin move. The clamped rim must stay still too, so only certain vibration patterns fit. A circular skin does not give the evenly spaced frequencies of a string. Added central mass slows each pattern according to how much that part of the skin moves.
investigations.limits: Uniform membrane modes are calculated. The central-load case uses a Rayleigh trial-shape estimate, not an exact tabla simulation; it does not force the frequencies onto integer multiples. The same calculated frequency drives optional audio.

investigations.title: Choose who hears the moving horn
investigations.question: What does the driver hear compared with the platform listener?
investigations.explanation: Each wavefront expands from its emission position through the air. A listener moving with the source receives the emitted frequency; a stationary listener ahead receives crests more often.
investigations.limits: One-dimensional radial Doppler relation in still air; offered speeds remain subsonic. Drawn crests sparsely sample the actual sound wave. The still view begins after several crests have already been emitted. The repeating animation resets its time window.

investigations.title: Light must arrive at the eye
investigations.question: Will an eye looking harder reveal an unlit mango?
investigations.explanation: A source illuminates the object. Some scattered light enters the eye. Removing the source or blocking that route removes the signal; nothing is emitted by the eye.
investigations.limits: Ray samples show possible light directions, not visible threads in clean air. The model view keeps apparatus visible even when the signal is zero.

investigations.title: Open the camera and follow the rays
investigations.question: Will making the hole larger improve both brightness and sharpness?
investigations.explanation: Straight rays from each object point cross through the opening to the opposite screen position. A finite opening gives each point a blur disc; enlarging it admits more light and more geometric blur.
investigations.limits: Geometrical optics only; very-small-hole diffraction and exposure are omitted. Object and screen dimensions are shown numerically. The 3D apparatus is an opened camera cutaway; longitudinal framing and aperture enlargement in the lower diagram are named.

investigations.title: A large lamp softens a shadow
investigations.question: Is a fuzzy shadow edge always diffraction?
investigations.explanation: Different points on an extended source cast displaced shadows. Umbra receives none of the source; penumbra receives only part.
investigations.limits: Geometric projection from a sampled line source. Light diffraction and multiple scattering are omitted.

investigations.title: Walk around a mirror image
investigations.question: Is the image painted on the glass?
investigations.explanation: Reflected rays obey equal angles. Their backward extensions meet at a virtual image behind a flat mirror. Curved mirrors can form real or virtual images depending on object distance.
investigations.limits: Flat-mirror paths are geometrical. The spoon comparison is an ideal paraxial concave/convex mirror; a real spoon has aberrations.

investigations.title: Bring back the hidden coin
investigations.question: Can water make the coin visible while eye and coin stay fixed?
investigations.explanation: Refraction at the surface creates a route past the rim. Back-projecting the arriving ray gives a shallower apparent position, while the real coin stays on the bottom.
investigations.limits: Illustrative tumbler dimensions; Snell’s law solves the surface crossing. The empty/full comparison keeps eye, coin and rim fixed.

investigations.title: Guide light around a bend
investigations.question: At which surface angle will the ray start leaking out?
investigations.explanation: A ray can reflect internally when it meets a higher-to-lower-index boundary beyond the critical angle. The path changes direction at successive contacts, not continuously between them.
investigations.limits: Exact two-dimensional ray intersections with a circular annulus, visualised as a bent light guide. Absorption and diffraction are omitted.

investigations.title: Why goggles restore underwater vision
investigations.question: Why does water blur an eye that works in air?
investigations.explanation: The air–cornea index jump supplies much of the focusing. Water reduces this jump. Goggles restore an air layer and the cornea’s refracting power.
investigations.limits: Reduced thin-lens teaching eye, not a prescription. Rays, focus and retinal intercepts use one physical conjugate state. Incoming rays are clipped near the eye; transverse scale is enlarged independently. The retinal image uses the calculated angular scale and pupil blur diameter; the Gaussian blur rendering is illustrative. The retinal inset shows one point’s spread on a fixed 1 mm reference scale, with a small centre marker kept visible at zero blur.

investigations.title: Emission time is not arrival time
investigations.question: Can the same eclipse be observed at different times from different distances?
investigations.explanation: An event emits a signal at one time; arrival occurs after distance divided by light speed. Changing Earth’s position changes the light-travel delay.
investigations.limits: Circular coplanar Earth/Jupiter geometry with schematic Io eclipse events; not an ephemeris or reconstruction of Rømer’s fitted observations.

investigations.title: A cogwheel times a light round trip
investigations.question: How fast must the next tooth replace the outgoing gap?
investigations.explanation: Light leaves through a gap and makes the journey to the distant mirror and back. Meanwhile the wheel turns. At the first fully dark return, the neighbouring tooth has replaced that gap and blocks the returning light. The known tooth spacing, wheel speed and round-trip distance tell us how long the light took.
investigations.limits: Equal-width teeth and gaps; transmission averages launch and return openings over a wheel cycle. The marker follows one ray launched at the gap centre. Full extinction occurs at gap-to-tooth centre alignment. Predicts timing with modern c; Fizeau’s approximate observed speed was 12.6 Hz. Apparatus and tiny phase advance are separately magnified.

investigations.title: Select one colour for the second prism
investigations.question: Will a second prism add colours to selected red light?
investigations.explanation: The first prism separates wavelengths because its refractive index depends on wavelength. Selecting one narrow band leaves that band alone; the second prism refracts it without inventing other wavelengths.
investigations.limits: A 60-degree ideal crown-glass prism; index interpolated between red and violet textbook values. Ray directions follow the calculated refractions. Apparatus dimensions are schematic.

investigations.title: One drop becomes a rainbow cone
investigations.question: Where must the Sun be relative to the observer?
investigations.explanation: A primary-rainbow ray refracts into a drop, reflects once, and refracts out. Drops sending light towards one observer lie on a cone around the antisolar direction.
investigations.limits: Spherical water drops, one internal reflection and wavelength-dependent index. The scene shows a selected impact parameter, not a complete intensity calculation.

investigations.title: The spectrum an object returns
investigations.question: Will the banana remain yellow under blue-only light?
investigations.explanation: The returned spectrum is the illuminating spectrum multiplied by the object’s reflectance. Broad overlapping cone sensitivities combine the returned wavelengths into colour responses.
investigations.limits: Illustrative smooth spectra and cone sensitivity curves; screen RGB cannot reproduce every real spectrum or visual adaptation.

investigations.title: Direct light and scattered light take different routes
investigations.question: Is blue sky simply sunlight viewed straight through blue air?
investigations.explanation: Short wavelengths scatter more strongly. The sky receives light redirected into the eye; a long direct path removes more blue from the light that continues towards the observer.
investigations.limits: Uniform 8 km effective-air shell for optical depth; drawn shell enlarged. Scattering event lies inside air and both incoming rays share the Sun direction. Removed fraction includes all scattered directions, not a prediction of light entering one eye.

investigations.title: Turn the filter and delete the glare
investigations.question: Does rotating a filter change all light by the same amount?
investigations.explanation: A filter transmits the projection of the electric field onto its axis. Intensity follows the squared projection. Fresnel reflection makes water glare strongly polarised near Brewster’s angle.
investigations.limits: Ideal analyser; incoherent Fresnel s/p intensities add. Water incidence/reflection is geometric; fields enlarged 5×. Separate unpolarised returning-water colour is set to illustrative 0.080 incident units and always halves through the analyser.

investigations.title: Probe the path difference
investigations.question: What path difference makes a dark point on the screen?
investigations.explanation: When crests arrive together, the two waves reinforce. If one route is half a wavelength longer, its crest arrives with the other wave’s trough and equal amplitudes cancel. Adding whole wavelengths brings them back into step. Move the probe to connect that route difference with bright and dark points.
investigations.limits: Exact source-to-probe distances; point-like coherent slits with equal amplitudes. The single-slit envelope and coherence loss are separate effects. The route sketch enlarges transverse distances independently. Each blue/yellow arrival arrow has half the common normalised amplitude; their red resultant has squared length equal to the plotted intensity.

investigations.title: Change an opening, a grating or a thin film
investigations.question: Does every rainbow-coloured object use a prism?
investigations.explanation: Waves leaving different parts of an opening reach the same screen point by different routes. They reinforce or cancel according to those route differences. A grating repeats the openings; a thin film supplies two reflected routes, including a phase reversal at one boundary. Changing spacing or thickness therefore selects different bright directions or colours.
investigations.limits: Fraunhofer model: 64 equal midpoint samples across one slit, eight equal grating sources, or two equal reflected film amplitudes. Plots and visible phasors use identical sums. Film one-reflection phase reversal is included; longitudinal and transverse apparatus scales are framed separately.

investigations.title: A bright spot in the middle of a shadow
investigations.question: What happens when equal-length rim paths meet at the centre?
investigations.explanation: At the centre, contributions from all around a circular obstacle’s rim arrive in phase. A near-axis rim-wave calculation predicts a central maximum.
investigations.limits: Near-axis paraxial rim model, 96 coherent samples converging to J₀²; not full Fresnel irradiance. Disc and probe transverse scales are separately enlarged; both geometry and phase use the selected physical radius.

investigations.title: Account for a changed photon colour
investigations.question: If the outgoing photon loses energy, what gains it?
investigations.explanation: Compare the two bars on one energy scale. When the outgoing photon has less energy, the molecule gains exactly the difference as vibration: this is Stokes scattering. In anti-Stokes scattering the vibration supplies energy to the outgoing photon. Elastic scattering transfers no net vibrational energy. A longer outgoing wavelength means a smaller photon energy.
investigations.limits: Schematic vibrational energy levels and selectable Raman shift. Shifted peaks are magnified; no assertion of an actual molecule’s spectrum or classical photon path.

widgets.cutaway: Inside the taut string: fibres transmit the inward tension force T = mv²/r; the instant the clip opens, T drops to 0 N.
widgets.idealised: The ball whirls on a frictionless horizontal table so gravity does not tilt the string downward into a cone.

widgets.cutaway: Inside Newton’s gravitational field: gravity pulls toward Earth’s centre at every point; at 7.9 km/s the ground curves away by 4.9 m every second—matching the fall.
widgets.idealised: Air is omitted even at the 10 km launch altitude. Reaching the 4.2 Earth-radius drawing horizon is a display limit; the sign of orbital energy decides bound motion or escape.

widgets.idealised: The Earth is drawn covered by a uniform deep ocean without continents or shallow coastal bays that amplify real tides.

widgets.cutaway: Inside the fluid column: every horizontal layer supports the weight of all the liquid and air stacked above it, pushing equally in all directions at that depth.
widgets.idealised: The liquid is treated as strictly incompressible (constant density ρ at all depths).

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.title: Buoyancy
widgets.challengePrompt: Set Block density to 7,800 kg/m³ (steel) in water, then click "Hollow it out" so the steel hull floats!
widgets.cutaway: Inside the pressure difference: water is deeper at the bottom face of the block than at the top face, so upward pressure force exceeds downward pressure force by ρ_liq V g.
widgets.idealised: Surface tension at the waterline and viscous water drag are simplified for clarity.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Solid steel (7,800 kg/m³) weighs more than an equal volume of water, so it sinks.

widgets.title: Sankey & Energy Stores Ledger
widgets.challengePrompt: Select "Bouncing tennis ball" and scrub Transfer progress to the bottom of the bounce (≈ 50%) where elastic store peaks.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the pathway tubes: mechanical work is an ordered force push, electrical work is drift of electrons, heating is random molecular jiggling, and radiation is electromagnetic waves.
widgets.idealised: Each jar groups microscopic kinetic and potential energies into a single macroscopic store label.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.challengePrompt: With Friction at 0.10, find the lowest Release height that still lets the marble clear the 0.80 m bump (1.1 m).
widgets.cutaway: Inside the sliding bead and track: friction converts ordered motion into random lattice vibrations (thermal store) without changing the total joules.
widgets.idealised: The marble slides without rotational inertia (½Iω²), so all its motion energy is translational ½mv².

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.title: Conduction
widgets.challengePrompt: Compare steel, wood, and aluminium with a 37 °C hand; every surface starts at the same 30 °C room temperature.
widgets.cutaway: Mobile electrons help transfer energy in metals. Wood is a much poorer conductor. This lumped-layer model shows contact transfer without calibrating a material’s cooling time.
widgets.idealised: Heat flow is modelled in one dimension along the bar without convective heat loss to the surrounding room air.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: All three surfaces start at 30 °C, cooler than the 35 °C hand.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Two fingers" and set Rhythm to 2.0 Hz to create a crisp two-source interference pattern.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the water surface: water parcels move in tiny vertical circles as the crest passes—the wave travels across the tank while the water stays in place.
widgets.idealised: The tank walls are non-reflecting so outgoing ripples are not muddied by echoes from the edges.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: A single tap sends out circular ripples at constant wave speed.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Both" (waveform + frequency spectrum) to see time-domain oscillations and harmonic peaks side by side.
widgets.cutaway: In a capacitive microphone, sound bends a flexible diaphragm and changes its capacitance; the electronics turn that change into a signal. The plot is an uncalibrated signal, not pressure in pascals.
widgets.idealised: Without the microphone active, the scope displays a clean synthetic reference tone free of room background noise.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: The oscilloscope plots relative microphone signal against time in milliseconds; the initial trace is a simulated reference tone.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Tabla" and set Upper overtones to 60% to compare its near-harmonic frequency ladder with the plain drum.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the tabla head: C. V. Raman showed that the iron-paste syahi mass-loads the centre of the membrane so its modes shift into integer harmonic ratios 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5.
widgets.idealised: Six partials are summed. The small drum views illustrate mode families; a real loaded tabla needs a full membrane model and has many higher modes.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: A plucked string vibrates in standing-wave loops with ratios 1 : 2 : 3 : 4.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away

widgets.cutaway: Inside the wavefront bunching: each sound crest leaves the horn and expands at 348.7 m/s in 30 °C air, but the moving horn emits the next crest closer to the previous one.
widgets.idealised: The listener stands close to the track so the cosine angle factor approaches ±1 except right at the moment of passing.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: When the train stands still (0 km/h), sound circles are concentric and everyone hears the same pitch.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away

widgets.title: Mirror
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Whole body" and move to 120 cm from the mirror to confirm that a half-height mirror still shows you head to toe!
widgets.cutaway: Inside the silvered glass: incoming photons reflect off the thin aluminium/silver backing at θ_i = θ_r; your visual cortex projects diverging rays straight backward to a virtual image.
widgets.idealised: The mirror is treated as a front-surface reflector, ignoring the weak second reflection from the front face of household glass.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Every ray from the object bounces off the mirror at an angle equal to its arrival angle.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Extended straight back behind the mirror, all reflected rays meet at one virtual image point.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Why no light actually goes behind the wall—virtual rays are sightlines traced by your eye.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: In "Whole body" mode, similar triangles guarantee that a mirror half your height shows your full body at any distance.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Walk closer or farther and toggle the traced-back rays.

widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Diamond (2.419)", flip direction to "material → air", and increase the angle above 25° to trigger Total Internal Reflection!
widgets.cutaway: Inside the wavefront boundary: light slows down to c/n inside glass or diamond, so the edge of each wavefront that enters first falls behind and pivots the beam.
widgets.idealised: The beam is monochromatic; real white light splits into a rainbow (dispersion) because n varies slightly with wavelength.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Light entering water (n = 1.333) slows down and bends toward the normal.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Diamond (n = 2.419) slows light to 41% of c, bending the ray sharply.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Wavefront crests march closer together in the slower medium, pivoting the ray direction.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Going from diamond into air above the 24.4° critical angle traps 100% of the light inside.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Explore angles, materials, and critical angles.

widgets.cutaway: The cornea provides most of the bending. Ciliary muscles change the crystalline lens shape to adjust focus; this drawing combines both into one effective thin lens.
widgets.idealised: The cornea and crystalline lens are combined into a single thin adjustable lens for ray-tracing clarity.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: An ideal eye adjusts its lens curvature so rays from any distance meet sharply on the retina.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn

widgets.title: Interference
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Stripes on a screen", set Wavelength to 650 nm (red) and Source spacing to 0.25 mm to widen the bright fringes.
widgets.cutaway: Inside path difference Δr = d sin θ: where crests from both slits arrive in step (Δr = mλ) amplitudes add; where a crest meets a trough (Δr = (m+½)λ) they cancel to darkness.
widgets.idealised: The slits are treated as infinitely narrow point sources, so the wide single-slit diffraction envelope does not dim the outer fringes.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Two coherent sources send overlapping waves whose crests and troughs add or cancel.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: On a distant screen, constructive lanes form evenly spaced bright bands.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Light plus light makes darkness wherever the two paths differ by half a wavelength.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Longer red wavelength (650 nm) or closer slits (0.25 mm) spreads the fringes wider apart.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Sweep wavelength across the spectrum and watch fringe spacing respond.

widgets.challengePrompt: In "Light on a white wall", mix Red = 100%, Green = 100%, and Blue = 0% to make pure additive Yellow light!
widgets.cutaway: The retina has three cone types with overlapping wavelength responses. Different spectra can produce similar response patterns and appear the same colour; this RGB display illustrates that principle rather than modelling cone sensitivities.
widgets.idealised: Screen sRGB primaries approximate monochromatic spectral lights and idealised block-filter pigments.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Adding Red, Green, and Blue spotlights on a dark wall makes white where all three overlap.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend

widgets.title: Skycolour
widgets.challengePrompt: Lower Sun height to 2° (sunset) on Earth to see why the low Sun turns deep orange-red while the overhead sky stays blue.
widgets.cutaway: Inside Rayleigh scattering: N₂ and O₂ molecules (0.3 nm wide) are much smaller than light wavelengths, oscillating like tiny dipole antennas that radiate strongly as 1/λ⁴.
widgets.idealised: Only Rayleigh molecular scattering (1/λ⁴) is calculated; larger dust and water droplets add whiter Mie scattering near the horizon.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: With the Sun high overhead, short blue wavelengths scatter across the sky into your eyes.

watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: In this model, 450 nm blue light scatters 5.86 times as strongly as 700 nm red light.

widgets.title: Circuit
widgets.challengePrompt: Set Battery to 9.0 V and choose "3 LEDs": find the current and the voltage left for the 330 Ω resistor.
widgets.cutaway: The wire already contains mobile charge. A change in the electric field spreads around the circuit; carriers do not travel from the battery to fill an empty wire. When current flows, each coulomb transfers about 2 J at each LED and the remaining energy at the resistor.
widgets.idealised: Each conducting red LED is approximated by a 2 V drop and a 330 Ω resistor limits the current. Below the combined threshold the model gives zero current and does not resolve individual LED voltages; real LED curves are gradual.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Existing charge circulates around a closed loop; the same current crosses A, B and C.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: The battery raises energy per coulomb; the resistor and LEDs transfer it to their surroundings.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Charge is conserved; energy is transferred at the circuit components.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: At 9 V, three 2 V LEDs leave 3 V across 330 Ω, giving about 9.1 mA.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Lower the supply below the combined LED threshold and compare the whole-loop current.

widgets.title: Series & Parallel Circuit Bench
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Parallel", set LEDs to 3, and click "Unclip LED 1" to see why the other two lamps stay at full brightness!
widgets.cutaway: Inside the parallel junction node: Kirchhoff’s current law (I_in = I_1 + I_2 + I_3) splits the charge stream into independent lanes, each connected across the full battery voltage.
widgets.idealised: The battery has zero internal resistance, so adding parallel branches never makes the battery terminal voltage sag.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: In series, one single loop carries the same reduced current through every lamp.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: In parallel, each lamp gets its own direct lane across the battery and shines at full brightness.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: At the branch junction, current adds up while voltage stays equal across each rung.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Unclipping one lamp breaks a series loop completely, but leaves the other parallel branches running.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Compare 1, 2, or 3 lamps in series and parallel.

widgets.title: Field 3D
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Coil and magnet", set Current to 2.5 A, and click "Reverse current" to flip the coil’s North and South poles.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the solenoid coil: circular magnetic field loops around each turn add together down the central tunnel to form a uniform North–South bar-magnet field.
widgets.idealised: The wire calculation uses vacuum permeability μ₀. Its separate compass view includes Mumbai’s 38.4 μT horizontal background; the coil/magnet field shapes are schematic dipoles.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Current in a straight wire wraps magnetic field rings around the conductor (Ørsted’s discovery).

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Winding the wire into a coil stacks those rings into a strong electromagnet.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Inside the coil core, magnetic field lines run continuously from South to North.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn

widgets.title: Magnetometer
widgets.challengePrompt: Explore the 3-axis magnetic readout or click "Hold" to freeze a reading in microteslas (μT).
widgets.cutaway: One possible chip design uses the Hall effect: moving charges are deflected sideways by a magnetic field, producing a voltage. Other phone chips use magnetoresistive materials; the displayed axes do not identify the chip design.
widgets.idealised: Phone calibration varies. Internal magnets, nearby steel and sensor offsets can shift the readings; this display does not guarantee hard-iron correction or world-coordinate orientation.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Even far from any fridge magnet, a magnetometer reads Earth’s ~43 μT background field.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: A small magnet’s far field falls approximately as 1/r³; a long straight current-carrying wire instead gives B ∝ 1/r.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Three sensor axes measure B_x, B_y and B_z; keep the screen flat before interpreting the screen-normal component as vertical.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Flipping the magnet reverses the sign of the component along the sensor axis.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Use a device magnetometer or inspect the reference reading.

widgets.title: Induction
widgets.challengePrompt: Set Turns to maximum (index 3) and click "Nudge in / out" (or drag the magnet fast) to generate a strong induced voltage spike!
widgets.cutaway: Inside Faraday’s law: a changing magnetic flux Φ_B through the coil curls an electric field around the copper loops, pushing conduction electrons only while the magnet moves.
widgets.idealised: Self-inductance of the coil is neglected so current follows the induced EMF instantaneously.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: A magnet sitting still inside the coil produces zero voltage, no matter how strong it is.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Plunging the magnet in or pulling it out deflects the galvanometer in opposite directions.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Only changing magnetic flux (ΔΦ_B/Δt) drives an induced current.

widgets.idealised: Atmospheric absorption and seasonal thermal lag of the oceans (which delays peak summer temperatures by ~4 weeks) are omitted.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

widgets.idealised: The lunar orbit is circular and coplanar in this illustration. Orbital inclination, eclipse dates and libration are omitted.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

widgets.cutaway: Inside the 1 AU triangle: 1 parsec is the distance where Earth’s 150-million-km orbital radius subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond (1/3,600 of a degree, the width of a rupee coin at 5 km).
widgets.idealised: The overhead triangle exaggerates angles. The telescope view uses its labelled 1.0 arcsecond scale bar; the circular annual trace applies near an orbital pole.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

widgets.title: Vectors
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Parallelogram law", set P = 60 N, Q = 80 N, and find the angle θ where the resultant R is exactly 100 N (Pythagoras!).
widgets.cutaway: Every 2D vector equation is two independent 1D equations at right angles: what happens along x has zero projection along y because cos 90° = 0.
widgets.idealised: Vectors here lie in a flat 2D plane; in 3D space a third perpendicular component R_z joins so R = √(R_x² + R_y² + R_z²).

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: In the Parallelogram Law, projecting P into P cos θ and P sin θ builds a right triangle of base Q + P cos θ.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: At θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0 so the 2PQ cos θ alignment bonus vanishes and R = √(P² + Q²).

widgets.title: Atwood
widgets.challengePrompt: Dilute gravity to exactly one-tenth of free fall (a = 0.98 m/s²): set m₁ = 0.55 kg and m₂ = 0.45 kg.
widgets.cutaway: Unfolding the rope reveals a 1D coupled train: internal tensions +T and −T cancel across the rope while the external weight difference (m₁ − m₂)g accelerates the combined inertia m₁ + m₂.
widgets.idealised: The rope is treated as massless and unstretchable, and the pulley wheel as frictionless and massless (a real pulley adds rotational inertia I/R² to the denominator).

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Two nearly equal masses (0.55 kg and 0.45 kg) dilute free fall to a gentle 0.98 m/s².

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Equal masses (0.50 kg each) give zero net driving force and T = mg = 4.90 N.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Inside the Tension Sandwich, T must beat the lighter weight m₂g so m₂ rises, yet stay below m₁g so m₁ falls.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: A large imbalance (1.00 kg vs 0.20 kg) drives acceleration up to two-thirds of g (6.53 m/s²).

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Adjust m₁ and m₂ to test any mass ratio on Atwood’s pulley.

cards.definition: A simplified representation that explains observations and makes testable predictions.
cards.example: Two explanations both fit yesterday’s observations. How could you decide which is more useful? Find a new situation in which the explanations predict different results. Test it and compare the observations with each prediction.
cards.confusion: A model is not established merely because an explanation sounds convincing.
cards.question: Explain scientific model from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A simplified representation that explains observations and makes testable predictions. A model is not established merely because an explanation sounds convincing.

cards.definition: The smallest change a measuring instrument can distinguish.
cards.example: A balance displays mass in steps of 1 g. Can it directly distinguish masses of 8.2 g and 8.3 g? Explain. No: the difference is 0.1 g. That difference is smaller than the 1 g display step.
cards.confusion: Resolution is different from closeness to the true value.
cards.question: Explain measurement resolution from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: The smallest change a measuring instrument can distinguish. Resolution is different from closeness to the true value.

cards.definition: Precision concerns agreement among repeated readings; accuracy concerns agreement with the true value.
cards.example: A stopwatch gives 2.1 s, 2.5 s and 2.2 s for repeated journeys. State one way to improve the estimate and one limitation of that improvement. Repeat and calculate a mean, investigating any unusual result. A mean reduces the influence of random variation but cannot by itself remove a systematic error.
cards.confusion: Repeated identical values can all share a systematic error.
cards.question: Explain precision and accuracy from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Precision concerns agreement among repeated readings; accuracy concerns agreement with the true value. Repeated identical values can all share a systematic error.

cards.definition: The same physical quantity can be expressed in different units using the defined conversion factor.
cards.example: A survey records a model track length as 1850 m. Express this length in kilometres and explain whether its physical length changes. 1 km = 1000 m, so divide the metre value by 1000. 1850 ÷ 1000 = 1.85 km. Changing the unit changes the numerical value, not the physical length.
cards.confusion: Changing the unit does not change the physical size of the quantity.
cards.question: Explain unit conversion from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: The same physical quantity can be expressed in different units using the defined conversion factor. Changing the unit does not change the physical size of the quantity.

cards.definition: An approximate calculation based on stated, reasonable inputs.
cards.example: A camp estimates it needs 19200 L of water for 240 people each day. What daily allowance per person does this estimate assume? Give one reason the real demand may differ. Assumed allowance = total volume ÷ number of people. 19200 ÷ 240 = 80 L per person per day. Actual use may differ with weather, activities or individual needs.
cards.confusion: An estimate does not justify more significant figures than its weakest inputs.
cards.question: Explain estimation from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: An approximate calculation based on stated, reasonable inputs. An estimate does not justify more significant figures than its weakest inputs.
cards.formula: total = number × estimated quantity per item

cards.definition: Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ a < 10 and integer n.
cards.confusion: A negative exponent means a small positive number, not a negative length.
cards.question: Explain standard form from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ a < 10 and integer n. A negative exponent means a small positive number, not a negative length.

cards.definition: The viewpoint and coordinate system used to describe position and motion.
cards.example: A seated passenger is at rest relative to her bus and moving relative to a roadside tree.
cards.confusion: Moving relative to one frame does not mean moving relative to every frame.
cards.question: Can a parcel be at rest and moving in the same event?
cards.answer: Yes, relative to different frames: at rest on its walkway, moving relative to the floor.

cards.definition: Distance is path length. Displacement is the change in position, including direction.
cards.example: Walking 10 m east and 10 m west gives 20 m distance and zero displacement.
cards.confusion: A zero displacement does not mean no journey took place.
cards.question: After a complete lap, which can be zero: distance or displacement?
cards.answer: Displacement is zero. Distance is the lap length.

cards.definition: Total distance travelled divided by total elapsed time.
cards.example: A 100 m journey in 20 s has average speed 5 m/s.
cards.confusion: Do not divide displacement by time when asked for average speed.
cards.question: A 30 m journey takes 10 s. What is the average speed?
cards.formula: average speed = total distance ÷ total elapsed time

cards.definition: The rate of change of position, including direction.
cards.example: 4 m/s east and 4 m/s west have the same speed and different velocities.
cards.confusion: Changing direction changes velocity even if the speed stays the same.
cards.question: A runner turns a corner at steady speed. Is velocity constant?
cards.answer: No. The direction changes, so the velocity changes.

cards.definition: Units that match the equation and the requested answer.
cards.confusion: A number without its unit may describe the wrong quantity.
cards.question: How do you convert 90 cm to metres and 2 min to seconds?

cards.definition: Change in the vertical-axis quantity divided by change in the horizontal-axis quantity.
cards.example: Position rises uniformly by 12 m in 4 s: velocity is +3 m/s in the positive direction.
cards.confusion: A graph is not a drawing of the path; a flat position line means stationary.
cards.question: What does a negative gradient on a position–time graph mean?
cards.answer: Velocity is in the negative direction. It does not by itself say whether speed is increasing or decreasing.
cards.formula: gradient = change up the axis ÷ change along the axis

cards.definition: Rate of change of velocity.
cards.example: Velocity changes from 1 m/s to 7 m/s in 3 s: average acceleration is 2 m/s².
cards.confusion: Negative acceleration means the negative direction; whether speed decreases depends on the velocity direction.
cards.question: Can something accelerate while travelling at constant speed?
cards.answer: Yes. Turning at constant speed changes the direction of velocity.
cards.formula: average acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ elapsed time

cards.definition: The distance travelled during the time interval.
cards.example: A constant 3 m/s for 4 s gives rectangle area 12 m.
cards.confusion: Area under a signed velocity–time graph gives displacement; speed–time area gives distance.
cards.question: A straight line rises from 0 to 4 m/s in 3 s. What distance is covered?
cards.answer: The triangular area is ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 m.
cards.formula: distance = area under the speed–time graph

cards.definition: Repeated measurements reveal variation; a fair comparison controls relevant variables.
cards.example: When varying ramp height, keep the car, timed distance, surface and release method the same.
cards.confusion: A mean can reduce random variation but cannot fix every systematic error.
cards.question: Does repeating a measurement fix a distance marked incorrectly every time?
cards.answer: No. Check and correct the distance measurement; repeating a shared systematic error does not remove it.

cards.definition: Motion under gravity alone, with other forces negligible.
cards.example: Ignoring air, a ball has downward acceleration about 9.8 m/s² even when its velocity is zero at the top.
cards.confusion: Zero velocity at an instant is different from zero acceleration.
cards.question: At the top of a vertical throw, which is zero: velocity or acceleration?
cards.answer: Velocity is zero. Acceleration remains downward because gravity still acts.
cards.formula: near Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m/s²; use the value stated in the question

questions.title: A journey and its endpoints
questions.prompt: State the difference between distance travelled and displacement.
points: Distance is the total length of the path travelled.
Displacement is the change from the starting position to the final position, including direction.
model: Distance follows the whole route. Displacement describes where you finish relative to where you started.
questions.common: A long journey can end at its starting point, giving zero displacement.
hints: Compare the whole path with the start and finish.

questions.title: How fast, and which way?
questions.prompt: State the equation for average speed and give its SI unit.
points: Average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total elapsed time.
The SI unit is metres per second, m/s.
model: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, in m/s when distance is in metres and time in seconds.
questions.common: Speed is not distance multiplied by time. A velocity also needs a direction.
hints: Ask how many metres are covered in each second.

questions.title: A change each second
questions.prompt: State what acceleration measures and give its SI unit.
points: Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity.
Its SI unit is m/s².
model: Acceleration tells you how much the velocity changes each second. Its unit is m/s².
questions.common: Acceleration includes a change in direction, even when speed stays constant.
hints: Velocity includes direction.

questions.title: A flat line

questions.title: Worked example: a cycle ride

questions.title: Your turn: find the time

model: Time = distance ÷ average speed.

questions.title: Worked example: gaining speed
questions.prompt: A toy vehicle moving in a straight line increases its velocity from 2.0 m/s to 10.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s².

Divide the change by 4.0 s.
Obtain 2.0 m/s².
model: Average acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ time.
The velocity changes by an average of 2 m/s each second.

questions.title: Your turn: a slowing scooter
questions.prompt: A scooter moving east slows from 12.0 m/s to 4.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Take east as positive. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s².

Divide by 4.0 s.
Obtain −2.0 m/s².

questions.common: A minus sign gives direction; here it also corresponds to slowing because the velocity is positive.

questions.title: Worked example: distance under a graph
questions.prompt: A trolley starts from rest. Its speed increases uniformly to 6.0 m/s in 4.0 s, as shown. Calculate its distance travelled in those four seconds, in metres.
points: Identify the triangular area under the speed–time graph.
Use ½ × 4.0 s × 6.0 m/s.
Obtain 12 m.
model: Distance is the area under the speed–time graph.

questions.common: Using 6 × 4 assumes the trolley was at its final speed for the whole interval.

questions.title: Your turn: two parts of a journey
questions.prompt: The graph shows a cart at 3.0 m/s for 4.0 s, then slowing uniformly to rest over the next 2.0 s. Calculate the total distance travelled in metres.
points: Find the rectangle: 4.0 × 3.0 = 12 m.
Find the triangle: ½ × 2.0 × 3.0 = 3 m.
Add the areas to obtain 15 m.
model: Distance = rectangle area + triangle area.
questions.common: The final two seconds begin at t = 4 s, so their width is 2 s rather than 6 s.
hints: Split the area at t = 4 s.

questions.title: Worked example: walking inside a carriage
questions.prompt: In a model, a carriage moves east at 8.0 m/s relative to the ground. A passenger walks east at 1.0 m/s relative to the carriage. Calculate the passenger’s speed relative to the ground in m/s.
points: Recognise that both velocities point east.
Add 8.0 + 1.0 to obtain 9.0 m/s.

Relative to the ground she moves 9 m east in that second: 9.0 m/s.
questions.common: The 1 m/s and 8 m/s refer to different frames. State the frame when describing motion.
hints: Imagine where the passenger ends up after one second.

questions.title: Your turn: read a gradient
questions.prompt: A walker’s position changes uniformly from 2.0 m to 10.0 m east of a marker between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s. Calculate her velocity in m/s, taking east as positive.
points: Find the change in position: 10.0 − 2.0 = 8.0 m.
Find the elapsed time: 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 s.
Divide to obtain +2.0 m/s.
model: Velocity = change in position ÷ elapsed time.
questions.common: Use changes in both coordinates; 10 ÷ 5 would ignore the starting point.
hints: Choose two points and subtract their coordinates.

questions.title: Back at the starting gate
questions.prompt: A child walks 120 m east along a straight path, then 120 m west to the starting gate. The whole trip takes 160 s. Calculate (a) total distance, (b) displacement, and (c) average speed.
points: Total distance is 120 + 120 = 240 m.
Displacement is zero because the final position equals the starting position.
Average speed is 240 ÷ 160 = 1.5 m/s.
model: (a) Total distance = 240 m.
(b) Displacement = 0 m.
(c) Average speed = 1.5 m/s. The zero displacement does not make the distance or average speed zero.
questions.common: Using zero displacement in the speed equation would calculate average velocity, not average speed.

Obtain 3.0 m/s.

questions.title: Away, waiting, and back
questions.prompt: The graph shows a walker’s position east of a marker. Describe her motion during 0–4 s, 4–7 s and 7–9 s.

From 7 to 9 s she moves west at a constant velocity, ending 2 m east of the marker.

The horizontal segment means no change in position.

hints: Use the direction and steepness of each segment.

questions.title: A model train changes velocity
questions.prompt: A model train’s velocity changes from 3.0 m/s north to 9.0 m/s north in 3.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s², taking north as positive.
points: Use the velocity change 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 m/s.
Divide by 3.0 s.
Obtain +2.0 m/s².
model: a = (9.0 − 3.0) ÷ 3.0 = +2.0 m/s², towards the north.
questions.common: An answer in m/s is a velocity rather than an acceleration.
hints: Find how much the velocity changes in the whole interval.

questions.title: A journey made of three shapes
questions.prompt: The graph shows a robot speeding up uniformly, moving steadily, then slowing uniformly. Calculate its total distance travelled in metres.
points: First triangle: ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 m.
Rectangle: 3 × 4 = 12 m.
Last triangle: ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 m.

questions.title: Measure a toy car’s average speed
questions.prompt: Plan how to measure a toy car’s average speed between two marks on a clear indoor floor. State what you would measure, how you would calculate the speed, and one way to reduce timing uncertainty. You only need to describe the plan.
points: Measure the distance between the marks with a ruler or tape measure.
Measure the elapsed time between the car crossing the two marks.
Calculate average speed as measured distance divided by elapsed time.
Use a suitable improvement such as timing from video frames or increasing the timed distance while keeping the route clear.
model: Read the plan with an adult before trying it. Keep the floor clear and use a small toy car; keep away from stairs and doorways.
Measure the marked distance. Time from the front of the car crossing the first mark to the same part crossing the second. Divide distance by elapsed time.
A fixed-camera video with a known frame rate lets you identify the crossings more consistently. A longer safe timed distance also reduces the effect of reaction time.
questions.common: A speed measured over the whole interval is an average; it does not prove the car had that speed at every instant.
hints: Which two measured quantities does the speed equation need?

questions.title: At the highest point
questions.prompt: A small ball has been thrown vertically upwards. At its highest point, state its velocity and its acceleration. Ignore air resistance and use g = 9.8 m/s². Explain why zero velocity at that instant does not mean zero acceleration.
points: The instantaneous velocity is zero.
The acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downwards.
Gravity still acts and the velocity continues changing through that instant.
model: At the highest point the ball has zero velocity, but its acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downwards.
The ball is changing from upward velocity to downward velocity; gravity has not switched off.
questions.common: Zero velocity at one instant does not imply zero acceleration.
hints: Think about the velocity just before and just after the highest point.

questions.title: A parcel on a moving walkway
questions.prompt: A parcel rests on a moving walkway that travels steadily east. A person standing on the floor says the parcel moves; a person moving beside it on the walkway says it is at rest. Explain whether their descriptions can both be correct.
points: The parcel has zero velocity relative to the walkway.
The parcel has eastward velocity relative to the floor.
Both descriptions can be correct because they use different stated reference frames.
model: The parcel keeps the same position on the walkway, so it is at rest in that frame.
Its position relative to the floor changes eastwards, so it is moving in the floor frame. Both observations describe the same event.
questions.common: There is no single privileged frame that makes the other steady-motion description an illusion.
hints: Name what each person uses as the reference.

questions.title: The turn on the athletics track
questions.prompt: A runner goes around a curved section of a track at a constant speed of 4.0 m/s. Explain whether her velocity changes and whether she is accelerating.
points: Her velocity changes because its direction changes.
Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity.
She is therefore accelerating even though her speed is constant.
model: The speedometer could keep the same reading while the direction of motion changes.
Velocity includes direction. A changing velocity means acceleration.
questions.common: Constant speed implies zero acceleration only when direction is also unchanged.
hints: Write down what velocity contains that speed does not.

questions.title: Compare two journeys
questions.prompt: Two model boats travel at steady speeds. Boat A covers 240 m in 2.0 min. Boat B moves at 7.2 km/h. Compare their speeds using a common unit and state which is faster.
points: The speeds are equal.
model: Boat A takes 2 × 60 = 120 s, so its speed is 2.0 m/s.
Boat B travels 7200 m in 3600 s, also 2.0 m/s. Neither is faster.
questions.common: Numbers with different units cannot be compared directly.
hints: Put both speeds in metres per second.

questions.title: Turn observations into a graph
questions.prompt: The table gives illustrative measurements of distance travelled by a toy car. On paper, draw a distance-travelled–time graph. Label both axes with units, choose a sensible scale, plot the readings and join adjacent points with straight segments for this question.
points: Put time (s) on the horizontal axis and distance travelled (m) on the vertical axis.
Choose uniform scales that include 0–8 s and 0–12 m.
Plot all five supplied points correctly.
Join adjacent points with straight segments, including a horizontal segment from 4 s to 6 s.
model: Time belongs on the horizontal axis. The distance-travelled axis needs to reach at least 12 m.
Plot (0,0), (2,4), (4,8), (6,8), (8,12). Join adjacent points with a ruler.
The horizontal section from 4 to 6 s shows that the car was stationary during that interval.
questions.common: The line is a graph against time, not a picture of the car’s route across the floor.

questions.title: Negative acceleration, increasing speed

questions.title: Which measurement should be improved?

cards.definition: Energy is conserved when transfers across the chosen system boundary are fully counted.

cards.definition: For the low-speed classical model, kinetic energy is half mass times speed squared.

questions.prompt: Compare parallaxes of two stars at different distances under the same observing baseline. Explain.
points: The nearer star has the larger parallax angle.
The same baseline subtends a larger angle for a nearer object.
model: The nearer star has the larger parallax angle.
The same baseline subtends a larger angle for a nearer object.
questions.common: A light-year is a distance, and faintness alone does not determine distance.
hints: Distances can be inferred from geometric parallax and calibrated relationships between intrinsic brightness and other properties.

questions.title: Stellar distance · A changed setting
questions.prompt: Explain why apparent brightness alone cannot tell you which of two stars is farther away.
points: Their intrinsic luminosities can differ.
A faint star might be nearby and intrinsically faint, or distant and intrinsically bright.
model: Their intrinsic luminosities can differ.
A faint star might be nearby and intrinsically faint, or distant and intrinsically bright.
questions.common: A light-year is a distance, and faintness alone does not determine distance.
hints: Distances can be inferred from geometric parallax and calibrated relationships between intrinsic brightness and other properties.

questions.title: Stellar remnants · On your own
questions.prompt: Describe the expected broad fate of a Sun-like star, without claiming it becomes a black hole.
points: It expands during later evolution and loses outer material.
It leaves a white dwarf that cools, rather than undergoing the usual massive-star core-collapse route.
model: It expands during later evolution and loses outer material.
It leaves a white dwarf that cools, rather than undergoing the usual massive-star core-collapse route.
questions.common: The Sun is not expected to become a core-collapse supernova or a black hole.
hints: A star’s later evolution depends strongly on its mass and the physical support of its remaining core.

questions.title: Stellar remnants · Revisit the idea
questions.prompt: Explain why a white dwarf need not keep fusing hydrogen to remain supported for a long time.
points: Electron degeneracy pressure can support it against gravity.
Its glow can come from residual thermal energy as it cools rather than ongoing normal stellar fusion.
model: Electron degeneracy pressure can support it against gravity.
Its glow can come from residual thermal energy as it cools rather than ongoing normal stellar fusion.
questions.common: The Sun is not expected to become a core-collapse supernova or a black hole.

questions.title: Cosmic expansion · On your own
questions.prompt: Explain cosmological redshift in terms of a light wave travelling through expanding space.
points: The wavelength stretches as space expands during the journey.
The observed wavelength is longer than when emitted.
model: The wavelength stretches as space expands during the journey.
The observed wavelength is longer than when emitted.
questions.common: The expanding universe is not a conventional explosion from a special centre into pre-existing empty space.
hints: Large-scale observations support expansion of space, with distant unbound galaxies generally showing redshift.

questions.title: Cosmic expansion · A changed setting
questions.prompt: Explain why an expanding-dot model can show more distant dots receding faster from every dot without a special central dot.
points: Uniform expansion stretches each separation by the same fractional amount.
Larger initial separations therefore gain more distance per unit time; any dot can be used as the viewpoint.
model: Uniform expansion stretches each separation by the same fractional amount.
Larger initial separations therefore gain more distance per unit time; any dot can be used as the viewpoint.

questions.title: Photons · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Compare photon energy for two frequencies f and 2f. State the relationship used.
points: E = hf.
The 2f photon has twice the energy.
model: E = hf.
The 2f photon has twice the energy.
questions.common: More light intensity does not automatically mean greater energy per photon at the same frequency.
hints: Light exchanges energy in packets whose energy is E = hf.

questions.title: Nuclei and radioactivity · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Compare alpha and gamma radiation in terms of what they are and their usual penetration through material.
points: Alpha particles are helium nuclei; gamma radiation consists of high-energy electromagnetic photons.
Alpha is generally stopped much more readily than gamma, although actual penetration depends on energy and material.
model: Alpha particles are helium nuclei; gamma radiation consists of high-energy electromagnetic photons.
Alpha is generally stopped much more readily than gamma, although actual penetration depends on energy and material.
questions.common: Irradiation is not the same as radioactive contamination.
hints: Unstable nuclei can emit ionising radiation as they change.

questions.title: Fusion and mass-energy · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Distinguish fission from fusion.
points: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei.
Fusion combines light nuclei into heavier nuclei under suitable conditions.
model: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei.
Fusion combines light nuclei into heavier nuclei under suitable conditions.
questions.common: Fusion in the Sun is not chemical burning, and total energy is conserved.
hints: In nuclear reactions a decrease in system rest mass can correspond to energy released according to ΔE = Δmc².

questions.title: Stellar spectra · Paper practice
questions.prompt: A cooler gas lies in front of a continuous-spectrum source. Describe an absorption spectrum and its origin.
points: Dark lines occur at particular wavelengths in the transmitted spectrum.
Gas atoms absorb photons corresponding to allowed energy transitions.
model: Dark lines occur at particular wavelengths in the transmitted spectrum.
Gas atoms absorb photons corresponding to allowed energy transitions.
questions.common: Different line strengths need not mean completely different chemical ingredients.
hints: Patterns of spectral lines provide evidence about atoms and physical conditions in stars.

questions.title: Stellar distance · Paper practice
questions.prompt: What additional calibration is needed to turn a Cepheid’s period into a distance estimate?
points: Use a calibrated period–luminosity relation to infer intrinsic luminosity.
Compare that with apparent brightness, allowing for relevant effects such as extinction.
model: Use a calibrated period–luminosity relation to infer intrinsic luminosity.
Compare that with apparent brightness, allowing for relevant effects such as extinction.
questions.common: A light-year is a distance, and faintness alone does not determine distance.
hints: Distances can be inferred from geometric parallax and calibrated relationships between intrinsic brightness and other properties.

questions.title: Stellar remnants · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to say every star ends in the same kind of remnant?
points: Initial mass and subsequent mass loss affect core conditions and evolution.
Different outcomes include white dwarfs and, for sufficiently massive stellar cores, neutron stars or black holes.
model: Initial mass and subsequent mass loss affect core conditions and evolution.
Different outcomes include white dwarfs and, for sufficiently massive stellar cores, neutron stars or black holes.
questions.common: The Sun is not expected to become a core-collapse supernova or a black hole.
hints: A star’s later evolution depends strongly on its mass and the physical support of its remaining core.

questions.title: Nuclei and radioactivity · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Explain why saying that every kind of radiation makes an exposed object radioactive is too broad.
points: Exposure and contamination are different, and many ordinary exposures leave no radioactive material.
Some nuclear processes, such as neutron activation, can induce radioactivity, so the radiation and process must be specified.
model: Exposure and contamination are different, and many ordinary exposures leave no radioactive material.
Some nuclear processes, such as neutron activation, can induce radioactivity, so the radiation and process must be specified.
questions.common: Irradiation is not the same as radioactive contamination.
hints: Unstable nuclei can emit ionising radiation as they change.

questions.title: Fusion and mass-energy · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Explain why a statement that the Sun’s fusion energy is produced mainly at its surface is incorrect.
points: The required high temperatures and pressures occur in the core.
Energy then reaches the surface by transport through the star before being radiated.
model: The required high temperatures and pressures occur in the core.
Energy then reaches the surface by transport through the star before being radiated.
questions.common: Fusion in the Sun is not chemical burning, and total energy is conserved.
hints: In nuclear reactions a decrease in system rest mass can correspond to energy released according to ΔE = Δmc².

questions.title: Stellar spectra · Paper practice
questions.prompt: State what a stellar spectrum can reveal besides composition, with an explanation.
points: A systematic shift of spectral wavelengths can reveal line-of-sight motion or cosmological redshift in the appropriate context.
Compare the observed line pattern with known reference wavelengths.
model: A systematic shift of spectral wavelengths can reveal line-of-sight motion or cosmological redshift in the appropriate context.
Compare the observed line pattern with known reference wavelengths.
questions.common: Different line strengths need not mean completely different chemical ingredients.
hints: Patterns of spectral lines provide evidence about atoms and physical conditions in stars.

questions.title: Stellar distance · Paper practice
questions.prompt: State what a light-year measures and explain its definition.
points: It measures distance.
It is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year.
model: It measures distance.
It is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year.
questions.common: A light-year is a distance, and faintness alone does not determine distance.
hints: Distances can be inferred from geometric parallax and calibrated relationships between intrinsic brightness and other properties.

questions.title: Stellar remnants · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Explain why exceeding the maximum supported white-dwarf mass does not simply mean a stable white dwarf has zero radius.
points: The support model no longer permits a stable white dwarf above its limit.
A different physical outcome must occur; the limit is not a literal stable point-sized white dwarf.
model: The support model no longer permits a stable white dwarf above its limit.
A different physical outcome must occur; the limit is not a literal stable point-sized white dwarf.
questions.common: The Sun is not expected to become a core-collapse supernova or a black hole.
hints: A star’s later evolution depends strongly on its mass and the physical support of its remaining core.

questions.title: Cosmic expansion · Paper practice
questions.prompt: Give two complementary types of evidence used in the modern Big Bang account.
points: The large-scale redshift–distance relationship supports expansion.
The cosmic microwave background supports an earlier hot dense state.
model: The large-scale redshift–distance relationship supports expansion.
The cosmic microwave background supports an earlier hot dense state.
questions.common: The expanding universe is not a conventional explosion from a special centre into pre-existing empty space.
hints: Large-scale observations support expansion of space, with distant unbound galaxies generally showing redshift.

questions.title: Cosmic expansion · Revisit the idea
questions.prompt: A supplied distant-galaxy sample has these redshifts. State the trend and one reason a redshift value alone is not a complete account of cosmic history.
points: The more distant model galaxy has the larger positive redshift, consistent with expansion.
A full interpretation needs an expansion model and other evidence; one correlation is not a complete history.
model: The more distant model galaxy has the larger positive redshift, consistent with expansion.
A full interpretation needs an expansion model and other evidence; one correlation is not a complete history.
questions.common: The expanding universe is not a conventional explosion from a special centre into pre-existing empty space.
hints: Large-scale observations support expansion of space, with distant unbound galaxies generally showing redshift.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Boyle's Law in the human chest: how diaphragm contraction drives airflow
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Lungs have no skeletal muscle of their own. When the diaphragm flattens and external intercostals lift the ribs, thoracic volume V increases, dropping alveolar gas pressure P below atmospheric pressure (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂) so air rushes in.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: During inhalation, thoracic volume increases while temperature stays constant at 37 °C. Why does air flow into the lungs?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Increasing volume reduces the collision frequency of gas molecules with alveolar walls, so internal pressure drops below atmospheric pressure and outside air is pushed in.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Forearm bones and biceps/triceps as Class 3 mechanical levers
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: The elbow hinge joint acts as a pivot (fulcrum). Because the biceps tendon inserts only ~4 cm from the elbow while a load in the hand sits ~32 cm away, the biceps must exert 8× the load's weight — trading force advantage for rapid, wide-arc motion.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: M = F × d⊥   (F_biceps × d_in = F_load × d_out)
